name: Normal Physiology
description: Complete study manual · 30 practical class topics

topics.title: Introduction. Physiology as a science and the regulation of functions. Bioelectric phenomena in excitable tissues

goals.text: To introduce the student to the subject, tasks, research methods and history of normal physiology; to master the concepts of nervous and humoral regulation of functions in the body, homeostasis and the integrity of the organism; to explain the mechanisms by which the resting and action potentials arise in excitable tissues.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the subject of physiology, its branches and its links with other sciences;
the methods of physiological research (observation, acute and chronic experiments, modern instrumental methods);
the main stages in the development of physiology and its scientists (W. Harvey, R. Descartes, I.M. Sechenov, I.P. Pavlov, Avicenna (Ibn Sina));
the concepts of homeostasis, functional system and feedback;
the nervous, humoral and local mechanisms of the regulation of functions;
excitable tissues and their general properties;
the structure of the cell membrane, ion channels and the function of the Na^+^/K^+^ pump;
the mechanisms and phases of the resting potential and the action potential.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform and explain Galvani's first and second experiments (Matteucci's experiment);
point out the phases on a graph of the action potential and explain the ionic mechanism of each;
draw a regulatory loop (receptor — center — effector — feedback) with examples.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main method of physiology is **experiment**. An acute experiment gives quick results, but the integrity of the organism is disrupted; a chronic experiment makes it possible to study the organism in its natural state. In humans, mainly **noninvasive** methods are used (ECG, spirography, blood pressure measurement).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Negative feedback** returns a deviated parameter to normal (the main mechanism of homeostasis): if blood thyroxine rises, the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone decreases. **Positive feedback** amplifies a process and is rare: oxytocin release during labor, the blood coagulation cascade, the opening of Na^+^ channels in the rising phase of the action potential.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main cause of the resting potential is the **diffusion of K^+^ ions out of the cell**. Therefore, if the K^+^ concentration in the extracellular fluid rises (hyperkalemia), the gradient decreases and the membrane **depolarizes**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **critical level of depolarization (CLD)** is the membrane potential at which an action potential arises (≈ −50…−55 mV in a nerve). The difference between the resting potential and the CLD is called the **threshold depolarization** (≈ 15–20 mV): the smaller it is, the higher the excitability. After an action potential the ion concentrations hardly change (very few ions cross in a single impulse); they are restored by the Na^+^/K^+^ pump.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the order of the action potential as **“NaK”**: first **Na** enters (depolarization), then **K** leaves (repolarization). At rest, “potassium escapes, the anions stay” — that is why the inside is negative.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Local anesthetics (lidocaine, procaine (novocaine)) **block voltage-gated Na^+^ channels**: no action potential arises and the pain impulse is not conducted. Tetrodotoxin (puffer fish poison) also blocks Na^+^ channels and causes paralysis of the respiratory muscles. Tetraethylammonium, on the other hand, blocks K^+^ channels and slows repolarization.

sections.title: 1. Physiology as a science: its tasks and methods

blocks.text: **Physiology** (Greek physis — nature, logos — study) is the science that studies the vital activity (functions) of the living organism, its organs and systems, tissues and cells, the mechanisms that regulate these functions and the interaction of the organism with the external environment. **Normal physiology** studies the functions of the healthy human body and is the theoretical foundation of medicine: to understand disease (pathological physiology), one must first know the norm.

blocks.title: Table 1.1. The main branches of physiology
head: Branch
What it studies
rows: Processes common to all tissues: excitability, excitation, inhibition, principles of regulation
Individual systems: blood, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, excretory, endocrine and nervous systems, sensory systems (analyzers)
Changes in functions during ontogenesis (childhood, old age)
Adaptation of the organism to physical and mental load
Adaptation to climate, altitude and underwater conditions

blocks.text: Methods of physiological research

items: **Observation** — the oldest method; recording a process without interfering with it.
**Acute experiment (vivisection)** — under anesthesia an organ is exposed and acted on directly; the experiment is short-term. Drawback: anesthesia and surgical trauma affect function.

**Chronic experiment** — long-term observation under natural conditions in an animal prepared in advance by surgery (a fistula, organ transplantation). I.P. Pavlov studied the physiology of digestion with this method and was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1904.
**Method of isolated organs and tissues** — the frog nerve-muscle preparation, the isolated heart (Langendorff method).
**Modern instrumental methods** — electrophysiological (ECG, EEG, EMG), the microelectrode technique, patch clamp, telemetry, tomography, molecular genetic methods, computer modeling.

parts.text: The main method of physiology is **experiment**. An acute experiment gives quick results, but the integrity of the organism is disrupted; a chronic experiment makes it possible to study the organism in its natural state. In humans, mainly **noninvasive** methods are used (ECG, spirography, blood pressure measurement).

blocks.text: A brief history of physiology

items: **Hippocrates** (5th–4th century BC) — the doctrine of temperaments.
**Galen** (2nd century) — vivisection experiments on animals.
**Avicenna (Abu Ali ibn Sina)** (980–1037) — in “The Canon of Medicine” he described in detail the heartbeat, the types of pulse, and questions of nutrition and hygiene.
**William Harvey** (1628) — discovered the circulation of the blood; scientific physiology dates from this year.
**René Descartes** (17th century) — founder of the concept of the reflex.
**Luigi Galvani** (1791) — discovered “animal electricity”.
**I.M. Sechenov** (1863) — “Reflexes of the Brain”; discovered central inhibition.
**I.P. Pavlov** — the physiology of digestion, conditioned reflexes and the doctrine of higher nervous activity.
**P.K. Anokhin** — the theory of functional systems.
**Claude Bernard** (19th century) — the idea of the “constancy of the internal environment”; **W. Cannon** (1929) — the term “homeostasis”.

sections.title: 2. Regulation of functions in the body

blocks.text: Homeostasis

**Homeostasis** is the relative constancy of the composition and properties of the internal environment of the body (blood, lymph, tissue fluid) and the stability of the basic physiological functions. Homeostatic parameters may be **rigid** (pH, osmotic pressure, body temperature — kept within very narrow limits) or **plastic** (blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose — vary within wider limits).

blocks.title: Table 1.2. The main homeostatic parameters (in adults)
head: Parameter

blocks.text: Regulatory mechanisms

blocks.text: Nervous and humoral regulation do not work separately but as a single **neurohumoral regulation**: the nervous system controls the endocrine glands, and hormones influence the activity of nerve cells.

A **reflex** is the response of the organism to stimulation of receptors, carried out with the participation of the central nervous system. A reflex is carried out through a **reflex arc**: receptor → afferent (sensory) pathway → nerve center → efferent (motor) pathway → effector (working organ). Information about the result of the response returns to the center — this is called **reverse afferentation (feedback)**; therefore modern physiology uses the concept of a **reflex ring** instead of a “reflex arc”.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: The regulatory loop of physiological functions: negative feedback

parts.text: **Negative feedback** returns a deviated parameter to normal (the main mechanism of homeostasis): if blood thyroxine rises, the release of thyroid-stimulating hormone decreases. **Positive feedback** amplifies a process and is rare: oxytocin release during labor, the blood coagulation cascade, the opening of Na^+^ channels in the rising phase of the action potential.

blocks.text: Functional system (P.K. Anokhin)

A **functional system** is a dynamic association of various organs and tissues directed toward achieving a result useful for the adaptation of the organism. Its components are the **useful result** (the system-forming factor), the **receptors** that evaluate the result, **reverse afferentation**, the **central architecture** (afferent synthesis, decision making, the acceptor of the action result) and the **executive mechanisms** (autonomic, hormonal, behavioral). For example, the functional system that maintains blood pO~2~ includes the respiratory, circulatory and blood systems.
The integrity of the organism

The organism is not a sum of separate organs but a single system. Its integrity is ensured by the nervous system (especially its higher divisions), the endocrine system and the circulation of blood and lymph. A change in the function of one organ leads to changes in other systems as well (for example, during physical work breathing, heart rate and sweating change together with muscle activity).

Tissues that can pass from a state of rest to an active state in response to a stimulus and generate an **action potential** in doing so are called **excitable tissues**. They include **nerve**, **muscle** (skeletal, cardiac, smooth) and **glandular** tissue.

blocks.text: By their nature, **stimuli** are **physical** (mechanical, thermal, electrical, light, sound), **chemical** (acids, alkalis, hormones, neurotransmitters) and **physicochemical** (changes in osmotic pressure or pH). By biological significance, **adequate** stimuli (to which a receptor is specially adapted — light for the eye) and **inadequate** stimuli (“seeing sparks” after a blow to the eye) are distinguished. In experiments **electric current** is used most often: it can be dosed precisely, does not damage the tissue and is close to natural biocurrents.

sections.title: 4. The cell membrane and ion channels

blocks.text: The cell membrane, 7–10 nm thick, consists of a **phospholipid bilayer** with proteins embedded in it (the fluid mosaic model). The lipid layer is almost impermeable to ions; ions pass through **ion channels** and **carrier proteins**.

blocks.title: Table 1.5. Transport of substances across the membrane
head: Type
Energy
Examples
rows: Not required, down the concentration gradient
Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^, Cl^-^ ion channels
Not required, with a carrier protein
Absorption of glucose and amino acids together with Na^+^ (SGLT)

blocks.text: **Ion channels** are protein molecules that span the membrane; they have a **selectivity filter** (letting through only a particular ion) and a **gating mechanism**. By the way they open, channels are **voltage-gated** (open when the membrane potential changes — fast Na^+^ channels), **ligand-gated** (open when a neurotransmitter binds — the N-cholinergic receptor for acetylcholine), **mechanosensitive** (open on stretch) and **“leak” channels** (always open — the K^+^ channels at rest). The fast Na^+^ channel has two gates: the outer **activation (m)** gate and the inner **inactivation (h)** gate.

blocks.label: Figure 1.2
blocks.caption: Ion channels and the Na^+^/K^+^ pump (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **The Na^+^/K^+^ pump (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase)**, using the energy of one ATP molecule, moves **3 Na^+^** ions out of the cell and **2 K^+^** ions into it. As a result: 1) the ion concentration gradients are maintained; 2) the pump is **electrogenic** — one extra positive charge is moved out in each cycle, contributing to the membrane potential (−5…−10 mV); 3) cell volume is regulated. The pump accounts for 30–40% of the energy expenditure of a tissue (up to 70% in nervous tissue).

Inside the cell

Ratio

blocks.text: The **resting potential (membrane potential)** is the potential difference between the inner and outer surfaces of the membrane of a cell at rest. The inner surface of the membrane is negatively charged relative to the outer surface. Its magnitude is −60…−70 mV in a nerve cell, −80…−90 mV in skeletal muscle and −50…−60 mV in smooth muscle.
The mechanism of the resting potential (membrane-ion theory: J. Bernstein, A. Hodgkin, A. Huxley)

items: **Unequal distribution** of ions inside and outside the cell (the result of the work of the Na^+^/K^+^ pump).
**Different permeability** of the resting membrane to different ions: the permeability to K^+^ is 25–100 times higher than to Na^+^ (K^+^ “leak” channels are always open).

K^+^ ions **leave the cell** down their concentration gradient, while the large organic anions cannot cross the membrane and stay inside — the inner surface of the membrane becomes negative and the outer surface positive.

The electric field that arises opposes further exit of K^+^; the point at which the concentration and electrical forces balance is called the **potassium equilibrium potential** (≈ −90 mV). It can be calculated with the **Nernst equation**.
A small leak of Na^+^ into the cell makes the potential somewhat less negative than the K^+^ equilibrium potential (−70 mV); the Na^+^/K^+^ pump adds an electrogenic contribution.

parts.text: The main cause of the resting potential is the **diffusion of K^+^ ions out of the cell**. Therefore, if the K^+^ concentration in the extracellular fluid rises (hyperkalemia), the gradient decreases and the membrane **depolarizes**.

Changes in blood potassium are dangerous for the heart and muscles. In **hyperkalemia** (renal failure, extensive tissue damage) the resting potential decreases and Na^+^ channels become inactivated — cardiac conduction is disturbed and cardiac arrest is possible. In **hypokalemia** (vomiting, diuretics) the membrane becomes hyperpolarized — muscle weakness and arrhythmias appear.

blocks.label: Figure 1.3
blocks.caption: Ionic mechanisms of the resting and action potentials: A — resting potential; B — phases of the action potential and ion permeability (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **action potential** is a rapid, short-lasting change in the membrane potential during excitation, in which the membrane charge is reversed (the inner surface becomes positive). In a nerve fiber it lasts 0.5–2 ms and its amplitude is 100–120 mV.

blocks.label: Figure 1.4
blocks.caption: Phases of the action potential (drawn after Alavia O.T., 2018; Costanzo L.S., 2018)

Membrane potential

Na^+^ channels are inactivated (the h gate closes), voltage-gated K^+^ channels open and K^+^ leaves the cell

parts.text: The **critical level of depolarization (CLD)** is the membrane potential at which an action potential arises (≈ −50…−55 mV in a nerve). The difference between the resting potential and the CLD is called the **threshold depolarization** (≈ 15–20 mV): the smaller it is, the higher the excitability. After an action potential the ion concentrations hardly change (very few ions cross in a single impulse); they are restored by the Na^+^/K^+^ pump.

parts.text: Remember the order of the action potential as **“NaK”**: first **Na** enters (depolarization), then **K** leaves (repolarization). At rest, “potassium escapes, the anions stay” — that is why the inside is negative.

blocks.text: Changes in excitability during the action potential

items: During the **local response** excitability increases.
**Absolute refractory period** (depolarization and the beginning of repolarization) — even a very strong stimulus cannot evoke a new action potential: the Na^+^ channels are open or inactivated.
**Relative refractory period** (the end of repolarization) — only a suprathreshold stimulus evokes a response.
**Supernormal period (exaltation)** — during after-depolarization excitability is above normal.
**Subnormal period** — during after-hyperpolarization excitability is reduced. These periods are discussed in detail in the next topic (laws of stimulation).

parts.text: Local anesthetics (lidocaine, procaine (novocaine)) **block voltage-gated Na^+^ channels**: no action potential arises and the pain impulse is not conducted. Tetrodotoxin (puffer fish poison) also blocks Na^+^ channels and causes paralysis of the respiratory muscles. Tetraethylammonium, on the other hand, blocks K^+^ channels and slows repolarization.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: preparing the frog nerve-muscle preparation

items: Immobilize the frog as instructed by the teacher (destruction of the spinal cord — a “spinal frog”).
Cut the body just below the forelimbs and remove the internal organs; leave the hind limbs and the lumbar part of the vertebral column.
Pull the skin downward like a stocking.
Divide the vertebral column in the middle and separate the two legs into individual preparations.
Carefully isolate the sciatic nerve in the thigh region, and dissect out the calf muscle (m. gastrocnemius) together with the Achilles tendon.
Keep the preparation moist with Ringer's solution (if it dries, excitability is lost).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: Galvani's first experiment

items: Take bimetallic forceps made of copper and zinc.
Touch the tips of the forceps simultaneously to the nerves of the preparation (in front of the vertebral column).

Watch the muscle contract at each touch. **Results and analysis:** L. Galvani explained the contraction by “animal electricity”. A. Volta, however, proved that the cause of the contraction is the **current of a galvanic cell** formed by two different metals and the tissue fluid (an electrolyte). Thus the first experiment is not yet proof of animal electricity.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: Galvani's second experiment (without metal)

items: Lift the sciatic nerve of a nerve-muscle preparation with a glass hook.
Lower the nerve simultaneously onto the **injured** (cut) surface of the muscle and onto its uninjured surface.

Watch the muscle contract. **Results and analysis:** the muscle contracts even without metal. The injured surface is negatively charged relative to the uninjured one (the **injury current**, demarcation potential); the nerve acts as a bridge between the two surfaces and the current stimulates it. This experiment was the first proof of the **existence of bioelectric potentials** in tissues.

blocks.text: Experiment 4: Matteucci's secondary contraction experiment

items: Prepare two nerve-muscle preparations.
Place the nerve of the second preparation on the muscle of the first preparation.

Stimulate the nerve of the first preparation with an electric current. **Results and analysis:** both muscles contract. The **action potentials** generated when the first muscle contracts stimulate the second nerve lying on it. The experiment proves that bioelectric potentials are generated during excitation.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing a graph of the action potential

items: Mark the abscissa (time, ms) and ordinate (potential, mV) axes.
Draw the resting potential level (−70 mV) and the critical level of depolarization (−55 mV).
Show the phases of the local response, rapid depolarization, overshoot, repolarization and after-hyperpolarization.
Under each phase write its ionic mechanism (Na^+^ entry, inactivation of Na^+^ channels, K^+^ exit).
Below the graph mark the periods of excitability (absolute and relative refractoriness, supernormal, subnormal).

skills.title: Skill: constructing a regulatory loop

items: Choose a regulated parameter (for example, blood pressure).
Indicate the receptors that sense it (baroreceptors of the aortic arch and carotid artery).
Mark the afferent pathway, the center (the circulatory center in the medulla oblongata), the efferent pathway and the effectors (heart, vessels).
Determine the type of feedback (negative) and explain the direction of the response when the parameter changes.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a patient with chronic renal failure, blood potassium reached 7.2 mmol/l. The patient developed muscle weakness and a disturbance of the heart rhythm.
cases.ask: How does a rise in blood potassium affect the resting potential? Why is the activity of excitable tissues disturbed?
cases.answer: The resting potential is generated mainly by the diffusion of K^+^ out of the cell. When extracellular K^+^ increases, the concentration gradient decreases and less K^+^ leaves — the membrane depolarizes. At first excitability may increase, but with prolonged depolarization the voltage-gated Na^+^ channels are inactivated and a full action potential cannot arise. The result is muscle weakness, disturbed cardiac conduction and, in severe cases, cardiac arrest.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Before dental treatment, a dentist injected lidocaine. A few minutes later the patient no longer felt pain in that area, while sensation was preserved in other areas.
cases.ask: By what mechanism does lidocaine abolish pain? Which phase of the action potential is disturbed?
cases.answer: Lidocaine blocks the voltage-gated Na^+^ channels in the membrane of nerve fibers. The (painful) stimulus cannot open the Na^+^ channels, depolarization does not reach the critical level, and the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential does not develop. Excitation does not spread along the fiber and the pain signal does not reach the center. The effect is limited to the injected area, so sensation is preserved elsewhere.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student performed Galvani's first experiment: when the copper-zinc forceps touched the nerve, the muscle contracted. He explained this as “the muscle has its own electricity”.
cases.ask: Is the student's conclusion correct? Which experiment actually proves the presence of bioelectric potentials in tissue?
cases.answer: The conclusion is wrong. As A. Volta showed, in the first experiment the two different metals and the tissue fluid form a galvanic cell, and its current stimulates the nerve. The presence of bioelectric potentials in tissue is proved by Galvani's second experiment (without metal): when the nerve touches the injured and uninjured surfaces of the muscle, the muscle contracts under the action of the injury current. Matteucci's secondary contraction experiment shows that action potentials are generated during excitation.

topics.title: Laws of stimulation

goals.text: To teach the student the laws by which excitable tissues respond to stimuli — the laws of strength, duration and rate of rise of stimulus strength (the gradient law), the “all-or-none” law, the polar law of direct current, the changes in excitability during excitation and the concept of lability; to teach the determination of threshold strength and chronaxie.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the relationship between the stimulation threshold (threshold strength) and excitability;
the law of strength and the “all-or-none” law, and the limits of their application;
the strength–duration curve (the Hoorweg–Weiss–Lapicque curve) and the concepts of rheobase, utilization time and chronaxie;
the phenomenon of accommodation and the gradient law;
Pflüger's polar law, catelectrotonus and anelectrotonus, and Verigo's cathodal depression;
the phasic changes in excitability during excitation;
the concept of lability (N.E. Vvedensky) and its value in different tissues.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the stimulation threshold of a nerve and a muscle in a nerve-muscle preparation;
demonstrate the law of strength experimentally (threshold, submaximal and maximal contraction);
demonstrate the polar law with direct current;
explain the clinical significance of chronaxie.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Excitability is **inversely proportional** to the threshold. The threshold of a nerve is lower than that of a muscle — the nerve is more excitable; this is why, in a preparation, it is easier to stimulate a muscle through its nerve (indirect stimulation).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The “all-or-none” law is **relative**: 1) a subthreshold stimulus is not “nothing” either — it evokes a local response and increases excitability; 2) the size of the response depends not on the stimulus but on the state of the tissue at that moment (fatigue, temperature, ions). A whole skeletal muscle obeys not this law but the law of strength, while the heart, as a syncytium, obeys the “all-or-none” law.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The rate of accommodation differs between tissues: it is high in motor nerve fibers and low in smooth muscles and sensory fibers. Tissues with low accommodation respond even to slowly rising stimuli.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Cathode on make, anode on break”**: when the circuit is closed (current switched on) excitation arises at the cathode, and when it is opened (current switched off) — at the anode. The cathode “warms up” the membrane (depolarization), the anode “cools it down” (hyperpolarization).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Absolute refractoriness ensures that excitation spreads in **one direction** and sets the upper limit of the lability of a tissue. Because the refractory period of the heart is long, cardiac muscle **cannot contract tetanically**.

blocks.text: To evoke excitation, a stimulus must meet three conditions: **sufficient strength**, **sufficient duration** and **a sufficiently fast rise in strength**. Each has its own law.

The **stimulation threshold (threshold strength)** is the smallest strength of a stimulus that can evoke excitation. The threshold is the main measure of excitability, and the two are **inversely proportional**: the lower the threshold, the higher the excitability.

parts.text: Excitability is **inversely proportional** to the threshold. The threshold of a nerve is lower than that of a muscle — the nerve is more excitable; this is why, in a preparation, it is easier to stimulate a muscle through its nerve (indirect stimulation).

sections.title: 2. The law of strength and the “all-or-none” law

blocks.text: **The law of strength:** a tissue of complex structure (a whole skeletal muscle, a nerve trunk) **increases its response** as the stimulus strength rises from threshold to maximal; beyond the maximal strength the response no longer changes. The reason is that a muscle consists of thousands of fibers with different excitability: as the strength rises, more and more fibers are recruited into excitation. With a very strong stimulus the response may decrease — the phenomenon of **pessimum**.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: The law of strength: change in the contraction of a whole muscle as stimulus strength increases (drawn after data of Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **The “all-or-none” law** (H. Bowditch, 1871): a single excitable structure (one nerve or muscle fiber) or a functional syncytium (cardiac muscle) does not respond to a subthreshold stimulus (“none”), while to a threshold or stronger stimulus it **always gives the same, maximal** response (“all”).

parts.text: The “all-or-none” law is **relative**: 1) a subthreshold stimulus is not “nothing” either — it evokes a local response and increases excitability; 2) the size of the response depends not on the stimulus but on the state of the tissue at that moment (fatigue, temperature, ions). A whole skeletal muscle obeys not this law but the law of strength, while the heart, as a syncytium, obeys the “all-or-none” law.

sections.title: 3. The law of duration: the strength–duration curve

blocks.text: To evoke excitation, a stimulus must last for a certain time. There is an **inverse relationship** between the strength of a stimulus and its duration: the shorter the stimulus, the greater the strength required. This relationship is expressed by the **strength–duration curve** (the Hoorweg–Weiss–Lapicque hyperbola).

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: The strength–duration curve: rheobase, utilization time and chronaxie (drawn after Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Parameters of the strength–duration curve
head: Parameter
Definition
Meaning
rows: The smallest strength of direct current that evokes excitation when applied for a long time
Threshold strength; a measure of excitability in terms of strength
The shortest time for which a current equal to the rheobase must act to evoke excitation
Difficult to measure precisely (the curve is flat there)
The shortest time for which a current equal to twice the rheobase must act to evoke excitation
A measure of excitability in terms of time; measured precisely

blocks.text: On the left part of the curve, very short stimuli (shorter than 0.01 ms) do not evoke excitation at any strength — the Na^+^ channels do not have time to open. On the right part, a current weaker than the rheobase is ineffective even if it acts for a very long time.

blocks.title: Table 2.3. Chronaxie of different tissues (approximate)
head: Tissue
Chronaxie, ms

parts.text: **Chronaximetry** is a method of electrodiagnosis in neurology. When a nerve is damaged, the chronaxie of the muscle increases (excitability decreases) and it becomes difficult to stimulate the muscle through its nerve; when the nerve recovers, chronaxie returns to normal. It is used to follow peripheral nerve injuries and to choose the parameters of electrical stimulation in physiotherapy.

blocks.text: **The gradient law (du Bois-Reymond):** excitation depends not only on the absolute strength of a stimulus but also on its **rate of rise per unit of time**. If the strength rises steeply (quickly), excitation occurs; if it rises slowly, excitation may not occur even when the strength exceeds the threshold.

**Accommodation** is the adaptation of a tissue to a slowly rising stimulus; the critical level of depolarization rises (the threshold increases). Mechanism: during slow depolarization the Na^+^ channels are gradually **inactivated** and K^+^ permeability increases; as a result the regenerative Na^+^ current does not arise.

blocks.label: Figure 2.3
blocks.caption: Accommodation: rate of rise of current strength and the threshold (diagram)

parts.text: The rate of accommodation differs between tissues: it is high in motor nerve fibers and low in smooth muscles and sensory fibers. Tissues with low accommodation respond even to slowly rising stimuli.

sections.title: 5. The polar law of direct current

blocks.text: **Pflüger's polar law** (1859): direct current stimulates a tissue only when the circuit is **made (closed)** and **broken (opened)**; while the current is flowing there is no excitation. When the circuit is **closed, excitation arises under the cathode**, and when it is **opened — under the anode**. The cathodal effect on closing is stronger than the anodal effect on opening.

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: The polar law: change in the membrane potential under the cathode and anode when direct current is switched on (diagram)

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Electrotonic phenomena
head: Phenomenon
Where
Effect on the membrane
Excitability
rows: Under the cathode, with prolonged current
Prolonged depolarization — inactivation of Na^+^ channels
Under the anode, when the current is switched off
After hyperpolarization the CLD is lowered

blocks.text: The appearance of excitation under the anode **when the current is switched off** is explained as follows: while the current flows, the membrane is hyperpolarized, the inactivation of Na^+^ channels is removed and the CLD falls. When the current is switched off, the membrane potential is quickly restored, reaches the new, lowered CLD and evokes excitation.

parts.text: **“Cathode on make, anode on break”**: when the circuit is closed (current switched on) excitation arises at the cathode, and when it is opened (current switched off) — at the anode. The cathode “warms up” the membrane (depolarization), the anode “cools it down” (hyperpolarization).

In physiotherapy, **galvanization** and the introduction of drugs by current (**electrophoresis**) are based on the polar law. Because excitability is reduced under the anode, the anode is placed over a painful area to relieve pain, while the cathode is used to increase excitability.

blocks.text: When an action potential arises, the excitability of the tissue changes in phases. These phases explain the response to rhythmic stimuli, the development of tetanus and the features of the heart's work.

blocks.label: Figure 2.5
blocks.caption: The action potential (top) and the phases of excitability (bottom) (drawn after a figure by Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Phases of excitability
head: Phase
Corresponding part of the action potential
Excitability
Cause
rows: The membrane is close to the CLD
Depolarization and the beginning of repolarization
Na^+^ channels are open or inactivated
Some Na^+^ channels are still inactivated, K^+^ permeability is high
The membrane potential is close to the CLD
The membrane potential is farther from the CLD

blocks.text: Duration of the absolute refractory period: 0.5–1 ms in a nerve fiber, 2–3 ms in skeletal muscle, 250–300 ms in cardiac muscle (almost the entire duration of the action potential).

parts.text: Absolute refractoriness ensures that excitation spreads in **one direction** and sets the upper limit of the lability of a tissue. Because the refractory period of the heart is long, cardiac muscle **cannot contract tetanically**.

blocks.text: **Lability** (N.E. Vvedensky, 1886) is the maximum number of action potentials that an excitable tissue can generate per unit of time (per 1 s) in step with the rhythm of stimulation, without transforming it.
Lability depends primarily on the **duration of the absolute refractory period**: the shorter it is, the higher the lability.

blocks.title: Table 2.6. Lability of different structures
head: Structure
Lability, impulses/s

blocks.text: Lability is not a constant value: training, temperature and rhythmic stimulation change it. The increase in lability under rhythmic stimulation is called **assimilation of rhythm** (A.A. Ukhtomsky). The structure with the lowest lability determines the operating frequency of the whole system (for example, the synapse in a nerve-muscle preparation).
Experiment 1: determining the stimulation threshold of a nerve and a muscle

items: Prepare a frog nerve-muscle preparation and attach the muscle to the lever of a myograph (or kymograph).
Place the electrodes of the electrical stimulator on the sciatic nerve; increase the voltage gradually, starting from zero.
Record the voltage at which the muscle first contracts noticeably — this is the **threshold of the nerve** (indirect stimulation).
Place the electrodes directly on the muscle and repeat the experiment — the **threshold of the muscle** (direct stimulation).

Compare the two values. **Expected results and analysis:** the threshold of the nerve is lower than that of the muscle, i.e., the excitability of the nerve is higher. This is related to the membrane properties of nerve fibers (closer to the CLD).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: studying the law of strength

items: Starting from the threshold strength, increase the stimulus strength step by step (for example, by 0.1 V each time).
At each strength record the amplitude of the single contraction on the kymograph tape.
Mark the strength at which the amplitude stops increasing — the **maximal strength**.

Increase the strength further and show that the amplitude does not change (supramaximal strength). **Expected results and analysis:** from threshold to maximal strength the contraction amplitude increases, because the muscle consists of fibers of different excitability and, as the strength rises, more fibers are excited (the law of strength). At maximal strength all fibers are excited, so a further increase does not enhance the response. Each individual fiber, however, obeys the “all-or-none” law.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: demonstrating Pflüger's polar law

items: Place the nerve of a nerve-muscle preparation on two nonpolarizable electrodes; connect a direct current source through a switch.
Place the cathode closer to the muscle and the anode farther away; close and open the circuit and record the contractions.
Reverse the poles (anode closer to the muscle) and repeat the experiment.

Vary the current strength between weak, moderate and strong and record the results in a table. **Expected results and analysis:** with a weak current, contraction is seen only on closing the circuit (excitation under the cathode); with a moderate current — both on closing and on opening. With a strong current, if the anode is close to the muscle, the cathodal excitation on closing cannot pass through the hyperpolarized region under the anode (anodal block) — contraction occurs only on opening.

skills.title: Skill: determining chronaxie from the strength–duration curve

items: Mark the stimulus strength on the ordinate and the duration on the abscissa.
Find the rheobase level from the flat part of the curve.
Multiply the rheobase by two and mark this point on the ordinate.
From this point draw a horizontal line until it crosses the curve.
From the point of intersection drop a perpendicular onto the abscissa — this is the **chronaxie**.
Compare the result with the type of tissue and draw a conclusion about its excitability.

skills.title: Skill: relating the phases of excitability to the action potential

items: Draw a graph of the action potential.
Below it, draw the corresponding excitability graph in time (normal = 100%).

Mark the periods: local response — exaltation; depolarization and the beginning of repolarization — absolute refractoriness; the end of repolarization — relative refractoriness; after-potentials — the supernormal and subnormal periods.
Briefly write the ionic mechanism of each phase.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient injured in the forearm has damage to the ulnar nerve. A neurologist performed electrodiagnosis and found that the chronaxie of the muscles innervated by this nerve was 10 times higher than normal. On repeat examination three months later, the chronaxie had begun to decrease.
cases.ask: What does chronaxie show? What do its increase and subsequent decrease mean?
cases.answer: Chronaxie is the shortest time for which a current equal to twice the rheobase must act to evoke excitation; it is a measure of excitability in terms of time. When a nerve is damaged, the muscle loses its innervation, indirect stimulation through nerve fibers becomes impossible, and the muscle's own excitability is low — so chronaxie rises sharply. The beginning of a decrease in chronaxie indicates regeneration of the nerve fibers and restoration of innervation. That is why chronaximetry is used to follow the course of nerve injuries.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student stimulated the nerve of a nerve-muscle preparation with a current of 2 V — the muscle contracted. He then raised the voltage from zero to 4 V very slowly (over several seconds) — the muscle did not contract.
cases.ask: Why did the stronger current not evoke a response? Which law does this illustrate?
cases.answer: This is the gradient law and the phenomenon of accommodation. When the current rises slowly, the membrane depolarizes gradually; meanwhile the Na^+^ channels are inactivated, K^+^ permeability increases and the critical level of depolarization rises. As a result, even when the current exceeds the initial threshold, no regenerative Na^+^ current arises and no action potential appears. For excitation, the stimulus strength must rise quickly enough.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A physiotherapist placed a direct current electrode over the painful area of a patient. A student asked: “Which pole should be placed over the painful area to reduce pain?”
cases.ask: Which pole should be placed there, and why? Which law is this based on?
cases.answer: The anode is placed over the painful area. According to Pflüger's polar law, the membrane under the anode is hyperpolarized (anelectrotonus), its potential moves away from the critical level and excitability decreases — pain receptors and fibers are excited less. Under the cathode, by contrast, excitability increases because of depolarization (catelectrotonus), so the cathode is used to stimulate muscles and nerves.

topics.title: Physiology of nerve fibers and synapses

goals.text: To teach the student the structure and types of nerve fibers, the mechanisms and laws of conduction of excitation along them, the lability of nerve fibers and the phenomenon of parabiosis, and the structure and types of synapses and the mechanism of synaptic transmission of excitation (using the neuromuscular synapse as an example).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure of the neuron and the nerve fiber, and the difference between myelinated and unmyelinated fibers;
the Erlanger–Gasser classification of nerve fibers (groups A, B, C);
the mechanism of continuous conduction in an unmyelinated fiber and saltatory conduction in a myelinated fiber;
the laws of conduction of excitation in a nerve;
N.E. Vvedensky's doctrine of parabiosis and the phases of parabiosis;
the classification of synapses and the stages of transmission of excitation in a chemical synapse;
the action of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular synapse and the end-plate potential;
the properties of synapses and the effects of drugs and poisons on them.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: demonstrate bilateral conduction and isolated conduction in a nerve fiber experimentally;
identify the phases of parabiosis in a nerve-muscle preparation;
prove that a synapse fatigues faster than a nerve.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Conduction velocity depends on the **diameter** of the fiber and its **myelination**: the thicker the fiber and the thicker its myelin, the higher the velocity. The fastest are Aα fibers (up to 120 m/s), the slowest are C fibers (0.5–2 m/s).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Vvedensky regarded parabiosis as **a peculiar localized, persistent (stationary) state of excitation**. This doctrine shows **the unity of the processes of excitation and inhibition**: inhibition can be a special form of excitation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The neuromuscular synapse has a high **safety factor**: the EPP produced by one impulse is 3–4 times larger than needed for an action potential. Therefore, normally every motor impulse is sure to excite the muscle fiber.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Steps of the synapse — **“Arrives–Enters–Releases–Binds–Opens–Breaks down”**: the impulse **arrives**, Ca^2+^ **enters**, the neurotransmitter is **released**, it **binds** to the receptor, the channel **opens**, the neurotransmitter is **broken down**.

sections.title: 1. Structure of the neuron and nerve fibers

blocks.text: The **neuron** is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It consists of a body (soma), short branching processes — **dendrites** (which receive information) — and one long process — the **axon** (which transmits information). The site where the axon leaves the body — the **axon hillock** (initial segment) — has the lowest threshold: this is where the action potential is generated (the trigger zone).

A **nerve fiber** is an axon surrounded by glial cells (**Schwann cells** in the periphery, **oligodendrocytes** in the CNS). In myelinated fibers the Schwann cell wraps the axon in many layers, forming a lipid-rich **myelin sheath**. The myelin is interrupted every 1–2 mm; these sites are called **nodes of Ranvier**, and voltage-gated Na^+^ channels are packed very densely in them.

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Structure of a myelinated nerve fiber: the myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Classification of nerve fibers (after Erlanger–Gasser)

Diameter, µm
Velocity, m/s
Myelin

rows: Motor fibers of skeletal muscles, afferents from muscle spindles

parts.text: Conduction velocity depends on the **diameter** of the fiber and its **myelination**: the thicker the fiber and the thicker its myelin, the higher the velocity. The fastest are Aα fibers (up to 120 m/s), the slowest are C fibers (0.5–2 m/s).

sections.title: 2. Conduction of excitation in a nerve fiber

blocks.text: The inner surface of an excited region is positive, while that of the neighboring unexcited region is negative. **Local (circular) currents** arise between them, depolarize the neighboring region to the critical level and evoke a new action potential in it. In this way excitation spreads **without decrement**.

items: **In an unmyelinated fiber** conduction is **continuous**: each neighboring segment of the membrane is excited in turn; the velocity is low.

**In a myelinated fiber** conduction is **saltatory (jumping)**: myelin acts as an electrical insulator, so the action potential is generated only at the nodes of Ranvier and “jumps” from one node to the next (even skipping 2–3 nodes). This increases the velocity 50-fold and saves energy (the Na^+^/K^+^ pump works only at the nodes).

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Conduction of excitation: I — continuous in an unmyelinated fiber; II — saltatory in a myelinated fiber (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: **Multiple sclerosis** and **Guillain–Barré syndrome** are demyelinating diseases. When myelin is destroyed, saltatory conduction is disturbed: impulses slow down or stop. The result is paralysis, sensory disturbances and impaired vision. Electroneuromyography reveals a decrease in conduction velocity.

sections.title: 3. Lability of the nerve and parabiosis

blocks.text: N.E. Vvedensky (1901) established that when various damaging agents (KCl, procaine (novocaine), ether, cold) act on part of a nerve, its lability decreases and it responds to excitation in a peculiar way. This state was called **parabiosis** (“beside life”). Parabiosis is a reversible process: when the damaging agent is removed, nerve function is restored.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: The parabiosis experiment (A) and the phases of parabiosis (B): 1 — muscle contraction; 2 — stimulus strength (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Phases of parabiosis
head: Phase
Response to a weak stimulus
Response to a strong stimulus
Mechanism
rows: Weakened — the same response to strong and weak stimuli
Lability decreases; frequently arriving impulses fall into the refractory period
A larger response to a weak stimulus
A weak response or none at all to a strong stimulus
Lability is reduced further; strong (frequent) impulses deeply inhibit the region
Persistent depolarization — inactivation of Na^+^ channels; excitation is not conducted

parts.text: Vvedensky regarded parabiosis as **a peculiar localized, persistent (stationary) state of excitation**. This doctrine shows **the unity of the processes of excitation and inhibition**: inhibition can be a special form of excitation.

The phases of parabiosis are seen in local anesthesia: after injection of procaine (novocaine), strong painful stimuli are blocked first (paradoxical phase), then all impulses stop (inhibitory phase). As the anesthetic is absorbed, the phases pass in reverse order and sensation is restored.

blocks.text: A **synapse** (Greek synapsis — connection; a term of C. Sherrington) is a special structure that transmits excitation from one cell to another. Every synapse consists of a **presynaptic membrane**, a **synaptic cleft** and a **postsynaptic membrane**.

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Classification of synapses
head: Feature
Types
rows: Central (in the CNS) and peripheral (neuromuscular, neuroglandular, in autonomic ganglia)
Chemical (via a neurotransmitter), electrical (via gap junctions — connexons), mixed
Cholinergic (acetylcholine), adrenergic (norepinephrine), dopaminergic, serotonergic, GABAergic, glycinergic, glutamatergic, peptidergic

blocks.text: In **electrical synapses** the synaptic cleft is very narrow (2–4 nm), and neighboring cells are connected directly through protein channels (connexons); excitation passes without delay and in both directions. They are found in cardiac muscle, smooth muscles and some parts of the CNS.

sections.title: 5. Transmission of excitation in a chemical synapse

blocks.text: Most synapses in the human body are **chemical** synapses. In them the synaptic cleft is 20–50 nm wide; the presynaptic terminal contains **synaptic vesicles** that store the neurotransmitter, and the postsynaptic membrane carries **receptors** sensitive to it.

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Stages of transmission of excitation in a chemical synapse

blocks.text: The amount of neurotransmitter in one vesicle is called a **quantum** (one quantum of acetylcholine ≈ 5–10 thousand molecules). Even at rest some vesicles are released spontaneously, producing small **miniature potentials**.
Neuromuscular synapse

The terminal of a motor neuron axon forms a **neuromuscular synapse (end plate)** with a skeletal muscle fiber. The neurotransmitter is **acetylcholine (ACh)**; the postsynaptic membrane carries **N-cholinergic receptors** (ligand-gated Na^+^/K^+^ channels).

items: The action potential arrives at the presynaptic terminal, and Ca^2+^ channels open.
Under the action of Ca^2+^, vesicles containing ACh undergo exocytosis (100–300 quanta per impulse).
ACh binds to N-cholinergic receptors, cation channels open and Na^+^ enters.
An **end-plate potential (EPP)** arises on the postsynaptic membrane — like the local response, it is graded and summates.
The EPP depolarizes the adjacent muscle membrane to the critical level and an **action potential** arises — the muscle contracts.
ACh is broken down within 1–2 ms by the enzyme **acetylcholinesterase (AChE)** into choline and acetic acid; choline returns to the presynaptic terminal and is used to synthesize new ACh.

blocks.label: Figure 3.5
blocks.caption: Structure of the neuromuscular synapse and transmission of excitation in it (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: The neuromuscular synapse has a high **safety factor**: the EPP produced by one impulse is 3–4 times larger than needed for an action potential. Therefore, normally every motor impulse is sure to excite the muscle fiber.

blocks.text: Properties of chemical synapses

items: **One-way conduction** — the neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic terminal, and the receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane.
**Synaptic delay** — 0.2–0.5 ms at each synapse (for release of the neurotransmitter, its diffusion and binding to the receptor).
**Low lability** — 100–150 impulses/s.
**Rapid fatigue** — depletion of the neurotransmitter store, desensitization of receptors.
**High sensitivity to chemicals** — drugs and poisons act selectively on synapses.
**Summation and facilitation** — with successive impulses, transmitter release increases because Ca^2+^ accumulates.

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Substances acting on the neuromuscular synapse
head: Site of action
Substance
Result
rows: Accumulation of ACh; in therapeutic doses muscle strength increases, in poisoning — convulsions and paralysis

parts.text: **Myasthenia gravis** is an autoimmune disease in which autoantibodies are formed against N-cholinergic receptors. The number of receptors decreases, the EPP becomes smaller and the safety factor falls: muscles tire quickly (drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty swallowing). Treatment uses AChE inhibitors (pyridostigmine), which increase the amount of ACh in the synapse.

Steps of the synapse — **“Arrives–Enters–Releases–Binds–Opens–Breaks down”**: the impulse **arrives**, Ca^2+^ **enters**, the neurotransmitter is **released**, it **binds** to the receptor, the channel **opens**, the neurotransmitter is **broken down**.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: demonstrating isolated conduction in a nerve

items: Isolate the frog's sciatic nerve together with its branches to both legs (or, in one leg, observe the branches to the gastrocnemius and other muscles).
Stimulate part of the nerve trunk and observe which muscles contract.

Change the site of stimulation. **Expected results and analysis:** each time only the muscles innervated by the stimulated fibers contract; excitation does not pass to neighboring fibers. This proves the law of isolated conduction.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: Vvedensky's parabiosis experiment

items: Prepare a nerve-muscle preparation. Place a piece of cotton wool soaked in KCl or procaine solution on the middle part of the nerve (the parabiotic region).
Place the stimulating electrodes above the parabiotic region (closer to the center).
Every 1–2 minutes stimulate alternately with weak and strong stimuli and record the muscle contractions.
Note the sequence of phases.
Remove the cotton wool, wash the nerve with Ringer's solution and observe the recovery of function.

blocks.text: **Expected results and analysis:** first the responses to strong and weak stimuli become equal (equalizing phase), then the response to a weak stimulus becomes larger than to a strong one (paradoxical phase), and finally there is no response at all (inhibitory phase). After washing, the phases pass in reverse order and conduction is restored — parabiosis is a reversible process.
Experiment 3: relative indefatigability of the nerve and rapid fatigue of the synapse

items: Stimulate the nerve of a nerve-muscle preparation for a long time at a frequency of 30–50 Hz.
Wait until the muscle stops contracting (becomes fatigued).

Immediately place the electrodes directly on the muscle and stimulate it. **Expected results and analysis:** the muscle that does not contract when stimulated through the nerve contracts again when stimulated directly. Hence neither the muscle nor the nerve is fatigued — the **neuromuscular synapse** fatigues first (its neurotransmitter store is depleted). This shows that the synapse has the lowest lability.

quiz.q: Which feature is not a property of chemical synapses?
What causes muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis?
options: Autoantibodies to N-cholinergic receptors and a decrease in the number of receptors

quiz.q: What fatigues first in a nerve-muscle preparation stimulated for a long time?
What is a characteristic feature of electrical synapses?

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 30-year-old woman complains that in the evening her eyelids droop, she tires quickly when speaking and swallowing food becomes difficult. After rest in the morning her condition improves. After injection of neostigmine (Proserin), muscle strength was temporarily restored.
cases.ask: What disease can be suspected? Explain the mechanism of the disease and the action of neostigmine.
cases.answer: Myasthenia gravis. In this disease autoantibodies are formed against N-cholinergic receptors, and the number of receptors on the postsynaptic membrane decreases. As a result the end-plate potential becomes smaller and the safety factor of the neuromuscular synapse falls; with repeated activity, when transmitter release decreases slightly, the EPP falls below threshold — the muscles tire quickly (worse toward evening). Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, acetylcholine persists longer in the synaptic cleft and activates the remaining receptors more — muscle strength is temporarily restored.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient who had eaten home-canned food developed double vision, drooping eyelids, impaired swallowing and later weakness of the respiratory muscles. Sensation was not affected.
cases.ask: The action of which poison can be suspected? Which stage of synaptic transmission does it disrupt?
cases.answer: Botulinum toxin (botulism). The toxin enters the presynaptic terminal and cleaves the proteins that ensure fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the membrane — exocytosis of the neurotransmitter stops. Even when the action potential reaches the terminal, acetylcholine is not released, no end-plate potential arises and flaccid paralysis develops. Sensation is preserved because sensory pathways do not use cholinergic neuromuscular synapses. Paralysis of the respiratory muscles is life-threatening.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student stimulated the nerve of a nerve-muscle preparation rhythmically for a long time. The muscle stopped contracting. He concluded that “the muscle is fatigued”.
cases.ask: Is the conclusion correct? How can it be checked? Explain the result.
cases.answer: The conclusion may be wrong. To check it, the electrodes should be placed directly on the muscle: if the muscle contracts, it is not fatigued. The nerve also practically does not fatigue (the law of relative indefatigability). Hence the neuromuscular synapse fatigues first — it has the lowest lability, and with prolonged stimulation its neurotransmitter store is depleted and its receptors are desensitized.

topics.title: Methods of studying the properties of muscle. Incomplete (serrated) and complete (smooth) tetanus

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, physiological properties and mechanism of contraction of skeletal and smooth muscles, the types and modes of muscle contraction (single twitch, incomplete and complete tetanus), motor units, and the laws of muscle strength, work and fatigue; to master the methods of studying muscle activity in humans (dynamometry, ergography, electromyography).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the types of muscle and their main physiological properties;
the structure of the skeletal muscle fiber and the sarcomere;
excitation–contraction coupling and the sliding filament theory;
the types of contraction (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic) and its modes (single twitch, incomplete and complete tetanus);
the phenomena of optimum and pessimum;
the motor unit and its types;
muscle strength, work and fatigue, and the law of average loads;
the features of smooth muscles.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: record a single twitch, incomplete and complete tetanus of a nerve-muscle preparation on kymograph tape;
perform and evaluate hand dynamometry in a human;
record an ergogram and analyze the dynamics of fatigue.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: ATP performs three tasks in muscle: 1) energy for the movement of cross-bridges; 2) **detachment** of the myosin head from actin; 3) the work of the Ca^2+^ pump and the Na^+^/K^+^ pump. After death ATP runs out and the cross-bridges remain attached — **rigor mortis** develops.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The type of tetanus is determined by the **interval between stimuli**: if the interval is shorter than a single twitch but longer than the contraction phase — incomplete (serrated) tetanus; if it is shorter than the contraction phase — complete (smooth) tetanus.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the past, **accumulation of lactic acid** was considered the main cause of fatigue. According to modern data, muscle fatigue involves accumulation of inorganic phosphate, decreased Ca^2+^ release, exhaustion of glycogen stores, accumulation of K^+^ outside the cells and central factors (motivation, CNS fatigue).

sections.title: 1. Types of muscle and their properties

blocks.text: There are three kinds of muscle tissue in the human body: **striated skeletal**, **striated cardiac** and **smooth** muscle.

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Comparative characteristics of the types of muscle
head: Feature
Skeletal muscle
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
rows: Cells with one or two nuclei, cross-striated, intercalated discs
Involuntary (autonomic nervous system, hormones), automaticity in some

blocks.text: The physiological properties of muscle are **excitability**, **conductivity**, **contractility**, **elasticity** (return to the original state after stretching) and **extensibility**; smooth muscles additionally have **plasticity** (keeping their tone unchanged in the stretched state) and **automaticity**.

**The main functions of muscles:** movement of the body in space and maintenance of posture, respiratory movements, heat production (60–70% of the energy of contraction becomes heat), assisting the movement of blood and lymph (the muscle pump), and movement of internal organs (smooth muscles).

sections.title: 2. Structure of the skeletal muscle fiber

blocks.text: Muscle → muscle bundles → **muscle fibers** (multinucleated cells, up to several cm long) → **myofibrils** → **sarcomeres**. The sarcomere is the part of a myofibril between two **Z lines** (2–2.5 µm long at rest), the functional unit of the contractile apparatus.

items: **Thick filaments** — myosin; located in the middle of the sarcomere, they form the **A band** (anisotropic, dark).
**Thin filaments** consist of actin, tropomyosin and troponin; they are attached to the Z line and form the **I band** (isotropic, light).
The light part in the middle of the A band containing only thick filaments is the **H zone**, with the **M line** at its center.

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Structure of skeletal muscle: muscle — fiber — myofibril — sarcomere (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The membrane of the muscle fiber (sarcolemma) dips into the fiber as **transverse tubules (the T system)**. On both sides of them lie the terminal cisterns of the **sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)**, forming a **triad**. The SR is the store of Ca^2+^ ions.
Excitation–contraction coupling

items: The action potential generated at the neuromuscular synapse spreads along the sarcolemma and passes into the fiber through the **T tubules**.
The voltage-sensitive **dihydropyridine receptors** (L-type Ca^2+^ channels) in the T tubule change their conformation and mechanically open the **ryanodine receptors** (Ca^2+^ channels) of the SR.
Ca^2+^ leaves the SR for the sarcoplasm: its concentration rises from 10^-7^ to 10^-5^ mol/l.
Ca^2+^ binds to **troponin C**; the troponin–tropomyosin complex shifts and the myosin-binding sites on actin are exposed.

blocks.text: The sliding filament theory (A. Huxley, H. Huxley)

During contraction the filaments themselves do not shorten: **the thin actin filaments slide between the thick myosin filaments**. As a result the Z lines approach each other, **the I band and H zone narrow, while the width of the A band does not change**.

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: The sarcomere at rest (top) and contracted (bottom) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 4.3
blocks.caption: The cross-bridge cycle

blocks.text: Relaxation

Relaxation is also an **active process**: the **Ca^2+^-ATPase (calcium pump)** in the SR membrane pumps Ca^2+^ back into the SR using the energy of ATP; once Ca^2+^ falls, troponin–tropomyosin covers the active sites and the muscle relaxes.

parts.text: ATP performs three tasks in muscle: 1) energy for the movement of cross-bridges; 2) **detachment** of the myosin head from actin; 3) the work of the Ca^2+^ pump and the Na^+^/K^+^ pump. After death ATP runs out and the cross-bridges remain attached — **rigor mortis** develops.
In sliding, **“A stays Always”** (the A band does not change), **“I and H get thIn”** (the I band and H zone narrow).

Definition
Example

Flexing the arm without a load
The length does not change, the tension increases
Holding a load that cannot be lifted, maintaining posture

blocks.text: Single twitch

A single threshold or stronger stimulus evokes a **single twitch**. Its periods (in the frog gastrocnemius, ≈ 0.1 s in total) are the **latent period** (from the stimulus to the start of contraction, ≈ 0.01 s — for excitation–contraction coupling), the **contraction phase** (≈ 0.04 s) and the **relaxation phase** (≈ 0.05 s). The action potential (1–3 ms) is much shorter than the contraction — therefore the muscle can be excited again during the contraction.
Summation and tetanus
If a second stimulus arrives before the first contraction has ended, the contractions add up (**summation**). Rhythmic stimuli produce a long-lasting strong contraction — **tetanus**.

blocks.title: Table 4.3. Types of tetanus
head: Type
Stimulus frequency (frog muscle)
Condition
Curve
rows: Each subsequent stimulus falls into the relaxation phase of the previous contraction
Each subsequent stimulus falls into the contraction phase of the previous contraction

blocks.label: Figure 4.4
blocks.caption: Modes of muscle contraction: A — single twitch; B — incomplete tetanus; C — complete tetanus; D — pessimum (drawn after Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 4.5
blocks.caption: Single twitch and summation (A, B), kymograms of incomplete and complete tetanus (C) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: In tetanus the contraction amplitude is 2–4 times greater than that of a single twitch, because Ca^2+^ is maintained at a high concentration in the sarcoplasm and all cross-bridges are active. In natural human movements, skeletal muscles contract **tetanically**: motor neurons send impulses at a frequency of 10–50 Hz.
Optimum and pessimum (N.E. Vvedensky)

As the stimulus frequency increases, the amplitude of tetanus grows and becomes greatest at a certain frequency — the **optimum**: each impulse falls into the phase of exaltation after the previous excitation. If the frequency is increased further, the impulses fall into the refractory period and the contraction decreases or stops — the **pessimum**. Pessimum is mainly related to the low lability of the neuromuscular synapse.

parts.text: The type of tetanus is determined by the **interval between stimuli**: if the interval is shorter than a single twitch but longer than the contraction phase — incomplete (serrated) tetanus; if it is shorter than the contraction phase — complete (smooth) tetanus.

In **tetanus** (the disease), tetanus toxin stops the release of glycine and GABA from inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord. Motor neurons send impulses continuously at a high frequency, and skeletal muscles contract tetanically and painfully (spasm of the masticatory muscles — “risus sardonicus”, opisthotonus). In **hypocalcemia**, on the other hand, the excitability of nerves and muscles increases and tetanic convulsions (tetany) appear.

blocks.text: A **motor unit** is a set consisting of one motor neuron, its axon and the muscle fibers innervated by that axon. It is the functional unit of muscle: when the motor neuron is excited, all its fibers contract simultaneously.

blocks.title: Table 4.4. Types of motor units
head: Feature
Slow (S, type I, “red”)
Fast fatigue-resistant (FR, IIa)
Fast fatigable (FF, IIb, “white”)
rows: Postural muscles that keep the body upright

blocks.text: In the eye muscles one motor unit consists of 3–10 fibers, in finger muscles 10–25, and in the large calf and thigh muscles up to 1500–2000 fibers: the smaller the motor unit, the more precise the movement. Muscle force is controlled by the **number of active motor units** and their **impulse frequency**; small (slow) units are recruited first, then larger ones (**Henneman's size principle**).

**Muscle strength** is the maximum load a muscle can lift or its maximum isometric tension. It depends on the **physiological cross-section** (the sum of the cross-sections of all fibers). **Absolute muscle strength** is the ratio of maximum strength to the physiological cross-section (5–10 kg/cm^2^ in humans). Pennate muscles are stronger because their physiological cross-section is large.

**Muscle work** is the product of the mass of the lifted load and the height to which it is lifted (A = P × h). If the load is zero or maximal, the work is zero; the greatest work is done at an **average load** — **the law of average loads**. Likewise, the most work is done when the rhythm of work is also average (**the law of average rhythm**).

**Fatigue** is a temporary decrease in working capacity as a result of prolonged or intense work; it is restored after rest. In an isolated preparation, fatigue occurs first at the **neuromuscular synapse**; in the whole organism, mainly in the **nerve centers** (I.M. Sechenov). Sechenov showed the effect of **active rest**: if, while the tired arm is resting, work is done with the other arm, working capacity is restored faster.

parts.text: In the past, **accumulation of lactic acid** was considered the main cause of fatigue. According to modern data, muscle fatigue involves accumulation of inorganic phosphate, decreased Ca^2+^ release, exhaustion of glycogen stores, accumulation of K^+^ outside the cells and central factors (motivation, CNS fatigue).

blocks.text: Smooth muscles are found in the walls of internal organs (stomach, intestine, urinary bladder, uterus), blood vessels and bronchi. Their contraction is slow but long-lasting and requires little energy (**tone**).

items: **Single-unit (visceral)** smooth muscles — the cells are connected by gap junctions and contract as a functional syncytium; most of them have **automaticity** (pacemaker cells): intestine, stomach, ureter.

**Multi-unit** smooth muscles — each cell is innervated separately: the muscles of the pupil, the ciliary muscle, large arteries. **Mechanism of contraction:** Ca^2+^ (entering mainly from outside the cell) binds to **calmodulin** → the complex activates **myosin light-chain kinase** → myosin is phosphorylated and its interaction with actin begins. Smooth muscles contract in response to stretch (the **myogenic response**, the Bayliss effect in vessels).

parts.text: Disturbed contraction of smooth muscles underlies many diseases: spasm of bronchial smooth muscle in **bronchial asthma**, increased arteriolar tone in **arterial hypertension**, intestinal spasm in **intestinal colic**. That is why Ca^2+^ channel blockers (nifedipine), β~2~-adrenergic agonists (salbutamol (albuterol)) and antispasmodics (drotaverine) are widely used.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: recording a single twitch, incomplete and complete tetanus

items: Prepare a frog nerve-muscle preparation, attach the muscle tendon to the myograph lever and bring the tip of the lever into contact with the kymograph drum.
Stimulate the nerve with a single suprathreshold stimulus — record the curve of a single twitch. With the drum rotating fast, mark the latent period and the contraction and relaxation phases.
Set the stimulus frequency on the electrical stimulator to 10–15 Hz and stimulate for 2–3 s — record incomplete tetanus.
Increase the frequency to 30–50 Hz — record complete tetanus.

Increase the frequency further (100 Hz and higher) and observe the pessimum; show that contraction is restored when the frequency is reduced (optimum). **Expected results and analysis:** at low frequency each stimulus falls into the relaxation phase of the previous contraction and incomplete tetanus arises; at high frequency the stimuli fall into the contraction phase, the contractions fuse completely and complete tetanus appears. The amplitude of tetanus is larger than that of a single twitch. At a very high frequency the impulses fall into the refractory period and exceed the lability of the synapse — pessimum.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: hand dynamometry

items: The subject stands upright and extends the arm to the side; the dynamometer is held in the palm with the dial facing inward.
It is squeezed with maximum force 2–3 times (with 1 minute of rest in between); the best result is recorded.
Both hands are measured.

The **strength index** is calculated: hand strength (kg) / body mass (kg) × 100%. **Interpretation:** the normal strength index is 65–80% in men and 48–50% in women. The working hand is usually 5–10% stronger.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: ergography (the Mosso ergograph)

items: The subject's arm is fixed in the ergograph, and a cord with a 2–4 kg load is tied to the middle finger.
To the rhythm of a metronome (every 1–2 s) the load is lifted as high as possible; the lifting height is recorded on the kymograph tape.
The work continues until the load can no longer be lifted (until fatigue).
The experiment is repeated after 5 minutes of passive rest and 5 minutes of active rest (work with the other arm).

The work done is calculated: A = mass of the load × sum of the lifting heights. **Expected results and analysis:** the ergogram first shows warming up (the height increases slightly), then stable work and fatigue (the height decreases). After active rest working capacity recovers better than after passive rest — the Sechenov phenomenon.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing a kymogram

items: Find the stimulus mark and the time line.
Measure the duration of the latent period and the contraction and relaxation phases of a single twitch.
Determine whether the tetanus curve has teeth.
Compare the interval between stimuli with the phases of a single twitch and justify the type of tetanus.
Calculate the ratio of the tetanus amplitude to the single twitch amplitude.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating an electromyogram (EMG)

items: Place surface electrodes over the muscle and the ground electrode nearby.
Record at rest (bioelectric “silence”) and during weak and maximal voluntary contraction.
Note the increase in EMG amplitude and frequency as force increases (recruitment of new motor units and increased firing frequency).
Evaluate the change in amplitude and the decrease in frequency during fatigue.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An unvaccinated patient whose foot had been pierced by a rusty nail developed, a week later, spasm of the masticatory muscles (inability to open the mouth), “risus sardonicus” of the face and later strong spasms of the back muscles.
cases.ask: What disease is this? Why do the skeletal muscles contract strongly for a long time? Which mode of contraction does this resemble?
cases.answer: Tetanus. Tetanus toxin stops the release of glycine and GABA from inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. Motor neurons remain uninhibited and continuously send impulses at a high frequency. Each impulse then falls into the contraction phase of the previous contraction, and the muscles stay contracted for a long time in a state of complete tetanus. The muscles themselves and the neuromuscular synapse are not damaged — the disturbance lies in central inhibition.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 20-year-old athlete performs well in the 100 m sprint but has poor endurance in a marathon. His friend, on the contrary, runs long distances well.
cases.ask: How can this difference be explained by the types of muscle fibers (motor units)?
cases.answer: The sprinter's muscles contain many fast fatigable (FF, IIb, “white”) motor units: they contract quickly and strongly and obtain energy from anaerobic glycolysis, but tire quickly. In the marathon runner, slow (S, type I, “red”) and fast fatigue-resistant (FR) units predominate: they have many mitochondria, much myoglobin and many capillaries and obtain energy by oxidation — so they can work for a long time. Although the fiber ratio is mainly inherited, training partly changes their properties.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student stimulated a nerve-muscle preparation on a kymograph at a frequency of 20 Hz and obtained a wavy curve. The duration of a single twitch is 0.1 s, the contraction phase 0.04 s.
cases.ask: Which type of tetanus did the student obtain? What frequency is needed to obtain complete tetanus?
cases.answer: At 20 Hz the interval between stimuli is 0.05 s. This is shorter than the duration of a single twitch (0.1 s) but longer than the contraction phase (0.04 s) — each stimulus falls into the relaxation phase of the previous contraction, so incomplete tetanus arose. For complete tetanus the interval must be shorter than the contraction phase: less than 0.04 s, i.e., a frequency above 25 Hz (in practice 30–50 Hz).
