topics.title: Biological fluids of the body. Physicochemical properties of blood. ESR

goals.text: To teach the student the internal environment of the body and its fluid compartments, the concept of the blood system, the functions, volume and composition of blood, the composition of plasma, the main physicochemical properties of blood (viscosity, specific gravity, osmotic and oncotic pressure, pH and buffer systems), and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and its significance; to master the determination of the hematocrit and ESR.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the fluid compartments of the body and their volumes;
the concept of the blood system (G.F. Lang) and the functions of blood;
the blood volume, hematocrit and composition of plasma;
the plasma proteins and their functions;
osmotic and oncotic pressure, and isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions;
the active reaction of blood (pH), the buffer systems, acidosis and alkalosis;
the factors affecting the ESR and its normal values.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the hematocrit;
determine and evaluate the ESR by the Panchenkov method;
determine the osmotic resistance of erythrocytes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Albumin** generates **80%** of the oncotic pressure (its molecule is small and there are many of them). When albumin decreases (starvation, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), oncotic pressure falls and **oncotic (hypoproteinemic) edema** develops.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: For the bicarbonate buffer remember the ratio **“1 to 20”**: H~2~CO~3~ : NaHCO~3~ = 1 : 20. If the ratio is maintained, the pH is 7.4.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The ESR is a **nonspecific** parameter: it shows whether inflammation is present and how active it is, but does not establish the diagnosis. The ESR changes late (rises 1–2 days after the onset of disease) and may remain high for several weeks after recovery. **C-reactive protein** is more sensitive for early assessment of acute inflammation.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In modern laboratories the **Westergren method** (a longer tube, 200 mm scale) is the international standard; its normal values are close to those of the Panchenkov method, but at high values the Westergren method is more accurate.

sections.title: 1. The internal environment of the body and biological fluids

blocks.text: In the adult body water makes up **≈ 60%** of body mass (75–80% in a newborn, less in the elderly and in obese people). Water is located in two main compartments.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Fluid compartments of the body (for a 70 kg man; drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 5.1. Fluid compartments and their main ions
head: Compartment
Percentage of body mass
Main cation
Main anion
rows: Transcellular fluids (cerebrospinal, synovial, pleural, ocular fluids)

blocks.text: The **internal environment** is formed by the fluids surrounding the cells: **blood**, **lymph** and **tissue fluid**. They constantly exchange with one another: blood plasma filters from the capillaries into the tissues and forms tissue fluid, part of which returns to the blood through the lymphatic vessels.

sections.title: 2. The blood system and the functions of blood

blocks.text: The **blood system** (G.F. Lang, 1939) is a single system consisting of the peripheral blood, the hematopoietic organs (red bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, thymus), the organs of blood destruction (spleen, liver) and the neurohumoral apparatus that regulates them.

blocks.title: Table 5.2. Functions of blood
head: Function
Content
rows: Transport of all substances — the general function
Transport of O~2~ from the lungs to the tissues and of CO~2~ from the tissues to the lungs
Delivery of nutrients to the cells
Transport of the end products of metabolism (urea, uric acid, creatinine) to the excretory organs
Maintaining the constancy of pH, osmotic pressure and ion composition
Transport of hormones and other active substances

blocks.text: Blood volume and composition

In adults the blood volume is **6–8%** of body mass, i.e., 4.5–6 l (≈ 70 ml/kg). At rest part of the blood is kept in **reservoirs** (spleen, liver, subcutaneous vessels, lungs) and joins the circulating blood during physical work or blood loss.
Blood consists of **plasma** (55–60%) and **formed elements** (40–45%). The ratio of the volume of formed elements to the total blood volume is called the **hematocrit**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Determination of the hematocrit: blood collection, centrifugation and separation into layers (Alavia O.T., 2018)

Men

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Composition of blood (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Plasma consists of 90–92% water and 8–10% dry matter. The main part of the dry matter is **proteins** (65–85 g/l).

blocks.title: Table 5.4. Plasma proteins
head: Protein
Amount
Function
rows: Generate 80% of the oncotic pressure; transport bilirubin, fatty acids, drugs and hormones; a reserve of amino acids
α, β — transport of lipids, iron (transferrin), copper (ceruloplasmin); γ-globulins — antibodies (immunoglobulins)

blocks.text: The **albumin/globulin ratio** is normally 1.2–2.0. If fibrinogen is removed from plasma, **serum** is obtained.

**Functions of plasma proteins:** generating oncotic pressure (holding water in the vessels), transport, protection (immunity), blood coagulation, buffering, providing viscosity and serving as a protein reserve.

Other substances in plasma: **glucose** (3.3–5.5 mmol/l), lipids, **residual nitrogen** (nonprotein nitrogenous substances: urea 2.5–8.3 mmol/l, creatinine, uric acid, amino acids), mineral substances (≈ 0.9%; Na^+^ 135–145, K^+^ 3.5–5.0, Ca^2+^ 2.2–2.6, Cl^-^ 98–107 mmol/l), hormones, enzymes, vitamins.

blocks.text: Osmotic pressure

**Osmotic pressure** is the force with which dissolved substances (mainly ions) draw the solvent (water) to themselves through a semipermeable membrane. **NaCl** generates 60% of the osmotic pressure of plasma. Solutions whose osmotic pressure equals that of plasma are called **isotonic** (0.9% NaCl — “physiological saline”, 5% glucose); those with a lower pressure are **hypotonic**, and those with a higher one are **hypertonic**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: Erythrocytes in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions (Alavia O.T., 2018)

items: **In a hypotonic solution** water enters the erythrocyte, which swells and bursts — **osmotic hemolysis** (“lacquered blood”).

**In a hypertonic solution** water leaves the erythrocyte, which shrinks — **plasmolysis** (crenation). **The osmotic resistance of erythrocytes** is their resistance to bursting in hypotonic solutions. Normally hemolysis begins at **0.46–0.48%** NaCl (minimal resistance) and is complete at **0.32–0.34%** NaCl (maximal resistance).

parts.text: Only isotonic solutions are infused intravenously in large volumes. If a hypotonic fluid (for example, distilled water) is infused, hemolysis develops and the kidneys are damaged. In **hereditary microspherocytosis** (Minkowski–Chauffard disease) the erythrocytes are spherical and their osmotic resistance is sharply reduced — hemolysis begins already at 0.6–0.7% NaCl.

blocks.text: Oncotic pressure

**Oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure** is the part of osmotic pressure generated by plasma proteins; it is small (25–30 mm Hg) but very important, because proteins hardly pass through the capillary wall. Oncotic pressure **holds water inside the vessels** and returns tissue fluid to the blood in the venous part of the capillaries (the Starling balance).

parts.text: **Albumin** generates **80%** of the oncotic pressure (its molecule is small and there are many of them). When albumin decreases (starvation, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), oncotic pressure falls and **oncotic (hypoproteinemic) edema** develops.

blocks.text: The active reaction of blood (pH) and buffer systems

Blood pH is a very rigid homeostatic parameter: the limits compatible with life are 6.8–7.8. The constancy of pH is ensured by the **buffer systems**, the **lungs** (removal of CO~2~) and the **kidneys** (excretion of H^+^, reabsorption of HCO~3~^-^).

blocks.title: Table 5.6. Buffer systems of blood
head: Buffer system
Composition
Share of buffer capacity
Features
rows: The most powerful; works in erythrocytes
An open system — CO~2~ is removed through the lungs; works quickly
Important inside cells and in urine

blocks.text: The **alkaline reserve** is the amount of bicarbonate in plasma; it shows the capacity to neutralize acids (normally 24 ± 2 mmol/l, 50–65 vol% CO~2~).

**Acidosis** is a fall in pH below 7.35, **alkalosis** a rise above 7.45. By origin they are **respiratory** (accumulation or excessive loss of CO~2~) and **metabolic** (nonrespiratory); if the pH is kept normal by the buffer systems, they are **compensated**; if the pH changes, they are **decompensated**.

parts.text: For the bicarbonate buffer remember the ratio **“1 to 20”**: H~2~CO~3~ : NaHCO~3~ = 1 : 20. If the ratio is maintained, the pH is 7.4.

blocks.text: When anticoagulated blood stands upright in a tube, the erythrocytes gradually settle and a layer of plasma forms above them. The **ESR** is the height of the plasma layer formed in one hour (mm/h).

**Mechanism:** erythrocytes carry a negative charge and repel each other. Sedimentation depends on the erythrocytes sticking together into “coin stacks” (rouleaux, aggregates): aggregates are heavier and settle faster. Aggregation is enhanced by **large, positively charged protein molecules** — **fibrinogen**, **γ-globulins**, paraproteins; **albumin** reduces it.

blocks.title: Table 5.7. Factors affecting the ESR
head: Increase the ESR
Decrease the ESR
rows: Increase in fibrinogen and globulins (inflammation, infection, rheumatic fever)
Pregnancy (especially the second half, up to 40–50 mm/h)
Change in erythrocyte shape (sickle cell anemia)

parts.text: The ESR is a **nonspecific** parameter: it shows whether inflammation is present and how active it is, but does not establish the diagnosis. The ESR changes late (rises 1–2 days after the onset of disease) and may remain high for several weeks after recovery. **C-reactive protein** is more sensitive for early assessment of acute inflammation.

A sharp rise in ESR (100 mm/h and higher) occurs in multiple myeloma, sepsis, giant cell arteritis and metastases of malignant tumors. The dynamics of the ESR are useful for monitoring the effectiveness of treatment (rheumatic fever, tuberculosis).

blocks.text: Experiment 1: determining the hematocrit

items: Rinse a hematocrit capillary with an anticoagulant (heparin).
Fill the capillary to 7/8 of its length with blood taken from a finger and seal one end with plasticine.
Place the capillary in a hematocrit centrifuge and spin for 1.5–3 minutes (or 30 minutes at 3000 rpm in an ordinary centrifuge).

Using the scale, determine the ratio of the height of the column of formed elements to the total column height. **Interpretation:** 40–48% in men, 36–42% in women. A decreased hematocrit indicates anemia or hydremia; an increased one — erythrocytosis or dehydration (hemoconcentration).

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining the ESR by the Panchenkov method

items: Rinse a Panchenkov capillary with 5% sodium citrate solution, draw citrate up to the “P” mark (50 divisions) and expel it onto a watch glass.
Draw blood from a finger into the capillary up to the “K” mark twice, add it to the citrate on the watch glass (blood : citrate = 4 : 1) and mix.
Draw the mixture into the capillary up to the “K” (0) mark.
Place the capillary in the stand strictly upright and note the time.

After one hour measure the height of the plasma column in mm. **Interpretation:** 1–10 mm/h in men, 2–15 mm/h in women. A high result suggests an inflammatory process or a change in protein composition.

parts.text: In modern laboratories the **Westergren method** (a longer tube, 200 mm scale) is the international standard; its normal values are close to those of the Panchenkov method, but at high values the Westergren method is more accurate.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: determining the osmotic resistance of erythrocytes

items: Pour 1 ml of NaCl solutions from 0.7% to 0.2% (in steps of 0.02%) into test tubes.
Add 1 drop of blood to each tube, mix and leave for 1 hour (or centrifuge).
The tube in which the solution has turned pink but a sediment is still present — **minimal resistance** (onset of hemolysis).

The tube in which the solution is completely red and transparent (“lacquered blood”) and there is no sediment — **maximal resistance** (complete hemolysis). **Interpretation:** normally the minimal resistance is 0.46–0.48% and the maximal 0.32–0.34% NaCl.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating the main physicochemical parameters in a complete blood count

items: Compare the hematocrit with the normal range for the person's sex.
Compare the ESR with the normal range for sex and age.
Evaluate the total protein (65–85 g/l) and albumin (35–50 g/l).
If the ESR is increased, suspect conditions associated with increased fibrinogen and globulins (inflammation, pregnancy).
If albumin is decreased, point out the risk of oncotic edema.

skills.title: Skill: a simple assessment of acid–base status

items: Determine the pH: below 7.35 — acidosis, above 7.45 — alkalosis.
Evaluate pCO~2~ (normal 35–45 mm Hg): if the direction of change matches the pH — a respiratory disorder.
Evaluate HCO~3~^-^ (normal 22–26 mmol/l): if it changes in the same direction as the pH — a metabolic disorder.
Determine whether compensation is present.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis has fluid accumulation in the legs and the abdominal cavity (edema, ascites). Total blood protein is 52 g/l, albumin 24 g/l.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the edema. Which parameter has changed?
cases.answer: The liver is the main organ that synthesizes albumin; in cirrhosis albumin synthesis decreases (24 g/l, normal 35–50 g/l). Albumin generates 80% of the oncotic pressure of plasma, so oncotic pressure falls. The force holding water inside the capillaries decreases: more fluid leaves at the arterial end and less returns at the venous end. As a result fluid accumulates in the tissues — oncotic (hypoproteinemic) edema. In cirrhosis, increased pressure in the portal vein also contributes to ascites.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A healthy woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy has an ESR of 42 mm/h. Other parameters are normal, and she has no complaints.
cases.ask: Is this a pathology? Explain the cause of the increased ESR.
cases.answer: This is a physiological state. In the second half of pregnancy the blood levels of fibrinogen and globulins rise, albumin decreases relatively, and the erythrocyte concentration falls slightly because of hydremia. Large protein molecules reduce the charge of erythrocytes and enhance their aggregation into “coin stacks” (rouleaux) — the aggregates settle faster. In pregnancy the ESR may rise to 40–50 mm/h.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: By mistake a nurse infused 500 ml of distilled water intravenously into a patient. A few hours later the urine turned red-brown.
cases.ask: What condition has developed? Explain the mechanism. What solutions should be infused intravenously in large volumes?
cases.answer: Osmotic hemolysis. Distilled water is sharply hypotonic relative to blood; water enters the erythrocytes down the osmotic gradient, they swell and burst, and hemoglobin is released into the plasma. Free hemoglobin is excreted through the kidneys, colors the urine red-brown (hemoglobinuria) and may damage the renal tubules. Only isotonic solutions (0.9% NaCl, Ringer's solution, 5% glucose) are infused intravenously in large volumes.

topics.title: Erythrocytes. Hemoglobin and its types

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, number, functions and life cycle of erythrocytes, erythropoiesis and its regulation, the structure, types, compounds and amount of hemoglobin, the color index and the erythrocyte indices; to master counting erythrocytes, determining hemoglobin and calculating the color index.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the functional significance of the shape, size and structure of erythrocytes;
the normal erythrocyte count and its physiological changes;
the functions of erythrocytes;
the stages of erythropoiesis and its regulation (erythropoietin, vitamins, iron);
the destruction of erythrocytes and the formation of bilirubin;
the structure, physiological types and compounds of hemoglobin;
the color index and the erythrocyte indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: count erythrocytes in a Goryaev chamber;
determine hemoglobin by the Sahli method or the hemiglobincyanide method;
calculate and evaluate the color index.

The MCH also shows the amount of hemoglobin in one erythrocyte, but in absolute units (picograms). blocks.text: **Erythrocytes** (red blood cells) in mammals and humans are anucleate cells shaped like biconcave discs. Their diameter is **7.2–7.5 µm**, their thickness 2.5 µm at the edge and 1 µm in the center, and their volume 80–94 fl.
Advantages of the erythrocyte shape:

items: **Large surface area** — a biconcave disc has a surface area 1.7 times greater than a sphere, which speeds up gas diffusion.
**Short diffusion distance** — the distance from any point to the surface is small.
**Deformability** — the erythrocyte folds to pass through capillaries 3 µm in diameter (thanks to the membrane skeleton formed by spectrin, actin and ankyrin).

**Absence of a nucleus and mitochondria** — there is much room for hemoglobin; the erythrocyte does not consume the oxygen it carries (it obtains energy from anaerobic glycolysis). **Hemoglobin** makes up ≈ 34% of the erythrocyte (95% of its dry mass). Blood group antigens (A, B, Rh) are located on its membrane.

blocks.text: Erythrocyte count

items: **Erythrocytosis** is an increase in the number of erythrocytes. It may be **relative** (hemoconcentration: dehydration, heavy sweating, vomiting) or **absolute** (increased erythropoiesis: high altitude, chronic lung and heart diseases, athletes; pathological — erythremia).
**Erythropenia** is a decrease: anemias, hydremia (large fluid intake, pregnancy).

blocks.title: Table 6.1. Functions of erythrocytes
head: Function
Content
rows: Transport of O~2~ from the lungs to the tissues and of part of the CO~2~ from the tissues to the lungs
The hemoglobin buffer system — 75% of the buffer capacity of blood
Carrying amino acids, lipids and drugs on their surface
Antigens on the membrane (blood groups), transport of immune complexes
Procoagulants are released when they are destroyed

blocks.text: **Erythropoiesis** is the formation of erythrocytes; in adults it takes place in the **red bone marrow** (flat bones, vertebrae, sternum, pelvic bones). In the embryo erythropoiesis occurs first in the yolk sac, then in the liver and spleen. About 200 billion erythrocytes (2–3 million per second) are produced per day.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Stages of erythropoiesis

blocks.text: **Reticulocytes** are young erythrocytes; residual ribosomes (a reticular substance) become visible in them with special staining. Normally they make up **0.5–1.5%** (5–15‰) of the peripheral blood. The reticulocyte count reflects the erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow: it increases after blood loss or treatment with iron preparations (**reticulocyte crisis**).
Regulation of erythropoiesis

**Erythropoietin (EPO)** is the main humoral regulator of erythropoiesis, a glycoprotein hormone. It is produced mainly in the **kidneys** (90%) and in small amounts in the liver. The main factor that increases its synthesis is **tissue hypoxia**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Regulation of erythropoiesis by erythropoietin

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Factors affecting erythropoiesis
head: Factor
Effect
rows: Enhances proliferation and differentiation of erythroid progenitors
Enhance erythropoiesis (this is why men have more erythrocytes)
Needed for heme synthesis (20–25 mg is required daily, mostly recycled from destroyed erythrocytes; 1–2 mg is absorbed from food)
Needed for DNA synthesis and cell division
For heme synthesis and iron absorption
Produced by the parietal cells of the stomach; needed for the absorption of B~12~ in the small intestine
Enhances erythropoiesis; the parasympathetic system suppresses it

parts.text: **In chronic renal failure** EPO synthesis decreases and severe anemia develops; such patients are treated with recombinant erythropoietin. In sport EPO is used illegally as **doping** — the hematocrit rises, the blood thickens and the risk of thrombosis increases. **After gastric resection** Castle's intrinsic factor is lost and B~12~-deficiency (megaloblastic) anemia develops.

sections.title: 3. Life cycle and destruction of erythrocytes

blocks.text: Erythrocytes live in the blood for an average of **120 days**. The membrane of aging erythrocytes becomes rigid, and they are phagocytosed by macrophages mainly in the **spleen** (and in the liver and bone marrow) (**intracellular hemolysis**). A small proportion is destroyed inside the blood vessels (**intravascular hemolysis**).

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: The erythron: formation, circulation and destruction of erythrocytes (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Breakdown of hemoglobin: **globin** is split into amino acids; **iron** returns to the bone marrow with transferrin or is stored in the liver as ferritin and hemosiderin; **heme** → biliverdin → **bilirubin** (unconjugated, carried by albumin) → conjugated with glucuronic acid in the liver (conjugated bilirubin) → into the intestine with bile → stercobilin (color of stool) and urobilin (color of urine).

parts.text: The **erythron** (Castle) is the set of erythrocytes in the peripheral blood, their precursors in the bone marrow and the erythrocytes at the sites of their destruction. Normally the formation and destruction of erythrocytes are in balance.

blocks.text: **Hemoglobin (Hb)** is a complex protein (chromoprotein) with a molecular mass of 64,500 Da. It consists of **4 hemes** and **globin** (4 polypeptide chains). **Heme** is a compound of protoporphyrin IX with **ferrous iron (Fe^2+^)**; oxygen is bound by the iron in heme. One Hb molecule can bind **4 molecules of O~2~**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: The hemoglobin molecule: four subunits and the structure of heme (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Hemoglobin content

**130–160 g/l** in men and **120–140 g/l** in women. 1 g of Hb binds **1.34 ml of O~2~** (Hüfner's number). Therefore, with Hb of 150 g/l the **oxygen capacity** of blood is ≈ 200 ml O~2~/l (20 vol%).
Physiological types of hemoglobin

parts.text: **Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning** — from gas stoves, coal stoves and car exhaust. Carboxyhemoglobin does not carry O~2~ and also hinders the release of O~2~ by the remaining Hb — severe hypoxia. A “cherry-red” color of the skin is typical. Treatment: fresh air, 100% oxygen and, in severe cases, hyperbaric oxygenation. In **methemoglobinemia** (nitrate-containing water, aniline) the skin is bluish-gray; treatment — methylene blue, ascorbic acid.

**“CO — the Cherry Con”**: carbon monoxide “occupies” Hb and the skin becomes cherry-colored, yet the tissues suffocate. A pulse oximeter is “fooled” into reading HbCO as HbO~2~ — the saturation may look normal!

blocks.text: The **color index (CI)** is the relative saturation of one erythrocyte with hemoglobin:
CI = (Hb, g/l × 3) / (the first three digits of the erythrocyte count)
For example: Hb 150 g/l, erythrocytes 5.0 × 10^12^/l → CI = 150 × 3 / 500 = 0.9.

parts.text: The color index is a traditional parameter widely used in the practice of our country and the CIS; in international practice it has been replaced by the **MCH**. The MCH also shows the amount of hemoglobin in one erythrocyte, but in absolute units (picograms). The **MCV** (microcytic, normocytic, macrocytic) is the most important index for determining the type of anemia.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: counting erythrocytes in a Goryaev chamber

items: Put 4 ml of 3% NaCl solution (or Hayem's fluid) into a test tube.
Take 0.02 ml of blood from a finger, add it to the tube (dilution 1 : 200) and mix.
Cover the Goryaev chamber with a coverslip (rub it on until “Newton's rings” appear); put a drop of the diluted blood under the coverslip.

After 1 minute, count the erythrocytes under the microscope (×8 objective) in 5 large squares along the diagonal (each consisting of 16 small squares — 80 small squares in total). Count cells on the borders by the rule “those on the left and upper lines are counted”.

Calculation: X = (A × 4000 × 200) / 80, where A is the number of erythrocytes in 80 small squares; the count per 1 µl; simplified: X = A × 10,000 (per 1 µl) or A / 100 × 10^12^/l. **Interpretation:** compare the result with the normal range for the person's sex.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining hemoglobin by the Sahli method

items: Pour 0.1 N HCl up to the mark into the middle tube of the Sahli hemometer.
Take 20 µl (0.02 ml) of blood, add it to the HCl and mix; wait 5 minutes — hemoglobin forms **hematin hydrochloride** (brown) with hydrochloric acid.
Add distilled water drop by drop until the color matches the standard tubes.
Read the hemoglobin content (g/dl or g/l) from the tube scale.

parts.text: The Sahli method is subjective and has a large error (± 10%). In modern laboratories the international standard is the **hemiglobincyanide method** (photometric) or automated analyzers. The Sahli method is used for teaching purposes.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: calculating the color index

items: Take the results of the erythrocyte count and hemoglobin content.
Calculate by the formula CI = Hb (g/l) × 3 / the first three digits of the erythrocyte count.
Evaluate the result: normo-, hypo- or hyperchromia.

skills.title: Skill: suggesting the type of anemia from a blood test

items: Compare Hb and the erythrocyte count with the normal values (whether anemia is present).
Calculate the color index (or MCH).
Evaluate erythrocyte size from the MCV.
Evaluate the reticulocyte count: if increased, the bone marrow is active (blood loss, hemolysis); if decreased, erythropoiesis is suppressed.
Hypochromic microcytic — think of iron deficiency; hyperchromic macrocytic — B~12~/folate deficiency; normochromic — acute blood loss or hemolysis.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the oxygen capacity from the hemoglobin content

items: Take the Hb content in g/l.
Multiply by Hüfner's number (1.34 ml O~2~/g).
Express the result in ml O~2~/l (normally ≈ 190–210 ml/l).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman complains of weakness, fatigability, dizziness and hair loss. For many years her menstrual periods have been heavy. Blood test: Hb 85 g/l, erythrocytes 3.6 × 10^12^/l, MCV 72 fl.
cases.ask: Calculate the color index. What anemia can be suspected? Explain its cause.
cases.answer: CI = 85 × 3 / 360 = 0.71 — hypochromia. The MCV is reduced (72 fl) — microcytosis. Hypochromic microcytic anemia — iron-deficiency anemia. Chronic blood loss (heavy menstruation) has depleted the iron stores; iron is needed for heme synthesis, so hemoglobin synthesis decreases and the erythrocytes are small and pale. The weakness and dizziness are due to the reduced oxygen capacity of the blood and tissue hypoxia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In winter, family members who slept in a closed room with a burning coal stove were found in the morning with headache, nausea and weakness. One of them had cherry-red skin and mucous membranes. A pulse oximeter showed a saturation of 98%.
cases.ask: What kind of poisoning is this? Why is the pulse oximeter reading normal? What is the principle of first aid?
cases.answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO binds to hemoglobin 200–300 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin; it does not carry oxygen and also hinders the release of oxygen to the tissues by the remaining oxyhemoglobin — severe tissue hypoxia. Because carboxyhemoglobin has a color similar to oxyhemoglobin, an ordinary pulse oximeter cannot distinguish them and shows a falsely normal saturation. First aid: move the patient to fresh air and give 100% oxygen (which speeds up the elimination of CO); in severe cases, hyperbaric oxygenation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A mountaineer who moved from Tashkent to the Pamir mountains (3500 m) was found a month later to have erythrocytes of 5.8 × 10^12^/l, hemoglobin of 175 g/l and reticulocytes of 2.5%.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of these changes. Is this a relative or an absolute erythrocytosis?
cases.answer: This is an absolute (true) compensatory erythrocytosis. At high altitude the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmospheric air is low, so arterial pO~2~ decreases and tissue hypoxia develops. Hypoxia enhances erythropoietin synthesis in the kidneys; erythropoietin accelerates the proliferation of erythroid progenitors in the red bone marrow. The increase in reticulocytes reflects the activity of the bone marrow. The increase in erythrocytes and hemoglobin raises the oxygen capacity of the blood and compensates for the hypoxia.

topics.title: Leukocytes

goals.text: To teach the student the general properties, types, number and functions of leukocytes, the leukocyte formula (differential count) and its analysis, leukopoiesis and its regulation, and the role of leukocytes in nonspecific and specific (immune) defense; to master counting leukocytes and determining the leukocyte formula in a blood smear.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general properties and number of leukocytes;
the types of physiological and pathological leukocytosis and leukopenia;
the leukocyte formula and its normal values;
the functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes and lymphocytes;
the stages of leukopoiesis and its regulation;
the stages of phagocytosis;
cellular and humoral immunity and the role of T and B lymphocytes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: count leukocytes in a Goryaev chamber;
prepare and stain a blood smear and calculate the leukocyte formula;
detect and evaluate a “shift to the left” in the leukocyte formula.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the leukocyte formula in decreasing order: **“Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas”** — **N**eutrophils > **L**ymphocytes > **M**onocytes > **E**osinophils > **B**asophils (60 – 30 – 6 – 3 – 0.5%).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Evaluating the leukocyte formula only in percentages can be misleading. For example, even if lymphocytes are 50%, when the total leukocyte count is 3 × 10^9^/l their absolute number (1.5 × 10^9^/l) is normal — this is a **relative lymphocytosis** (in fact, neutropenia). Therefore **absolute counts** should always be calculated as well.

blocks.text: **Leukocytes** (white blood cells) are nucleated, colorless cells 6–20 µm in size. They are only **transported** in the blood and perform their main function **in the tissues**: they pass through the capillary wall (**diapedesis**) and move toward the focus of inflammation.
**General properties:** amoeboid movement, diapedesis, **chemotaxis** (movement toward chemical substances), phagocytosis and secretion of biologically active substances.
**Number:** **4–9 × 10^9^/l** in adults (4–10 × 10^9^/l in some sources). Up to 10–30 × 10^9^/l in newborns.

items: **Leukocytosis** is an increase above 9 (10) × 10^9^/l.
**Leukopenia** is a decrease below 4 × 10^9^/l.

blocks.text: Physiological leukocytoses are of a **redistributive** nature (release from reservoirs and from the marginal layer into the circulating blood), whereas pathological leukocytoses are associated with increased leukopoiesis.
Causes of **leukopenia**: viral infections (influenza, measles), ionizing radiation, cytostatics and some other drugs, autoimmune diseases, bone marrow damage.

sections.title: 2. Types of leukocytes and the leukocyte formula

blocks.text: By the presence or absence of specific granules in the cytoplasm, leukocytes are divided into two groups:

items: **Granulocytes (granular)** — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.
**Agranulocytes (nongranular)** — monocytes and lymphocytes.

blocks.caption: Types of leukocytes: neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, monocyte (smear stained by Romanowsky–Giemsa; Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **leukocyte formula (leukogram)** is the percentage ratio of the individual types of leukocytes.

blocks.caption: Normal ranges of the leukocyte formula (adults)

parts.text: To remember the leukocyte formula in decreasing order: **“Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas”** — **N**eutrophils > **L**ymphocytes > **M**onocytes > **E**osinophils > **B**asophils (60 – 30 – 6 – 3 – 0.5%).

blocks.text: Shifts of the leukocyte formula
By degree of maturity, neutrophils pass through: myelocyte → metamyelocyte (juvenile) → band → segmented. Normally only band and segmented neutrophils are present in the peripheral blood.

items: A **shift to the left** is an increase in young neutrophils (band forms, metamyelocytes and even myelocytes). In acute bacterial infection and inflammation it shows that the bone marrow is working intensively. Nuclear shift index = (myelocytes + metamyelocytes + band forms) / segmented forms; normally 0.05–0.08.
A **shift to the right** is an increase in segmented neutrophils with 5 or more segments (hypersegmentation); seen in B~12~-deficiency anemia and radiation sickness.

parts.text: The leukogram aids diagnosis: **neutrophilia** with a shift to the left — bacterial infection (pneumonia, appendicitis); **lymphocytosis** — viral infections (pertussis, mononucleosis), tuberculosis; **eosinophilia** — helminth infestation, allergic diseases (bronchial asthma); **monocytosis** — tuberculosis, infectious mononucleosis, recovery from sepsis; **agranulocytosis** — a sharp decrease in granulocytes, with a risk of severe infections.

sections.title: 3. Functions of the types of leukocytes

blocks.text: Neutrophils

The most numerous (50–70% of leukocytes) and mobile cells; they are the **first** to reach the focus of infection. They circulate in the blood for 6–8 hours and live in the tissues for 1–2 days. Functions: **phagocytosis** of bacteria (“microphages” — I.I. Mechnikov); killing bacteria with lysozyme, lactoferrin, cationic proteins, oxygen radicals and myeloperoxidase; release of pyrogens (fever). Pus consists mainly of dead neutrophils.
Eosinophils

Their granules stain deep pink with eosin. Functions: **defense against helminths** (they damage the parasite with major basic protein and peroxidase); **limiting allergic reactions** — they release histaminase (which breaks down histamine) and arylsulfatase; phagocytosis of antigen–antibody complexes. There are fewer of them in the blood by day and more at night (the effect of cortisol).
Basophils

The least numerous. Their granules contain **histamine** (dilates vessels and increases their permeability) and **heparin** (an anticoagulant). IgE receptors are located on their membrane; when an allergen binds, degranulation occurs — **immediate-type allergy** (anaphylaxis). Similar cells in the tissues are mast cells.
Monocytes

The largest leukocytes (15–20 µm), with a bean-shaped nucleus. After circulating in the blood for 2–3 days they pass into the tissues and become **macrophages** (“macrophages” — Mechnikov): Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lungs, osteoclasts in bone, microglia in the CNS. Functions: phagocytosis of large particles and dead cells (“scavengers”), **antigen presentation** (to T lymphocytes) and secretion of cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α).

blocks.label: Figure 7.3
blocks.caption: Stages of phagocytosis

blocks.text: Lymphocytes
The main cells of specific (acquired) immunity. Some of them live for years and even decades (**memory cells**).

head: Type
Share in blood
Site of maturation
Function
rows: Cellular immunity: T killers (CD8) kill virus-infected and tumor cells; T helpers (CD4) regulate the immune response; T regulatory cells limit it
Humoral immunity: under the action of an antigen they become plasma cells and produce antibodies (immunoglobulins)
Kill tumor and virus-infected cells without prior sensitization

parts.text: **HIV infection** damages CD4^+^ T helpers; when their number falls below 200 cells/µl, AIDS develops — the immune response is sharply weakened and opportunistic infections and tumors appear.

blocks.text: Granulocytes and monocytes are formed in the **red bone marrow**, and lymphocytes in the bone marrow and lymphoid organs (thymus, lymph nodes, spleen, Peyer's patches).

blocks.label: Figure 7.4
blocks.caption: Scheme of leukopoiesis

blocks.text: Leukopoiesis is regulated by **colony-stimulating factors (CSF)**: **G-CSF** (granulocytes), **M-CSF** (monocytes), **GM-CSF**; and also by **interleukins** (IL-3 — general, IL-5 — eosinophils, IL-7 — lymphocytes). They are produced by macrophages, endothelium, T lymphocytes and fibroblasts; their synthesis increases in infection and inflammation. Substances formed when leukocytes break down also enhance leukopoiesis (feedback).

parts.text: Recombinant **G-CSF** (filgrastim) is used to treat neutropenia after chemotherapy and to collect stem cells from donors.

blocks.text: **Immunity** is the ability of the organism to defend itself against genetically foreign substances and living organisms.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Types of immunity
head: Type
Factors
Features
rows: Fast, against any foreign agent, no memory
Against a particular antigen, immunological memory present
B lymphocytes → plasma cells → antibodies (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD)
Against a particular antigen, memory present

blocks.text: Specific immunity may be **active** (after disease or through vaccination) or **passive** (maternal antibodies via the placenta and milk, ready-made serum).
Experiment 1: counting leukocytes in a Goryaev chamber

items: Put 0.4 ml of 3–5% acetic acid solution (tinted with methylene blue) into a test tube — it hemolyzes the erythrocytes and stains the leukocyte nuclei.
Take 0.02 ml of blood from a finger, add it to the tube (dilution 1 : 20) and mix.
Fill the Goryaev chamber and wait 1 minute.
At low magnification (×8) count the leukocytes in 100 large squares (1600 small squares).
Calculation: X = A × 50 (per 1 µl), where A is the number of leukocytes in 100 large squares; or A / 20 × 10^9^/l. **Interpretation:** normal 4–9 × 10^9^/l.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: preparing a blood smear and determining the leukocyte formula

items: Place a small drop of blood near the edge of a clean, degreased glass slide.

Touch the drop with a ground-edge spreader slide at an angle of 45°; once the blood spreads along its edge, draw the smear with one even movement (the smear should be thin, with a “broom-shaped” end).
Air-dry the smear and fix it in methyl alcohol for 3–5 minutes.
Stain with Romanowsky–Giemsa stain for 20–30 minutes, rinse with water and dry.
Using the immersion objective (×90), move along the edges of the smear in a “meander” pattern and count 100 (or 200) leukocytes, classifying them by type.

Calculate the percentage of each type and its absolute count: absolute count = total leukocyte count × percentage / 100. **Interpretation:** compare the result with the normal leukogram and determine whether there is a shift to the left.

parts.text: Evaluating the leukocyte formula only in percentages can be misleading. For example, even if lymphocytes are 50%, when the total leukocyte count is 3 × 10^9^/l their absolute number (1.5 × 10^9^/l) is normal — this is a **relative lymphocytosis** (in fact, neutropenia). Therefore **absolute counts** should always be calculated as well.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting a leukogram

items: Evaluate the total leukocyte count (leukocytosis, normal, leukopenia).
Compare the percentage of each type with the normal range.
Calculate absolute counts and distinguish relative from absolute changes.
Evaluate the proportion of band forms among the neutrophils and calculate the nuclear shift index.
Name the likely condition from the predominant change: neutrophilia + shift to the left — bacterial inflammation; lymphocytosis — viral infection; eosinophilia — allergy or helminths.

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing leukocytes in a blood smear

items: Look at the shape of the nucleus: segmented (neutrophil), bilobed (eosinophil), indistinct and covered with granules (basophil), bean-shaped (monocyte), large and round (lymphocyte).

Evaluate the color of the cytoplasm and its granules: fine pinkish-violet (neutrophil), large orange-red (eosinophil), large dark violet (basophil), grayish-blue (monocyte), a thin blue rim (lymphocyte).
Compare the size of the cell with an erythrocyte.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old man came to the hospital with pain in the right lower abdomen, nausea and a body temperature of 38 °C. Blood test: leukocytes 15.8 × 10^9^/l; band neutrophils 14%, segmented 70%, lymphocytes 12%, monocytes 4%.
cases.ask: Analyze the leukogram. What do these changes indicate?
cases.answer: Leukocytosis (15.8 × 10^9^/l), neutrophilia (84%) and an increase in band neutrophils (14%, normal 1–6%) — a shift of the leukocyte formula to the left. Lymphocytes are relatively decreased. Such a change is typical of acute bacterial inflammation (the clinical picture matches acute appendicitis). Cytokines formed in the focus of inflammation (IL-1, TNF-α) and G-CSF release neutrophils, including young forms, from the bone marrow into the blood and enhance granulopoiesis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student gave blood after breakfast. The leukocyte count was 10.5 × 10^9^/l. When retested on an empty stomach the next day, it was 6.2 × 10^9^/l.
cases.ask: What caused the first result? Why is a blood test taken on an empty stomach?
cases.answer: This is alimentary (postprandial) physiological leukocytosis. After food intake leukocytes accumulate in the intestinal submucosa and partly enter the circulating blood; this is redistributive in nature and passes within a few hours. To avoid misinterpreting the result (mistaking it for inflammation), the blood test is taken in the morning on an empty stomach, without physical exertion or emotional stress.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient seen in spring with nasal congestion, sneezing and itchy eyes had a blood test showing leukocytes of 7.0 × 10^9^/l and eosinophils of 12%.
cases.ask: What change has been found? Explain its mechanism and the role of eosinophils in this condition.
cases.answer: Eosinophilia (12%, normal 0.5–5%). The clinical picture matches allergic rhinitis (pollinosis). The allergen degranulates mast cells and basophils that carry bound IgE — histamine and other mediators are released. Mast cells release a chemotactic factor for eosinophils, and Th2 lymphocytes enhance eosinophil production through IL-5. Eosinophils release histaminase and arylsulfatase, breaking down histamine and leukotrienes, and so limit the allergic reaction. That is why the eosinophil count rises in allergy.

In the thymus; cellular immunity (killers, helpers)

Founder of the theory of phagocytosis

topics.title: Platelets

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, number, formation and life span of platelets, their role in hemostasis and their other functions (angiotrophic, adhesion, aggregation, secretion, retraction), the platelet factors and the methods for evaluating platelet number and function; to master determining the bleeding time and testing capillary resistance.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure, size and number of platelets;
thrombocytopoiesis and its regulation (thrombopoietin);
the receptors of the platelet membrane and the contents of its granules;
the functions of platelets;
the stages of vascular-platelet hemostasis;
the platelet factors and their significance;
the causes and consequences of thrombocytopenia and thrombocytosis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: count platelets by the Fonio method;
determine the bleeding time by the Duke method;
test capillary resistance (tourniquet and pinch tests);
evaluate clot retraction.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Normally the endothelium **prevents** platelets from sticking: it produces **prostacyclin (PGI~2~)** and **nitric oxide (NO)**, which inhibit aggregation and dilate the vessel. Platelet **thromboxane A~2~**, on the contrary, enhances aggregation and vasoconstriction. The balance of these two substances determines the state of the platelets.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The sequence of platelet action — **“Stick–Activate–Aggregate–Retract”**: **S**ticking (adhesion) → **A**ctivation → **A**ggregation → **R**etraction.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Clotting time** and **bleeding time** are two different parameters. The bleeding time evaluates **vascular-platelet** hemostasis, while the clotting time (5–10 minutes by Lee–White) evaluates **coagulation** hemostasis. In hemophilia the bleeding time is normal but the clotting time is prolonged; in thrombocytopenia, the reverse — the bleeding time is prolonged and the clotting time is normal.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Today platelets are counted in automated hematology analyzers. In blood collected with EDTA, platelets sometimes aggregate and the analyzer shows them as low — **pseudothrombocytopenia**. If the result is doubtful, a smear should be examined or the sample recollected with citrate.

blocks.text: **Platelets** (thrombocytes) are anucleate, disc-shaped cell fragments **2–4 µm** in diameter. They are shed from the cytoplasm of the giant bone marrow cells — **megakaryocytes**.

**Number:** **180–320 × 10^9^/l** in adults (150–400 × 10^9^/l in international practice). Their life span is **7–10 days**; aged platelets are destroyed in the spleen and liver. About 1/3 of platelets are stored **in the spleen**.

items: **Thrombocytopenia** is a decrease below 150 (180) × 10^9^/l. Below 50 × 10^9^/l bleeding after injury increases, and below 20 × 10^9^/l spontaneous hemorrhages appear (petechiae, nosebleeds).

**Thrombocytosis** is an increase above 400 × 10^9^/l: physiological (physical work, after meals, pregnancy — redistributive), reactive (after blood loss, inflammation, after splenectomy) or neoplastic (essential thrombocythemia). The risk of thrombosis increases.

blocks.text: Structure

A platelet has a peripheral **hyalomere** (a light part containing microtubules and the contractile protein **thrombosthenin** — actomyosin) and a central **granulomere** (granules). The membrane has an **open canalicular system**, through which the contents of the granules are released.

Ligand

Aggregation — linking platelets to one another

blocks.label: Figure 8.1
blocks.caption: Scheme of thrombocytopoiesis

blocks.text: The main regulator of thrombocytopoiesis is **thrombopoietin**; it is synthesized mainly in the **liver** at a constant rate. Thrombopoietin binds to receptors on the membranes of platelets and megakaryocytes and is “captured” and destroyed by them. Therefore, when platelets decrease, free thrombopoietin increases and thrombocytopoiesis intensifies; when they increase, it weakens (feedback). IL-3, IL-6 and IL-11 also stimulate thrombocytopoiesis.

parts.text: **In liver cirrhosis** thrombopoietin synthesis decreases and the enlarged spleen (hypersplenism) “traps” many platelets — thrombocytopenia develops and a bleeding tendency appears. Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim) are used to treat immune thrombocytopenia.

blocks.title: Table 8.3. Functions of platelets
head: Function
Content
rows: They nourish endothelial cells and maintain the integrity of the vessel wall; every day ≈ 15% of platelets merge with the endothelium for this purpose. In thrombocytopenia the capillaries become fragile
Sticking to the damaged vessel wall
Sticking to one another to form a platelet plug
Release of the active substances in the granules
Concentrating plasma clotting factors on their surface (the phospholipid matrix — PF3) and speeding up coagulation
Compacting the clot and drawing the vessel edges together through contraction of thrombosthenin
Release of serotonin and thromboxane A~2~ to constrict the damaged vessel
PDGF and other growth factors speed up wound healing
Transport of serotonin and histamine; binding of immune complexes

blocks.text: **Vascular-platelet hemostasis** stops bleeding from microcirculatory vessels (diameter up to 100 µm, low pressure) within 1–3 minutes. It consists of the following stages:

items: **Reflex spasm** — contraction of the damaged vessel (a pain reflex, then the action of serotonin, thromboxane A~2~ and epinephrine released from platelets and endothelin from the endothelium).
**Adhesion** — subendothelial collagen is exposed; von Willebrand factor binds to collagen and links to the **GPIb** receptor of platelets.
**Activation and secretion** — platelets change shape (put out processes), release ADP, serotonin and Ca^2+^ and synthesize **thromboxane A~2~** (TxA~2~) from arachidonic acid.
**Reversible aggregation** — under the action of ADP and TxA~2~ the **GPIIb-IIIa** receptors are activated, and platelets stick to one another through fibrinogen “bridges”.
**Irreversible aggregation** — under the action of thrombin the platelet membranes break down and the platelets turn into a solid mass; a white (platelet) thrombus is formed.
**Retraction** — thrombosthenin contracts and compacts the thrombus.

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Functions of platelets in hemostasis

blocks.label: Figure 8.3
blocks.caption: Stages of vascular-platelet hemostasis: vascular spasm, platelet adhesion and aggregation (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: Normally the endothelium **prevents** platelets from sticking: it produces **prostacyclin (PGI~2~)** and **nitric oxide (NO)**, which inhibit aggregation and dilate the vessel. Platelet **thromboxane A~2~**, on the contrary, enhances aggregation and vasoconstriction. The balance of these two substances determines the state of the platelets.

**Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)** in a low dose (75–100 mg) irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase in platelets and stops the synthesis of thromboxane A~2~. Because platelets have no nucleus, the enzyme is not resynthesized — the effect lasts for the rest of the platelet's life (7–10 days). That is why aspirin is used to prevent myocardial infarction and stroke and is stopped 5–7 days before elective surgery. **Clopidogrel** blocks the P2Y~12~ (ADP) receptors.

parts.text: **Clotting time** and **bleeding time** are two different parameters. The bleeding time evaluates **vascular-platelet** hemostasis, while the clotting time (5–10 minutes by Lee–White) evaluates **coagulation** hemostasis. In hemophilia the bleeding time is normal but the clotting time is prolonged; in thrombocytopenia, the reverse — the bleeding time is prolonged and the clotting time is normal.

blocks.text: Experiment 1: counting platelets by the Fonio method

items: Wipe the skin of a finger with alcohol and place a drop of 14% magnesium sulfate solution on it (to prevent platelet aggregation).
Puncture the finger through this drop; the blood that emerges mixes with the magnesium sulfate.
Make a smear from the mixture, fix it and stain with Romanowsky–Giemsa stain.
Using the immersion objective, count 1000 erythrocytes and the platelets in the same fields of view.

Calculation: platelet count (× 10^9^/l) = erythrocyte count (× 10^12^/l) × the number of platelets per 1000 erythrocytes. **Example:** erythrocytes 4.5 × 10^12^/l, 55 platelets per 1000 erythrocytes → 4.5 × 55 = 247.5 × 10^9^/l.

parts.text: Today platelets are counted in automated hematology analyzers. In blood collected with EDTA, platelets sometimes aggregate and the analyzer shows them as low — **pseudothrombocytopenia**. If the result is doubtful, a smear should be examined or the sample recollected with citrate.

blocks.text: Experiment 2: determining the bleeding time by the Duke method

items: Wipe the earlobe with alcohol and let it dry.
Puncture it with a scarifier to a depth of 3–4 mm and start a stopwatch.
Every 30 seconds blot the emerging drop of blood with filter paper (without touching the skin).

Note the time when no new spot is left on the paper — the time when bleeding stopped. **Interpretation:** normally 2–4 minutes. Prolongation may be due to thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathy, von Willebrand disease or aspirin intake.

blocks.text: Experiment 3: testing capillary resistance (tourniquet test)

items: Put a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm and keep the pressure midway between systolic and diastolic pressure (≈ 90–100 mm Hg) for 5 minutes.
Remove the cuff and, after 5 minutes, draw a circle 2.5 cm in diameter below the elbow crease.
Count the petechiae inside the circle. **Interpretation:** up to 10 petechiae — normal; 10–20 — doubtful; more than 20 — capillary fragility (thrombocytopenia, vasculitis, vitamin C deficiency).

blocks.text: Experiment 4: evaluating clot retraction

items: Take 5 ml of venous blood into a graduated test tube and place it in a thermostat at 37 °C.
After 1 hour separate the clot and measure the volume of the expressed serum.
Retraction index = serum volume / blood volume × 100%. **Interpretation:** normally 44–65%. Retraction is impaired in thrombocytopenia and Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of hemostatic disorder in a hemorrhagic syndrome

items: Evaluate the type of bleeding: petechiae, ecchymoses, bleeding from mucous membranes (platelet type) or hemorrhages into joints and muscles (hematoma type — coagulation).
Evaluate the platelet count.
Compare the bleeding time and the clotting time.
Add the result of the tourniquet test.
If the bleeding time is prolonged and the clotting time is normal, conclude that vascular-platelet hemostasis is disturbed; if the reverse, that coagulation hemostasis is disturbed.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating antiplatelet therapy and surgical risk

items: Find out whether the patient takes aspirin or clopidogrel.
Take into account that the drug effect persists for the life span of the platelets (7–10 days).
Agree with the physician on when to stop the drug before elective surgery.
Check the bleeding time.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Two weeks after influenza an 8-year-old child developed small pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin (petechiae), bruises and nosebleeds. Platelets 18 × 10^9^/l, bleeding time 12 minutes, clotting time 7 minutes.
cases.ask: Which link of hemostasis is disturbed? Why did the bleeding time and clotting time change differently?
cases.answer: Vascular-platelet (primary) hemostasis is disturbed — severe thrombocytopenia (18 × 10^9^/l), probably immune thrombocytopenia (antibodies to platelets formed after a viral infection). Because there are few platelets, adhesion and aggregation are insufficient and no platelet plug forms — the bleeding time is prolonged. The angiotrophic function is also impaired and the capillaries become fragile — petechiae appear. The clotting time depends on the plasma clotting factors; since they are normal, the clotting time has not changed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with coronary heart disease takes 100 mg of aspirin daily. An elective tooth extraction has been scheduled. The dentist advised stopping aspirin 7 days beforehand.
cases.ask: How does aspirin act on platelets? Why should it be stopped a week before the operation?
cases.answer: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase in platelets and stops the formation of thromboxane A~2~ from arachidonic acid. Thromboxane A~2~ is a powerful inducer of platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; without it the platelet plug forms slowly and the bleeding time is prolonged. Because platelets have no nucleus, they cannot synthesize new enzyme — the effect lasts for the whole life of each platelet (7–10 days). After aspirin is stopped, most platelets are renewed within 5–7 days and hemostasis is restored. (In patients at high cardiac risk, the decision to stop aspirin is made by a cardiologist.)

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis has an enlarged spleen and platelets of 65 × 10^9^/l. He complains of bleeding gums.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanisms of the thrombocytopenia.
cases.answer: There are two main mechanisms. First, thrombopoietin is synthesized mainly in the liver; in cirrhosis its production decreases and the formation of platelets from megakaryocytes weakens. Second, the pressure in the portal vein rises and the spleen enlarges (splenomegaly, hypersplenism); normally 1/3 of the platelets are in the spleen, but in an enlarged spleen up to 80–90% are trapped and destroyed. In addition, in cirrhosis the liver also synthesizes fewer clotting factors, which further increases bleeding.

cards.back: A giant bone marrow cell; the source of platelets
Synthesized in the liver; regulator of thrombocytopoiesis
Aggregation and vasoconstriction; stopped by aspirin

topics.title: Hemostasis. Fibrinolysis

goals.text: To teach the student the hemostatic system and its components, the plasma clotting factors, the stages and mechanisms of coagulation hemostasis (blood coagulation), the anticoagulant system, and fibrinolysis and its regulation; to master determining the clotting time and evaluating the parameters of the coagulogram.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the components of the hemostatic system and the types of hemostasis;
the plasma clotting factors and their numbering;
the extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways and the stages of blood coagulation;
the significance of vitamin K;
the primary and secondary anticoagulants;
the stages of fibrinolysis, its activators and inhibitors;
the role of nervous and humoral factors in the regulation of hemostasis;
the main parameters of the coagulogram.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the clotting time by the Lee–White method;
determine the clotting time of capillary blood by the Sukharev method;
interpret the results of the prothrombin time, INR and APTT.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X** (and also the anticoagulants protein C and S). In the liver vitamin K γ-carboxylates these factors, giving them the ability to bind Ca^2+^. If vitamin K is deficient or its antagonists (warfarin) are taken, the factors are inactive and blood coagulation slows down.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Vitamin K-dependent factors: **“1972”** — **10, 9, 7, 2** (X, IX, VII, II).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The classical scheme of “extrinsic and intrinsic pathways” is convenient for understanding laboratory tests, but in the body they do not work separately. According to the modern **cell-based model**, coagulation **is initiated** by the tissue factor–VIIa complex (a small amount of thrombin), then thrombin **amplifies** the process by activating factors V, VIII and XI and the platelets, and a large amount of thrombin is formed on the surface of activated platelets (**propagation**). That is why factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding, whereas deficiency of factors VIII and IX causes severe bleeding (hemophilia).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Anticoagulants used in clinical practice: **heparin** (acts through antithrombin III; fast-acting, given intravenously or subcutaneously; monitored by the APTT), **warfarin** (a vitamin K antagonist; reduces the synthesis of II, VII, IX and X; its effect begins in 3–5 days; monitored by the INR), and new oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban — Xa inhibitors; dabigatran — a thrombin inhibitor). To prevent blood from clotting in a test tube, **sodium citrate** or EDTA (which bind Ca^2+^) are used.

blocks.text: **Hemostasis** is the system that stops bleeding when blood vessels are damaged and at the same time keeps the blood in a liquid state inside the vessels. The hemostatic system includes the **vessel wall** (endothelium), **blood cells** (mainly platelets), **plasma clotting factors**, **anticoagulants** and the **fibrinolytic system**.

rows: Large vessels; all vessels for a firm thrombus

blocks.text: The two mechanisms are closely interrelated: platelets concentrate clotting factors on their surface (PF3), and thrombin activates platelets.
According to the international nomenclature, clotting factors are designated by **Roman numerals** (in the order of their discovery). The active form is indicated by the letter “a” (for example, Xa).

blocks.text: (Factor VI was removed from the list because it turned out to be activated factor V.) In addition, **prekallikrein** (Fletcher factor) and **high-molecular-weight kininogen** (Fitzgerald factor) also take part in contact activation.

parts.text: **Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X** (and also the anticoagulants protein C and S). In the liver vitamin K γ-carboxylates these factors, giving them the ability to bind Ca^2+^. If vitamin K is deficient or its antagonists (warfarin) are taken, the factors are inactive and blood coagulation slows down.
Vitamin K-dependent factors: **“1972”** — **10, 9, 7, 2** (X, IX, VII, II).

blocks.text: Blood coagulation is an enzymatic **cascade**: each activated factor activates the next, and the signal is amplified at every step. In the classical scheme blood coagulation proceeds in three stages:

items: **Formation of prothrombinase** (the longest stage, 5–7 minutes) — through the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways.
**Formation of thrombin** — under the action of prothrombinase, prothrombin (II) is converted into thrombin (IIa) (2–5 seconds).
**Formation of fibrin** — thrombin cleaves peptides from fibrinogen and the fibrin monomers polymerize; factor XIIIa links them covalently, turning them into insoluble fibrin (2–5 seconds).

parts.text: The classical scheme of “extrinsic and intrinsic pathways” is convenient for understanding laboratory tests, but in the body they do not work separately. According to the modern **cell-based model**, coagulation **is initiated** by the tissue factor–VIIa complex (a small amount of thrombin), then thrombin **amplifies** the process by activating factors V, VIII and XI and the platelets, and a large amount of thrombin is formed on the surface of activated platelets (**propagation**). That is why factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding, whereas deficiency of factors VIII and IX causes severe bleeding (hemophilia).

blocks.text: Functions of thrombin

Thrombin is the central enzyme of hemostasis: it converts fibrinogen into fibrin; activates factors V, VIII, XI and XIII (positive feedback); strongly activates platelets; and, by binding to thrombomodulin on the endothelium, activates **protein C** (an anticoagulant effect — negative feedback).
Retraction

After the clot has formed, it is compacted by the contraction of platelet thrombosthenin and serum is squeezed out of it (**retraction**). This draws the edges of the vessel together and makes the thrombus firmer.

parts.text: **Hemophilia A** (factor VIII deficiency, 80–85%) and **hemophilia B** (factor IX deficiency) are X-linked recessive hereditary diseases; they occur mainly in boys, with mothers as carriers. Hemorrhages into the joints (hemarthrosis), hematomas in the muscles and prolonged bleeding after injury are typical. The APTT is prolonged, while the prothrombin time and bleeding time are normal. Treatment: concentrates of the missing factor.

blocks.text: Factors that prevent blood from clotting in the vessels: **the smooth, negatively charged surface of the endothelium**, with its glycocalyx and heparan sulfate; prostacyclin and NO; the speed of blood flow (which dilutes and carries away active factors); the liver, which clears activated factors; and **anticoagulants**.

rows: Inactivates thrombin, Xa, IXa, XIa and XIIa; heparin enhances its action 1000-fold

parts.text: **The Leiden mutation** (factor V Leiden) is the most common hereditary thrombophilia: the altered factor V is not broken down by activated protein C and the risk of venous thrombosis increases. Deficiency of **antithrombin III**, protein C and protein S also predisposes to thrombosis.

Anticoagulants used in clinical practice: **heparin** (acts through antithrombin III; fast-acting, given intravenously or subcutaneously; monitored by the APTT), **warfarin** (a vitamin K antagonist; reduces the synthesis of II, VII, IX and X; its effect begins in 3–5 days; monitored by the INR), and new oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban — Xa inhibitors; dabigatran — a thrombin inhibitor). To prevent blood from clotting in a test tube, **sodium citrate** or EDTA (which bind Ca^2+^) are used.

blocks.text: **Fibrinolysis** is the enzymatic dissolution of a fibrin clot; it restores the patency of the vessel. The main enzyme is **plasmin**, which is formed from inactive **plasminogen**.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: The fibrinolytic system

head: Stage
Process
rows: Tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) is released from the endothelium; urokinase is formed in the kidney; intrinsic route: XIIa, kallikrein
Plasminogen binds t-PA on the fibrin surface and is converted into plasmin (in the presence of fibrin the activity of t-PA increases 100-fold)

blocks.text: **Inhibitors of fibrinolysis:** PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor — from the endothelium and platelets), α~2~-antiplasmin (rapidly inactivates free plasmin), α~2~-macroglobulin.

parts.text: **Thrombolytic therapy** — in acute myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke and massive pulmonary embolism, t-PA (alteplase) or streptokinase is given to dissolve the thrombi; to be effective it must be used as soon as possible (within hours) after the onset of disease. An increase of **D-dimer** in the blood shows that fibrin is being formed and broken down in the body — it is used to rule out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Aminocaproic and tranexamic acids inhibit fibrinolysis and reduce bleeding.

items: The **sympathetic nervous system** and **adrenaline** (stress, pain, fear) accelerate blood coagulation (**stress enhancement of hemocoagulation**) — an evolutionary defense that reduces blood loss from wounds. At the same time fibrinolysis is also enhanced.
The **parasympathetic nervous system** slightly slows coagulation.
**Cortisol and vasopressin** accelerate coagulation; at the end of pregnancy the clotting factors increase (preparation for blood loss in childbirth).
The cerebral cortex influences the rate of coagulation through conditioned reflexes.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining the venous blood clotting time by the Lee–White method

items: Take 1 ml of venous blood into a clean, dry glass test tube and start the stopwatch.
Place the tube in a 37 °C water bath.
Tilt the tube by 45° every 30 seconds.

Note the time when the blood stops flowing (the clot does not fall out when the tube is inverted). **Interpretation:** normally 5–10 minutes. Prolongation — clotting factor deficiency (hemophilia), heparin therapy; shortening — hypercoagulation.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: determining the capillary blood clotting time by the Sukharev method

items: Wipe away the first drop from the finger with cotton wool.
Draw blood to a height of 25–30 mm into a Panchenkov capillary (or Sukharev capillary) and start the stopwatch.
Tilt the capillary right and left every 30 seconds.

The time when the blood column stops moving is the start of clotting; the appearance of fibrin threads in the blood is the end of clotting. **Interpretation:** start of clotting 30 seconds – 2 minutes, end 3–5 minutes.

skills.title: Skill: determining the level of the disorder from the coagulogram

items: Evaluate the platelet count and bleeding time (primary hemostasis).
Evaluate the PT (INR): only PT prolonged — factor VII deficiency, warfarin effect, early vitamin K deficiency.
Evaluate the APTT: only APTT prolonged — deficiency of factors VIII, IX, XI (hemophilia), heparin effect.
If both are prolonged — deficiency of common pathway factors (X, V, II, fibrinogen), liver diseases, DIC syndrome.
Additionally evaluate the state of fibrinolysis by D-dimer and fibrinogen.

skills.title: Skill: monitoring anticoagulant therapy

items: Find out which drug the patient is taking.
For warfarin, monitor the INR (target usually 2.0–3.0).
For (unfractionated) heparin, monitor the APTT (it should be prolonged 1.5–2.5 times above normal).
Watch for signs of bleeding; in warfarin overdose the antidote is vitamin K, for heparin — protamine sulfate.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a fall, a 6-year-old boy has a swollen, painful knee joint (bleeding into the joint). Earlier he had prolonged bleeding when his teeth erupted. His mother's brother has the same disease. Platelets 250 × 10^9^/l, bleeding time 3 minutes, prothrombin time 13 s, APTT 78 s.
cases.ask: What disease can be suspected? Explain the laboratory results. How is the disease inherited?
cases.answer: Hemophilia (probably A — factor VIII deficiency). The platelet count and bleeding time are normal — vascular-platelet hemostasis is not disturbed. The prothrombin time is normal — the extrinsic pathway is preserved. The APTT is sharply prolonged — deficiency of intrinsic pathway factors (VIII or IX). Bleeding into joints and muscles (hematoma type) is typical of a coagulation hemostasis disorder. The disease is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner: the mother is a carrier and boys are affected (the mother's brother is also ill). The exact type is determined by measuring factor VIII and IX activity.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with a mechanical heart valve prosthesis takes warfarin. After starting an antibiotic his gums began to bleed and the INR rose to 5.8.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of action of warfarin. Why did the INR rise, and what help is given?
cases.answer: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist: in the liver it stops the γ-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X); they cannot bind Ca^2+^ and become inactive — blood coagulation slows down. The intestinal microflora synthesizes part of vitamin K~2~; because the antibiotic suppressed the microflora (and affected warfarin metabolism), vitamin K decreased and the effect of warfarin increased — the INR exceeded the therapeutic range (2.5–3.5) and bleeding appeared. Help: stop or reduce the warfarin dose, give vitamin K, and in severe bleeding — fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a long bus journey a 45-year-old patient's left calf became swollen and painful. Then sudden shortness of breath and chest pain appeared. Blood D-dimer 3.2 µg/ml.
cases.ask: What complication can be suspected? Explain the mechanism of the rise in D-dimer. What are the principles of treatment?
cases.answer: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. During prolonged immobile sitting the blood flow in the leg veins slows (part of Virchow's triad) and a thrombus forms; a fragment of it breaks off and lodges in the pulmonary artery. The body's fibrinolytic system tries to break down the fibrin of the formed thrombus: plasmin splits covalently cross-linked fibrin, forming D-dimer — its rise shows that fibrin is being formed and broken down in the body. Treatment: anticoagulants (heparin, then oral anticoagulants) — to stop new thrombus formation; in massive embolism, thrombolytics (t-PA) — to dissolve the thrombus.

cards.back: The system that stops bleeding and keeps blood liquid
Fibrinogen → fibrin; activates V, VIII, XI, XIII
Factor VIII / IX deficiency; APTT prolonged
Breaks down fibrin; formed from plasminogen
Fibrin degradation product; marker of thrombosis

topics.title: Blood groups. Rh factor. Principles of blood transfusion

goals.text: To teach the student the doctrine of erythrocyte antigen systems, the ABO blood groups, agglutinogens and agglutinins, the Rh system and Rh incompatibility, the rules of blood transfusion and compatibility tests; to master determining the blood group and Rh factor with standard sera and monoclonal reagents (tsoliclones).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the history of the discovery of blood groups (K. Landsteiner, J. Jansky);
the agglutinogens and agglutinins of the ABO system and the description of the four blood groups;
the mechanism of the agglutination reaction;
the inheritance of the ABO system;
the Rh system, Rh-positive and Rh-negative blood;
Rh conflict and the mechanism of hemolytic disease of the newborn;
the rules for transfusion of blood and its components and the compatibility tests;
transfusion complications.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the blood group with standard sera and tsoliclones;
determine the Rh factor;
explain the procedure for the individual (ABO) and Rh compatibility tests and the biological test.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The ABO rule: **“Whatever is on the erythrocyte, its enemy is absent from the plasma”**. Group A — A antigen and anti-B; group B — B antigen and anti-A; group 0 — no antigen, both antibodies; group AB — both antigens, no antibodies.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Today **only group-specific blood (ABO- and Rh-compatible) is transfused**. The concept of the “universal donor” is outdated: group 0 (I) blood contains high-titer α and β agglutinins and, when transfused in large amounts, can hemolyze the recipient's erythrocytes. Only in emergencies, when group-specific blood is unavailable, may up to 500 ml of 0 (I) Rh^-^ **packed red cells** (without plasma) be transfused. In addition, whole blood is rarely transfused: the patient receives only the needed **component** (packed red cells, platelet concentrate, fresh frozen plasma).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Tsoliclones** (monoclonal antibodies) are the main reagents in current practice: compared with standard sera they are more accurate, have a high titer and do not depend on donor blood. Tsoliclones directly detect the **agglutinogen** (the antigen on the erythrocyte).

blocks.text: A **blood group** is the set of hereditarily determined antigens (**agglutinogens**) on the erythrocyte membrane. Blood groups were discovered in 1901 by the Austrian scientist **K. Landsteiner** (three groups; Nobel Prize in 1930); the fourth group was described in 1907 by the Czech scientist **J. Jansky**. Today more than 400 antigens and more than 40 systems are known on erythrocytes (ABO, Rh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd, MNSs and others), but in clinical practice the most important are the **ABO** and **Rhesus (Rh)** systems.

In the ABO system erythrocytes may carry two kinds of agglutinogen — **A** and **B**; the plasma contains natural antibodies against them — **agglutinins α (anti-A)** and **β (anti-B)**. When an agglutinogen and agglutinin of the same name (A and α, B and β) meet, the erythrocytes stick together — the **agglutination** reaction occurs, followed by hemolysis. Therefore one person's blood never contains an agglutinogen and agglutinin of the same name.

blocks.caption: The ABO system: agglutinogens and agglutinins, the agglutination reaction and a scheme of blood group compatibility (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Agglutinins (IgM class) appear 2–8 months after birth and reach their highest titer at 5–10 years of age; they form in response to similar antigens of intestinal bacteria and food (which is why they are called “natural” antibodies). Agglutinogen A has subtypes **A~1~** and **A~2~** (A~2~ is weaker).
Inheritance of the ABO groups
The ABO groups are inherited through a single gene on chromosome 9 with three alleles (**I^A^, I^B^, i**). I^A^ and I^B^ are **codominant**, i is recessive.
