parts.text: The ABO rule: **“Whatever is on the erythrocyte, its enemy is absent from the plasma”**. Group A — A antigen and anti-B; group B — B antigen and anti-A; group 0 — no antigen, both antibodies; group AB — both antigens, no antibodies.

blocks.text: The **Rh factor (Rh)** was identified in 1940 by K. Landsteiner and A. Wiener on the erythrocytes of rhesus monkeys. The Rh system has several antigens (D, C, c, E, e); the most immunogenic is the **D antigen**. People who carry it are **Rh-positive (Rh^+^)** — ≈ 85% of Europeans; the rest are **Rh-negative (Rh^-^)** — ≈ 15% (Rh^-^ is less common among Asian peoples).

**Difference from the ABO system:** the Rh system has **no natural antibodies**. Anti-D antibodies (IgG class) in an Rh^-^ person form only after **sensitization** by Rh^+^ erythrocytes: when Rh^+^ blood is transfused or when an Rh^-^ woman is pregnant with an Rh^+^ fetus.
Rh conflict

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Rh conflict and the development of hemolytic disease of the newborn

parts.text: **Hemolytic disease of the newborn** — anti-D IgG antibodies formed in an Rh^-^ mother cross the placenta and destroy the erythrocytes of the Rh^+^ fetus: anemia, jaundice (bilirubin is toxic to the brain — “kernicterus”), and in severe cases hydrops fetalis. Usually the first pregnancy passes without conflict (antibodies form during childbirth); the risk increases in subsequent pregnancies. **Prevention:** an Rh^-^ woman is given **anti-D immunoglobulin** at 28 weeks of pregnancy and within 72 hours after the birth of an Rh^+^ child — it removes the fetal erythrocytes that entered the mother's blood before the immune system “notices” them. Conflict by the ABO system is also possible (most often the mother is group 0 and the child A or B), but it is usually milder.

blocks.text: Formerly **Ottenberg's rule** was applied in blood transfusion: “the donor's erythrocytes must not be agglutinated by the recipient's plasma” (the donor plasma was assumed to be diluted in the recipient's blood). Accordingly, group 0 (I) was called the “universal donor” and AB (IV) the “universal recipient”.

parts.text: Today **only group-specific blood (ABO- and Rh-compatible) is transfused**. The concept of the “universal donor” is outdated: group 0 (I) blood contains high-titer α and β agglutinins and, when transfused in large amounts, can hemolyze the recipient's erythrocytes. Only in emergencies, when group-specific blood is unavailable, may up to 500 ml of 0 (I) Rh^-^ **packed red cells** (without plasma) be transfused. In addition, whole blood is rarely transfused: the patient receives only the needed **component** (packed red cells, platelet concentrate, fresh frozen plasma).

blocks.title: Table 10.3. ABO compatibility in transfusion of blood components (basic principle)
head: Recipient group
Packed red cells
Fresh frozen plasma

blocks.text: For plasma the compatibility is reversed: plasma contains agglutinins, so AB (IV) plasma is “universal” (it has no agglutinins).
Mandatory tests before blood transfusion

items: Determine (confirm) the ABO and Rh group of the recipient's and donor's blood.
**Individual ABO compatibility test**: recipient serum + donor erythrocytes (10 : 1) at room temperature for 5 minutes; if there is no agglutination — compatible.
**Rh compatibility test** (with polyglucin or gelatin, at 37 °C).

**Biological test**: 10–15 ml of blood is given as a stream and the patient is observed for 3 minutes; this is repeated three times. If signs of incompatibility appear (pain in the lower back and chest, facial flushing, shortness of breath, tachycardia, a fall in blood pressure), the transfusion is stopped immediately.

parts.text: **Hemotransfusion shock** — when incompatible blood is transfused, acute intravascular hemolysis develops: pain in the lower back, chills, a fall in blood pressure, hemoglobinuria (“black urine”), acute kidney failure and DIC syndrome. The main cause of these complications is organizational errors (mixing up the patient or the bag), so before every transfusion the documents and the blood group are checked again.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining the blood group with standard sera

Place 1 drop (≈ 0.1 ml) of the corresponding standard serum in each place (it is recommended to use two batches of serum for each group).
Next to each serum place a drop of finger-prick blood 10 times smaller (≈ 0.01 ml) (serum : blood = 10 : 1).
Mix each drop with a separate clean glass rod.
Rock the plate gently and observe for 5 minutes; add a drop of saline to the drops in which agglutination appears (to exclude pseudo-agglutination).
Evaluate the result using the table.

skills.title: Skill: algorithm for preparing a blood transfusion

items: Establish the indication for transfusion and decide which component is needed.
Re-determine the patient's ABO and Rh group.

Confirm the donor blood group with tsoliclones.
Perform the individual ABO and Rh compatibility tests.
Carry out the biological test (3 times 10–15 ml, at 3-minute intervals).
During and after the transfusion observe the patient's condition, blood pressure, pulse, temperature and urine color; record all data in the documents.

quiz.q: Which group is considered “universal” for transfusion of fresh frozen plasma?

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An Rh^-^ woman is in her third pregnancy. Her first child was born healthy; the second pregnancy ended in abortion, and no prophylaxis was given. Her husband is Rh^+^. At 30 weeks of pregnancy a high titer of anti-D antibodies was found in her blood.
cases.ask: What condition is developing? Explain its mechanism and the danger to the fetus. What prophylaxis should have been given?
cases.answer: Rh conflict (Rh sensitization). During the first birth and the abortion, Rh^+^ fetal erythrocytes entered the mother's blood; the mother has no natural anti-D antibodies, but after sensitization IgG-class anti-D antibodies were formed. IgG can cross the placenta and hemolyzes the Rh^+^ fetal erythrocytes — hemolytic disease of the newborn: anemia, jaundice, toxic effect of bilirubin on the brain, and in severe cases hydrops fetalis and fetal death. Prophylaxis: anti-D immunoglobulin should have been given within 72 hours after each birth (of an Rh^+^ child), abortion or miscarriage, and at 28 weeks of pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After an accident, a patient who has lost a lot of blood needs emergency surgery. The patient's blood group is A (II) Rh^+^. The blood bank has run out of group A (II) blood, but 0 (I) Rh^-^ packed red cells are available.
cases.ask: Can group 0 (I) packed red cells be transfused in this situation? Under what conditions? Why are packed red cells chosen rather than whole blood?
cases.answer: In an emergency, when group-specific blood is unavailable, up to 500 ml of 0 (I) Rh^-^ packed red cells may be transfused. Group 0 (I) erythrocytes have no A or B agglutinogens, so the recipient's β agglutinins do not agglutinate them. Packed red cells rather than whole blood are chosen because 0 (I) plasma contains high-titer α and β agglutinins — in large volumes they can hemolyze the recipient's A erythrocytes. In any case, individual compatibility and biological tests are performed; group-specific blood is used as soon as possible.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student determined a blood group with standard sera: agglutination appeared in all three sera — 0 (I), A (II), B (III).
cases.ask: What is the blood group? How should the result be confirmed?
cases.answer: If agglutination occurs in all three sera, the erythrocytes carry A and B agglutinogens — group AB (IV). However, this result may also be due to nonspecific (pseudo-) agglutination (for example, rouleaux formation or serum contamination). To confirm it, a control test with standard serum of group AB (IV) is performed: it has no agglutinins, so there should be no agglutination. Saline is also added to the agglutinated drops, and the result is confirmed with tsoliclones.

topics.title: The hemodynamic function of the heart. Physiological properties of cardiac muscle. Methods of studying cardiac activity

goals.text: To teach the student the pumping function of the heart, the physiological properties of cardiac muscle (automaticity, excitability, conductivity, contractility) and their specific features, the phases of the cardiac cycle, the main parameters of cardiac activity, the electrical, mechanical and acoustic phenomena of the heart and the methods of studying them (ECG, auscultation, phonocardiography, echocardiography).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure and hemodynamic function of the heart;
the conduction system of the heart and the gradient of automaticity;
the ionic mechanisms of the action potential in typical and atypical cardiomyocytes;
the excitability and refractoriness of cardiac muscle and the mechanism of the extrasystole and compensatory pause;
the phases of the cardiac cycle and their duration;
parameters such as stroke and minute volume, ejection fraction and cardiac index;
the ECG leads, waves and intervals and their meaning;
the heart sounds and their origin.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform the Stannius ligature experiment on the frog heart and explain the gradient of automaticity;
record an extrasystole and compensatory pause in the frog heart;
record an ECG in a human and determine its main parameters;
auscultate the heart sounds.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The 4 properties of cardiac muscle: **automaticity, excitability, conductivity, contractility**. Its main differences from skeletal muscle: automaticity, a functional syncytium (“all or nothing”), a long refractory period (no tetanus), and the need for extracellular Ca^2+^ for contraction.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When the heart rate increases, it is mainly **diastole that shortens**; systole changes less. At a very high heart rate (more than 180 /min) the ventricles do not fill adequately and the coronary vessels (which receive blood mainly in diastole) are poorly supplied with blood — the efficiency of the heart decreases.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the ECG as “**P — the atria (they fire first); QRS — the ventricles; T — recovery (repolarization)**”. HR = 60 / RR (s).

sections.title: 1. The hemodynamic function of the heart

blocks.text: The heart is the central organ of the circulatory system, a rhythmically working **pump**. By ejecting blood into the vessels it creates a pressure gradient in them and ensures the continuous movement of blood through the systemic and pulmonary circulations. The heart consists of two pumps: the **left heart** (systemic circulation, high pressure) and the **right heart** (pulmonary circulation, low pressure). Both ventricles contract simultaneously and eject the same volume of blood.

The heart **valves** ensure one-way movement of blood: the **atrioventricular (cuspid) valves** (bicuspid — mitral — on the left, tricuspid on the right) between the atria and ventricles; the **semilunar valves** (aortic and pulmonary) between the ventricles and arteries. The valves open and close passively under the action of the pressure difference.
Cardiac muscle consists of two kinds of cells: **working (typical) cardiomyocytes**, which provide contraction, and **atypical cells of the conduction system**, which generate and conduct impulses.
Automaticity

**Automaticity** is the ability of the heart to be rhythmically excited and to contract under the influence of impulses generated within the heart itself. Automaticity is **myogenic** in nature: an isolated heart works for hours in a nutrient solution (the Langendorff method). The source of automaticity is the **conduction system**.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: The conduction system of the heart and the gradient of automaticity

blocks.text: **Gradient of automaticity** (W. Gaskell): the level of automaticity is high in the upper parts of the conduction system and decreases further down. Normally the rhythm is set by the fastest impulse generator, the **sinoatrial node** (**sinus rhythm**); the other centers are subordinate to its rhythm (latent pacemakers).

**Action potential in pacemaker cells:** the resting potential is not stable (maximum diastolic potential −60 mV). In phase 4 **slow diastolic depolarization** occurs, due to the “funny” **I~f~ current** (Na^+^ entry), T-type Ca^2+^ channels and a decrease in K^+^ efflux. On reaching threshold (−40 mV), depolarization proceeds slowly through **L-type Ca^2+^ channels**; then repolarization occurs with K^+^ efflux.

Phases of the action potential in **working cardiomyocytes** (duration 250–300 ms): **0** — rapid depolarization (fast Na^+^ channels); **1** — early rapid repolarization (K^+^ and Cl^-^); **2** — **plateau** (Ca^2+^ enters through L-channels, balanced by K^+^ efflux); **3** — rapid final repolarization (K^+^ leaves); **4** — rest (−90 mV).

blocks.label: Figure 11.2
blocks.caption: Action potentials of a pacemaker cell (A) and a ventricular cardiomyocyte (B) (drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

blocks.text: Excitability and refractoriness
Because of the plateau phase, the **absolute refractory period** of cardiomyocytes is very long (≈ 0.27 s) — it covers almost all of systole. Therefore:

items: cardiac muscle **cannot contract tetanically** — relaxation and filling with blood are ensured;
excitation does not circulate in a ring (re-entry) and return.

blocks.label: Figure 11.3
blocks.caption: Cardiomyocyte action potential, contraction curve and phases of excitability (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: An **extrasystole** is a premature contraction. If an extra stimulus arrives in **diastole** (after relative refractoriness has ended), the heart contracts prematurely. After a ventricular extrasystole a **compensatory pause** is observed: the next impulse from the sinus node falls into the refractory period of the ventricle and gets no response, and the ventricle waits for the following impulse.
Conductivity

Excitation spreads in the heart through **gap junctions between cardiomyocytes** (nexuses, intercalated discs) — the heart works as a **functional syncytium** and obeys the “all or nothing” law. Conduction velocity: in the atria ≈ 1 m/s, in the AV node 0.02–0.05 m/s, in the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers 2–4 m/s, in the ventricular myocardium 0.3–1 m/s. The **AV delay** (≈ 0.1 s) ensures that the atria finish contracting and the ventricles fill with blood.
Contractility

For contraction of cardiac muscle part of the Ca^2+^ enters **from outside the cell** (in the plateau phase) and triggers the release of additional Ca^2+^ from the SR (**calcium-induced calcium release**). Therefore the force of contraction depends on extracellular Ca^2+^. The force of contraction is regulated by the **Frank–Starling law** (the more the myocardium is stretched, the stronger it contracts) and by neurohumoral factors (topic 12).

parts.text: The 4 properties of cardiac muscle: **automaticity, excitability, conductivity, contractility**. Its main differences from skeletal muscle: automaticity, a functional syncytium (“all or nothing”), a long refractory period (no tetanus), and the need for extracellular Ca^2+^ for contraction.

blocks.text: The **cardiac cycle** is the period consisting of one contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole). At a heart rate of 75 /min the cycle lasts **0.8 s**: atrial systole 0.1 s, atrial diastole 0.7 s; ventricular systole 0.33 s, ventricular diastole 0.47 s. The period when the atria and ventricles are relaxed at the same time is the **general pause** (≈ 0.4 s).

blocks.text: Electrocardiography (ECG)
The **ECG** is the curve of electrical potentials generated during cardiac excitation, recorded from the body surface. It was first recorded by W. Einthoven (1903).

Other methods

items: **Echocardiography (ultrasound)** — evaluation of the heart chambers, wall thickness, valves and ejection fraction; Doppler — speed and direction of blood flow.
**Palpation of the apex beat** — normally in the 5th intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line.
**Sphygmography, polycardiography** — recording of the arterial pulse and the phase structure of the cycle.
**Holter monitoring** — recording the ECG over 24 hours.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: Stannius ligatures (frog heart)

items: Immobilize the frog, open the chest and expose the heart. Count the heart rate for 1 minute.

**Ligature I** — tie a thread at the boundary between the sinus venosus and the right atrium. The sinus venosus continues to contract at its previous rhythm; the atria and ventricle stop temporarily and then begin to contract at a slower rhythm.
**Ligature II** — tie it at the boundary between the atria and the ventricle (the AV node region). The ventricle contracts at an even slower rhythm.

**Ligature III** — tie it at the lower third of the ventricle. The apex of the heart does not contract (it has no center of automaticity). **Result and analysis:** the experiment proves the **gradient of automaticity**: the main center of automaticity is in the sinus venosus (in humans, in the sinoatrial node), the lower centers have slower rhythms, and the apex of the heart has no automaticity.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: extrasystole and compensatory pause (frog heart)

items: Connect the apex of the heart to a kymograph lever with a serrefine and record the contractions.
Stimulate the ventricle with a single electrical stimulus in different phases of systole and then in diastole.
Compare the results on the kymogram.

blocks.text: **Result and analysis:** a stimulus given in systole causes no response (absolute refractoriness). A stimulus given in diastole causes a premature contraction — an **extrasystole**; it is followed by a prolonged **compensatory pause**, because the next impulse from the sinus venosus falls into the refractory period of the ventricle after the extrasystole.
Exercise 3: recording an ECG in a human

items: Lay the subject on a couch; wipe the electrode sites with alcohol and apply contact gel.
Place the limb electrodes: red — right arm, yellow — left arm, green — left leg, black (ground) — right leg.
Place the chest electrodes at points V~1~–V~6~.
Check the calibration signal (1 mV = 10 mm) and the paper speed (50 or 25 mm/s); record the ECG in 12 leads.
In standard lead II measure the amplitude of the waves and the duration of the intervals.
Determine the rhythm (sinus rhythm — a P wave before every QRS, equal RR intervals) and the HR (60 / RR).

blocks.text: Exercise 4: auscultation of the heart sounds

items: Listen to the subject in a sitting or lying position.
Place the stethoscope successively at the auscultation points.
At the same time palpate the carotid pulse and identify the first sound (simultaneous with the pulse).
Compare the first and second sounds by pitch, duration and pauses: the first sound is louder at the apex, the second at the base of the heart.

skills.title: Skill: determining the HR and main intervals on the ECG

items: Determine the paper speed (at 50 mm/s 1 mm = 0.02 s; at 25 mm/s 1 mm = 0.04 s).
Measure the distance between two adjacent R waves and calculate RR (s).
HR = 60 / RR.
Measure PQ, QRS and QT and compare them with the norm.
Check the criteria of sinus rhythm: the P wave is positive (in lead II) and precedes each QRS, PQ is constant, RR intervals are equal.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the minute volume and ejection fraction

items: Stroke volume (SV) = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume.
Ejection fraction = SV / end-diastolic volume × 100%.
Minute volume = SV × HR.
Compare the results with the norm and evaluate cardiac activity.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 70-year-old patient has attacks of dizziness and fainting. On the ECG the P waves are regular (70 /min), while the QRS complexes are independent of them, widened, at a rate of 35 /min.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Under the influence of which pacemaker are the ventricles contracting? Explain from the standpoint of the gradient of automaticity.
cases.answer: Complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block. The sinus node excites the atria at a normal rhythm (70 /min), but the impulses do not pass through the AV node to the ventricles. The ventricles contract under the influence of lower pacemakers — the bundle of His or Purkinje fibers; according to the gradient of automaticity their rate is low (30–40 /min or less), and because excitation does not spread through the conduction system in the usual way, the QRS is widened. The slow rhythm reduces the minute volume — the brain receives too little blood and fainting occurs (Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attacks). Treatment — an artificial pacemaker (electrocardiostimulator).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An athlete at rest has a HR of 50 /min and a stroke volume of 100 ml. His non-athlete peer has a HR of 75 /min and a stroke volume of 66 ml.
cases.ask: Calculate the minute volume of both. Explain the difference.
cases.answer: Athlete: 100 ml × 50 = 5000 ml/min (5 l/min). Non-athlete: 66 ml × 75 ≈ 4950 ml/min (≈ 5 l/min). At rest the minute volume is almost the same, because the body's needs are the same. In the athlete regular training has enlarged the left ventricular cavity and strengthened the myocardium (physiological hypertrophy) — the stroke volume is large; therefore the same minute volume is achieved with fewer contractions (bradycardia; vagal tone is also high). This makes the work of the heart economical and provides a large reserve during physical load.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student stimulated a frog heart with an electric current during the diastole phase. A premature contraction followed by a long pause appeared on the kymogram. A stimulus given during systole caused no response.
cases.ask: Explain the results.
cases.answer: During systole cardiac muscle is in the absolute refractory period (long because of the plateau phase), so the stimulus caused no response. In diastole excitability had been restored, and the stimulus caused a premature excitation and contraction — an extrasystole. After it, the next impulse from the sinus venosus coincided with the refractory period of the ventricle following the extrasystole and got no response; the ventricle waited for the next sinus impulse — a compensatory pause arose.

topics.title: Regulation of cardiac activity

goals.text: To teach the student the intracardiac (myogenic and intracardiac nervous system) and extracardiac (nervous and humoral) mechanisms of regulating cardiac activity, the types of influence of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves on the heart, cardiac reflexes, and the effects of hormones and ions; to master studying reflex changes in cardiac activity in humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the levels of regulation of cardiac activity;
the heterometric (Frank–Starling) and homeometric (Anrep, Bowditch) regulatory mechanisms;
the intracardiac peripheral reflexes;
the types (chrono-, ino-, dromo-, bathmo-, tonotropic) and mechanisms of the influence of the vagus and sympathetic nerves on the heart;
the tone of the cardiac nerve centers;
the intrinsic and conjugate reflexes of the heart (Goltz, Dagnini–Aschner, Bainbridge, baroreceptor reflexes);
the effects of hormones, mediators and ions on cardiac activity.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: stimulate the vagus nerve in the frog and demonstrate its effect on the heart;
perform the Dagnini–Aschner oculocardiac reflex and the orthostatic test in humans;

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The Frank–Starling law **equalizes the work of the two ventricles**: if the right ventricle ejects more blood, more blood comes from the lungs to the left ventricle, and it too contracts more strongly. As a result the blood volumes in the systemic and pulmonary circulations remain balanced. **“The more the heart receives, the more it ejects.”**

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Five effects — **“CIDBT”**: **C**hronotropic (rate), **I**notropic (force), **D**romotropic (conduction), **B**athmotropic (excitability), **T**onotropic (tone). Sympathetic — all “+”, vagus — all “−”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Potassium** stops the heart in **diastole**, and **calcium** in **systole**. That is why cardioplegic solutions (used to stop the heart temporarily during heart surgery) are high in potassium.

sections.title: 1. Levels of regulation of cardiac activity

blocks.text: Cardiac activity constantly changes according to the body's needs: if the minute volume is 5 l at rest, during heavy physical work it reaches 25–30 l/min. This is achieved by changing the **heart rate** and the **stroke volume**.

blocks.title: Table 12.1. Mechanisms of regulation of cardiac activity
head: Level
Mechanism
Example
rows: Reflexes of the intracardiac (metasympathetic) nervous system
Autonomic nervous system (vagus and sympathetic nerves), central reflexes

blocks.text: Heterometric regulation (Frank–Starling law)

**Frank–Starling law:** the more the myocardium is stretched in diastole (the more blood enters the ventricle), the more strongly it contracts in the next systole. Mechanism — the sarcomere approaches its optimal length (2.2 µm), the area of interaction between actin and myosin filaments increases, and the Ca^2+^ sensitivity of troponin C rises.

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: Frank–Starling curves and their shift under inotropic influences (drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

parts.text: The Frank–Starling law **equalizes the work of the two ventricles**: if the right ventricle ejects more blood, more blood comes from the lungs to the left ventricle, and it too contracts more strongly. As a result the blood volumes in the systemic and pulmonary circulations remain balanced. **“The more the heart receives, the more it ejects.”**

blocks.text: Homeometric regulation
Change in the force of contraction without a change in the initial length of the myocardial fiber:

items: **Anrep phenomenon** — when the pressure (resistance) in the aorta rises, the force of ventricular contraction increases gradually and the stroke volume is maintained.
**Bowditch “staircase”** (rate dependence) — when the contraction frequency increases, the force of each contraction increases step by step (accumulation of Ca^2+^ inside the cell).

blocks.text: Peripheral intracardiac reflexes

Inside the heart there is an **intracardiac (metasympathetic) nervous system** consisting of afferent, intercalary and efferent neurons; it carries out reflexes even without the central nervous system. For example, when the right atrium is stretched, contraction of the left ventricle increases (when the atrium is underfilled — the reverse). These reflexes are preserved even after heart transplantation.

blocks.label: Figure 12.2
blocks.caption: The intracardiac nervous system: adrenergic and cholinergic efferent neurons, an afferent neuron and myocardial stretch receptors (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The heart has **dual autonomic innervation**.
Parasympathetic (vagus nerve) influence

The preganglionic neurons are located in the **medulla oblongata** (the dorsal nucleus of the vagus and the nucleus ambiguus); the postganglionic neurons are inside the heart. The mediator is **acetylcholine**, the receptors are **M~2~-cholinergic receptors**. The right vagus acts mainly on the sinus node, the left on the AV node.

**Experiment of I. and E. Cyon (1866)**: stimulation of the vagus nerve in the frog slows and stops the heart. With prolonged stimulation the heart begins to contract again — **“escape” from the vagal effect** (lower pacemakers become active).

**Mechanism:** acetylcholine activates a G protein via M~2~ receptors and **opens K^+^ channels (I~K-ACh~)** — the membrane hyperpolarizes; it inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cAMP — the I~f~ and Ca^2+^ currents decrease; slow diastolic depolarization slows down.
Sympathetic influence

The preganglionic neurons are in the lateral horns of the upper thoracic segments of the spinal cord (Th~1~–Th~5~); the postganglionic neurons are in the cervical and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia (stellate ganglion). The mediator is **noradrenaline**, the receptors are **β~1~-adrenergic receptors**. Sympathetic nerves go to all parts of the heart, including the ventricles.

**Mechanism:** β~1~ receptors → G~s~ protein → adenylate cyclase → **cAMP** ↑ → protein kinase A → L-type Ca^2+^ channels and I~f~ channels are phosphorylated, and the return of Ca^2+^ to the SR is accelerated (phospholamban).

parts.text: Five effects — **“CIDBT”**: **C**hronotropic (rate), **I**notropic (force), **D**romotropic (conduction), **B**athmotropic (excitability), **T**onotropic (tone). Sympathetic — all “+”, vagus — all “−”.

blocks.text: Tone of the cardiac centers

At rest the vagal centers have constant (tonic) activity — **vagal tone**. Therefore the intrinsic rate of the sinus node (≈ 100 /min — its “own rhythm”) is normally slowed to 60–80 /min. When the vagus is cut or atropine (an M-cholinergic blocker) is given, the heart rate increases. Athletes have high vagal tone — bradycardia at rest. In newborns vagal tone is low — HR 120–140 /min.
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia

HR increases on inspiration and decreases on expiration. The reason is that during inspiration the lung stretch receptors and the activity of the respiratory center reduce the tone of the vagal center. This is a **physiological** condition and is well expressed in young people.

blocks.text: **Intrinsic reflexes** start from the receptors of the cardiovascular system itself; **conjugate reflexes** from the receptors of other systems.

parts.text: An attack of **paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia** can sometimes be stopped by **vagal maneuvers**: the Valsalva maneuver (straining against a closed glottis), immersing the face in cold water, carotid sinus massage. They raise vagal tone and slow AV conduction. Pressure on the eyeballs (Dagnini–Aschner) is no longer recommended because of the risk of eye injury. In **carotid sinus hypersensitivity** a tight collar or a sharp turn of the head can cause bradycardia and fainting.

blocks.text: Influence of the cerebral cortex

Cardiac activity changes under the influence of emotions (fear, anger, excitement) and conditioned reflexes (an increase in HR in an athlete before the start). The hypothalamus and limbic system control the sympathetic and parasympathetic centers.

parts.text: **Potassium** stops the heart in **diastole**, and **calcium** in **systole**. That is why cardioplegic solutions (used to stop the heart temporarily during heart surgery) are high in potassium.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: effect of vagus nerve stimulation on the frog heart

items: Immobilize the frog, expose the heart and isolate the vagosympathetic trunk in the neck.
Record the heart contractions with a kymograph.
Stimulate the vagosympathetic trunk with a rhythmic electric current (weak and strong) for 10–20 s.

Continue the stimulation and observe the “escape from the vagal effect”. **Result and analysis:** with weak stimulation the heart rate slows and the force of contraction decreases (negative chrono- and inotropic effects); with strong stimulation the heart stops in diastole. With prolonged stimulation the heart begins to contract again (escape). After stimulation is stopped, the rhythm is restored.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: the Goltz reflex (in the frog)

items: Open the frog's abdominal cavity and count the heart contractions.
Tap the abdominal organs (stomach, intestine) lightly several times with the handle of forceps.

Record the change in HR. **Result and analysis:** the heart slows or stops temporarily. Afferent impulses from the abdominal organs (celiac plexus) go to the medulla oblongata and excite the vagal center. After the vagus nerve is cut or atropine is given, the reflex disappears.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: the Dagnini–Aschner oculocardiac reflex in humans

items: The subject rests lying down for 5 minutes; the pulse is counted for 15 s and converted to 1 minute.
With the eyes closed, light pressure is applied to the eyeballs from both sides for 20–30 s (the pressure should not cause pain).

The pulse is counted again during the pressure (the last 15 s). **Interpretation:** a decrease in pulse of 4–12 /min — normal; more than 12 — high parasympathetic tone (vagotonia); no decrease or an increase — predominance of sympathetic tone (sympathicotonia).

blocks.text: Exercise 4: the orthostatic test

items: The subject's pulse is counted while lying for 5 minutes.
The subject stands up quickly; the pulse is counted after 1 minute.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** an increase in pulse of 10–16 /min — normal (in the upright position venous return decreases, impulses from the baroreceptors decrease and the sympathetic influence increases). An increase of more than 20 /min — high sympathetic tone or low orthostatic stability.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating autonomic tone

items: Determine the HR and blood pressure at rest.
Perform the Dagnini–Aschner reflex.
Perform the orthostatic test.
Evaluate respiratory sinus arrhythmia (the difference in HR during deep inspiration and expiration).
Summarize the results and determine the type of autonomic tone (eutonia, vagotonia, sympathicotonia).

skills.title: Skill: detecting respiratory sinus arrhythmia on the ECG

items: Record the ECG with deep inspiration and expiration.
Measure the RR intervals during inspiration and expiration.
If the RR difference is more than 0.15 s and the P waves are unchanged — respiratory sinus arrhythmia (physiological).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After heart transplantation, a patient's resting HR is 95–100 /min. During physical load the HR increases slowly, but the stroke volume increases well.
cases.ask: Why is the HR high at rest? By what mechanisms does the heart increase its work during exercise?
cases.answer: The transplanted heart is denervated — the vagus and sympathetic nerves do not reach it. Normally at rest vagal tone acts on the heart and slows the intrinsic rhythm of the sinus node (≈ 100 /min) to 60–80 /min; after denervation this influence is absent, so the HR is close to the intrinsic rhythm. During exercise the increase in cardiac work is provided by intracardiac mechanisms (the Frank–Starling law: venous return increases, the ventricles are stretched more and contract more strongly; intracardiac reflexes) and by humoral factors (adrenaline released from the adrenal glands, which acts more slowly).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 20-year-old young man was examined because his heart was “beating fast”: at rest HR 72 /min, 88 on deep inspiration, 64 /min on expiration. On the ECG every complex is preceded by a P wave of unchanged shape.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism. Is it a pathology?
cases.answer: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a physiological condition, especially well expressed in young people. During inspiration the stretch receptors of the lungs and the activity of the respiratory center lower the tone of the vagal centers; in addition, venous return increases and the Bainbridge reflex is triggered — HR increases. During expiration vagal tone is restored and HR decreases. The rhythm comes from the sinus node (the P waves are identical) — it is not a pathology.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A nurse mistakenly gave a rapid intravenous injection of potassium chloride solution to a patient with kidney failure. The patient developed bradycardia, followed by cardiac arrest.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the effect of potassium on the heart. In which phase does the heart stop?
cases.answer: When blood K^+^ rises sharply, the resting potential of the cardiomyocyte membrane decreases (depolarization) and the fast Na^+^ channels are inactivated — excitability and conduction decrease and action potentials can no longer be generated. Excess K^+^ also slows diastolic depolarization in the sinus node. As a result, bradycardia, conduction blocks and cardiac arrest in diastole develop. That is why potassium preparations are given intravenously only slowly, diluted and under ECG monitoring.

topics.title: Arterial blood pressure and peripheral pulse. Microcirculation. Blood flow in the veins. Regulation of vascular tone

goals.text: To teach the student the basic laws of hemodynamics, the functional groups of blood vessels, arterial blood pressure and the factors that determine it, the arterial pulse and its characteristics, blood flow and exchange of substances in the microcirculatory bed, the mechanisms of blood flow in the veins, and the local, nervous and humoral regulation of vascular tone; to master measuring arterial pressure by the Korotkov method and examining the pulse.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the basic laws of hemodynamics (Poiseuille's law, continuity of flow);
the functional classification of blood vessels;
the types and norms of arterial pressure and the factors that determine it;
the characteristics of the arterial pulse and the sphygmogram;
the structure of the microcirculatory bed, filtration and reabsorption in capillaries (Starling equilibrium);
the factors that ensure venous return;
the basal, myogenic, nervous and humoral regulation of vascular tone;
the vasomotor center and the reflex regulation of blood pressure.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: measure arterial pressure by the Korotkov method;
calculate the pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure;
examine the pulse on the radial artery and evaluate its characteristics.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The criteria for arterial hypertension differ between international guidelines. According to WHO and European guidelines, an office blood pressure of **140/90 mm Hg or higher** is arterial hypertension; 120–139/80–89 is high-normal or elevated pressure. In the American (ACC/AHA, 2017) guidelines the threshold for hypertension is 130/80. Arterial hypotension is below 90/60.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: By the speed of regulation of arterial pressure there are three groups of mechanisms: **fast** (seconds — baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes), **intermediate** (minutes–hours — the renin–angiotensin system, fluid shifts in capillaries, stress relaxation of vessels) and **long-term** (days — regulation of blood volume through the kidneys: aldosterone, vasopressin, natriuretic peptide, pressure natriuresis).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Measurement errors: a cuff that is too narrow (falsely high pressure in obese people), an arm positioned below heart level (reads high), deflating too fast (incorrect diastolic pressure), smoking or drinking coffee before measurement. **“Auscultatory gap”** — in some people (in hypertension) the sounds disappear temporarily after the systolic pressure and then reappear; therefore the cuff is inflated sufficiently under palpation control.

blocks.text: The main cause of blood movement in the vessels is the **pressure difference** between the initial (aorta) and final (venae cavae) parts of the vascular system. Blood flow (Q) is directly proportional to the pressure difference (ΔP) and inversely proportional to vascular resistance (R): **Q = ΔP / R**.

According to **Poiseuille's law**, resistance R = 8ηl / πr^4^ — it is directly proportional to viscosity (η) and vessel length (l) and inversely proportional to **the fourth power of the radius**. Therefore, if the radius of a vessel decreases 2 times, the resistance increases 16 times. By changing the radius of its vessels the body regulates blood flow very effectively.

**Continuity of flow:** the same volume of blood passes through every cross-section of the vascular system per unit time. The **linear velocity** is inversely proportional to the **total cross-sectional area** of the vessels: 50 cm/s in the aorta, 0.05 cm/s in the capillaries (total cross-section 500–800 times larger), and it rises again in the veins (20–25 cm/s in the venae cavae). The circulation time (one complete circuit) is ≈ 20–23 s.

parts.text: The criteria for arterial hypertension differ between international guidelines. According to WHO and European guidelines, an office blood pressure of **140/90 mm Hg or higher** is arterial hypertension; 120–139/80–89 is high-normal or elevated pressure. In the American (ACC/AHA, 2017) guidelines the threshold for hypertension is 130/80. Arterial hypotension is below 90/60.

blocks.text: Factors that determine arterial pressure:

items: **Minute volume (cardiac work)** — affects mainly systolic pressure.
**Total peripheral resistance** (arteriolar tone) — affects mainly diastolic pressure.
**Circulating blood volume**.
**Blood viscosity**.

**Elasticity of the walls of the large arteries** — in the elderly elasticity decreases, systolic pressure rises and the pulse pressure widens. **Mean arterial pressure = minute volume × total peripheral resistance.**

blocks.text: **Physiological changes:** it increases with age; rises during physical work, excitement and pain; falls during sleep; changes slightly on standing; fluctuates over the day (circadian rhythm).
Methods of measuring arterial pressure

items: **Direct (invasive)** method — a cannula is inserted into an artery and connected to a manometer (S. Hales, 1733); today it is used as invasive monitoring in intensive care.

**Indirect (non-invasive)** methods: the **Riva-Rocci** palpatory method (systolic pressure only) and **N.S. Korotkov's auscultatory method** (1905) — systolic and diastolic pressure; also the oscillometric method (automatic blood pressure monitors).

blocks.label: Figure 13.3
blocks.caption: Measuring arterial pressure by the Korotkov method (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 13.4
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the Korotkov sounds: A — cuff pressure above systolic, the artery is compressed; B — pressure between systolic and diastolic, blood flows turbulently (sounds are heard); C — pressure below diastolic, laminar flow (sounds disappear) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **arterial pulse** is the rhythmic oscillation of the arterial walls caused by the ejection of blood into the aorta during cardiac systole. The pulse wave travels much faster than the blood itself: 4–6 m/s in the aorta, 8–12 m/s in the peripheral arteries (the velocity increases when the wall stiffens).

The **sphygmogram** is a graphic recording of the pulse. It shows the **anacrotic limb** (the ascending part — ejection of blood), the **catacrotic limb** (the descending part) and on it the **dicrotic wave** (closure of the aortic valves and the rebound of blood from them; preceded by the incisura).

parts.text: **Pulse deficit** — the heart rate (on auscultation) is greater than the pulse rate; in atrial fibrillation some contractions are so weak that the pulse wave does not reach the periphery. A difference in the pulse between the two arms may indicate narrowing of the aorta or its branches.

blocks.text: The **microcirculatory bed** is a functional unit consisting of arterioles, metarterioles, precapillary sphincters, capillaries, venules and arteriovenous anastomoses. At rest only 25–35% of capillaries are open; in a working organ their number increases.

The **capillary** wall consists of a single layer of endothelium; its length is 0.5–1 mm, its diameter 5–10 µm, and blood stays in it for 1–2 s. Types of capillaries: **somatic** (continuous — muscle, skin, lung; in the CNS the blood–brain barrier), **visceral** (fenestrated — renal glomeruli, intestine, endocrine glands) and **sinusoidal** (discontinuous — liver, spleen, bone marrow).
**Mechanisms of exchange of substances:** diffusion (the main one — O~2~, CO~2~, glucose), filtration and reabsorption (water and substances dissolved in it), micropinocytosis (large molecules).
Starling equilibrium

Fluid movement across the capillary wall is determined by the balance of four forces: the **hydrostatic pressure** in the capillary (pushes fluid out), the **oncotic pressure** of plasma (holds fluid in), and the hydrostatic and oncotic pressures of tissue fluid.

blocks.label: Figure 13.5
blocks.caption: Filtration and reabsorption in a capillary (Starling equilibrium)

blocks.text: At the arterial end of the capillary the hydrostatic pressure exceeds the oncotic pressure — **filtration**; at the venous end the hydrostatic pressure has fallen — **reabsorption**. Filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption; the excess fluid and proteins return to the blood through the **lymphatic vessels** (2–4 l of lymph per day).

parts.text: Edema develops when the Starling equilibrium is disturbed: **increased hydrostatic pressure** (heart failure, venous thrombosis), **decreased oncotic pressure** (hypoalbuminemia — liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, starvation), **increased capillary permeability** (inflammation, allergy — histamine) and **impaired lymph flow** (lymphostasis).

blocks.text: Pressure in the veins is low (15–20 mm Hg in venules, 0–5 mm Hg in the venae cavae, negative during inspiration). Factors that ensure venous return:

items: **The residual force of the heart** (vis a tergo — the force pushing from behind) — the main factor.
**The suction effect of the chest** — during inspiration the negative pressure in the thoracic cavity increases, dilating the venae cavae and drawing in blood.
**Movement of the diaphragm** — during inspiration intra-abdominal pressure rises and squeezes blood out of the abdominal veins.
**The skeletal muscle “pump”** — when muscles contract the veins are compressed, and the valves allow blood to flow only toward the heart.
**Venous valves** (especially in the leg veins).
**The suction effect of the heart** — during ventricular systole the downward displacement of the AV boundary dilates the atria.
**Pulsation of the arteries** — compresses the adjacent veins.

parts.text: During prolonged standing and immobility blood pools in the leg veins; with valve insufficiency **varicose disease** develops. During prolonged bed rest and travel venous flow slows and the risk of **deep vein thrombosis** increases — therefore early mobilization, leg exercises and compression stockings are recommended.

blocks.text: **Vascular tone** is the constant state of partial contraction of vascular smooth muscle. It consists of two parts:

items: **Basal (myogenic) tone** — independent of innervation; the automaticity of smooth muscle and its response to stretch (the **Bayliss effect**: when pressure rises and the vessel is stretched, it contracts). This is the basis of **autoregulation**: in the kidney, brain and heart blood flow is kept constant even when pressure changes within 60–160 mm Hg.
**Neurohumoral tone** — under the influence of autonomic nerves and humoral factors.

blocks.text: Local (metabolic) regulation

In working tissue a decrease in O~2~, an increase in CO~2~, H^+^, lactate, adenosine and K^+^, and a rise in temperature dilate the arterioles — **working (functional) hyperemia**. The endothelium produces **nitric oxide (NO)**, prostacyclin (vasodilators) and **endothelin** (a powerful vasoconstrictor). NO is released continuously under the action of the shear stress of blood flow.
Nervous regulation

items: **Vasoconstrictors** — mainly **sympathetic** adrenergic fibers (noradrenaline, α~1~-adrenergic receptors). They are tonically active: at rest they send impulses at 1–3 Hz. If the stimulation frequency increases, the vessels constrict; if it decreases, they dilate.

**Vasodilators** — parasympathetic fibers (in the tongue, salivary glands, genital organs — acetylcholine, NO), sympathetic cholinergic fibers (in skeletal muscles), β~2~-adrenergic receptors (in the vessels of skeletal muscle, heart and liver under the action of adrenaline), the axon reflex. The **vasomotor (circulatory) center** is in the **medulla oblongata** (F.V. Ovsyannikov, 1871): it has **pressor** (ventrolateral, exciting sympathetic neurons) and **depressor** parts. It is constantly tonically active; after transection above the medulla oblongata the pressure hardly changes, after transection below it the pressure falls sharply. Higher centers — the hypothalamus, limbic system and cerebral cortex (changes in pressure during emotions).

blocks.text: Reflex regulation of pressure

items: **Depressor reflexes** — from the **baroreceptors** of the aortic arch and carotid sinus (topic 12): when pressure rises, sympathetic tone decreases and the vagus is activated — pressure falls. The baroreceptors provide short-term (“second-to-second”) regulation.
**Pressor reflexes** — from the carotid and aortic **chemoreceptors** (hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis) — pressure rises.

parts.text: By the speed of regulation of arterial pressure there are three groups of mechanisms: **fast** (seconds — baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes), **intermediate** (minutes–hours — the renin–angiotensin system, fluid shifts in capillaries, stress relaxation of vessels) and **long-term** (days — regulation of blood volume through the kidneys: aldosterone, vasopressin, natriuretic peptide, pressure natriuresis).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: measuring arterial pressure by the Korotkov method

items: The subject sits quietly for 5 minutes; the arm is placed on the table at heart level, palm up.
The cuff is wrapped around the upper arm 2–2.5 cm above the elbow crease, loosely enough for one finger to fit under it.
The pulsation of the brachial artery is found in the cubital fossa and the stethoscope is placed there.
After the radial pulse disappears, the cuff is inflated a further 20–30 mm Hg.
The air is released slowly (2–3 mm Hg/s); the pressure at which the **first clear sound** appears is the **systolic pressure**.
The pressure at which the sounds **disappear completely** is the **diastolic pressure**.

The measurement is repeated after 2–3 minutes and the mean value is recorded; the first time, it is measured on both arms. **Calculate:** pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic; mean dynamic pressure = diastolic + pulse pressure / 3.

parts.text: Measurement errors: a cuff that is too narrow (falsely high pressure in obese people), an arm positioned below heart level (reads high), deflating too fast (incorrect diastolic pressure), smoking or drinking coffee before measurement. **“Auscultatory gap”** — in some people (in hypertension) the sounds disappear temporarily after the systolic pressure and then reappear; therefore the cuff is inflated sufficiently under palpation control.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: examining the pulse

items: Palpate the radial artery of both arms in the region of the styloid process of the radius with three fingers (index, middle, ring).
Compare the pulse on the two sides.
Count for 30 s and multiply by 2 (if the rhythm is irregular — a full 1 minute).
Evaluate its rhythm, tension and filling.
Also examine the pulse on the carotid, femoral and dorsalis pedis arteries.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: effect of physical load on arterial pressure and pulse

items: Measure the pressure and pulse at rest.
The subject does 20 squats in 30 s (Martinet–Kushelevsky test).

Measure the pressure and pulse again immediately and every minute (for 3–5 minutes). **Interpretation:** normally the pulse increases by 50–75%, systolic pressure rises by 15–30 mm Hg, diastolic pressure does not change or falls slightly (vessels dilate in the working muscles), and the parameters recover within 3 minutes.

skills.title: Skill: calculating hemodynamic parameters

items: Take the systolic and diastolic pressures.
Calculate the pulse pressure (normal 40–50).
Calculate the mean dynamic pressure.
If the minute volume is known, find the total peripheral resistance: R = mean pressure / minute volume.
Evaluate the results: a large pulse pressure — aortic valve insufficiency or reduced arterial elasticity in the elderly; a small one — aortic stenosis, blood loss.

items: Has the capillary hydrostatic pressure changed (venous stasis, heart failure)?
Has the plasma oncotic pressure changed (albumin level)?
Has capillary permeability increased (inflammation, allergy)?
Is lymph flow impaired?
Identify the predominant factor and name the type of edema.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 72-year-old patient has an arterial pressure of 170/70 mm Hg. In youth his pressure was 120/80.
cases.ask: Calculate the pulse pressure and mean pressure. How can the rise in systolic and fall in diastolic pressure in old age be explained?
cases.answer: Pulse pressure = 170 − 70 = 100 mm Hg (normal 40–50). Mean pressure = 70 + 100/3 ≈ 103 mm Hg. In old age the walls of the aorta and large arteries lose their elastic fibers and stiffen (atherosclerosis, collagen accumulation). The shock-absorbing function weakens: in systole the stiff aorta dilates little — systolic pressure rises sharply; in diastole the aorta cannot recoil and push the blood onward — diastolic pressure falls. This condition is called isolated systolic hypertension and increases cardiovascular risk.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient in the surgical ward has heart failure: edema of the legs and distended neck veins. Blood albumin is normal.
cases.ask: What is the main mechanism of the edema? Explain it on the basis of the Starling forces.
cases.answer: In heart failure the heart cannot pump the venous blood adequately — blood accumulates in the veins and venous pressure rises (distended neck veins). The increased venous pressure raises the hydrostatic pressure at the venous end of the capillaries; reabsorption decreases and filtration increases. The oncotic pressure is normal (albumin is normal), so the main factor is the increase in hydrostatic pressure (congestive edema). Because of gravity, the edema appears in the lower parts of the body — the legs. In addition, sodium and water retention in the kidneys (RAAS activation) increases blood volume and aggravates the edema.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After standing motionless in formation for a long time, a student's vision darkened and he lost consciousness. After he was laid down and his legs were raised, he quickly came round.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the fainting. Why did raising the legs help?
cases.answer: During prolonged motionless standing, gravity causes blood to pool in the leg veins; the skeletal muscle pump does not work — venous return decreases. According to the Frank–Starling mechanism, ventricular filling and stroke volume decrease and arterial pressure falls. When compensation by the baroreceptor reflex (sympathetic activation) is insufficient, cerebral blood flow decreases and fainting (orthostatic syncope) develops. In the horizontal position with the legs raised, venous return is restored, stroke volume and cerebral blood flow increase — the patient quickly comes round.

Filtration at the arterial end, reabsorption at the venous end

topics.title: Study of metabolism and energy exchange. Thermoregulation. Physiology of the endocrine glands. The hypothalamo-pituitary system

goals.text: To teach the student energy exchange in the body and the methods of measuring it, basal metabolism and daily energy expenditure, the constancy of body temperature and the mechanisms of thermoregulation, the general principles of the endocrine system, the classification of hormones and their mechanisms of action, and the structure and hormones of the hypothalamo-pituitary system; to master calculating basal metabolism and measuring body temperature.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the methods of direct and indirect calorimetry of energy exchange, the respiratory quotient and the caloric equivalent of oxygen;
the concept of basal metabolism, its magnitude and the factors affecting it;
the specific dynamic action of food and daily energy expenditure;
the norms of body temperature and its daily variations;
the mechanisms of chemical and physical thermoregulation and the thermoregulatory center;
the general properties, chemical classification and mechanisms of action of hormones;
the regulation of endocrine gland activity and the feedback principle;
the hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary and their functions.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the predicted basal metabolism using tables and formulas;
calculate the deviation of basal metabolism from the norm using Read's formula;
calculate energy expenditure from the results of the Douglas–Haldane method;
measure body temperature and evaluate the temperature curve.

summary.text: When the ambient temperature is **higher** than body temperature, heat cannot be lost by radiation, convection or conduction — the body gains heat. The only route then is **evaporation of sweat**. If the air humidity is high, evaporation becomes difficult and the risk of heatstroke increases.

summary.text: Hormones of the adenohypophysis — **“FLAT PiG”**: **F**SH, **L**H, **A**CTH, **T**SH, **P**rolactin, (**i**), **G**rowth hormone (GH).

sections.title: 1. Energy exchange and methods of measuring it

blocks.text: Metabolism in the body consists of two processes: **assimilation (anabolism)** — synthesis of complex substances, which consumes energy; and **dissimilation (catabolism)** — breakdown of substances, which releases energy (topic 21). Ultimately all the energy that enters the body is converted into **heat** (apart from external mechanical work). Therefore energy expenditure can be estimated from the amount of heat released.

blocks.title: Table 14.1. Methods of determining energy expenditure
head: Method
Essence
Features
rows: The person stays in a special insulated chamber (Atwater–Benedict calorimeter); the heat released is measured by the warming of water flowing through the chamber wall
Most accurate, but complex and expensive
The O~2~ consumed and the CO~2~ released are measured (Douglas–Haldane method: the expired air is collected in a Douglas bag)
Calculated from the respiratory quotient and caloric equivalent
Only the O~2~ consumed is measured (spirometabolograph); the respiratory quotient is taken as 0.85
Tables and formulas based on sex, age, height and weight (Harris–Benedict)

blocks.text: The **respiratory quotient (RQ)** is the ratio of the volume of CO~2~ released to the volume of O~2~ consumed. It depends on which substance is being oxidized.

blocks.title: Table 14.2. Respiratory quotient and caloric equivalent of oxygen
head: Substance oxidized
RQ
Caloric equivalent of 1 l O~2~, kcal
Energy value of 1 g of substance, kcal (kJ)

blocks.text: The **caloric equivalent of oxygen** is the amount of heat released when 1 l of O~2~ is consumed. Energy expenditure = volume of O~2~ consumed × caloric equivalent.

parts.text: The RQ can exceed 1.0 — **when fat is synthesized from carbohydrates** (in obesity) or in hyperventilation (when CO~2~ is “washed out”), and after heavy physical work. An RQ below 0.7 — in prolonged starvation and diabetes mellitus (fats and ketone bodies are oxidized).

blocks.text: **Basal metabolism** is the minimum energy expenditure of the body needed for life (cellular metabolism, breathing, the work of the heart, kidneys and CNS, maintenance of body temperature). It is determined **under standard conditions** : in the morning, after waking, on an empty stomach (12–14 hours after the last meal), at physical and mental rest, lying down, at a **“comfort temperature”** (18–20 °C).

**Magnitude:** on average **1 kcal/kg/hour** (4.19 kJ); in a 70 kg man ≈ **1700 kcal/day** (7100 kJ), 10% less in women. Relative to body surface area: ≈ 40 kcal/m^2^/hour. **Rubner's surface law**: in warm-blooded animals of different mass, basal metabolism is proportional not to body mass but to **body surface area**.

**Factors affecting basal metabolism:** sex (higher in men), age (relatively high in children, low in the elderly), height and weight, **thyroid hormones** (the strongest — it increases by up to 50–100% in thyrotoxicosis and decreases by 30–40% in hypothyroidism), temperature (in fever it increases by ≈ 10–13% for every 1 °C), season, nutrition, pregnancy.

parts.text: **Read's formula** gives an approximate estimate of the deviation of basal metabolism from the norm (%) from the pulse and arterial pressure: BM (%) = 0.75 × (pulse + pulse pressure × 0.74) − 72. Up to ± 10% is normal. This formula was used for screening thyroid function; today, for an accurate diagnosis, TSH and thyroid hormones are measured in the blood.

blocks.text: Specific dynamic action of food

After food intake energy expenditure increases (for digestion, absorption and metabolic transformations). With protein intake it reaches 30%, with carbohydrates 4–6%, with fats 2–4%; with mixed food — 10–15%.
Daily energy expenditure
Daily energy expenditure = basal metabolism + specific dynamic action + work increment (physical activity).

blocks.title: Table 14.3. Daily energy expenditure by work intensity (approximate)
head: Group
Occupations
Daily expenditure, kcal

blocks.text: The **physical activity ratio** is the ratio of daily expenditure to basal metabolism (1.4 in group I; 2.4 in group V).

Humans are **homeothermic (warm-blooded)** organisms: the core body temperature is kept relatively constant regardless of the ambient temperature. The body **core** (internal organs, brain — ≈ 37 °C) and **shell** (skin, subcutaneous tissue, limbs — variable temperature) are distinguished.

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Temperature of the body core and shell in a cold (left) and hot (right) environment (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 14.4. Normal values of body temperature
head: Site of measurement
Norm, °C

blocks.text: **Daily variations** of 0.5–1 °C: lowest at 3–6 a.m., highest in the evening at 4–7 p.m. In women after ovulation (under the influence of progesterone) the basal temperature rises by 0.3–0.6 °C.
Chemical thermoregulation (heat production)
The main sources of heat are the **skeletal muscles** (20% at rest, up to 90% during work), the **liver** and other internal organs. In the cold, heat production increases:

items: **Shivering thermogenesis** — involuntary rhythmic contraction of skeletal muscles; it increases heat production 3–5 times.

**Non-shivering thermogenesis** — intensification of metabolism under the influence of the sympathetic nervous system, noradrenaline and thyroid hormones; **brown adipose tissue** (abundant in infants; in its mitochondria thermogenin — the UCP-1 protein — uncouples oxidation from phosphorylation and converts energy directly into heat).

blocks.text: Physical thermoregulation (heat loss)

blocks.title: Table 14.5. Routes of heat loss (at rest, at comfort temperature)
head: Route
Essence
Share
rows: By infrared rays to colder objects
Evaporation of water from sweat and the respiratory tract (0.58 kcal per 1 g of water evaporated)
Through currents of air or water in contact with the skin

parts.text: When the ambient temperature is **higher** than body temperature, heat cannot be lost by radiation, convection or conduction — the body gains heat. The only route then is **evaporation of sweat**. If the air humidity is high, evaporation becomes difficult and the risk of heatstroke increases.

blocks.text: Heat loss is regulated through the **tone of skin vessels** (they constrict in the cold and dilate in the heat — the skin blood supply varies from 0.2 to 3 l/min), sweating, breathing, clothing and behavior (changing posture).
The thermoregulatory center

The **thermoregulatory center** is in the **hypothalamus**: its anterior part (the preoptic area) is mainly the center of heat loss; the posterior part is the center of heat production and conservation. The hypothalamus has a temperature “set point”; the center receives information from peripheral (skin) and central (hypothalamus, blood) thermoreceptors and keeps body temperature at this point.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Mechanisms of thermoregulation

parts.text: **Fever** — under the action of pyrogens (bacterial toxins, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) prostaglandin E~2~ is formed in the hypothalamus and the “set point” shifts upward; the body raises its temperature to the new level (chills, shivering). Antipyretics (paracetamol, ibuprofen) reduce prostaglandin synthesis. **Hyperthermia (heatstroke)**, in contrast, results from insufficient heat loss with an unchanged “set point” — antipyretics are ineffective and external cooling is needed.

sections.title: 4. General physiology of the endocrine system

blocks.text: The **endocrine system** is the set of endocrine glands and hormone-producing cells. **Hormones** are biologically active substances formed in specialized cells, released into the blood and acting at a distance on target cells.

blocks.label: Figure 14.3
blocks.caption: The endocrine glands and their hormones (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **General properties of hormones:** high biological activity (they act in very small concentrations — 10^-12^–10^-6^ mol/l), specificity of action (only on target cells that have receptors), action at a distance, and a relatively short life span (inactivation in the liver and kidneys).

blocks.title: Table 14.6. Chemical classification and mechanisms of action of hormones
head: Group
Examples
Receptor location
Mechanism
rows: Insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones, PTH
Second messengers (cAMP, Ca^2+^, IP~3~, DAG) or tyrosine kinase — rapid action
Cortisol, aldosterone, estrogens, testosterone, calcitriol (vitamin D)
The hormone–receptor complex binds to DNA and alters protein synthesis

blocks.text: The activity of the endocrine glands is regulated mainly by the principle of **negative feedback**; the nervous system (directly or through the hypothalamus) and blood metabolites (glucose, Ca^2+^) also have an influence.

**Methods of studying endocrine gland function:** removal of the gland (extirpation) followed by hormone administration; transplantation of the gland; determination of hormones and their metabolites in blood and urine (radioimmune and enzyme immunoassay methods); functional (stimulation and suppression) tests; radioisotope methods; imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI).

The **hypothalamus** is part of the diencephalon; it is the highest center of autonomic, endocrine and behavioral functions. It converts nervous signals into hormonal signals. The **pituitary gland** is a small gland (0.5–0.6 g) located in the fossa of the sella turcica, the “conductor of the endocrine system”.

blocks.label: Figure 14.4
blocks.caption: The hypothalamo-pituitary system and negative feedback

blocks.text: **Neurosecretory cells** of the hypothalamus:

items: **Parvocellular nuclei** produce liberins and statins; they reach the adenohypophysis through the **hypophyseal portal blood system** and regulate the secretion of its hormones.
**Magnocellular nuclei** (supraoptic and paraventricular) synthesize vasopressin and oxytocin; they are transported along the axons to the **neurohypophysis** and released from there into the blood.

parts.text: **GH excess**: in childhood (growth plates not yet closed) — **gigantism**; in adults — **acromegaly** (enlargement of the hands and feet, nose, lower jaw and tongue). **GH deficiency** in childhood — **pituitary dwarfism** (short stature with preserved body proportions and intelligence). **ADH deficiency** — **diabetes insipidus**: 5–20 l of dilute urine per day, intense thirst.
Hormones of the adenohypophysis — **“FLAT PiG”**: **F**SH, **L**H, **A**CTH, **T**SH, **P**rolactin, (**i**), **G**rowth hormone (GH).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining the predicted basal metabolism using tables and a formula

items: Determine the subject's sex, age, height (cm) and weight (kg).

Calculate the predicted basal metabolism by the Harris–Benedict formula: for men 66.5 + 13.75 × weight + 5.0 × height − 6.76 × age (kcal/day); for women 655.1 + 9.56 × weight + 1.85 × height − 4.68 × age.
Compare the result with the approximate estimate of 1 kcal/kg/hour.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: determining the deviation of basal metabolism by Read's formula

items: In the morning, on an empty stomach, after 10–15 minutes of lying rest, the subject's pulse and arterial pressure are measured three times; the lowest values are taken.
Calculate the pulse pressure.
BM (%) = 0.75 × (pulse + pulse pressure × 0.74) − 72.

**Interpretation:** ± 10% — normal; more than 10% — basal metabolism is increased (thyrotoxicosis suspected). **Example:** pulse 70, pressure 120/80 (pulse pressure 40) → 0.75 × (70 + 29.6) − 72 = 2.7% — normal.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: calculating energy expenditure from the results of the Douglas–Haldane method

items: Use the given data: for example, 40 l of air expired in 5 minutes, containing 16.6% O~2~ and 3.6% CO~2~ (atmospheric air contains 20.94% O~2~ and 0.03% CO~2~).
RQ = 1.43 / 1.74 = 0.82; from the table the caloric equivalent is ≈ 4.83 kcal.
Energy expenditure in 5 minutes: 1.74 × 4.83 = 8.4 kcal; in 1 hour: 8.4 × 12 = 101 kcal.

blocks.text: Exercise 4: measuring body temperature

items: Place the thermometer (if it is a mercury thermometer, shake it down below 35 °C) in the dry axilla; hold it with the arm pressed against the body for 10 minutes (with an electronic thermometer, until the signal).
Record the result; measure in the morning and evening and determine the daily difference.
Measure the sublingual temperature and compare it with the axillary temperature.

skills.title: Skill: calculating daily energy requirement

items: Calculate basal metabolism (Harris–Benedict).
Choose the physical activity ratio according to the work group (1.4–2.4).
Daily requirement = basal metabolism × ratio.
Compare the result with calorie intake and evaluate the energy balance.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating a disorder of the hypothalamo-pituitary system (scheme)

items: Determine the level of the peripheral hormone (for example, T~4~).
Determine the corresponding tropic hormone (TSH).
If the peripheral hormone is low and the tropic hormone high — the gland itself is damaged (primary insufficiency).
If both are low — the pituitary or hypothalamus is damaged (secondary or tertiary).
Explain the result according to the feedback principle.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 30-year-old woman complains of weight loss, sweating, heat intolerance, palpitations and hand tremor. Pulse 110 /min, arterial pressure 140/70 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Calculate the deviation of basal metabolism by Read's formula. Which gland's function may be disturbed?
cases.answer: Pulse pressure = 140 − 70 = 70. BM = 0.75 × (110 + 70 × 0.74) − 72 = 0.75 × 161.8 − 72 ≈ 49%. Basal metabolism is increased by ≈ 50% above the norm. The clinical signs (weight loss, sweating, heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor, wide pulse pressure) are typical of thyroid hyperfunction — thyrotoxicosis. Thyroid hormones increase oxidative processes and Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase activity in almost all cells, increase heat production and raise the sensitivity of β-adrenergic receptors. The diagnosis is confirmed by blood TSH (decreased) and free T~4~, T~3~ (increased).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In summer, on a day with an air temperature of 40 °C and high humidity, a worker who had been working in the field for a long time suddenly developed headache, nausea and was close to losing consciousness. Body temperature 40.5 °C, skin dry and hot.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism. Why does paracetamol not help in this condition?
cases.answer: Heatstroke (hyperthermia). When the ambient temperature is higher than body temperature, heat loss by radiation, convection and conduction is impossible; the only route is evaporation of sweat. Because the humidity was high, evaporation was ineffective; prolonged sweating led to dehydration and salt loss, and eventually sweating stopped (dry skin). Muscle work produced a lot of heat. The heat accumulated and the temperature rose. In this condition the “set point” in the hypothalamus has not changed — the thermoregulatory mechanisms are simply insufficient; therefore antipyretics, which reduce prostaglandin synthesis, are ineffective. Help: move the person to shade and a cool place, external cooling (wet sheets, ice, a fan), and restoration of fluids and salts.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An 8-year-old child is 105 cm tall (the norm for his age ≈ 127 cm), with normal body proportions and age-appropriate mental development. Blood GH and IGF-1 are low.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the mechanism of action of GH.
cases.answer: Pituitary dwarfism (somatotropin deficiency). GH is formed in the adenohypophysis and stimulates the synthesis of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1, somatomedin) mainly in the liver and other tissues; IGF-1 stimulates the proliferation of chondrocytes in the growth plates of bones and ensures longitudinal growth. GH also enhances protein synthesis. In deficiency growth slows, but because thyroid hormones are normal, body proportions and mental development are preserved (the difference from cretinism). Treatment — recombinant GH until the growth plates close.

topics.title: Physiology of the thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreatic and sex glands

goals.text: To teach the student the formation, biological effects and regulation of secretion of the hormones of the peripheral endocrine glands — the thyroid, parathyroid and adrenal glands, the endocrine part of the pancreas and the sex glands — and the main manifestations of their dysfunction; to master evaluating hormonal status on the basis of clinical and laboratory parameters.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the synthesis, effects and regulation of thyroid hormones and the signs of hypo- and hyperthyroidism;
the hormonal regulation of calcium metabolism (parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, calcitriol);
the effects of the hormones of the adrenal cortex (mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, androgens) and of the adrenal medulla;
the hormones of the pancreatic islet apparatus and the regulation of blood glucose;
the male and female sex hormones and the hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle;
stress and the general adaptation syndrome (H. Selye).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: interpret thyroid hormone, cortisol, glucose and calcium parameters;
evaluate the result of a glucose tolerance test;
explain the main signs of endocrine disorders from a physiological point of view.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Aldosterone** is essential for life: without it the body loses sodium and water and potassium accumulates — in acute adrenal insufficiency blood pressure falls and hyperkalemia can stop the heart. **Cortisol** is the main “stress hormone”: its secretion increases several times during stress.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: There are many hormones that raise blood glucose (**counter-insulin** hormones): glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH, thyroid hormones. Only one lowers it — **insulin**. That is why the body is better protected against hypoglycemia.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Estrogen builds, progesterone preserves”**: estrogen makes the endometrium grow (proliferation), and progesterone prepares it for pregnancy and maintains it (“pro-gestation” — for pregnancy).

blocks.text: The thyroid gland (20–30 g) lies on the anterior surface of the neck. Its structural and functional unit is the **follicle**: a vesicle lined by a single layer of thyrocytes and filled with **colloid** (thyroglobulin). Between the follicles lie the **parafollicular C cells**, which produce **calcitonin**.

blocks.label: Figure 15.1
blocks.caption: Thyroid follicles (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Synthesis of thyroid hormones

items: Thyrocytes actively take up **iodide** (I^-^) from the blood through the Na^+^/I^-^ symporter.
Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues of **thyroglobulin** (monoiodotyrosine, diiodotyrosine).
Iodotyrosines combine to form **thyroxine (T~4~)** and **triiodothyronine (T~3~)**; they are stored in the colloid.

Under the action of TSH thyroglobulin is taken back up by endocytosis and proteolyzed, and T~4~ and T~3~ are released into the blood. 90% of the secreted hormone is T~4~, but the active form is **T~3~** (3–5 times more potent); T~4~ is converted to T~3~ in peripheral tissues by deiodinase. In the blood the hormones are carried mainly bound to proteins. Adults need ≈ 150 µg of iodine per day.

rows: Increase basal metabolism, O~2~ consumption and heat production (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase, mitochondria)
Essential for the CNS (myelination, neuronal development) and bone growth; enhance the effect of GH
Enhance protein synthesis (at physiological doses), gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and cholesterol breakdown
Increase the number of β-adrenergic receptors — HR and force of contraction increase
Increase excitability, reflex speed and mental activity

blocks.text: **Regulation:** hypothalamus (TRH) → pituitary (TSH) → thyroid gland (T~4~, T~3~) — negative feedback. Cold stimulates TRH secretion.

Weight gain, cold sensitivity, bradycardia, drowsiness, memory impairment, dry and swollen skin (myxedema)
Cretinism — delayed mental and physical development, dwarfism
Congenital hypothyroidism, severe iodine deficiency in pregnancy
Enlargement of the gland (TSH rises in iodine deficiency)

parts.text: If congenital hypothyroidism is not detected early, irreversible mental retardation (cretinism) develops. Therefore **TSH screening** is performed in all newborns, and if the disease is detected, treatment with thyroxine starts in the first weeks. **Iodized salt** is used to prevent iodine deficiency.

sections.title: 2. Regulation of calcium and phosphorus metabolism

blocks.text: Total blood calcium is **2.2–2.6 mmol/l**, ionized (active) calcium 1.1–1.3 mmol/l. Calcium is necessary for muscle contraction, mediator release, blood coagulation and excitability. It is regulated by three hormones.

blocks.label: Figure 15.2

blocks.text: PTH secretion is stimulated by a **decrease in ionized Ca^2+^** in the blood (through calcium-sensing receptors on the gland cells).

parts.text: **Hypoparathyroidism** (most often when the parathyroid glands are accidentally removed during thyroid surgery) — hypocalcemia: the excitability of nerves and muscles increases, **tetany** (cramps, “obstetrician's hand”, Chvostek and Trousseau signs), and in severe cases laryngospasm. In **hyperparathyroidism** — leaching of calcium from bone (osteoporosis, fractures), kidney stones, peptic ulcer. **Vitamin D deficiency** leads to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

blocks.text: The adrenal gland consists of two independent parts: the **cortex** (mesodermal, steroid hormones) and the **medulla** (neuroectodermal, catecholamines).

parts.text: **Aldosterone** is essential for life: without it the body loses sodium and water and potassium accumulates — in acute adrenal insufficiency blood pressure falls and hyperkalemia can stop the heart. **Cortisol** is the main “stress hormone”: its secretion increases several times during stress.
