blocks.text: The medulla

The chromaffin cells of the medulla are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons; they are innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers (acetylcholine, N-cholinergic receptors). They secrete **adrenaline** (80%) and **noradrenaline** (20%). The effects of catecholamines resemble those of the sympathetic nervous system (the “fight or flight” reaction) and are discussed in detail in topic 26: increased HR and pressure, bronchodilation, glycogenolysis and lipolysis (hyperglycemia), pupil dilation, and redistribution of blood flow to the muscles.
Stress and the general adaptation syndrome

**Stress** (H. Selye, 1936) is the body's nonspecific adaptive reaction to strong stimuli (stressors). The **general adaptation syndrome** consists of three stages: the **alarm stage** (sharp activation of the sympathoadrenal system and the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal system), the **stage of resistance** and the **stage of exhaustion** (if the stressor acts for a long time, the adaptive capacities are exhausted and diseases develop). The main hormones are **catecholamines and cortisol**.
The endocrine part of the pancreas is the **islets of Langerhans** (1–2% of the gland mass, 1–2 million islets).

blocks.text: Insulin is the body's only hypoglycemic hormone. Its effects: it enhances the entry of glucose into muscle and fat cells (by bringing GLUT4 transporters to the membrane); in the liver and muscle it increases glycogen synthesis and inhibits gluconeogenesis; it enhances lipogenesis, inhibits lipolysis and the formation of ketone bodies; it enhances protein synthesis; it increases the entry of K^+^ into cells.

**Regulation of insulin secretion:** the main stimulus is a **rise in blood glucose** (glucose metabolism in β cells → ATP ↑ → ATP-sensitive K^+^ channels close → depolarization → Ca^2+^ entry → exocytosis of insulin). Amino acids, intestinal hormones — **incretins** (GLP-1, GIP; that is why oral glucose releases more insulin than intravenous glucose) and the vagus nerve also enhance it; the sympathetic nerves (α~2~), adrenaline and somatostatin inhibit it.

parts.text: There are many hormones that raise blood glucose (**counter-insulin** hormones): glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH, thyroid hormones. Only one lowers it — **insulin**. That is why the body is better protected against hypoglycemia.

**Diabetes mellitus** is chronic hyperglycemia resulting from insulin deficiency (type 1, autoimmune destruction of β cells) or insulin resistance with relative deficiency (type 2, often with obesity). Classic signs: **polyuria** (glucosuria — osmotic diuresis), **polydipsia** (thirst), **polyphagia**, weight loss. Diagnostic criteria: fasting venous plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/l, ≥ 11.1 mmol/l 2 hours into a glucose tolerance test, HbA~1c~ ≥ 6.5%.

blocks.text: Male sex glands (testes)

In the testes, **Leydig cells** produce **testosterone** under the influence of LH; **Sertoli cells** support spermatogenesis under the influence of FSH and testosterone and secrete **inhibin** (which inhibits FSH).

**Effects of testosterone:** formation of the male genital organs in the fetal period; primary and secondary sexual characteristics at puberty (deepening of the voice, growth of hair and beard, muscle mass); spermatogenesis; a strong **anabolic** effect (protein synthesis, muscle and bone mass); stimulation of erythropoiesis; sexual drive and behavior. In many tissues testosterone is converted into a more active form — **dihydrotestosterone**.

blocks.text: Female sex glands (ovaries) and the menstrual cycle
The ovaries produce **estrogens** (estradiol — in follicle cells), **progesterone** (in the corpus luteum) and small amounts of androgens and inhibin.

blocks.label: Figure 15.6
blocks.caption: Structure of the ovary and effects of progesterone and estrogens (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: If there is no pregnancy, the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls and menstruation begins. In pregnancy **chorionic gonadotropin** (detected by pregnancy tests) maintains the corpus luteum; later the placenta produces progesterone and estrogens.

parts.text: **“Estrogen builds, progesterone preserves”**: estrogen makes the endometrium grow (proliferation), and progesterone prepares it for pregnancy and maintains it (“pro-gestation” — for pregnancy).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: evaluating the results of a glucose tolerance test

items: From the given results take the fasting glycemia and the glycemia 2 hours after drinking 75 g of glucose.
Plot the glycemic curve (0, 30, 60, 90, 120 minutes) on graph paper.
Interpretation (venous plasma): fasting < 6.1 and at 2 hours < 7.8 mmol/l — normal; at 2 hours 7.8–11.0 — impaired glucose tolerance; ≥ 11.1 — diabetes mellitus.
Analyze the shape of the curve (time and height of the peak, return to the baseline level).

blocks.text: Exercise 2: interpreting thyroid status parameters

items: Take the results of TSH (normal 0.4–4.0 mIU/l) and free T~4~ (10–23 pmol/l).
TSH low, T~4~ high — primary hyperthyroidism.
TSH high, T~4~ low — primary hypothyroidism.
Both TSH and T~4~ low — secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism.
Compare the result with the clinical signs.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: testing the Chvostek and Trousseau signs (demonstration)

items: **Chvostek sign**: contraction of the facial muscles (corner of the mouth) when the exit point of the facial nerve in front of the ear is tapped lightly with a hammer.
**Trousseau sign**: spasm of the hand muscles (“obstetrician's hand”) when a blood pressure cuff is placed on the upper arm and kept above systolic pressure for 3 minutes.
If the signs are positive, neuromuscular excitability is increased (hypocalcemia).

Evaluate the levels of estrogen, progesterone, LH and FSH.
Analyze the basal temperature chart: a rise of 0.3–0.6 °C after ovulation — the effect of progesterone.
Determine the phase and whether ovulation has occurred.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman complains of weakness, weight loss, dizziness and darkening of the skin. Arterial pressure 85/55 mm Hg, blood Na^+^ 128, K^+^ 5.8 mmol/l, glucose 3.4 mmol/l. Blood cortisol is low, ACTH high.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain each sign by linking it to the hormone deficiency.
cases.answer: Primary adrenal cortical insufficiency (Addison's disease). Because of aldosterone deficiency, Na^+^ and water are lost in the kidney and K^+^ is retained — hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, decreased blood volume and arterial hypotension. Because of cortisol deficiency, gluconeogenesis weakens — hypoglycemia, weakness; the effect of catecholamines on the vessels (permissive effect) decreases and the hypotension worsens. When cortisol falls, the pituitary releases a lot of ACTH by negative feedback; ACTH and MSH are formed from a common precursor (proopiomelanocortin) and stimulate melanocytes — the skin darkens.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: On the second day after thyroid resection, the patient developed numbness of the lips and fingertips, followed by painful cramps of the hand muscles. The Chvostek and Trousseau signs are positive.
cases.ask: What complication has developed? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: During the operation the parathyroid glands were removed or damaged — hypoparathyroidism. Because of parathyroid hormone deficiency, the release of calcium from bone and calcium reabsorption in the kidney decrease, calcitriol synthesis falls and intestinal calcium absorption decreases — hypocalcemia develops. When extracellular Ca^2+^ falls, the opening threshold of Na^+^ channels decreases (membrane stability decreases) — the excitability of nerves and muscles increases and spontaneous impulses arise: paresthesias, tetany. Treatment — intravenous calcium preparations, then calcium and active vitamin D.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient treated with prednisolone (a glucocorticoid) for a long time has a rounded face, fat accumulation in the upper body, purple stripes on the abdomen, arterial pressure 160/100 mm Hg and blood glucose 8.2 mmol/l.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the mechanism of the signs. Why is it dangerous to stop the treatment abruptly?
cases.answer: Drug-induced (iatrogenic) Itsenko–Cushing syndrome. Glucocorticoids enhance gluconeogenesis and reduce glucose uptake by tissues — hyperglycemia; protein catabolism thins the skin and collagen — striae, muscle weakness, osteoporosis; they redistribute fat — “moon face”, obesity of the upper body; through mineralocorticoid action and increased vascular sensitivity to catecholamines — hypertension. During long-term treatment, exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, and the patient's own adrenal glands atrophy. If treatment is stopped abruptly, acute adrenal insufficiency may develop; therefore the dose is reduced gradually.

topics.title: Respiratory physiology. Mechanism of breathing. Alveolar-capillary gas exchange. Regulation of breathing

goals.text: To teach the student the stages of respiration, the biomechanics of inspiration and expiration, intrapleural pressure and its significance, lung compliance and the role of surfactant, the laws of gas exchange in the alveoli, the structure of the respiratory center and the reflex and humoral regulation of breathing; in laboratory work, to master recording respiratory movements and analyzing their changes under the influence of various factors.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the stages of respiration (external respiration, transport of gases in the blood, tissue respiration);
the inspiratory and expiratory muscles and the biomechanics of the respiratory cycle;
intrapleural pressure and its origin, pneumothorax;
the elastic recoil of the lungs and the function of surfactant;
the composition of gases in air and in the alveoli, partial pressures;
the diffusion of gases across the alveolar-capillary membrane;
the structure of the respiratory center and the rhythm generator;
the central and peripheral chemoreceptors and the Hering–Breuer reflex.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: demonstrate the mechanism of breathing with the Donders model;
record respiratory movements by pneumography and analyze the effects of hyperventilation, breath-holding and exercise;
perform and evaluate the Stange and Genchi tests.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Two extreme states of V/Q mismatch: **dead space** (ventilation present, no blood flow — pulmonary embolism) and **shunt** (blood flow present, no ventilation — pneumonia, atelectasis). In a shunt, even giving 100% oxygen does not fully correct the hypoxemia.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main humoral stimulus of breathing is **CO~2~** (more precisely, H^+^): a rise in pCO~2~ of 1 mm Hg increases ventilation by 2–3 l/min. Hypoxia strongly stimulates breathing only when pO~2~ falls below 60 mm Hg. **Fredericq's experiment** (cross-circulation of the heads of two dogs) and Haldane's experiments proved the humoral regulation of breathing.

blocks.text: **Respiration** is the set of processes that ensure gas exchange between the body and the external environment (uptake of O~2~ and elimination of CO~2~).

blocks.label: Figure 16.1
blocks.caption: Stages of respiration: external respiration, transport of gases in the blood, tissue respiration (Alavia O.T., 2018)

items: **External respiration (pulmonary ventilation)** — exchange of air between the atmosphere and the alveoli.
**Gas exchange in the lungs** — between alveolar air and the blood of the pulmonary capillaries.
**Transport of gases in the blood** (topic 17).
**Gas exchange in the tissues** — between blood and tissues.
**Cellular (tissue) respiration** — the use of O~2~ in oxidative processes in the mitochondria.

blocks.text: Because the lung has no muscle tissue of its own, it cannot expand actively; it passively follows the movements of the chest. Between the lung and the chest wall there is a sealed **pleural cavity** (a thin layer of fluid).
Inspiration — an active process

**Main inspiratory muscles: the diaphragm** (70–80% of the volume change in quiet breathing; its dome descends 1.5–2 cm, up to 10 cm in deep breathing) and the **external intercostal muscles** (they raise the ribs and expand the chest anteroposteriorly and laterally). **Accessory muscles** (in deep breathing): sternocleidomastoid, scalene, pectoralis major and minor.

Sequence: impulse from the respiratory center → the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract → chest volume increases → intrapleural pressure becomes more negative → the lungs expand → alveolar pressure falls 1–2 cm H₂O below atmospheric → air enters the lungs.
Expiration

In quiet breathing it is **passive**: the respiratory muscles relax, and the **elastic recoil** of the lungs and the weight of the chest return it to the initial position; alveolar pressure exceeds atmospheric and air leaves. In forced expiration (physical work, coughing, bronchial asthma) it is **active**: the **internal intercostal muscles** and the **abdominal muscles** contract.

blocks.label: Figure 16.2
blocks.caption: Donders model: A — resting state; B — when the “diaphragm” (rubber) is pulled down, the lungs expand (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Intrapleural pressure

**Intrapleural pressure** is **lower** than atmospheric (“negative”): −3…−5 cm H₂O (−2…−4 mm Hg) at the end of quiet expiration, −6…−8 during quiet inspiration, and down to −20 cm H₂O during deep inspiration.

**Origin:** the **elastic recoil** of the lungs (which tends to shrink the lung toward its root) and the outward pull of the chest wall act in opposite directions; the pleural layers cannot separate from each other and a negative pressure arises in the cavity. In the postnatal period the faster growth of the chest relative to the lungs also contributes.

blocks.label: Figure 16.3
blocks.caption: Changes in lung volume and alveolar and intrapleural pressure during the respiratory cycle (drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

parts.text: **Pneumothorax** is the entry of air into the pleural cavity (chest injury, rupture of a bulla). The negative pressure disappears and the lung collapses due to its elastic recoil — it no longer takes part in breathing.

**Valvular (tension) pneumothorax** is life-threatening: with each inspiration air enters but does not leave, pressure rises and the mediastinum shifts. Emergency help — puncture and drainage of the pleural cavity.

blocks.text: Elastic recoil of the lungs and surfactant
The elastic recoil of the lungs is due to two factors: the **elastic fibers** of lung tissue (≈ 1/3) and the **surface tension** of the fluid layer on the inner surface of the alveoli (≈ 2/3).

**Surfactant** is a complex of phospholipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and proteins produced by type II alveolocytes. Its functions: it **reduces surface tension** and increases lung compliance (reducing the work of breathing); it **prevents the collapse of small alveoli (atelectasis)** — according to Laplace's law the pressure in a small alveolus should be greater, but surfactant is denser in it and reduces the tension more; it keeps the alveoli dry (prevents pulmonary edema); and it has a protective function.

parts.text: Surfactant begins to be synthesized in the fetus at 24–28 weeks and becomes sufficient by 34–35 weeks. In premature infants surfactant deficiency leads to **respiratory distress syndrome** (hyaline membrane disease): the alveoli collapse and breathing becomes difficult. Prevention — glucocorticoids for the mother when preterm birth is threatened (they accelerate surfactant synthesis); treatment — endotracheal administration of surfactant.

blocks.text: **Lung compliance** is the change in lung volume per 1 cm H₂O change in pressure; normally ≈ 200 ml/cm H₂O (lungs and chest together — 100). It decreases in fibrosis and increases in emphysema.
**Airway resistance** is mainly in the medium-sized bronchi; it rises sharply when the bronchi narrow (asthma, bronchitis) (Poiseuille's law: the fourth power of the radius).

blocks.text: Because expired air is a mixture of alveolar air and “dead space” air, it contains more O~2~ and less CO~2~.

The **partial pressure of a gas** is the pressure attributable to that gas in a gas mixture: Pgas = Ptotal × gas fraction (%) / 100. In the alveoli the water vapor pressure (47 mm Hg) is taken into account: pO~2~ alv = (760 − 47) × 0.14 ≈ 100 mm Hg.

blocks.title: Table 16.2. Partial pressures and tensions of gases (mm Hg)

pO~2~

blocks.label: Figure 16.4
blocks.caption: Partial pressures of gases in the pulmonary and tissue capillaries (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Gases pass from the alveoli into the blood and from the blood into the tissues only by **diffusion**, down the partial pressure gradient. In the lungs the gradient for O~2~ is 100 − 40 = **60 mm Hg**, and for CO~2~ 46 − 40 = **6 mm Hg**. Nevertheless CO~2~ diffuses well: its solubility is 20–25 times higher than that of O~2~.
The alveolar-capillary membrane

The air–blood barrier is only **0.3–0.5 µm** thick: the surfactant layer, the alveolar epithelium (type I alveolocytes), the common basement membrane and the capillary endothelium; plus a layer of plasma and the erythrocyte membrane. The total diffusion surface is **70–100 m^2^**. An erythrocyte passes through a capillary in ≈ 0.75 s, while gas equilibrium is reached in 0.25 s — there is a large reserve.

blocks.label: Figure 16.5
blocks.caption: The alveolar-capillary membrane and the diffusion of gases (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: According to **Fick's law**, the rate of diffusion is directly proportional to the partial pressure difference, the membrane area and the solubility of the gas, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. **The diffusing capacity of the lung** is the volume of gas that diffuses in 1 minute at a gradient of 1 mm Hg; for O~2~ at rest it is ≈ 25 ml/min/mm Hg.
The ventilation-perfusion ratio

For effective gas exchange, alveolar ventilation (≈ 4.2 l/min) and pulmonary blood flow (≈ 5 l/min) must be matched: **V/Q ≈ 0.8–1.0**. At the lung apices V/Q is high (ventilation predominates), at the base it is low (blood flow predominates). **Hypoxic vasoconstriction** — when O~2~ falls in a poorly ventilated area, the vessels there constrict and blood is directed to well-ventilated areas.

parts.text: Two extreme states of V/Q mismatch: **dead space** (ventilation present, no blood flow — pulmonary embolism) and **shunt** (blood flow present, no ventilation — pneumonia, atelectasis). In a shunt, even giving 100% oxygen does not fully correct the hypoxemia.

blocks.text: The respiratory center
The **respiratory center** is the set of CNS neurons that generate the respiratory rhythm and adapt it to the body's needs. Its main part is in the **medulla oblongata** (N.A. Mislavsky, 1885):

items: the **dorsal respiratory group** (in the region of the nucleus of the solitary tract) — mainly inspiratory neurons; it receives afferent information;
the **ventral respiratory group** — inspiratory and expiratory neurons; within it the **pre-Bötzinger complex** is the respiratory **rhythm generator** (neurons with pacemaker properties);

the **pneumotaxic center in the pons** — terminates inspiration on time and ensures the switch to expiration; its damage makes breathing deep and slow. After transection between the medulla oblongata and the spinal cord breathing stops; after transection above the pons breathing is preserved.

blocks.caption: The system of respiratory control

blocks.text: Humoral regulation — chemoreceptors

blocks.title: Table 16.3. Chemoreceptors regulating breathing

Location
What they sense

rows: Ventral surface of the medulla oblongata
An increase in H^+^ in the cerebrospinal fluid (mainly due to a rise in pCO~2~ — CO~2~ crosses the blood–brain barrier easily)

parts.text: The main humoral stimulus of breathing is **CO~2~** (more precisely, H^+^): a rise in pCO~2~ of 1 mm Hg increases ventilation by 2–3 l/min. Hypoxia strongly stimulates breathing only when pO~2~ falls below 60 mm Hg. **Fredericq's experiment** (cross-circulation of the heads of two dogs) and Haldane's experiments proved the humoral regulation of breathing.

In patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, because pCO~2~ is constantly high, the central chemoreceptors “adapt” to it and breathing is driven mainly by **hypoxia** (the peripheral chemoreceptors). If such a patient is given high-concentration oxygen, the hypoxic drive disappears and breathing may weaken and hypercapnia worsen. Therefore oxygen is given to them under control, at a low flow.

blocks.text: Reflex regulation

items: **Hering–Breuer reflex** — during inspiration the stretch receptors of the lungs are excited, and impulses travel along the vagus nerve to the respiratory center and stop inspiration (the switch from inspiration to expiration). In adults it is of little importance in quiet breathing and is activated in deep breathing (volume > 1–1.5 l); it is well expressed in newborns.
**Protective reflexes** — coughing (irritant receptors of the larynx, trachea and bronchi), sneezing (nasal mucosa), reflex cessation of breathing (pungent substances, diving into water).
**Proprioceptors** (muscles and joints) — rapidly increase ventilation at the start of physical work.
**The cerebral cortex** — voluntary control of breathing (speech, singing, breath-holding), conditioned reflexes (increased breathing before the start).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: demonstrating the mechanism of breathing with the Donders model

items: Examine the model: the lungs of an animal are suspended by the trachea inside a glass bell jar (its lower part closed by a rubber membrane); the cavity of the jar is connected to a manometer.
Pull the rubber membrane down (imitating contraction of the diaphragm).
Observe the change in pressure inside the jar and in lung volume.

Release the membrane. **Result and analysis:** when the membrane is pulled, the pressure inside the jar falls (the manometer shows negative pressure) and the lungs expand and air enters them — inspiration. When it is released, the lungs shrink because of their elastic recoil — expiration. The model shows that the lungs passively follow changes in chest volume.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: pneumography — recording respiratory movements

items: Tie the pneumograph cuff (or sensor) around the subject's chest and connect it to a kymograph or computer system.
Record quiet breathing for 1 minute and count the respiratory rate (normal 12–18 /min).
The subject breathes rapidly and deeply for 30 s (hyperventilation), then returns to normal breathing — continue recording.

Record breathing during voluntary breath-holding, speaking, swallowing and after 20 squats. **Expected result and analysis:** after hyperventilation a short **apnea** or weakening of breathing is observed — CO~2~ has been “washed out” (hypocapnia), and the main stimulus of the respiratory center has decreased. After breath-holding breathing becomes deeper and faster — CO~2~ has accumulated. During swallowing breathing stops reflexly. During physical load the rate and depth of breathing increase.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: the Stange and Genchi tests

items: **Stange test**: the seated subject takes a deep (not maximal) breath, pinches the nose and holds the breath; the time is measured with a stopwatch.
**Genchi test**: the breath-holding time after a quiet expiration is measured.

Repeat the Stange test after 1 minute of hyperventilation. **Interpretation:** the Stange test is 40–60 s in healthy adults (60–120 s in athletes), the Genchi test 20–40 s. After hyperventilation the breath-holding time increases — blood CO~2~ decreases, and it takes longer to reach the “threshold” that excites the respiratory center.

skills.title: Skill: calculating the partial pressure of a gas in alveolar air

items: Determine the atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg at sea level).
Subtract the water vapor pressure in the alveoli (47 mm Hg).
Multiply by the percentage of the gas: pO~2~ = (760 − 47) × 14 / 100 ≈ 100 mm Hg.
Repeat the calculation for the lower atmospheric pressure at altitude and assess the risk of hypoxia.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating the type and rate of breathing

items: Without the subject noticing (as if counting the pulse), count the respiratory movements for 1 minute.
Determine the type of breathing: thoracic (mainly in women), abdominal (diaphragmatic — mainly in men), mixed.
Evaluate the rhythm and depth.
Compare the result with the age norm (12–18 /min in adults; 40–60 in newborns).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A tall, thin 20-year-old young man suddenly developed sharp pain in the right side of the chest and shortness of breath. No breath sounds are heard on the right. On X-ray the right lung has collapsed toward its root, with air in the pleural cavity.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Why did the lung collapse? Why does this lung not expand during inspiration?
cases.answer: Spontaneous pneumothorax (a bulla on the lung surface has ruptured). Normally the pressure in the pleural cavity is lower than atmospheric — it keeps the lung “stuck” to the chest wall. When air enters, the pressure equalizes with atmospheric and the lung shrinks toward its root because of its own elastic recoil (elastic fibers and alveolar surface tension). Even when the chest expands during inspiration, no negative pressure is created in the pleural cavity — air simply enters the pleural cavity, and the lung does not expand passively. Treatment — removal of the air (puncture, drainage).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A baby born at 29 weeks of pregnancy developed rapid breathing a few hours after birth; the soft parts of the chest are drawn inward, there is grunting on expiration, and cyanosis is increasing.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism on the basis of the function of surfactant.
cases.answer: Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn. Surfactant is synthesized in sufficient amounts after 34–35 weeks; a premature baby lacks it. As a result the surface tension in the alveoli remains high: according to Laplace's law the small alveoli collapse during expiration (atelectasis), lung compliance falls sharply and each inspiration requires great effort — chest retraction, shortness of breath. No gas exchange takes place in the collapsed alveoli (shunt) — hypoxemia and cyanosis. Treatment — administration of surfactant preparations into the trachea and respiratory support.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A student who was nervous before an exam breathed rapidly and deeply. He developed dizziness and numbness of the fingers and around the lips. He was advised to breathe in and out of a paper bag.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the signs. Why does breathing into a bag help?
cases.answer: Hyperventilation syndrome. Because of excessive ventilation a lot of CO~2~ is removed from the blood — hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis. The decrease in CO~2~ constricts the cerebral vessels — cerebral blood flow decreases and dizziness occurs. Alkalosis enhances the binding of ionized calcium to proteins — free Ca^2+^ decreases and nerve excitability increases — paresthesias (numbness), and in severe cases cramps. When breathing into a bag, the expired CO~2~ is re-inhaled, blood pCO~2~ is restored and the signs disappear (but this method is used only briefly and only when it is clear that the cause is hyperventilation).

goals.text: To teach the student lung volumes and capacities, the parameters of pulmonary ventilation, the methods of spirometry and spirography, the mechanisms of transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood, the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, gas exchange in the tissues and tissue respiration, and the principles of pulse oximetry; to master performing spirometry and evaluating the results.
By the end of the class the student should know:

minute ventilation, alveolar ventilation and dead space;
spirographic parameters (FEV~1~, Tiffeneau index, maximal voluntary ventilation);
the forms of oxygen transport in the blood and the oxygen capacity;
the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, its shape and shifts (Bohr effect);
the forms of CO~2~ transport in the blood, carbonic anhydrase and the chloride shift (Hamburger);
gas exchange in the tissues and tissue respiration;
the principle, norm and limitations of pulse oximetry.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: measure lung volumes with a spirometer and compare the VC with the predicted value;
analyze a spirogram and distinguish obstructive from restrictive disorders;
perform pulse oximetry and evaluate the result.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Rapid shallow breathing is ineffective**: for example, with a TV of 200 ml and a respiratory rate of 40 /min the MV is 8 l/min (close to normal), but alveolar ventilation is (200 − 150) × 40 = 2 l/min — hypoventilation. Therefore **deep, slow breathing** is more effective.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Shift to the right — **“CADET, face Right!”**: **C**O~2~, **A**cid (H^+^), **D**PG (2,3-DPG), **E**xercise (physical work), **T**emperature — when these increase the curve shifts **to the right** and the tissues receive more oxygen.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ is interrelated: **Bohr effect** — an increase in CO~2~ and H^+^ facilitates the release of O~2~ by Hb (in the tissues); **Haldane effect** — deoxyhemoglobin binds CO~2~ and H^+^ better than oxyhemoglobin, so in the tissues the release of O~2~ facilitates the uptake of CO~2~, and in the lungs oxygenation facilitates the release of CO~2~.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Limitations of pulse oximetry: in **carboxyhemoglobinemia** (carbon monoxide poisoning) and **methemoglobinemia** the result is wrong (falsely high or about ≈ 85%); peripheral vasospasm, cold hands, shock, movement, nail polish, bright ambient light and dark skin reduce accuracy. SpO~2~ shows only oxygenation — **it does not evaluate ventilation (CO~2~)**: in a patient receiving oxygen hypercapnia may be present even when SpO~2~ is normal.

blocks.text: The **functional residual capacity** is important: it dilutes the air entering with each breath (500 ml) and keeps the composition of alveolar air stable throughout the respiratory cycle — gas concentrations do not fluctuate sharply. The **residual volume** and FRC cannot be measured with an ordinary spirometer (helium dilution or body plethysmography is required).

parts.text: **In determining the cause of death**, whether the lung sinks in water is important: the lungs of a baby who breathed after birth contain residual (minimal) air, and a piece of lung does not sink in water; the lungs of a stillborn fetus sink (a forensic test).

blocks.text: **Minute ventilation (MV)** = tidal volume × respiratory rate = 500 ml × 14–16 = **6–8 l/min**. During heavy physical work it increases to 100–150 l/min.
**Dead space** is the volume of the airways that does not take part in gas exchange:

items: **Anatomical dead space** — from the nasopharynx to the terminal bronchioles: ≈ **150 ml** (≈ 2 ml/kg).

**Physiological (functional) dead space** — anatomical plus alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused; in a healthy person it is almost equal to the anatomical dead space. **Alveolar ventilation** = (TV − dead space) × respiratory rate = (500 − 150) × 14 ≈ **4.2–5 l/min**. It is alveolar ventilation that determines gas exchange.

parts.text: **Rapid shallow breathing is ineffective**: for example, with a TV of 200 ml and a respiratory rate of 40 /min the MV is 8 l/min (close to normal), but alveolar ventilation is (200 − 150) × 40 = 2 l/min — hypoventilation. Therefore **deep, slow breathing** is more effective.

blocks.text: **Spirometry** is the measurement of lung volumes; **spirography** is the graphic recording of respiratory movements and volume changes over time. Modern computer spirometers also record the **“flow–volume” curve**.

parts.text: **Bronchodilator test** — an increase in FEV~1~ of ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 ml 15–20 minutes after salbutamol inhalation shows that the obstruction is reversible and is typical of **bronchial asthma**; in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease the obstruction is not fully reversible.

blocks.text: The **predicted VC** is calculated by a formula (Baldwin, Cournand, Richards): for men VC (l) = (27.63 − 0.112 × age) × height (cm) / 1000; for women (21.78 − 0.101 × age) × height / 1000. If the actual VC is within ± 15–20% of the predicted value, it is normal.

sections.title: 4. Transport of oxygen in the blood

blocks.text: Oxygen is carried in the blood in two forms:

items: **Physically dissolved** — a small amount (0.3 ml per 100 ml of blood at a pO~2~ of 100 mm Hg). But it is the dissolved O~2~ that creates the partial pressure (tension) and ensures diffusion.

**Bound to hemoglobin (oxyhemoglobin)** — 98–99%. The **oxygen capacity of blood** is the maximum amount of O~2~ that 1 l of blood can bind: Hb 150 g/l × 1.34 ml ≈ **200 ml O~2~/l** (20 vol%). Arterial blood contains ≈ 190–200 ml/l of O~2~ (saturation 96–98%), venous blood ≈ 140–150 ml/l (saturation ≈ 75%).

blocks.text: **Arteriovenous difference** — the difference in O~2~ content between arterial and venous blood: ≈ 50 ml/l at rest. **Oxygen utilization coefficient** of the tissues = arteriovenous difference / O~2~ in arterial blood ≈ 25–30%; up to 50–60% during physical work, and 60–70% in heart muscle even at rest.
The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve

The relationship between the saturation of hemoglobin with O~2~ (saturation, SO~2~) and pO~2~ is expressed by an **S-shaped** curve. The S shape results from the **cooperative effect**: once one heme binds O~2~, the affinity of the others increases.

blocks.label: Figure 17.3
blocks.caption: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve and its shifts (drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

blocks.text: Physiological significance of the curve:

items: **The upper flat part** (pO~2~ 70–100 mm Hg) — in the lungs: even if pO~2~ falls slightly (altitude, lung diseases), the saturation remains high — oxygen supply is **reliable**.

**The steep lower part** (pO~2~ 10–40) — in the tissues: a small fall in pO~2~ releases a lot of O~2~ — the tissues **easily obtain** O~2~. **P~50~** is the pO~2~ at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated; normally ≈ **26–27 mm Hg.** An increase in P~50~ (a right shift of the curve) means that the affinity of Hb for O~2~ has decreased and the delivery of O~2~ to the tissues is facilitated.

blocks.title: Table 17.5. Factors affecting the shift of the curve

Left shift (O~2~ retention enhanced)

Fall in pCO~2~, rise in pH (alkalosis)

parts.text: Shift to the right — **“CADET, face Right!”**: **C**O~2~, **A**cid (H^+^), **D**PG (2,3-DPG), **E**xercise (physical work), **T**emperature — when these increase the curve shifts **to the right** and the tissues receive more oxygen.

head: Form
Share
Note
rows: Sodium bicarbonate in plasma, potassium bicarbonate in erythrocytes
CO~2~ binds to the amino groups of globin

blocks.text: Mechanism (in tissue capillaries):

items: CO~2~ diffuses from the tissue into the plasma and then into the erythrocyte.
In the erythrocyte the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** accelerates the reaction CO~2~ + H~2~O → H~2~CO~3~ 13,000-fold.
H~2~CO~3~ dissociates into H^+^ + HCO~3~^-^. H^+^ is bound by deoxyhemoglobin (buffer).
HCO~3~^-^ leaves the erythrocyte for the plasma and Cl^-^ enters the erythrocyte in its place — the **chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon)**.
In the pulmonary capillaries all processes go in the reverse direction and CO~2~ is released into the alveoli.

blocks.label: Figure 17.4
blocks.caption: Transport of CO~2~ in the blood: processes inside the erythrocyte in the tissue and pulmonary capillaries (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: The transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ is interrelated: **Bohr effect** — an increase in CO~2~ and H^+^ facilitates the release of O~2~ by Hb (in the tissues); **Haldane effect** — deoxyhemoglobin binds CO~2~ and H^+^ better than oxyhemoglobin, so in the tissues the release of O~2~ facilitates the uptake of CO~2~, and in the lungs oxygenation facilitates the release of CO~2~.

sections.title: 6. Gas exchange in the tissues and tissue respiration

blocks.text: In the tissue capillaries O~2~ diffuses from the blood (pO~2~ 95–100) into the tissue (pO~2~ 20–40, 5–10 mm Hg in working muscle), and CO~2~ from the tissue (pCO~2~ 46–60) into the blood (40). Diffusion is affected by capillary density, the number of open capillaries, the distance to the cells and the tissue's O~2~ consumption. In muscles **myoglobin** stores O~2~ and carries it inside the cell (its affinity for O~2~ is higher than that of hemoglobin — P~50~ ≈ 1–5 mm Hg).

**Tissue (cellular) respiration** is the use of O~2~ as the final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial respiratory chain (cytochromes, cytochrome oxidase) and the synthesis of ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. For normal mitochondrial function an intracellular pO~2~ of only 1–3 mm Hg is sufficient (**critical pO~2~**).

parts.text: **Cyanides** (bitter almonds, cyanide salts) block **cytochrome oxidase** — even if there is enough oxygen in the blood, the cells cannot use it (**tissue hypoxia**). Venous blood remains saturated with oxygen (the arteriovenous difference narrows) and the skin is pink.

blocks.text: **Pulse oximetry** is a non-invasive, continuous method of determining arterial oxygen saturation (**SpO~2~**). The sensor (usually placed on a finger) transmits light of two wavelengths — **red (660 nm)** and **infrared (940 nm)**. Oxyhemoglobin absorbs more infrared light, deoxyhemoglobin more red light. The device analyzes only the **pulsatile** (arterial) component, calculates SpO~2~ from the ratio of absorption of the two lights and at the same time shows the pulse rate.

parts.text: Limitations of pulse oximetry: in **carboxyhemoglobinemia** (carbon monoxide poisoning) and **methemoglobinemia** the result is wrong (falsely high or about ≈ 85%); peripheral vasospasm, cold hands, shock, movement, nail polish, bright ambient light and dark skin reduce accuracy. SpO~2~ shows only oxygenation — **it does not evaluate ventilation (CO~2~)**: in a patient receiving oxygen hypercapnia may be present even when SpO~2~ is normal.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining lung volumes with a water (or dry) spirometer

items: Wipe the mouthpiece with alcohol; the subject closes the nose with a clip.
**Tidal volume**: after a quiet inspiration, exhale quietly into the spirometer 3–5 times and calculate the mean.
**ERV**: after a quiet expiration, exhale maximally into the spirometer.
**VC**: take a maximal breath and exhale maximally into the spirometer; repeat three times and take the largest result.
**IRV** = VC − (TV + ERV).
Calculate the predicted VC by the formula and compare it with the actual VC.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: recording and analyzing a spirogram

items: Record quiet breathing (1 minute) on a computer spirograph — determine TV, respiratory rate and MV.
Perform the VC maneuver.
Forced expiration maneuver: take a maximal breath and exhale as quickly and completely as possible — determine FVC, FEV~1~ and PEF.
Calculate the Tiffeneau index.
Compare the results with the predicted values and determine the type of ventilatory disorder.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: pulse oximetry

items: The subject's finger should be warm and the nail free of polish; put the sensor on the finger.
Wait for the signal (plethysmogram wave) to stabilize (10–20 s); record the SpO~2~ and pulse readings.
Repeat the measurement after 30 s of breath-holding and after 20 squats.

Squeeze the finger tightly (reducing blood flow) and observe how the signal quality changes. **Expected result:** in a healthy person SpO~2~ is 96–99%; brief breath-holding and light exercise hardly change it (because of the upper flat part of the dissociation curve and the O~2~ reserve). When peripheral blood flow decreases, the signal deteriorates.

skills.title: Skill: interpreting a spirometry result

items: Evaluate the FVC (VC) as a percentage of the predicted value (≥ 80% — normal).
Evaluate the FEV~1~ relative to the predicted value.
Calculate the Tiffeneau index: < 70% — obstruction.
Index normal but FVC reduced — restriction is likely.
In obstruction, assess reversibility from the result of the bronchodilator test.

skills.title: Skill: calculating blood oxygen parameters

items: Oxygen capacity = Hb (g/l) × 1.34.
O~2~ in arterial blood = oxygen capacity × SaO~2~ + 0.003 × pO~2~ (ml/l).
Arteriovenous difference = arterial O~2~ − venous O~2~.
Utilization coefficient = arteriovenous difference / arterial O~2~ × 100%.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 25-year-old woman complains of cough and nocturnal attacks of breathlessness. Spirometry: FVC — 88% of predicted, FEV~1~ — 58%, Tiffeneau index 62%. 20 minutes after salbutamol inhalation the FEV~1~ increased by 22% (350 ml).
cases.ask: What type of ventilatory disorder is this? What does the result of the bronchodilator test show?
cases.answer: An obstructive disorder: the FEV~1~ and Tiffeneau index (< 70%) are reduced, while the FVC is almost normal. When the bronchi narrow, airway resistance increases (according to Poiseuille's law, inversely to the fourth power of the radius), and rapid expiration of air becomes difficult. The bronchodilator test is positive (≥ 12% and ≥ 200 ml) — the obstruction is reversible; the spasm of the bronchial smooth muscle relaxed under the action of a β~2~-adrenomimetic. This is typical of bronchial asthma.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A mountaineer climbed to an altitude of 5000 m, where the atmospheric pressure is ≈ 405 mm Hg. A few days later his blood 2,3-DPG was found to have increased.
cases.ask: Calculate the approximate alveolar pO~2~ at this altitude. What is the adaptive significance of the increase in 2,3-DPG?
cases.answer: In inspired air pO~2~ = (405 − 47) × 0.21 ≈ 75 mm Hg; taking alveolar CO~2~ and ventilation into account, alveolar pO~2~ falls to ≈ 45–50 mm Hg (hyperventilation raises it slightly). At this pO~2~ the saturation is about 80–85%. Hypoxia enhances 2,3-DPG synthesis in erythrocytes; 2,3-DPG binds to deoxyhemoglobin and reduces its affinity for O~2~ — the dissociation curve shifts to the right. As a result, although O~2~ binding in the lungs decreases slightly, O~2~ release in the tissues is greatly facilitated — the oxygen supply of the tissues improves.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with severe pneumonia is breathing rapidly and shallowly: respiratory rate 40 /min, tidal volume 200 ml. SpO~2~ 86%.
cases.ask: Calculate the MV and alveolar ventilation. Why is such breathing ineffective?
cases.answer: MV = 200 × 40 = 8 l/min (it appears close to normal). Alveolar ventilation = (200 − 150) × 40 = 2 l/min — more than two times lower than normal (4.2–5 l/min). A large part of each breath (150 ml) ventilates the dead space and does not reach gas exchange. The result is alveolar hypoventilation, hypoxemia (SpO~2~ 86%) and a risk of CO~2~ accumulation. In pneumonia the shunt in the inflamed alveoli also aggravates the hypoxemia.

topics.title: Methods of studying digestive function. Digestion in the oral cavity and stomach. Interrelation of the maxillofacial organs with the body's systems

goals.text: To teach the student the functions of the digestive system and the types of digestion, the methods of studying digestive function (I.P. Pavlov's chronic experimental methods and modern clinical methods), digestion in the oral cavity — the mechanisms of salivation, chewing and swallowing, digestion in the stomach — the composition of gastric juice and the phases and regulation of secretion, and the relationship of the maxillofacial organs with the other systems of the body.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the secretory, motor, absorptive, excretory, endocrine and protective functions of the digestive system;
the types of digestion (intrinsic, symbiotic, autolytic; cavity and membrane digestion);
I.P. Pavlov's fistula methods and modern methods of examination;
the composition and functions of saliva and the regulation of salivation;
the mechanisms of chewing and swallowing, masticatiography;
the composition of gastric juice and the significance of hydrochloric acid and pepsin;
the phases of gastric secretion and its neurohumoral regulation;
the relationship of the maxillofacial organs with digestion, respiration, speech and other systems.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: test the effect of salivary amylase on starch;
demonstrate the effect of pepsin on protein and the role of HCl in it;
evaluate the acidity parameters of gastric juice (total, free HCl);
evaluate chewing efficiency.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Both autonomic divisions **stimulate** salivation — unlike in other organs (synergism), but the composition of saliva differs: parasympathetic — “watery”, sympathetic — “thick” saliva.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The oral cavity is **the most important reflexogenic zone**: impulses from its receptors “start up” the whole digestive system. That is why chewing food well and perceiving its taste are also important for the subsequent stages of digestion.

sections.title: 1. Functions of the digestive system and types of digestion

blocks.text: **Digestion** is the mechanical and chemical processing of the complex substances of food (proteins, fats, carbohydrates) and their breakdown into simple compounds that have lost their species specificity and can be absorbed (amino acids, monosaccharides, fatty acids and monoglycerides).

blocks.title: Table 18.1. Functions of the digestive system
head: Function
Content
rows: Production of digestive juices (8–9 l per day)
Chewing, swallowing, mixing and propulsion of food, defecation
Passage of digestion products, water, salts and vitamins into the blood and lymph
Excretion of metabolic products, drugs and heavy metals
Gut hormones (gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin, GIP, motilin, ghrelin)

Participation in water-salt metabolism and acid–base balance

blocks.label: Figure 18.1
blocks.caption: Volume of digestive juices and the processes performed in different parts of the digestive system (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Types of digestion** (by the source of enzymes): **intrinsic** (the body's own enzymes), **symbiotic** (enzymes of the intestinal microflora — breakdown of fiber) and **autolytic** (the food's own enzymes, for example in breast milk). By location: **intracellular** (phagocytosis, pinocytosis) and **extracellular** — **cavity (distant)** digestion and **membrane (parietal)** digestion (A.M. Ugolev, topic 20).

**The conveyor principle of digestion:** each part of the digestive system processes the food in turn and prepares the next part; the activity of the preceding part influences that of the next (for example, the acid chyme formed in the stomach stimulates pancreatic secretion in the duodenum).
I.P. Pavlov's chronic experimental methods

Before Pavlov, digestion was studied in acute experiments. I.P. Pavlov developed **chronic experiment** methods, in which a surgical operation is performed on the animal beforehand, allowing long-term observation under natural conditions (Nobel Prize, 1904).

blocks.text: Modern methods used in humans

items: **Gastric juice sounding** (fractional examination with a thin tube) — basal and stimulated secretion, acidity.
**Intragastric pH-metry** (24-hour) — evaluation of the acid-forming function.
**Fibroesophagogastroduodenoscopy (FEGDS)**, colonoscopy, capsule endoscopy.
**Contrast radiography** (barium), ultrasound, CT, MRI.
**Electrogastrography**, manometry — motor activity.
**Sialometry** — measurement of salivary flow rate; **masticatiography**, **electromyography** — activity of the masticatory muscles.
**Radioisotope** and **breath tests** (for example, the urease breath test for Helicobacter pylori).

blocks.text: Food stays in the oral cavity for 15–20 s. Here food is processed **mechanically** (chewing), **moistened with saliva**, the **food bolus** is formed, partial chemical breakdown of carbohydrates begins and the taste of the food is evaluated.

blocks.label: Figure 18.2
blocks.caption: The oral cavity and the salivary glands (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Saliva

Saliva is produced by three pairs of major glands — the **parotid** (serous, watery, rich in enzymes), **submandibular** (mixed) and **sublingual** (mixed, rich in mucus) — and by many minor glands of the oral mucosa. **0.5–2 l** of saliva is secreted per day; 0.3–0.5 ml/min at rest and up to 3–4 ml/min when stimulated.

blocks.title: Table 18.3. Composition and functions of saliva
head: Component
Function
rows: Moistening and dissolving food (necessary for taste), forming the bolus
Breaks down starch and glycogen to dextrins and maltose (optimal pH 6.8–7)
Coats the bolus with mucus, facilitating swallowing; protects the mucosa
Buffer — protects tooth enamel from acids; pH 5.8–7.4
Active substances (kallikrein, growth factors, nerve growth factor)
Regeneration of the mucosa, wound healing

blocks.text: **Regulation of salivation** is mainly **reflex** (nervous): unconditioned reflexes (receptors of the oral cavity — taste, mechanical, temperature) and conditioned reflexes (the sight and smell of food, mealtime, kitchen sounds). The center is the **salivary nuclei of the medulla oblongata**.

items: **Parasympathetic** influence (superior and inferior salivary nuclei; via cranial nerves VII and IX) — a large amount of watery, enzyme-rich saliva; vessels dilate.
**Sympathetic** influence (Th~2~–Th~4~, superior cervical ganglion) — a small amount of thick, mucin-rich saliva (dry mouth during excitement).

parts.text: Both autonomic divisions **stimulate** salivation — unlike in other organs (synergism), but the composition of saliva differs: parasympathetic — “watery”, sympathetic — “thick” saliva.

**Xerostomia** (dry mouth) — in Sjögren syndrome, radiotherapy of the head and neck, many drugs (antidepressants, antihistamines, M-cholinergic blockers), dehydration. Because the protective and remineralizing functions of saliva are lost, **caries increases sharply**, and candidiasis and disorders of taste and swallowing occur. **Sialorrhea** (excessive drooling) — in Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, and during teething.

blocks.text: Chewing

**Chewing** is the grinding of food, mixing it with saliva and forming the bolus. The chewing center is in the **medulla oblongata** and pons (the chewing rhythm generator); chewing can also be controlled voluntarily (cortex). The masticatory muscles are innervated by the motor fibers of the **trigeminal nerve** (cranial nerve V). Receptors — the oral mucosa, the tooth periodontium (pressure receptors — regulate the biting force), and proprioceptors of the masticatory muscles and the temporomandibular joint.
**Chewing pressure** is 10–15 kg on the incisors and up to 50–80 kg on the molars (limited by the endurance of the periodontium).

**Masticatiography** is the graphic recording of the movements of the lower jaw. The masticatiogram shows the phases of one chewing period: I — rest; II — taking food into the mouth; III — the beginning of chewing (adaptation); IV — the main (rhythmic) chewing phase; V — formation of the bolus and swallowing.

blocks.label: Figure 18.3
blocks.caption: Masticatiogram: phases of the chewing period (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Swallowing
**Swallowing** is a complex reflex act that ensures the passage of the bolus from the oral cavity to the stomach (F. Magendie). It consists of three phases:

items: **Oral (voluntary) phase** — the tongue lifts the bolus toward the palate and pushes it into the pharynx.

**Pharyngeal (involuntary, rapid) phase** — the soft palate rises and closes the nasopharynx; the larynx rises and the **epiglottis** closes the laryngeal inlet; breathing stops reflexly (swallowing apnea); the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes. The center is in the medulla oblongata.
**Esophageal (involuntary, slow) phase** — a peristaltic wave carries the bolus to the stomach in 2–9 s (liquid 1–2 s); the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes reflexly.

blocks.label: Figure 18.4
blocks.caption: The pharyngeal phase of swallowing: the epiglottis closes the airway (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: When the swallowing center is damaged (stroke, bulbar palsy), **dysphagia** and entry of food into the airways (aspiration, aspiration pneumonia) are observed. In insufficiency of the lower esophageal sphincter the gastric contents return to the esophagus — **gastroesophageal reflux disease** (heartburn).

sections.title: 4. Interrelation of the maxillofacial organs with the body's systems

blocks.text: The maxillofacial region (oral cavity, teeth, jaws, temporomandibular joint, masticatory and facial muscles, salivary glands, tongue) is not only the initial part of digestion; it is closely linked with many systems of the body.

blocks.title: Table 18.4. Relationship of the maxillofacial organs with other systems
head: System
Nature of the relationship
rows: Reflexes from the receptors of the oral cavity start gastric and pancreatic secretion and bile release (the complex reflex phase). Poor chewing (missing teeth, faulty dentures) burdens the function of the stomach and intestine

The mouth and pharynx are a common pathway; the oral cavity takes part in breathing, and breathing stops reflexly during swallowing; when nasal breathing is impaired, mouth breathing affects the development of the teeth and occlusion
The tongue, lips, teeth and palate take part in the articulation of sounds; missing teeth and occlusal defects impair speech
Taste, smell (retronasal olfaction), pain, temperature, tactile and proprioceptive sensation; evaluation of food quality

Chronic foci of infection in the oral cavity (periodontitis, caries) contribute through bacteremia to infective endocarditis and atherosclerosis; reflex reactions during dental procedures (bradycardia, fainting)
Periodontitis and xerostomia in diabetes mellitus, while periodontitis worsens glycemic control; gingivitis during hormonal changes (puberty, pregnancy)
The tonsils (Waldeyer's ring), IgA and lysozyme in saliva — the first line of defense
Very extensive sensory innervation by the trigeminal nerve; toothache radiates to other areas; chewing has a toning effect on the central nervous system
The sensation of thirst (dry mouth), loss of water and bicarbonates with saliva
In animals (dogs) heat loss through evaporation of saliva and panting

parts.text: The oral cavity is **the most important reflexogenic zone**: impulses from its receptors “start up” the whole digestive system. That is why chewing food well and perceiving its taste are also important for the subsequent stages of digestion.

blocks.text: Functions of the stomach: **storage** of food (up to 1.5–2.5 l), mechanical and chemical processing, formation of **chyme** and its passage in portions into the intestine; protective (bactericidal), endocrine and excretory (urea, drugs) functions, and production of **Castle's intrinsic factor**.
Gastric juice
**2–2.5 l** of gastric juice is secreted per day; it is a colorless acidic fluid (pH **0.8–1.5**; 1.5–3.5 when mixed with food in the stomach cavity).

blocks.title: Table 18.5. Cells of the gastric glands and their products

Location
Product
rows: Glands of the fundus and body
Glands of the fundus and body

blocks.text: **Functions of hydrochloric acid:** converts pepsinogens into pepsin and creates the optimal pH for its action; denatures and swells proteins; bactericidal action; regulates the passage of food from the stomach to the intestine (pyloric reflex); stimulates the formation of secretin in the duodenum; aids iron absorption (Fe^3+^ → Fe^2+^).

blocks.label: Figure 18.5
blocks.caption: Formation of hydrochloric acid in the parietal cell and its regulation

blocks.text: **Pepsins** break down proteins into large polypeptides (optimal pH 1.5–2.0 and 3.2–3.5); they also break down collagen. **Gastric lipase** acts only on emulsified fats (milk fat); it is important in infants. In the stomach salivary amylase continues to work inside the bolus until the acid penetrates it.

The **gastric mucus-bicarbonate barrier** protects the stomach wall from self-digestion: the mucus gel layer, the bicarbonates beneath it (pH ≈ 7), the rapid renewal of epithelial cells, and prostaglandins (which enhance mucus and bicarbonate secretion and improve blood flow).

parts.text: **Helicobacter pylori** infection, **NSAIDs** (aspirin, ibuprofen — they reduce prostaglandin synthesis), alcohol, smoking and stress weaken the protective barrier — gastritis and **gastroduodenal ulcer** develop. Treatment uses **proton pump inhibitors** (omeprazole — blocks H^+^/K^+^-ATPase), H~2~-histamine blockers (famotidine) and eradication of H. pylori.

blocks.text: Phases and regulation of gastric secretion

blocks.label: Figure 18.6
blocks.caption: Phases of gastric secretion

blocks.text: **Main stimulants: acetylcholine** (vagus nerve; M~3~-cholinergic receptors), **gastrin** (G cells; released under the influence of peptides, amino acids, gastric distension and the vagus) and **histamine** (ECL cells; H~2~ receptors — the most powerful stimulant). **Inhibitors:** somatostatin, secretin, cholecystokinin, GIP, prostaglandins, a fall of pH in the stomach cavity below 1.5–2 (negative feedback), sympathetic influence.

**Adaptation to the type of food** (Pavlov): bread — the smallest amount of juice but the richest in enzymes; meat — the largest amount and the most acidic juice; milk — a small amount of juice poor in enzymes (fat has an inhibitory effect).
Motor activity of the stomach

When food enters, the proximal part of the stomach relaxes reflexly — **receptive relaxation** (via the vagus) — so food accumulates without a rise in pressure. In the distal part **peristaltic contractions** (≈ 3 /min; pacemaker — the Cajal cells on the greater curvature) mix the chyme and pass it in small portions through the pylorus into the duodenum. Food remains in the stomach for 3–10 hours: carbohydrate food is evacuated quickly, protein food more slowly, and fatty food most slowly. **Evacuation** is inhibited by acid, fats and hypertonic solutions in the duodenum (the **enterogastric reflex**, secretin, CCK).
**Vomiting** is a protective reflex; its center is in the medulla oblongata (the vomiting center and the trigger zone on the floor of the fourth ventricle, which is sensitive to toxins in the blood).
Exercise 1: effect of salivary amylase on starch

items: Rinse the mouth with water, collect 2 ml of saliva and dilute it 5 times with water.
Pour 2 ml of 1% starch solution into each of three test tubes.
Add diluted saliva to tube 1, boiled saliva to tube 2 and water to tube 3 (control).
Keep the tubes at 37 °C for 10–15 minutes.

Take a sample from each tube and test it with iodine solution (for starch) and the Trommer (Fehling) test (for reducing sugars). **Result and analysis:** in tube 1 there is no blue color with iodine (the starch has been broken down) and the Trommer test is positive — maltose has formed. In tube 2 (boiled saliva — the enzyme is denatured) and tube 3 the starch is preserved (blue color). This proves that salivary amylase breaks down starch and is an enzyme of protein nature.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: effect of pepsin on protein and the role of HCl

items: Put identical pieces of fibrin (or egg white) into four test tubes.
Add to tube 1 — gastric juice; tube 2 — boiled gastric juice; tube 3 — neutralized gastric juice (with NaHCO~3~); tube 4 — 0.5% HCl.

Keep at 37 °C for 30–40 minutes and compare the state of the protein. **Result and analysis:** the protein is digested (dissolves or becomes transparent) only in tube 1. Boiling inactivates pepsin; pepsin does not work in a neutral medium; HCl itself only swells the protein but does not break it down. Therefore protein digestion requires **pepsin and an acidic medium** together.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: evaluating the acidity of gastric juice (from results)
By the titration method, the acidity of gastric juice is expressed as the number of ml of 0.1 N NaOH needed to neutralize 100 ml of juice (titration units).

blocks.title: Table 18.6. Normal values of gastric juice acidity (in titration units)
head: Parameter
Basal secretion (fasting)
Stimulated secretion

blocks.text: Analyze the results: above normal — a hyperacid state (duodenal ulcer); low — a hypoacid state (atrophic gastritis); absence of free HCl — achlorhydria.
Exercise 4: evaluating chewing efficiency (Gelman test)

items: The subject chews 5 g of almonds (or standard nuts) for 50 s.
The chewed mass is passed through a sieve (2.4 mm mesh).

The percentage that passed through the sieve is calculated. **Interpretation:** with a healthy dentition chewing efficiency is close to 100%; when teeth are missing and the denture is unfit, it decreases sharply.

items: Indicate which receptors and which nerve take part in the complex reflex phase.
For the gastric phase, write down the mechanical (distension) and chemical (peptides) factors and the role of gastrin and histamine.

skills.title: Skill: measuring the salivary flow rate (sialometry)

items: In the morning, on an empty stomach, the subject spits saliva into a test tube for 5 minutes without swallowing (unstimulated saliva).
Measure the volume and calculate it in ml/min (normal 0.3–0.5 ml/min).
Stimulate with 2% citric acid solution and repeat the measurement (normal 1–3 ml/min).
Evaluate the result: unstimulated saliva < 0.1 ml/min — hyposalivation.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After radiotherapy for a head and neck tumor, a 55-year-old patient developed dry mouth, difficulty swallowing food and altered taste. Within six months caries developed in many teeth.
cases.ask: What are these changes associated with? Which functions of saliva are disturbed?
cases.answer: The radiotherapy damaged the salivary gland tissue — xerostomia (hyposalivation) developed. The water of saliva moistens food and dissolves taste substances — when it decreases, taste is impaired; mucin lubricates the bolus — when it is lacking, swallowing becomes difficult. The salivary buffer systems (bicarbonate, phosphate) neutralize the acids formed by bacteria in dental plaque, calcium and phosphate remineralize the enamel, and lysozyme, lactoferrin and IgA provide antibacterial protection — because these functions were lost, caries developed rapidly. Help: saliva substitutes, fluoride preparations, oral hygiene.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 40-year-old patient has epigastric pain on an empty stomach and at night; the pain decreases after eating. FEGDS revealed a duodenal ulcer and H. pylori. Gastric juice acidity is increased.
cases.ask: Explain the physiological mechanism of ulcer development on the basis of the balance of protective and aggressive factors. What is the effect of a proton pump inhibitor?
cases.answer: An ulcer develops when the balance between aggressive factors (HCl, pepsin, H. pylori) and protective factors (the mucus-bicarbonate barrier, prostaglandins, blood flow, epithelial regeneration) is disturbed. H. pylori reduces the somatostatin-producing D cells in the antrum — gastrin release and HCl secretion increase; the excess acid enters the duodenum and damages the mucosa. Food buffers the acid — the pain decreases. Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly block the H^+^/K^+^-ATPase in the parietal cell — the final stage of HCl secretion stops (the response to any stimulant decreases) and the ulcer heals; H. pylori is eliminated with antibiotics.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An elderly patient who has lost many teeth and does not wear a denture swallows food without chewing it well. He complains of heaviness in the stomach, bloating and constipation.
cases.ask: How does impaired chewing affect the subsequent stages of digestion?
cases.answer: Chewing grinds food, increases the surface on which digestive enzymes act and mixes it with saliva. Poorly chewed large pieces are digested slowly in the stomach and stay there long (a feeling of heaviness). The reflex influence from the receptors of the oral cavity (the complex reflex phase) weakens — the “start-up” of gastric and pancreatic secretion and bile release is reduced. Undigested residues enhance fermentation and putrefaction in the large intestine (bloating). That is why dental treatment and prosthetics matter for the whole digestive system.

topics.title: Motor activity of the gastrointestinal tract. The role of the liver in digestion. Bile secretion and its properties. Secretory activity of the pancreas

goals.text: To teach the student the properties of the smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract and the types of movement, their nervous (enteric nervous system and autonomic nerves) and humoral regulation, the digestive and non-digestive functions of the liver, the formation, composition, properties and secretion of bile, and the composition of pancreatic juice and the regulation of its secretion.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the electrical activity of the gastrointestinal smooth muscles (slow waves, Cajal cells);
the structure and function of the enteric (metasympathetic) nervous system;
the types of movement of the small and large intestine, the migrating motor complex;
the nervous and humoral factors regulating motility;
the functions of the liver;
the composition of bile, the function of bile acids and their enterohepatic circulation;
the regulation of bile formation and secretion;
the composition of pancreatic juice, its enzymes and their activation, and the phases and regulation of secretion.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: demonstrate experimentally the role of bile in emulsifying fats;
prove the importance of bile for the action of pancreatic lipase;
explain the effect of adrenaline and acetylcholine on intestinal motility.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Secretin** (the first hormone discovered — W. Bayliss and E. Starling, 1902) mainly evokes juice rich in **water and bicarbonates** — it neutralizes the acid chyme. **Cholecystokinin** mainly evokes juice rich in **enzymes** and contracts the gallbladder. Together they enhance each other's effect (potentiation).

sections.title: 1. Motor activity of the gastrointestinal tract

blocks.text: Properties of smooth muscles

The wall of the gastrointestinal tract (except the upper esophagus and the external anal sphincter) contains smooth muscles: an inner **circular** and an outer **longitudinal** layer. They work as a **functional syncytium** (gap junctions).

Smooth muscles show rhythmic oscillations of the membrane potential — **slow waves** (the basic electrical rhythm); they are generated by the **interstitial cells of Cajal** (pacemakers). Slow waves do not cause contraction by themselves; if the membrane reaches threshold at their peak, **action potentials (spikes)** appear and the muscle contracts. Frequency: ≈ 3 /min in the stomach, 11–12 /min in the duodenum, 8–9 /min in the ileum.
The enteric nervous system
The **enteric (metasympathetic) nervous system** is an independent network of ≈ 100 million neurons in the gastrointestinal wall (the “second brain”):

items: **The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus** — between the circular and longitudinal layers; mainly regulates **motor** activity.
**The submucosal (Meissner) plexus** — regulates **secretion**, absorption and local blood flow.

blocks.text: The enteric nervous system carries out peristaltic and secretory reflexes even without the central nervous system; the autonomic nerves only modify its activity.

blocks.label: Figure 19.1
blocks.caption: Layers of the intestinal wall and nerve plexuses (Alavia O.T., 2018)

The circular muscles contract above and relax below — the wave spreads in the distal direction (the “law of the intestine”, Bayliss–Starling)
A wave of strong contractions spreading from the stomach to the ileum every 90–120 minutes on an empty stomach (motilin)
The “intestinal housekeeper” — sweeps out residues and bacteria

blocks.text: The **ileocecal sphincter (Bauhin's valve)** regulates the passage of chyme from the ileum into the cecum in portions and prevents the reflux of colonic contents; it opens reflexly when food enters the stomach (the **gastroileal reflex**).
Regulation of motility

head: Stimulating
Inhibiting

Sharp distension of the intestine (irritation of the peritoneum)

blocks.text: **Gastrointestinal reflexes:** gastroileal, **gastrocolic** (when food enters the stomach, colonic motility and the urge to defecate increase), **enterogastric** (when the duodenum is distended, gastric motility and secretion are inhibited), **intestino-intestinal** (when one part of the intestine is strongly distended, the other parts are inhibited).

parts.text: **Paralytic ileus** is reflex inhibition of intestinal peristalsis (predominance of sympathetic influence) after abdominal surgery, in peritonitis and hypokalemia. The abdomen is distended and no peristalsis is heard. Treatment includes restoring electrolytes and AChE inhibitors (proserin/neostigmine).

sections.title: 2. The role of the liver in digestion

blocks.text: The liver is the largest gland in the body (1.5 kg), the “central biochemical laboratory”. It is the first to receive all the blood flowing from the intestine (through the portal vein).

blocks.title: Table 19.3. Functions of the liver
head: Function
Content
rows: Bile formation — for the digestion and absorption of fats
Synthesis and breakdown of glycogen, gluconeogenesis — maintaining blood glucose
Synthesis of plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin and other clotting factors); deamination of amino acids; synthesis of urea (detoxification of ammonia)
Synthesis of lipoproteins, cholesterol and phospholipids; β-oxidation of fatty acids; formation of ketone bodies
Detoxification of toxins from the intestine (indole, skatole, phenol), drugs and alcohol by the cytochrome P450 system and conjugation
Excretion of bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs and heavy metals with bile
Glycogen, iron (ferritin), vitamins (A, D, B~12~), blood depot

parts.text: **In liver failure** ammonia is not detoxified, accumulates in the blood and affects the brain (**hepatic encephalopathy**); synthesis of albumin and clotting factors decreases — edema, ascites and a tendency to bleed; bilirubin metabolism is disturbed and jaundice develops; the metabolism of drugs and hormones slows down (doses must be reduced).

blocks.text: **Bile** is formed **continuously** in liver cells (hepatocytes) (**0.5–1.2 l** per day), but it is released into the duodenum only during **digestion**. Between meals bile accumulates **in the gallbladder** and is concentrated 5–10 times (water and electrolytes are reabsorbed).

blocks.title: Table 19.4. Composition of hepatic and gallbladder bile
head: Parameter
Hepatic bile
Gallbladder bile

blocks.text: **Composition of bile:** water, **bile acids and their salts** (the main part), **bile pigments** (conjugated bilirubin — gives the color), cholesterol, phospholipids (lecithin), electrolytes (much bicarbonate), mucus.
Functions of bile:

items: **Emulsifies fats** — by reducing surface tension it breaks large fat droplets into small ones; the surface on which lipase acts increases thousands of times.
**Activates pancreatic and intestinal lipase**.
Forms **micelles** with fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and **fat-soluble vitamins** (A, D, E, K), ensuring their absorption.
**Neutralizes** the acid chyme coming from the stomach (bicarbonate) and stops the action of pepsin.
**Enhances intestinal peristalsis**.
**Bacteriostatic** action — reduces putrefactive processes.
**Excretory** — excretes bilirubin, cholesterol and drugs.
Stimulates bile formation and pancreatic secretion.

blocks.text: Enterohepatic circulation of bile acids

blocks.label: Figure 19.3
blocks.caption: Enterohepatic circulation of bile acids

blocks.text: Regulation of bile formation and secretion

items: **Bile formation (choleresis)** is enhanced by: bile acids returning to the blood (the strongest stimulus), **secretin** (water and bicarbonate), the vagus nerve, gastrin, and protein and fatty food.

**Bile release (cholekinesis)** is enhanced by: **cholecystokinin (CCK)** — contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the **sphincter of Oddi** (the main factor); the vagus nerve. The strongest stimulants are egg yolk, milk, meat and fats. The sympathetic nerves relax the gallbladder and contract the sphincter.

parts.text: **Gallstone disease** — if the amount of cholesterol in bile increases relative to bile acids and phospholipids (lithogenic bile), cholesterol crystallizes and forms stones. After fatty food CCK contracts the gallbladder, and when a stone blocks the neck of the gallbladder, pain appears under the right costal margin (biliary colic). When the duct is completely blocked, bile does not enter the intestine: fats are not digested (**steatorrhea**), the stool is discolored (acholic stool), vitamin K is not absorbed (tendency to bleed), and **obstructive jaundice** develops.

blocks.text: The exocrine part of the pancreas (acini and ducts) produces **1.5–2.0 l** of alkaline (pH **7.8–8.4**) juice per day. It is the most important digestive juice — it contains enzymes that break down all nutrients.

blocks.title: Table 19.5. Enzymes of pancreatic juice
head: Group
Enzyme (inactive form)
Activator
Effect
rows: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase; duodenal mucosa), then trypsin itself (autocatalysis)
Breaks down proteins and peptides at internal bonds; activates the other proenzymes
Breaks down peptides from the C-terminus
Starch and glycogen to maltose and oligosaccharides
Triglycerides to monoglycerides and fatty acids

blocks.text: The gland is protected from self-digestion: the proteolytic enzymes are secreted as **inactive proenzymes**; the acinar cells contain a **trypsin inhibitor** (SPINK1); the enzymes are activated only in the intestine.

blocks.label: Figure 19.4
blocks.caption: Pancreatic juice, the regulation of its secretion and the breakdown of nutrients in the small intestine (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Regulation of secretion

Pancreatic secretion also proceeds in three phases: **complex reflex** (vagus nerve, ≈ 20%), **gastric** (gastric distension — vagovagal reflex, gastrin; ≈ 10%) and **intestinal** (the main one — ≈ 70%).

blocks.label: Figure 19.5
blocks.caption: Humoral regulation of pancreatic secretion

parts.text: **Secretin** (the first hormone discovered — W. Bayliss and E. Starling, 1902) mainly evokes juice rich in **water and bicarbonates** — it neutralizes the acid chyme. **Cholecystokinin** mainly evokes juice rich in **enzymes** and contracts the gallbladder. Together they enhance each other's effect (potentiation).

blocks.text: **Adaptation to the type of food:** bread — much amylase; meat — much trypsin; milk and fatty food — much lipase.

parts.text: **Acute pancreatitis** — the enzymes are activated inside the gland and “digest” it (alcohol, blockage of the duct by a gallstone). **Amylase and lipase** rise sharply in the blood and urine (a diagnostic criterion). In **chronic pancreatitis** and **cystic fibrosis** exocrine insufficiency develops: fats are not digested (steatorrhea), protein digestion is impaired (creatorrhea), weight loss; treatment — enzyme preparations (pancreatin).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: emulsification of fats by bile

items: Pour 2 ml of water into each of two test tubes.
Add 1 ml of bile (or a solution of bile salts) to tube 1 and 1 ml of water to tube 2.
Add 3–5 drops of vegetable oil to both, shake vigorously and let stand for 5 minutes.

Put a drop from each on a slide and examine under the microscope. **Result and analysis:** in the tube with bile the oil remains broken into small droplets for a long time (a stable emulsion), and small uniform droplets are seen under the microscope. In the tube with water the oil quickly separates to the surface. Bile acids reduce surface tension and emulsify fats.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: the importance of bile for the action of pancreatic lipase

items: Put 5 ml of milk (or fat emulsion) and phenolphthalein (pink in an alkaline medium) into each of three test tubes; bring them to a pale pink color with a weak alkali.
Add to tube 1 — pancreatin (lipase) solution + bile; tube 2 — pancreatin + water; tube 3 — water only.

Keep at 37 °C and observe the time of color change. **Result and analysis:** the pink color disappears fastest (fatty acids are formed and the medium becomes acidic) in tube 1, more slowly in tube 2; in tube 3 the color does not change. Bile activates lipase and, by emulsifying fats, increases the surface on which the enzyme acts.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: effect of mediators on the motility of an isolated intestinal segment (demonstration or video)

items: An isolated segment of rabbit small intestine is suspended in a bath filled with Ringer–Tyrode solution at 37 °C and aerated with air, and its contractions are recorded.
Acetylcholine solution is added to the bath; recording continues.

After washing, adrenaline is added. **Result and analysis:** the isolated intestine contracts rhythmically on its own — automaticity (Cajal cells and the enteric nervous system). Acetylcholine increases the amplitude of contractions and the tone (parasympathetic effect), while adrenaline reduces them (sympathetic effect).

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing types of jaundice by bile pigment metabolism (schematic)

items: Determine which bilirubin fraction is increased in the blood: unconjugated (indirect) or conjugated (direct).
Evaluate the presence of bilirubin (only conjugated bilirubin passes) and urobilin in the urine.
Evaluate the color of the stool (stercobilin).
Unconjugated bilirubin increased, stool dark, much urobilin in the urine — hemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice.
Conjugated bilirubin increased, stool discolored, bilirubin in the urine, no urobilin — obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice.
Both fractions increased — parenchymal (hepatic) jaundice.

Identify weight loss and signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Evaluate fecal elastase-1 (normal > 200 µg/g).
Explain the result by linking it to the function of the pancreatic enzymes.
