cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After fatty food a 45-year-old obese woman developed severe pain under the right costal margin, followed by yellowing of the skin and sclerae, dark urine and pale stools. Blood conjugated bilirubin is increased.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the signs on the basis of the physiology of bile.
cases.answer: Gallstone disease with blockage of the common bile duct by a stone — obstructive jaundice. Fatty food enhances the release of CCK in the duodenum; the gallbladder contracts, the stone moves and blocks the duct — biliary colic. Bile does not enter the intestine: the conjugated bilirubin in the liver returns to the blood (jaundice), and because it is water-soluble it passes into the urine (dark urine); no stercobilin is formed in the intestine (pale stools). Because bile acids are lacking, fats are not emulsified or digested (steatorrhea), and fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin K — blood coagulation) are not absorbed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient who has consumed alcohol for many years has weight loss, abundant shiny, fatty, foul-smelling stools and bloating. Fecal elastase-1 is reduced.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the mechanism of the signs.
cases.answer: Chronic pancreatitis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. The acinar tissue has been replaced by fibrosis, and the production of lipase, proteases and amylase has decreased. Because of lipase deficiency triglycerides are not broken down or absorbed — steatorrhea (fatty, shiny stools); protein digestion is impaired — creatorrhea; undigested substances ferment and putrefy in the large intestine under the action of bacteria — bloating, foul smell. Because nutrients are not absorbed, weight loss develops. Treatment: stopping alcohol and enzyme preparations (pancreatin) with meals.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: On the second day after abdominal surgery the patient's abdomen is distended, no intestinal peristalsis is heard and no gas is passed. Blood K^+^ 3.1 mmol/l.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanisms of the arrest of intestinal motility.
cases.answer: Postoperative paralytic ileus. When the peritoneum and intestine are irritated, the sympathetic nervous system is reflexly activated — noradrenaline inhibits the intestinal smooth muscle and enteric neurons; pain and stress (catecholamines), anesthesia and opioid analgesics also weaken peristalsis. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the smooth muscle membrane and reduces excitability — motility weakens further. Treatment: restoration of potassium, early mobilization and, if needed, AChE inhibitors (proserin/neostigmine), which enhance the parasympathetic influence.

topics.title: Digestion in the small and large intestine. Ugolev's experiment

goals.text: To teach the student digestion in the small intestine — the composition and secretion of intestinal juice, A.M. Ugolev's doctrine of cavity and membrane (parietal) digestion, the mechanisms of absorption of nutrients, water and electrolytes, the processes in the large intestine, the role of the microflora and the mechanism of defecation; in laboratory work, to master demonstrating the efficiency of membrane digestion compared with cavity digestion (Ugolev's experiment).
By the end of the class the student should know:

the composition of intestinal juice and the regulation of its secretion;
cavity, membrane and intracellular digestion;
the final digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats;

water absorption in the large intestine, the microflora and its functions;
the defecation reflex and its regulation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Advantages of membrane digestion: 1) **high speed** — the enzymes are arranged in order over a large surface and the substrate is close to them; 2) **coupling of digestion and absorption** — the monomers formed are passed directly to the transport systems; 3) **sterility** — microorganisms cannot use the monomers.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When the spinal cord is damaged above the sacral segments, the defecation reflex is preserved but voluntary control is lost (reflex automatic emptying). When the sacral segments themselves are damaged, the reflex is lost — fecal retention and incontinence are observed.

sections.title: 1. Structural features of the small intestine

blocks.text: The small intestine (duodenum, jejunum and ileum) is 3–5 m long in a living person. Here digestion is completed and almost all nutrients are absorbed. Structures that increase the absorptive surface:

blocks.title: Table 20.1. Structures that increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine
head: Structure
Increase in surface
rows: Microvilli (1500–3000 on each enterocyte — the “brush border”)

blocks.text: In the center of each villus there is an arteriole, a capillary network, a venule and a lymphatic capillary (the **lacteal**); smooth muscle fibers contract the villus rhythmically, enhancing lymph and blood flow (the “villus pump”; its hormone is villikinin).

On the surface of the microvilli there is the **glycocalyx** — a mesh layer of glycoproteins and mucopolysaccharides; enzymes are adsorbed in it, and it acts as a barrier to the intestinal microflora.

Intestinal juice is produced by the **Brunner glands** (in the duodenum — rich in mucus and bicarbonate) and the **crypts of Lieberkühn** (throughout the intestine). **1.5–2.0 l** is secreted per day; pH **7.2–8.6**.

The juice consists of two parts: a **liquid part** (water, electrolytes, bicarbonates, mucus) and a **dense part** — shed enterocytes (they disintegrate and release their enzymes into the intestinal lumen). The intestinal epithelium is completely renewed in 3–5 days.

**Enzymes of intestinal juice** (more than 20): **enterokinase** (enteropeptidase — activates trypsinogen), peptidases (aminopeptidases, dipeptidases), disaccharidases (**maltase, saccharase (sucrase), lactase**, isomaltase), intestinal lipase, phospholipases, alkaline phosphatase, nucleases.

**Regulation of secretion** is mainly **local**: mechanical and chemical stimulation of the mucosa by chyme (enteric nervous system reflexes); humoral factors — VIP, gastrin, secretin, CCK and motilin enhance it; somatostatin inhibits it.

sections.title: 3. Cavity and membrane digestion (A.M. Ugolev's doctrine)

blocks.text: A.M. Ugolev (1958) identified two main types of digestion in the small intestine:

items: **Cavity (distant) digestion** — in the intestinal lumen, mainly under the action of pancreatic enzymes; large molecules (polymers) undergo initial breakdown (oligomers are formed).

**Membrane (parietal) digestion** — on the surface of the microvilli, under the action of enzymes located in the glycocalyx and membrane; the intermediate products are broken down to the final stage (monomers). Membrane digestion is **the final stage of digestion** and is directly coupled with **absorption**.

blocks.label: Figure 20.1
blocks.caption: Membrane digestion: A — microvilli and glycocalyx, substrate molecules reaching the membrane through the glycocalyx; B — location of the cavity and membrane enzymes and the transport systems (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 20.2
blocks.caption: Stages of digestion in the small intestine

blocks.title: Table 20.2. Comparative characteristics of cavity and membrane digestion
head: Feature
Cavity digestion
Membrane digestion
rows: Yes — the spaces between microvilli are too narrow for bacteria (glycocalyx barrier)
Very high (enzymes arranged in order, a “digestion-absorption conveyor”)

parts.text: Advantages of membrane digestion: 1) **high speed** — the enzymes are arranged in order over a large surface and the substrate is close to them; 2) **coupling of digestion and absorption** — the monomers formed are passed directly to the transport systems; 3) **sterility** — microorganisms cannot use the monomers.

**Lactase deficiency** is the most common disorder of membrane digestion (widespread in adults). Lactose passes undigested into the large intestine: it draws water osmotically and bacteria ferment it — bloating, pain and diarrhea after milk. In **celiac disease** (an immune response to gluten) the villi atrophy — membrane digestion and the absorptive surface decrease sharply (malabsorption syndrome).

blocks.text: **Absorption** is the passage of substances from the lumen of the digestive system into the blood and lymph. The main site is the **small intestine** (most substances in its proximal part, B~12~ and bile acids in the ileum). Little is absorbed in the oral cavity (nitroglycerin); water, alcohol and some drugs are absorbed in the stomach, and water and electrolytes in the large intestine.

**Mechanisms of absorption:** simple and facilitated diffusion, osmosis, filtration, primary and **secondary active transport** (driven by the Na^+^ gradient), endocytosis (pinocytosis — antibodies from breast milk in infants).

They reach the membrane in bile micelles and enter by diffusion; in the enterocyte triglycerides are resynthesized and chylomicrons are formed
Lymph (lacteals) — into the blood via the thoracic duct

blocks.text: Absorption of water, electrolytes, vitamins and iron

items: **Water** — 8–9 l of fluid enters the intestine per day (2 l with food + 7 l of digestive juices); ≈ 7–8 l is absorbed in the small intestine and 1–1.5 l in the large intestine; 100–150 ml leaves with the feces. Water is absorbed passively along the **osmotic** gradient, together with dissolved substances (Na^+^, glucose).
**Na^+^** — actively (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase); together with glucose and amino acids; aldosterone enhances it in the large intestine.
**Ca^2+^** — absorbed actively in the duodenum under the action of calcitriol (vitamin D).
**Iron** — in the duodenum; it is well absorbed as Fe^2+^ (ascorbic acid and HCl reduce Fe^3+^); heme iron by a separate route; regulated by hepcidin according to the body's needs.
**Vitamin B~12~** — forms a complex with Castle's intrinsic factor and is absorbed **in the terminal ileum**.
**Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)** — in micelles, with the participation of bile acids.

parts.text: **Oral rehydration** (in dehydration, for example in cholera) is based on the co-transport of glucose and sodium (SGLT1): when a glucose-salt solution is drunk, Na^+^ is absorbed together with glucose and water follows — even in severe secretory diarrhea. This discovery has saved the lives of millions of children.

blocks.text: 0.5–1.5 l of chyme enters the large intestine per day. Its main functions are **absorption of water and electrolytes** (formation of feces), microbial digestion, and storage and elimination of feces.

**Juice of the large intestine** — small in amount (50–60 ml per day), rich in mucus, alkaline (pH 8.5–9.0), with few enzymes. The mucus protects the intestinal wall and binds the fecal masses together.
The intestinal microflora

The large intestine contains 10^11^–10^12^ /g bacteria (more than 500 species), mainly anaerobes: bifidobacteria, lactobacilli, bacteroides, and also Escherichia coli and others. Their total mass is 1–1.5 kg.

blocks.title: Table 20.4. Functions of the intestinal microflora
head: Function
Content
rows: Ferments fiber (cellulose, pectin) to form short-chain fatty acids — an energy source for colonocytes
Vitamin K, B vitamins (B~1~, B~2~, B~6~, B~12~, folate, biotin)
Prevents the multiplication of pathogenic microorganisms
Metabolism of bile acids, bilirubin (urobilinogen, stercobilin) and cholesterol
Indole, skatole and phenol from protein residues (detoxified in the liver); gases

parts.text: Long-term antibiotic treatment disturbs the balance of the microflora (**dysbacteriosis**): diarrhea, vitamin K deficiency, candidiasis and Clostridioides difficile infection (pseudomembranous colitis) may develop. Fiber and fermented milk products support the beneficial microflora.

blocks.text: Motility of the large intestine and defecation

Movements in the large intestine are slow: **pendular**, **haustral** contractions (mixing, aiding water absorption), **peristaltic**, and 3–4 times a day, often after meals (**gastrocolic reflex**) — **strong propulsive contractions (mass movements)** that push the contents into the rectum. Food residues remain in the large intestine for 12–24 hours.

**Defecation** is a complex reflex act. When feces enter the rectum and stretch its wall (pressure 40–50 cm H₂O), the mechanoreceptors are excited. **The center of the defecation reflex** is in the **sacral** (S~2~–S~4~) segments of the spinal cord; through the pelvic (parasympathetic) nerves it ensures contraction of the rectum and relaxation of the **internal anal sphincter** (smooth muscle, involuntary). The **external anal sphincter** is striated muscle (pudendal nerve) and is controlled **voluntarily**: the cerebral cortex can delay or enhance defecation (this control develops by the age of two). Defecation is aided by contraction of the abdominal muscles and descent of the diaphragm (straining).

parts.text: When the spinal cord is damaged above the sacral segments, the defecation reflex is preserved but voluntary control is lost (reflex automatic emptying). When the sacral segments themselves are damaged, the reflex is lost — fecal retention and incontinence are observed.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: Ugolev's experiment — proving membrane digestion
**Aim:** to show the efficiency of digestion associated with the intestinal mucosa (membrane digestion) compared with cavity digestion.

items: Take the small intestine of a freshly killed rat (or another animal), wash it with Ringer's solution and divide it into three pieces of equal length.
**Sample 1** (membrane + cavity digestion): a piece of intestine is cut lengthwise and placed with the mucosa intact in a substrate solution (starch or maltose, 37 °C).

**Sample 2** (cavity digestion only): a piece of intestine is shaken several times in the same volume of solution and the “washings” are collected (non-adsorbed enzymes) — the substrate is added to these washings.
**Sample 3** (control): substrate and solution only.
Incubate all tubes at 37 °C for 20–30 minutes.

Determine the amount of glucose formed by the glucose oxidase method (or test strips, the Trommer test) and compare the results. **Expected result and analysis:** the most glucose is formed in the sample with the mucosa (1); considerably less in the washings (2); and none in the control (3). Therefore the main part of the enzymes is not free in the intestinal lumen but **bound to the membrane and glycocalyx of the enterocytes**, and the final stage of digestion proceeds efficiently precisely there. This experiment proves Ugolev's doctrine of membrane digestion.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: effect of intestinal juice on disaccharides

items: Pour 2 ml of 1% maltose, sucrose and lactose solution into three test tubes respectively.
Add intestinal mucosa homogenate (or intestinal juice) to each.

Keep at 37 °C for 20 minutes and determine glucose. **Result and analysis:** glucose is formed in all tubes — intestinal juice contains maltase, sucrase and lactase, which break down disaccharides to monosaccharides. Lactase activity is often lower in adults.

skills.title: Skill: physiological analysis of the signs of malabsorption

items: Evaluate the character of the stool: liquid and abundant (osmotic or secretory diarrhea), fatty (steatorrhea — impaired fat absorption).
Identify signs of deficiency: anemia (iron, B~12~, folate), tendency to bleed (vitamin K), bone fragility (Ca^2+^, vitamin D), edema (protein).
Determine the level of the disorder: cavity digestion (pancreas, bile), membrane digestion (lactase), absorption (celiac disease, ileal resection), transport (lymph).
Suggest diagnostic tests: fecal elastase, hydrogen breath test (lactose), celiac antibodies, endoscopy and biopsy.

skills.title: Skill: physiological justification of the composition of an oral rehydration solution

items: Show that the solution contains glucose and sodium in approximately equimolar proportion.
Explain the principle of operation of the SGLT1 transporter.
Explain how water is absorbed along the osmotic gradient following sodium and glucose.
State the importance of adding potassium and bicarbonate (citrate).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old young man complains of bloating, rumbling in the abdomen and watery diarrhea 1–2 hours after drinking milk. He tolerates yogurt and cheese well.
cases.ask: What condition can be suspected? Which type of digestion is disturbed? Why can he tolerate yogurt?
cases.answer: Lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance). Lactase is an enzyme bound to the membrane of the microvilli, i.e. membrane digestion is disturbed. Undigested lactose, as an osmotically active substance, draws water into the intestine, and in the large intestine bacteria ferment it, forming gases (H~2~, CO~2~) and organic acids — bloating, rumbling and osmotic diarrhea. In yogurt and cheese most of the lactose has been broken down by lactic acid bacteria, so they are well tolerated. The diagnosis is confirmed by the hydrogen breath test.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A year after resection of the terminal ileum (1 m) because of Crohn's disease, a patient developed weakness, macrocytic anemia and fatty stools.
cases.ask: Explain these signs by linking them to the functions of the ileum.
cases.answer: Two important processes take place in the terminal ileum: vitamin B~12~ is absorbed as a complex with Castle's intrinsic factor, and 90–95% of the bile acids are reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation). After resection B~12~ is not absorbed — when the stores are exhausted (months to years), DNA synthesis is disturbed and megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia develops. Bile acids are lost and the liver cannot replace them sufficiently — micelles are not formed, fat absorption is impaired (steatorrhea) and fat-soluble vitamins are also deficient. Treatment: B~12~ injections, fat restriction.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with cholera is losing 10–15 l of watery stool per day. In a setting where intravenous fluids were not available, drinking a glucose-salt solution was recommended.
cases.ask: What is the mechanism of diarrhea in cholera? Why is the glucose-salt solution absorbed by the intestine?
cases.answer: Cholera toxin permanently activates adenylate cyclase in enterocytes — cAMP increases, and Cl^-^, followed by Na^+^ and water, is secreted into the intestinal lumen through CFTR chloride channels (secretory diarrhea); the active absorption of NaCl is also inhibited. However, the glucose–sodium cotransporter (SGLT1) is not damaged by the toxin. When the glucose-salt solution is drunk, Na^+^ is actively absorbed together with glucose, and water is absorbed along the resulting osmotic gradient — the fluid loss is compensated. This is the physiological basis of oral rehydration.

topics.title: Metabolism. Metabolic bases of physiological functions. The plastic and energetic role of nutrients. Diet and nutritional norms

goals.text: To teach the student the essence of metabolism, the processes of assimilation and dissimilation, the plastic and energetic significance of proteins, fats, carbohydrates, water, minerals and vitamins in the body, the regulation of metabolism, and the principles of rational nutrition, diet and nutritional norms; to master compiling and evaluating a daily ration.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of metabolism, anabolism (assimilation) and catabolism (dissimilation);
the plastic and energetic functions of nutrients;
protein metabolism, nitrogen balance, essential amino acids, the protein minimum and optimum;
lipid and carbohydrate metabolism and their regulation;
the significance of water, minerals and vitamins;
the neurohumoral regulation of metabolism;
the principles of rational nutrition and the norms for nutrients and energy.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate and evaluate the nitrogen balance;
calculate the energy value and nutrient ratio of a daily ration;
calculate and evaluate the body mass index.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Essential amino acids: **“Val Leu Ile Lys Met Thr Trp Phe”** — **Va**line, **Le**ucine, **I**soleucine, **Ly**sine, **Met**hionine, **Th**reonine, **Tr**yptophan, **Phe**nylalanine.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E, K** (“ADEK”): absorbed with the participation of bile and fats and accumulate in the body (liver, adipose tissue) — there is a risk of hypervitaminosis. **Water-soluble vitamins** (B group, C) do not accumulate (except B~12~ — the liver stores enough for years), and the excess is excreted in the urine — they must be consumed regularly.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Norms differ according to age, sex, work intensity, climate, physiological state (pregnancy, lactation) and health; the figures in the table are for average adults. In children the protein and energy requirements per 1 kg of body mass are 2–3 times higher than in adults.

blocks.text: **Metabolism** is the exchange of substances and energy between the body and the external environment; it is the main sign of life. It consists of two interrelated processes:

items: **Assimilation (anabolism)** — the synthesis of complex compounds specific to the body from simple substances coming from outside; **energy is consumed** (ATP). This process ensures cell growth, renewal and the accumulation of reserves.
**Dissimilation (catabolism)** — the breakdown of complex organic substances to simple ones (CO~2~, H~2~O, urea); **energy is released** — it is stored as ATP and partly converted into heat.

blocks.label: Figure 21.1
blocks.caption: Metabolism: anabolism and catabolism, formation of ATP and heat (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: In childhood and during growth assimilation predominates; in adults the two processes are in balance; in old age and in diseases (fever, tumors, starvation) dissimilation predominates.

**Metabolic bases of physiological functions:** every function — muscle contraction, the nerve impulse, secretion, active transport, synthesis — is carried out with the energy of ATP. ATP is formed in the cell in three ways: **creatine phosphate** (seconds — fast but short), **anaerobic glycolysis** (minutes — lactate is formed) and **oxidative phosphorylation** (in mitochondria — the most efficient: ≈ 30–32 ATP from 1 molecule of glucose).

blocks.text: Protein metabolism

Proteins are not stored in reserve in the body and are constantly renewed (≈ 300–400 g of protein is renewed per day, mostly from recycled amino acids). When proteins are broken down, most of the nitrogen is excreted in the urine as **urea**.
**Nitrogen balance** is the ratio between the amount of nitrogen taken in with food and the amount excreted from the body (protein contains on average 16% nitrogen: 1 g nitrogen = 6.25 g protein).

items: **Nitrogen equilibrium** — intake = output (healthy adults).
**Positive nitrogen balance** — intake > output (growth, pregnancy, recovery from illness, anabolic hormones — GH, testosterone, insulin).

**Negative nitrogen balance** — intake < output (starvation, protein deficiency, severe diseases, burns, fever, glucocorticoid excess, old age). **Essential amino acids** are not synthesized in the body and must come with food: **valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, methionine, threonine, tryptophan, phenylalanine** (in children also **histidine**, and according to some sources arginine). Proteins that contain all the essential amino acids in adequate proportions are **complete** (meat, fish, eggs, milk); proteins lacking any of them are **incomplete** (many plant proteins; for example, maize protein is low in lysine and tryptophan).

parts.text: Essential amino acids: **“Val Leu Ile Lys Met Thr Trp Phe”** — **Va**line, **Le**ucine, **I**soleucine, **Ly**sine, **Met**hionine, **Th**reonine, **Tr**yptophan, **Phe**nylalanine.

blocks.text: **The protein minimum** (Rubner) is the smallest amount of protein needed to maintain nitrogen equilibrium (≈ 30–45 g/day; 0.6 g/kg). **The protein optimum** is the amount needed for full health and high working capacity: **0.8–1 g/kg** in adults (≈ 70–100 g/day), at least half of which should be animal protein; more is needed for children, pregnant and lactating women and athletes (1.2–2 g/kg).

parts.text: Protein-energy malnutrition in children: **kwashiorkor** (mainly protein deficiency — edema, enlarged abdomen, fatty liver, changes in skin and hair; the edema is due to the fall in oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia) and **marasmus** (general calorie deficiency — severe wasting without edema).

blocks.text: Lipid metabolism

Lipids are the energy reserve (10–15 kg in adipose tissue — energy for several weeks), a component of membranes, and a source of hormones and fat-soluble vitamins. **Essential fatty acids** are the polyunsaturated **linoleic** (ω-6) and **linolenic** (ω-3) acids; from them arachidonic acid and eicosanoids (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes) are formed. Sources — vegetable oils, fish oil.

**Regulation:** lipogenesis is enhanced by insulin; lipolysis is enhanced by adrenaline, noradrenaline, glucagon, GH, cortisol and thyroid hormones. Lipids are transported in the blood in **lipoproteins** (chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, HDL).
Carbohydrate metabolism

Carbohydrates are the main fast energy source. Glucose is stored in the **liver** and **muscles as glycogen** (100–120 g in the liver, 300–400 g in the muscles). Liver glycogen is used to maintain blood glucose, while muscle glycogen is used only by the muscle itself. When glycogen stores are exhausted (on days 1–2 of starvation), **gluconeogenesis** (from amino acids, lactate and glycerol) is activated.

The blood glucose level (**3.3–5.5 mmol/l**) is regulated by insulin and the counter-insulin hormones (glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, GH) (topic 15). The **brain** obtains almost all its energy from glucose (≈ 120 g per day); in prolonged starvation it partly uses ketone bodies.

**Fiber (dietary fiber)** — indigestible carbohydrates (cellulose, pectin): enhances intestinal peristalsis, is a substrate for the beneficial microflora, and slows the absorption of cholesterol and glucose (25–30 g per day is recommended).

**Water** makes up ≈ 60% of body mass; it is the substance most essential for life (without water a person lives 3–7 days, without food 30–50 days). The daily requirement is **2–2.5 l** (≈ 30–35 ml/kg): 1.2–1.5 l from drinks, ≈ 0.8–1 l from food, ≈ 0.3 l of metabolic (oxidation) water. Excretion: 1–1.5 l with urine, 0.5–0.7 l through the skin (sweat and insensible evaporation), 0.3–0.4 l with breath, 0.1–0.2 l with feces. Water metabolism is regulated by **thirst** (hypothalamus), **vasopressin**, **aldosterone** and natriuretic peptide.

blocks.text: **Vitamins** are organic substances that are not synthesized (or are insufficiently synthesized) in the body, are needed in very small amounts and work mainly as enzyme cofactors. Their deficiency is **hypovitaminosis** (complete absence — avitaminosis), their excess **hypervitaminosis** (mainly the fat-soluble ones: A, D).

parts.text: **Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E, K** (“ADEK”): absorbed with the participation of bile and fats and accumulate in the body (liver, adipose tissue) — there is a risk of hypervitaminosis. **Water-soluble vitamins** (B group, C) do not accumulate (except B~12~ — the liver stores enough for years), and the excess is excreted in the urine — they must be consumed regularly.

blocks.text: Metabolism is regulated by **neurohumoral** means. The highest center is the **hypothalamus**: it contains the **hunger** (lateral nuclei) and **satiety** (ventromedial nuclei, arcuate nucleus) centers; the centers of thermoregulation, thirst and the endocrine system are also located there. The hypothalamus influences metabolism through the endocrine glands (insulin, glucagon, thyroid hormones, cortisol, GH, sex hormones) and through the autonomic nervous system.

**Regulation of appetite and food intake: ghrelin** (secreted in the stomach on an empty stomach — enhances the sensation of hunger); **leptin** (from adipose tissue — a signal about fat stores, reduces appetite); **insulin**, **CCK**, **GLP-1**, **PYY** (satiety signals); gastric distension (via the vagus).

sections.title: 6. Principles and norms of rational nutrition

blocks.text: Principles of **rational (healthy) nutrition**:

items: **Energy balance** — the energy value of food should match the daily energy expenditure (topic 14).
**Balanced nutrition** — the optimal ratio of nutrients: proteins : fats : carbohydrates ≈ **1 : 1 : 4** (by mass); by energy, respectively 10–15%, 25–30%, 55–60%.
**Meal pattern** — at least 3–4 meals a day, at the same times; the last meal 2–3 hours before sleep.
**Variety** — obtaining sufficient amounts of all essential substances, vitamins and minerals.
**Food safety** and proper culinary processing.

parts.text: Norms differ according to age, sex, work intensity, climate, physiological state (pregnancy, lactation) and health; the figures in the table are for average adults. In children the protein and energy requirements per 1 kg of body mass are 2–3 times higher than in adults.

blocks.text: **Body mass index (BMI)** = body mass (kg) / height (m)^2^. Evaluation (WHO): < 18.5 — underweight; 18.5–24.9 — normal; 25–29.9 — overweight; ≥ 30 — obesity.

parts.text: **Obesity** results from energy intake exceeding expenditure over a long period; it increases the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, some tumors and joint diseases. Abdominal (visceral) obesity is especially dangerous: the risk increases when the waist circumference is > 94 cm in men and > 80 cm in women.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A week after extensive burns, a patient is excreting 25 g of nitrogen per day in the urine while taking 75 g of protein with food. The patient is losing weight and the wounds are healing slowly.
cases.ask: Calculate and evaluate the nitrogen balance. Why has this condition developed, and what measures are needed?
cases.answer: Nitrogen intake = 75 / 6.25 = 12 g; nitrogen output ≥ 25 g; balance = 12 − 25 = −13 g/day — a sharply negative nitrogen balance (catabolism predominates). In burns, stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon) and inflammatory cytokines enhance protein breakdown (mainly in muscles); amino acids are used for gluconeogenesis and wound healing; protein is also lost from the burn surface. As a result muscle mass decreases and immunity and regeneration weaken. Measures: increase protein to 1.5–2 g/kg, provide sufficient energy (otherwise protein is used for energy), vitamins (C, A) and trace elements (zinc).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student eats mainly bread, pasta and sweet tea every day, with little meat, milk, fruit or vegetables. His daily energy intake is 2800 kcal (expenditure 2400 kcal). In recent months his weight has increased, but he complains of fatigue and bleeding gums.
cases.ask: Evaluate the shortcomings of the ration from a physiological point of view.
cases.answer: The ration is excessive in energy (positive energy balance — weight gain) and far too rich in carbohydrates, especially rapidly absorbed (“free”) sugar. At the same time it is unbalanced: complete (animal) proteins, essential amino acids, calcium (milk) and iron (meat) are lacking; there are few fruit and vegetables — vitamin C deficiency (bleeding gums — impaired collagen synthesis) and little fiber. The fatigue may be related to deficiency of iron and B vitamins. Recommendation: match energy to expenditure, reduce sugar, add protein sources, dairy products and at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient who has consumed alcohol for a long time and eaten poorly has disturbed gait, impaired eye movements and a sharp decline in memory. Thiamine was prescribed before giving him glucose solution.
cases.ask: Deficiency of which vitamin is this? Why is thiamine given before glucose?
cases.answer: Vitamin B~1~ (thiamine) deficiency — Wernicke's encephalopathy (with Korsakoff syndrome). Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor of the enzymes pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase — it is necessary for the oxidation of carbohydrates. The brain obtains its energy mainly from glucose, so in thiamine deficiency the neurons suffer from an energy shortage. If glucose is given without thiamine, glucose metabolism increases and uses up the little thiamine that remains, and the neurological condition may worsen. In alcoholism thiamine intake is low, it is poorly absorbed and little is stored in the liver.

topics.title: Physiology of excretion. Physiology and regulation of the kidneys. Regulation of electrolytes, pH and extracellular fluid volume by the kidneys

goals.text: To teach the student the excretory organs and their functions, the structure of the nephron and the features of renal blood flow, the processes of urine formation — glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and secretion, the mechanism of urine concentration, the neurohumoral regulation of kidney function and the homeostatic functions of the kidneys (water-salt balance, osmotic pressure, blood volume, acid–base balance); to master evaluating clearance and urinalysis.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the excretory organs and the non-excretory functions of the kidneys;
the structure of the nephron, the types of nephron, renal blood flow and its autoregulation;
the mechanism of glomerular filtration, the effective filtration pressure and the GFR;
reabsorption and secretion in the proximal tubules, the loop of Henle, the distal tubule and the collecting ducts;
the renal threshold for glucose;
the countercurrent system and urine concentration;
the effects of vasopressin, aldosterone, the renin–angiotensin system, natriuretic peptide and parathyroid hormone on the kidney;
the role of the kidneys in regulating acid–base balance;
the amount, composition and properties of urine and the micturition reflex.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the GFR from creatinine clearance;
evaluate the Zimnitsky test;
interpret the results of a routine urinalysis from a physiological point of view.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Creatinine is secreted in small amounts in the tubules, so creatinine clearance is 10–20% higher than the true GFR. In the clinic, GFR estimated from blood creatinine by formulas (CKD-EPI) is widely used.

sections.title: 1. Excretory organs and functions of the kidneys

blocks.text: **Excretion** is the removal from the body of the end products of metabolism, excess water, salts and foreign substances. Excretory organs: the **kidneys** (the main ones — products of nitrogen metabolism, water, salts), the **lungs** (CO~2~, water vapor, volatile substances), the **skin** (sweat glands — water, salts, urea), the **digestive system** (bile pigments, cholesterol, heavy metals, undigested residues), the salivary glands.

blocks.title: Table 22.1. Functions of the kidneys
head: Function
Content
rows: Excretion of urea, creatinine, uric acid, drugs and toxins
Water balance, osmotic pressure (osmoregulation), ionic composition (Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^, phosphate), blood volume
Secretion of H^+^, reabsorption of HCO~3~^-^ and formation of new bicarbonate
Renin (arterial pressure), erythropoietin (erythropoiesis), calcitriol (the active form of vitamin D), prostaglandins, kinins
Gluconeogenesis (in prolonged starvation), breakdown of proteins and peptide hormones
Through blood volume (Na^+^ and water) and the renin–angiotensin system

sections.title: 2. The nephron and renal blood flow

blocks.text: The **nephron** is the structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney has ≈ 1 million nephrons. The nephron consists of the **renal corpuscle** (the network of glomerular capillaries and the surrounding **Shumlyansky–Bowman capsule**) and the system of **tubules**: **proximal tubule → loop of Henle** (descending and ascending limbs) **→ distal tubule → collecting duct**.

blocks.label: Figure 22.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the nephron (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Types of nephron: cortical** nephrons — 80–85%, with a short loop of Henle; **juxtamedullary** nephrons — 15–20%, with a long loop extending deep into the medulla; they play the main role in concentrating urine.

The **juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)** consists of the **juxtaglomerular cells** in the wall of the afferent arteriole (they secrete renin), the **macula densa** of the distal tubule (it senses NaCl in the tubule) and the mesangial cells.
Renal blood flow

Although the kidneys make up 0.5% of body mass, they receive **20–25%** of the minute volume (**≈ 1.2 l/min**) — not because of their own needs, but because of their function of forming urine. Features:

items: **two capillary networks**: the glomerular capillaries (high pressure — for filtration) and the peritubular capillaries (low pressure — for reabsorption);
the efferent arteriole has a smaller diameter than the afferent one — the pressure in the glomerulus is high;

**autoregulation**: when arterial pressure changes within **70–180 mm Hg**, renal blood flow and GFR hardly change (the myogenic mechanism — the Bayliss effect — and **tubuloglomerular feedback** via the macula densa).

blocks.text: Urine formation consists of three processes: **glomerular filtration**, **tubular reabsorption** and **tubular secretion**. Amount excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.
Glomerular filtration

Blood plasma, with almost all its components except proteins, is filtered from the glomerular capillaries into the capsular space — **primary urine** (ultrafiltrate) is formed. **The filtration barrier**: the fenestrated endothelium, the (negatively charged) basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between the foot processes of the podocytes. Substances with a molecular mass greater than 70,000 Da and negatively charged substances (albumin) hardly pass.

blocks.label: Figure 22.2
blocks.caption: Forces creating the filtration pressure in the glomerulus (drawn after Costanzo L.S., 2018)

blocks.text: **Effective filtration pressure** = hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries − (plasma oncotic pressure + hydrostatic pressure in the capsule) ≈ 60 − (32 + 18) ≈ **10 mm Hg**.

**Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** is the volume of primary urine formed by both kidneys per unit time: **≈ 125 ml/min** (≈ **180 l/day**). Of this, **99%** is reabsorbed and about **1.5 l** of final (secondary) urine is excreted. The **filtration fraction** is the ratio of GFR to renal plasma flow (≈ 20%).

**Factors affecting GFR:** a sharp fall in arterial pressure (< 70 mm Hg — filtration decreases; it stops at < 40–50), the tone of the afferent and efferent arterioles, plasma oncotic pressure (GFR increases in hypoproteinemia), the pressure in the capsule (GFR decreases when the urinary tract is obstructed), the number of active glomeruli and the filtration surface.

parts.text: **GFR** is the main indicator of kidney function; it is evaluated by **creatinine clearance** or by formulas (CKD-EPI) based on blood creatinine, age and sex. If GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m^2^ persists for more than 3 months — **chronic kidney disease**; < 15 — end-stage renal failure (dialysis or transplantation).

blocks.text: Tubular reabsorption

blocks.title: Table 22.2. Reabsorption in different parts of the nephron
head: Part
What and how much is reabsorbed
Features
rows: Na^+^ ≈ 65%, water ≈ 65%, K^+^, Cl^-^, HCO~3~^-^ ≈ 80–90%; glucose and amino acids ≈ 100%; phosphate, uric acid; filtered small proteins (pinocytosis)
Obligatory reabsorption; iso-osmotic; microvilli, many mitochondria
Descending limb of the loop of Henle
Impermeable to salts — the filtrate becomes concentrated
Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Impermeable to water — the “diluting segment”; the filtrate becomes hypotonic
Na^+^, Cl^-^ (NCC) ≈ 5%; Ca^2+^ (under the action of PTH)

blocks.text: **Glucose reabsorption** takes place in the proximal tubule together with Na^+^ through the **SGLT2** (mainly) and SGLT1 transporters and is limited by the number of transporters (the **transport maximum**). When blood glucose exceeds **8.9–10 mmol/l** (the **renal threshold**), the transporters are saturated and glucose appears in the urine — **glucosuria**.

parts.text: **Diuretics** block reabsorption in different parts of the nephron: **furosemide** — NKCC2 in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle (the strongest, “loop diuretics”); **hydrochlorothiazide** — NCC in the distal tubule; **spironolactone** — the aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct (potassium-sparing); **SGLT2 inhibitors** (empagliflozin) — glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule (in the treatment of diabetes).

blocks.text: Tubular secretion

The tubular epithelium **actively secretes** substances from the blood into the tubular lumen: **H^+^** (proximal and distal tubules, intercalated cells of the collecting ducts), **K^+^** (principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting ducts, under the action of aldosterone), **NH~3~/NH~4~^+^**, and organic acids and bases (para-aminohippuric acid, penicillin, many drugs, partly creatinine) — in the proximal tubule.
The human kidney can concentrate urine **up to 4 times** relative to plasma (up to 1200 mOsm/kg) or dilute it (down to 50 mOsm/kg). This is achieved by the **countercurrent multiplier system**:

items: In the descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle fluid flows in opposite directions.
The **ascending limb**, being impermeable to water, actively pumps NaCl into the interstitium — the interstitium becomes hypertonic.
The **descending limb** is permeable to water — water moves out into the hypertonic interstitium and the filtrate becomes concentrated.

Repeated along the loop, this process creates an **osmotic gradient** in the medulla from the cortex (300 mOsm/kg) to the tips of the papillae (1200 mOsm/kg). The return of **urea** from the collecting ducts to the interstitium (urea recycling) also contributes greatly.
The **vasa recta**, acting as a countercurrent exchanger, also do not wash out the gradient.

When **vasopressin** is present, **aquaporin-2** channels are inserted into the walls of the collecting ducts and water is reabsorbed into the hypertonic interstitium — **concentrated urine**; without vasopressin — **dilute urine**.

blocks.label: Figure 22.3
blocks.caption: Reabsorption of Na^+^ and water in the proximal tubule (A) and formation of the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla (B) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Humoral regulation

blocks.title: Table 22.3. Hormones regulating kidney function
head: Hormone
Source
Stimulus
Effect on the kidney
rows: Increase in plasma osmolarity (osmoreceptors; even 1–2% is enough), decrease in blood volume
Water reabsorption through aquaporin-2 in the collecting ducts ↑ — urine decreases and becomes concentrated
Na^+^ reabsorption ↑, K^+^ and H^+^ secretion ↑ — blood volume increases
Constricts the efferent arteriole and maintains GFR; Na^+^ reabsorption in the proximal tubule ↑; release of aldosterone and ADH, thirst

blocks.text: **Renin release** is enhanced by: a fall in pressure in the afferent arteriole (baroreceptor mechanism), a reduced NaCl supply to the macula densa, and the sympathetic nerves (β~1~).

blocks.label: Figure 22.4
blocks.caption: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system

blocks.text: Nervous regulation

The kidney is innervated mainly by **sympathetic** nerves: they constrict the arterioles (with strong influence GFR decreases — in pain and stress a **reflex decrease in diuresis** — pain anuria) and enhance renin release and Na^+^ reabsorption. The conditioned-reflex increase in diuresis with heavy drinking shows the influence of the cerebral cortex on the kidney (K.M. Bykov).
Regulation of acid–base balance by the kidneys
The kidneys excrete 50–100 mmol of **non-volatile acids** (sulfuric and phosphoric acids — from protein metabolism) from the body per day and conserve bicarbonate:

items: **Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate** (mainly in the proximal tubule, with the participation of carbonic anhydrase).
**Secretion of H^+^** and its binding by the **phosphate buffer** (**titratable acidity**: HPO~4~^2-^ + H^+^ → H~2~PO~4~^-^).

**Ammoniagenesis**: NH~3~ is formed from glutamine in the tubular cells, combines with H^+^ and is excreted as **NH~4~^+^**; in acidosis this route increases sharply. For each H^+^ excreted, one **new HCO~3~^-^** is returned to the blood. Urine pH can vary between **4.5 and 8.0** (on average 5.5–6.5).

blocks.title: Table 22.4. Main parameters of urine (adults)
head: Parameter
Normal value
rows: 5.0–7.0 (alkaline with plant food, acidic with meat food)
None or traces (< 0.033 g/l; < 150 mg per day)

blocks.text: **Disorders of diuresis: polyuria** (> 2 l/day — diabetes mellitus and insipidus, diuretics), **oliguria** (< 500 ml/day — dehydration, shock, acute kidney failure), **anuria** (< 100 ml/day), **nocturia** (nighttime diuresis exceeding daytime).
Micturition

Urine passes from the renal pelvis through the ureters into the bladder by peristaltic contractions. When 250–300 ml has accumulated in the bladder (pressure above 15–20 cm H₂O), the stretch receptors are excited and the urge to urinate appears. **The center of the micturition reflex** is in the **sacral segments of the spinal cord (S~2~–S~4~)**: the parasympathetic (pelvic) nerves contract the bladder muscle (detrusor) and relax the internal sphincter; the sympathetic nerves (Th~11~–L~2~), conversely, help to store urine. The **external sphincter** (striated, pudendal nerve) is controlled voluntarily; the **pontine micturition center** (Barrington's center) and the cerebral cortex coordinate the reflex and provide voluntary control (developed by 2–3 years of age).
Exercise 1: calculating GFR from creatinine clearance

**Clearance** is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a given substance by the kidneys per unit time: C = (U × V) / P, where U is the concentration of the substance in urine, V the minute diuresis (ml/min) and P its concentration in plasma. The clearance of a substance that is only filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted (inulin, in practice creatinine) equals the GFR.
**Given:** daily urine 1440 ml (V = 1 ml/min); urine creatinine 9 mmol/l; plasma creatinine 0.08 mmol/l.

items: **Interpretation:** normal 90–130 ml/min (decreases with age) — GFR is normal.
Calculate and evaluate the other variants given by the instructor.

parts.text: Creatinine is secreted in small amounts in the tubules, so creatinine clearance is 10–20% higher than the true GFR. In the clinic, GFR estimated from blood creatinine by formulas (CKD-EPI) is widely used.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: evaluating the Zimnitsky test

items: Eating as usual, the patient collects urine in a separate container every 3 hours over 24 hours (8 portions).
The volume and specific gravity (with a urometer) of each portion are determined.
Determine the daytime (6–18) and nighttime (18–6) diuresis, the daily diuresis and the maximum and minimum specific gravity.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** normally the daily diuresis is 70–80% of the fluid drunk, daytime diuresis is 2–3 times greater than nighttime; the specific gravity is ≥ 1.020 in at least one portion, and the difference between portions is ≥ 0.010–0.015. **Hyposthenuria** (specific gravity always < 1.012) or **isosthenuria** (specific gravity hardly changes, ≈ 1.010) — the concentrating ability of the kidney is impaired (chronic kidney failure, diabetes insipidus).
Exercise 3: determining the physicochemical properties of urine

items: Evaluate the color and clarity.
Measure the specific gravity with a urometer (fill the cylinder with urine and lower the urometer so that it does not touch the wall).
Determine the pH with indicator paper.
Test for protein, glucose, ketone bodies and blood with test strips.

skills.title: Skill: physiological interpretation of a routine urinalysis

items: Compare the volume, color, clarity, specific gravity and pH with the norm.
If there is glucosuria, compare it with blood glucose: ≥ 10 mmol/l in the blood — hyperglycemic; normal — renal glucosuria.
Proteinuria — damage to the glomerular filtration barrier or impaired tubular reabsorption.
Specific gravity always low — impaired concentrating ability (vasopressin deficiency or kidney disease).
Ketonuria — carbohydrate deficiency (starvation, decompensated diabetes).

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing the effects of vasopressin and aldosterone in clinical situations

items: Evaluate the urine volume and specific gravity: abundant and dilute — vasopressin is lacking; scanty and concentrated — much vasopressin (dehydration).
Evaluate blood Na^+^ and K^+^: Na^+^ retention and K^+^ loss — much aldosterone; the reverse — aldosterone is lacking.
Also evaluate arterial pressure and blood volume.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a head injury a patient began to excrete 8–10 l of urine per day with a specific gravity of 1.001–1.004, and intense thirst. Blood glucose is normal, sodium slightly increased.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: Central diabetes insipidus. The injury has damaged the hypothalamus–neurohypophysis system and vasopressin release has decreased. Without vasopressin, aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted into the membrane of the collecting ducts and water is not reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla — a large volume of dilute urine is excreted (polyuria, hyposthenuria). The loss of water raises plasma osmolarity and Na^+^ — the osmoreceptors and the thirst center are excited (polydipsia). Glucose is normal — it is not diabetes mellitus. Treatment — a synthetic vasopressin analogue (desmopressin).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a car accident with a blood loss of 1.5 l, a patient has an arterial pressure of 80/50 mm Hg and hourly urine output of 15 ml (normal ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/hour).
cases.ask: Why has urine output decreased sharply? What compensatory mechanisms have been activated?
cases.answer: Arterial pressure has fallen below the limit of renal autoregulation (70 mm Hg), and the sympathetic nerves have constricted the afferent arterioles — the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries and the effective filtration pressure have decreased sharply — GFR has fallen (oliguria). Compensatory mechanisms: sympathetic activation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction); the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (angiotensin II constricts vessels and, by constricting the efferent arteriole, partly maintains GFR; aldosterone retains Na^+^ and water); vasopressin release (through the baroreceptors in response to reduced blood volume) — water reabsorption increases, and urine decreases and becomes concentrated. These mechanisms are aimed at preserving blood volume; prolonged hypotension can lead to acute kidney injury.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus has blood glucose of 14 mmol/l, urine glucose of 2%, daily diuresis of 3 l and thirst.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of the glucosuria and polyuria.
cases.answer: In the proximal tubule glucose is reabsorbed through the SGLT2 and SGLT1 transporters, whose number is limited (the transport maximum). When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (8.9–10 mmol/l), the amount of filtered glucose exceeds the capacity of the transporters and the excess passes into the urine — hyperglycemic glucosuria. The glucose remaining in the tubules, as an osmotically active substance, retains water and reduces its reabsorption — osmotic diuresis (polyuria). The loss of water causes thirst (polydipsia).

topics.title: Properties of nerve centers. The spinal cord: spinal reflexes, conducting pathways, methods of examination

goals.text: To teach the student the reflex activity of the central nervous system, the concept of the nerve center and its properties, the transmission of excitation in central synapses, the types of inhibition in the CNS and the principles of reflex coordination, the reflex and conducting functions of the spinal cord, and spinal shock and the consequences of spinal cord injury; to master examining tendon reflexes in humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the reflex and the reflex arc, monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflexes;
the properties of the nerve center (one-way conduction, delay, summation, transformation, aftereffect, tone, fatigue, sensitivity to chemicals, plasticity);
excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials;
central inhibition (Sechenov's experiment), postsynaptic and presynaptic inhibition;
the principles of reflex coordination (convergence, divergence, irradiation, reciprocal innervation, dominant, final common path, occlusion, facilitation);
the segmental structure, reflexes and conducting pathways of the spinal cord;
spinal shock and Brown-Séquard syndrome.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the reflex time in a spinal frog and show the importance of an intact reflex arc;
perform Sechenov's experiment;
examine and evaluate the knee, Achilles, biceps, triceps and abdominal reflexes in humans.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Features of the dominant** (Ukhtomsky): high excitability; persistence of excitation; summation of excitations (“drawing them to itself”); inertia (it persists after the stimulus has stopped). The dominant is the basis of attention, motivation (hunger, thirst) and behavior.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Textbooks give the reflex segments with slight differences (for example, the knee reflex L~2~–L~4~ or L~3~–L~4~). The values most commonly used in clinical neurology are: biceps — C~5~–C~6~, triceps — C~7~–C~8~, abdominal — Th~7~–Th~12~, knee — L~3~–L~4~, Achilles — S~1~–S~2~.

sections.title: 1. Reflex activity of the central nervous system

blocks.text: A **reflex** is the body's response to stimulation of receptors with the participation of the CNS. The material basis of the reflex is the **reflex arc**: receptor → afferent (sensory) neuron → nerve center (interneurons) → efferent (motor) neuron → effector.

blocks.label: Figure 23.1
blocks.caption: Reflex arcs: A — polysynaptic (through an interneuron); B — monosynaptic (Alavia O.T., 2018)

items: **Monosynaptic** reflex arc — the afferent neuron ends directly on the motoneuron (one central synapse): **tendon (myotatic) reflexes** — knee, Achilles.

**Polysynaptic** reflex arc — through one or more interneurons: flexor (protective), skin and autonomic reflexes. **Reflex time** is the time from the stimulus to the beginning of the response. It consists of the excitation of the receptors, the conduction of excitation along the afferent and efferent fibers, and the **central reflex time** (the delay at the synapses of the center). When the stimulus strength increases, the reflex time shortens (summation).

blocks.text: A **nerve center** is the set of neurons that carry out a particular reflex or function. Functionally, the center of a complex function is located at different levels of the CNS (for example, the respiratory center — spinal cord, medulla oblongata, pons, hypothalamus, cortex).
There are thousands of synapses on the surface of a central neuron. Depending on the type of mediator and receptor:

items: **Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)** — **depolarization** of the postsynaptic membrane (Na^+^ entry); the main mediator is **glutamate** (AMPA, NMDA receptors), and also acetylcholine. A single EPSP is small (1–2 mV); for a neuron to be excited, many EPSPs must summate.

**Inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)** — **hyperpolarization** (Cl^-^ entry or K^+^ efflux); mediators — **GABA** (the main one in the brain) and **glycine** (in the spinal cord and brainstem). The neuron integrates all EPSPs and IPSPs at the **axon hillock**: if the result reaches the critical level, an action potential is generated.

blocks.label: Figure 23.2
blocks.caption: Summation of postsynaptic potentials: a, b — subthreshold EPSPs with one and two impulses; c — appearance of an action potential with summation (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: The **sensitivity of neurons to hypoxia** is very high: if blood supply to the brain stops, consciousness is lost within 10 s, and irreversible changes begin in cortical neurons within **4–6 minutes**. That is why resuscitation must start immediately after cardiac arrest. **Plasticity**, in turn, is the basis of partial recovery of functions after a stroke and of rehabilitation.

sections.title: 4. Inhibition in the central nervous system

blocks.text: **Inhibition** is an active nervous process that prevents the appearance or spread of excitation. It arises as a result of excitation and does not itself spread.

**Central inhibition was discovered by I.M. Sechenov** (1862): when the frog brain was transected at the level of the optic thalami and a crystal of NaCl was placed on the cut surface, the time of the withdrawal reflex on immersing the foot in sulfuric acid was sharply prolonged. Therefore the higher parts of the brain can inhibit spinal reflexes.

blocks.label: Figure 23.3
blocks.caption: A — Sechenov's experiment: when the optic thalami are stimulated with NaCl, the spinal reflex is inhibited; B — synaptic connections involving inhibitory neurons (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 23.2. Types of central inhibition

rows: An inhibitory interneuron evokes an IPSP (hyperpolarization) on the postsynaptic membrane; mediator GABA or glycine

parts.text: **Strychnine** blocks glycine receptors and **tetanus toxin** blocks the release of glycine and GABA — postsynaptic inhibition in the spinal cord is lost: any weak stimulus causes generalized convulsions. Conversely, **benzodiazepines** and **barbiturates** enhance the action of GABA~A~ receptors and have sedative and anticonvulsant effects.

sections.title: 6. Structure and functions of the spinal cord

blocks.text: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral canal and consists of 31 segments (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal). A pair of spinal nerves leaves each segment.
**Bell–Magendie law**: the dorsal roots consist of **sensory** (afferent) fibers, and the ventral roots of **motor** (efferent) fibers.

**Gray matter: dorsal horns** — sensory (inter)neurons; **ventral horns** — **α-motoneurons** (extrafusal fibers of skeletal muscles) and **γ-motoneurons** (muscle spindles); **lateral horns** (Th~1~–L~2~ — sympathetic, S~2~–S~4~ — parasympathetic preganglionic neurons). **White matter** — conducting pathways.

A **dermatome** is the area of skin receiving sensory innervation from one spinal segment; a **myotome** is the muscles innervated by one segment. One muscle usually receives innervation from several segments (the principle of reliability).
Reflexes of the spinal cord

blocks.text: Spinal shock

**Spinal shock** is the temporary loss of all reflexes below the level of transection (or injury) of the spinal cord. Its cause is the sudden interruption of the activating influence of the higher centers (brainstem, cortex). Its duration depends on the evolutionary level of the animal: minutes in the frog, days in the dog, weeks in the monkey, and **weeks–months** in humans. Later the reflexes recover and even become exaggerated (hyperreflexia), while voluntary movements and sensation do not recover.

parts.text: **Brown-Séquard syndrome** — in transverse damage to one half of the spinal cord: on the injured side — central paralysis (pyramidal tract) and loss of deep (proprioceptive) sensation (dorsal columns); on the opposite side — loss of pain and temperature sensation (the spinothalamic tract crosses in the spinal cord). It is a classic example for understanding where these pathways cross.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining the reflex time in a spinal frog (Türck method)

items: Suspend a spinal frog (with the brain removed) by the jaw on a stand; wait 5–10 minutes for spinal shock to pass.
Dip the tip of the hind foot into 0.5% sulfuric acid solution and measure the time until the leg is withdrawn with a metronome or stopwatch.
Wash the foot with water after each measurement.

Repeat the experiment with 0.3% and 1% acid. **Result and analysis:** as the acid concentration increases, the reflex time shortens — a strong stimulus excites more receptors, and summation in the center reaches threshold faster.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: the importance of an intact reflex arc

items: In a spinal frog make a circular cut in the skin of the leg and remove the skin from the foot (the receptors are removed) — there is no reflex on dipping into acid.
Cut the sciatic nerve in the other leg — the reflex disappears.

Destroy the spinal cord (with a probe) — all reflexes disappear. **Result and analysis:** when any part of the reflex arc (receptor, afferent pathway, center, efferent pathway) is damaged, the reflex is not carried out.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: Sechenov's experiment

items: Transect the frog brain in front of the optic thalami (removing the cerebral hemispheres) (a “thalamic frog”).
Determine the reflex time by the Türck method.
Place a NaCl crystal on the cut surface of the optic thalami and measure the reflex time again.

Remove the crystal, wash the surface with Ringer's solution and measure again. **Result and analysis:** when the NaCl crystal is applied, the reflex time is sharply prolonged or the reflex disappears; after washing it recovers. Excitation of neurons in the region of the optic thalami inhibits spinal reflexes — proof of **central inhibition**.

blocks.text: Exercise 4: examining tendon reflexes in humans

items: **Knee reflex**: the subject sits and crosses one leg over the other (or lets the legs hang freely); the tendon below the kneecap is struck with a neurological hammer — contraction of the quadriceps and extension of the lower leg.
**Achilles reflex**: the subject kneels on a chair with the feet hanging freely; the Achilles tendon is struck — plantar flexion of the foot.
**Biceps reflex**: the arm is half-flexed at the elbow; the examiner places a thumb on the biceps tendon and strikes it — flexion at the elbow.
**Triceps reflex**: the arm is flexed at the elbow at a right angle; the triceps tendon is struck above the olecranon — extension.
**Abdominal reflexes**: with the subject lying down, the abdominal skin is stroked quickly from the side toward the center (upper, middle, lower) — contraction of the abdominal muscles.

Compare the reflexes on the two sides (symmetry); **the Jendrassik maneuver** — the subject hooks the hands together and pulls, which enhances the knee reflex (distraction of attention and activation of γ-motoneurons). **Interpretation:** normally the reflexes are moderately brisk and symmetrical. Reduction or absence — damage to the reflex arc (peripheral nerve, root, segment); exaggeration (hyperreflexia, clonus) — loss of the inhibitory influence of the higher centers (upper motor neuron lesion).

Write down which reflexes are absent, reduced or exaggerated.

Exaggeration of the reflexes below (after spinal shock) shows that the influence of the higher centers has been interrupted.

items: Draw the receptor (muscle spindle), the afferent neuron (in the spinal ganglion), the center (ventral horn), the efferent neuron (α-motoneuron) and the effector.
Distinguish monosynaptic and polysynaptic arcs.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a motorcycle accident a patient has a complete spinal cord injury in the thoracic region (Th~10~). In the first weeks there were no movements, sensation or reflexes in the legs, and urinary retention was observed. After 2 months the knee and Achilles reflexes returned and even became exaggerated, but voluntary movements and sensation did not recover.
cases.ask: What is the condition in the first weeks called? Why did the reflexes later return and become exaggerated?
cases.answer: In the first weeks spinal shock developed — the spinal neurons below the injury were suddenly deprived of the constant activating impulses from the higher centers (brainstem, cortex), and their excitability fell sharply. Over time the excitability of the lower neurons recovers (increased receptor sensitivity, new synaptic connections — plasticity); the arcs of the knee (L~3~–L~4~) and Achilles (S~1~–S~2~) reflexes lie below the injury and are intact — the reflexes recover. Because the inhibitory influence of the higher centers is absent, they become exaggerated (hyperreflexia). Voluntary movement and sensation do not recover because the descending and ascending pathways needed for them have been severed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: After a stab wound a patient was found to have paralysis and loss of joint-position sensation in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg.
cases.ask: Where and how is the spinal cord damaged? Explain the signs on the basis of the conducting pathways.
cases.answer: The right half of the spinal cord has been damaged transversely (Brown-Séquard syndrome). The corticospinal (pyramidal) tract crosses in the medulla oblongata and descends in the spinal cord on its own side — paralysis on the injured (right) side. The dorsal columns (Goll and Burdach), which conduct proprioceptive sensation, do not cross in the spinal cord — deep sensation is lost on the right side. Pain and temperature sensation are conducted by the spinothalamic tract, which crosses in the spinal cord at the level of the entering segment — therefore pain and temperature sensation are lost on the opposite (left) side.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: During a neurological examination the patient's knee reflex was very weak on both sides. The doctor asked the patient to hook his hands together in front of him and pull hard, and the reflex became clearly visible.
cases.ask: What is this maneuver called? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: The Jendrassik maneuver. While pulling the hands hard, the patient's attention is distracted from the leg being tested (the voluntary inhibitory influence of the cortex decreases); in addition, excitation irradiates in the CNS, and spinal motoneurons and γ-motoneurons are activated — the sensitivity of the muscle spindles increases. As a result the knee reflex (a monosynaptic myotatic reflex) is enhanced. The maneuver helps to determine whether the reflex is truly reduced or only appeared weak because of the examination conditions.

topics.title: Activity of the different parts of the brain: the medulla oblongata, the pons, the midbrain

goals.text: To teach the student the structural features, reflex and conducting functions and vital centers of the brainstem (medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain), its role in regulating muscle tone and posture (decerebrate rigidity, static and statokinetic reflexes), and the descending and ascending influences of the reticular formation; in laboratory work, to master examining brainstem reflexes and cranial nerve function.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the composition of the brainstem and the location of the cranial nerve nuclei;
the vital centers and reflexes of the medulla oblongata;
the functions of the pons;
the functions of the midbrain nuclei (corpora quadrigemina, red nucleus, substantia nigra, nuclei of cranial nerves III–IV);
decerebrate rigidity and its mechanism;
static (postural and righting) and statokinetic reflexes (R. Magnus);
the structure of the reticular formation and its activating and inhibitory influences.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: observe brainstem reflexes in the frog and rat (video);
examine the pupillary, oculocardiac, swallowing and blink (corneal) reflexes and cranial nerve function in humans;
demonstrate statokinetic reflexes (nystagmus).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Damage to the medulla oblongata (injury, stroke, herniation of the brain into the foramen magnum) is **extremely dangerous to life**: the respiratory and circulatory centers are damaged — breathing stops and arterial pressure falls sharply. That is why the medulla oblongata is called the **“vital knot”** (Flourens).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remembering the tonic neck reflexes: **“Look up at the sky — the arms extend”** (head back — the arms extend and the legs flex: a cat looking up at a shelf), **“Look down — the arms flex”** (a cat looking down at a mouse hole).

blocks.text: The **brainstem** comprises the medulla oblongata, the pons and the midbrain (some authors also include the diencephalon). It connects the spinal cord with the higher parts of the brain and performs the following functions:

items: **Conducting** — all ascending and descending pathways pass through it.
**Reflex** — the nuclei of cranial nerves III–XII are located here; centers of vital reflexes.
**Regulation of muscle tone and posture** — through the vestibular, reticular and red nucleus systems.
**Integrative** — regulation of the general activity of the CNS through the reticular formation (sleep–wakefulness).

blocks.text: The medulla oblongata contains the nuclei of cranial nerves **IX–XII** (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal), as well as part of the nuclei of nerves V and VIII.

blocks.title: Table 24.1. Centers and reflexes of the medulla oblongata
head: Group
Center or reflex
rows: The respiratory center (dorsal and ventral groups), the circulatory (vasomotor) center, the center regulating cardiac activity (vagal nuclei)
Sucking, chewing, swallowing, salivation, gastric and pancreatic secretion, vomiting
Coughing, sneezing, lacrimation, blinking (corneal — often together with the pons), vomiting
Tonic neck and labyrinthine reflexes (vestibular nuclei)

parts.text: Damage to the medulla oblongata (injury, stroke, herniation of the brain into the foramen magnum) is **extremely dangerous to life**: the respiratory and circulatory centers are damaged — breathing stops and arterial pressure falls sharply. That is why the medulla oblongata is called the **“vital knot”** (Flourens).

blocks.text: **Conducting function:** in the medulla oblongata 80–90% of the **pyramidal tracts** cross (the pyramidal decussation); in the gracile and cuneate nuclei the proprioceptive pathways synapse on the second neuron and cross as the **medial lemniscus**.

parts.text: **Bulbar syndrome** — when the nuclei or nerves of cranial nerves IX, X and XII are damaged: impaired swallowing (dysphagia, return of liquid food through the nose), hoarseness (dysphonia), speech disturbance (dysarthria), atrophy and fibrillation of the tongue, loss of the pharyngeal and soft palate reflexes. The risk of aspiration pneumonia is high.

blocks.text: The pons contains the nuclei of cranial nerves **V–VIII** (trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear).
Functions:

items: **Conducting** — pathways from the cortex to the cerebellum (the **cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway**; pontine nuclei), ascending and descending pathways.

**Reflex** — chewing (nerve V), facial expression (nerve VII), turning the eyeball outward (nerve VI), the corneal reflex (afferent V, efferent VII), primary processing of auditory and vestibular information (nuclei of nerve VIII).
**Regulation of breathing** — the **pneumotaxic center** (controls the switch from inspiration to expiration).
**Regulation of sleep** — the locus coeruleus (noradrenergic neurons) and the mechanisms of paradoxical (REM) sleep.

blocks.text: The midbrain consists of the corpora quadrigemina (tectum), the cerebral peduncles, the red nucleus, the substantia nigra, the periaqueductal gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius and the nuclei of cranial nerves III–IV.

blocks.caption: Cross-section of the midbrain: superior and inferior colliculi, red nucleus, substantia nigra, reticular formation, conducting pathways (Alavia O.T., 2018)

parts.text: **Parkinson's disease** is the death of the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra: slowness of movement (bradykinesia), muscle rigidity (the “cogwheel” phenomenon), resting tremor and postural instability. Treatment — the dopamine precursor **levodopa** (dopamine itself does not cross the blood–brain barrier), dopamine agonists.

blocks.text: **The pupillary reflex:** when light enters the eye, the pupil constricts (direct reaction), and the pupil of the other eye constricts as well (**crossed (consensual) reaction**). Pathway: retina → optic nerve → pretectal nucleus (midbrain) → Yakubovich–Edinger–Westphal nuclei on both sides → nerve III (parasympathetic) → ciliary ganglion → pupillary constrictor muscle.

sections.title: 5. The role of the brainstem in regulating muscle tone

blocks.text: Decerebrate rigidity

When an animal's brainstem is transected **between the midbrain (red nucleus) and the vestibular nuclei** (between the colliculi), **decerebrate rigidity** develops (C. Sherrington): the **tone of all the extensor (antigravity) muscles rises sharply** — the legs are stretched straight, the head is thrown back and the tail raised; if the animal is set on its feet it stands like a “wooden” figure.

blocks.label: Figure 24.2
blocks.caption: Decerebrate rigidity — a sharp increase in extensor muscle tone in a cat (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Mechanism:** the transection interrupts the **inhibitory** influence of the red nucleus and the higher centers (cortex, basal ganglia) on the extensor muscles, while the **activating** influence of the vestibular nuclei (**Deiters' nucleus**) and the pontine reticular formation on the extensor motoneurons is preserved and becomes dominant. The rigidity is mediated mainly by activation of **γ-motoneurons** (γ-rigidity): if the dorsal roots are cut (afferent input from the muscle spindles is lost), the rigidity disappears. If the transection is made below the vestibular nuclei, rigidity does not develop.

parts.text: In humans, in severe brain injuries, stroke and brainstem compression, a **decerebrate posture** (arms and legs extended, forearms rotated inward) and a **decorticate posture** (arms flexed, legs extended — injury above the red nucleus) are observed. The decerebrate posture is considered a prognostically worse sign (the motor response is scored on the Glasgow scale).
