blocks.text: The **reticular formation (RF)** is a diffuse network of neurons with highly branched dendrites and axons located throughout the brainstem (from the upper spinal cord to the diencephalon).
Its neurons receive information from all sensory systems (via collaterals), but this information is **nonspecific** (it reflects the strength rather than the type of stimulus).

**The ascending activating system** (H. Magoun, G. Moruzzi, 1949): the RF diffusely activates the cerebral cortex — it maintains **wakefulness**, attention and consciousness. When the RF is stimulated, a sleeping animal wakes up and on the EEG the slow rhythms are replaced by fast ones (desynchronization); when the RF is damaged (or the brain is transected below the midbrain), the animal falls into a state resembling permanent sleep (coma).

blocks.label: Figure 24.4
blocks.caption: The ascending activating influence of the reticular formation: collaterals of the sensory pathways to the RF, and diffuse impulses from the RF to the cortex (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Descending influences** (Magoun): the **medial (medullary) part** of the RF **inhibits** the activity of spinal motoneurons, while the **lateral (pontine and midbrain) part** **facilitates** (activates) it. These influences act mainly through the γ-motoneurons and regulate muscle tone and reflexes.

blocks.label: Figure 24.5
blocks.caption: Descending facilitatory (b) and inhibitory (c) influences of the reticular formation: St — stimulator; a — initial state (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Other functions of the RF:** participation in the respiratory and circulatory centers; regulation of autonomic functions; regulation of the sleep–wake cycle (noradrenergic — locus coeruleus, serotonergic — raphe nuclei); modulation of pain; attention and orienting reactions.

parts.text: **Barbiturates** and general anesthetics cause sleep and narcosis mainly by inhibiting the ascending activating system of the RF. Damage to the brainstem RF (injury, stroke, tumors) leads to impaired consciousness — **stupor and coma**.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: observing brainstem reflexes in the frog

items: Observe a normal frog: its sitting posture at rest, jumping, swimming, righting when turned on its back, and the “croaking” reflex when the abdomen is lightly pressed.
Test the same reflexes in a frog with the cerebral hemispheres removed (the midbrain and lower parts preserved).
Test them in a frog transected above the medulla oblongata.

Test them in a spinal frog. **Result and analysis:** in the frog with the midbrain preserved, the postural and righting reflexes are retained (the center of these reflexes is in the midbrain); in the medullary frog the righting reflexes are lost, but breathing and some tonic reflexes are preserved; in the spinal frog only segmental reflexes remain, with no posture or breathing.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: examining brainstem reflexes and cranial nerves in humans

items: **Pupillary reflex** (nerve III, midbrain): cover the eye with the palm for a few seconds, then uncover it and observe the constriction of the pupil; check the crossed reaction in the other eye.
**Corneal (blink) reflex** (nerves V–VII, pons): when the cornea is touched carefully with the tip of a cotton wisp, the eye closes (instructor demonstration).
**Swallowing and pharyngeal reflex** (nerves IX–X, medulla oblongata): touching the posterior pharyngeal wall with a spatula — a gag movement.
**Oculocardiac (Dagnini–Aschner) reflex** (nerves V–X): light pressure on the eyeballs — slowing of the pulse (topic 12).
**Eye movements** (nerves III, IV, VI): the subject follows a hammer in all directions with the eyes.
**Facial muscles** (nerve VII): wrinkling the forehead, closing the eyes tightly, showing the teeth; **masticatory muscles** (nerve V): clenching the jaws.

**Protruding the tongue** (nerve XII): the tongue should be in the midline. **Interpretation:** the reflexes should be equal and brisk on both sides; asymmetry or absence indicates damage to the corresponding cranial nerve or the brainstem.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: demonstrating statokinetic reflexes (Bárány chair)

items: The subject sits in a rotating chair with the head bent 30° forward and the eyes closed.
He is rotated evenly 10 times over 20 s and then stopped suddenly.
The subject opens his eyes and looks ahead — rhythmic movements of the eyeballs (**post-rotational nystagmus**) are observed; their duration is measured with a stopwatch.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:** normally post-rotational nystagmus lasts 25–35 s. Prolonged nystagmus or nausea and pallor indicate increased excitability of the vestibular apparatus (in occupational selection — pilots, sailors).

skills.title: Skill: evaluating the pupillary reaction

items: Darken the room slightly.
Direct a flashlight beam at each eye from the side.
Observe the direct and crossed reactions.
Assess the equality of pupil size (absence of anisocoria).
If the reaction is absent or sluggish, consider damage to nerve III or the midbrain, or potent drugs (opioids — the pupil constricts; atropine — it dilates).

skills.title: Skill: estimating the level of brainstem damage from the syndromes

items: Disorders of breathing and circulation, impaired swallowing and speech — the medulla oblongata.
Paralysis of the facial muscles, inability to turn the eye outward, impaired chewing — the pons.
Absence of the pupillary reaction, inability to turn the eye up and in — the midbrain.
Impaired consciousness — the reticular formation.
If the cranial nerve disturbance is on one side and the paralysis on the opposite side — an **alternating (crossed) syndrome** (unilateral damage to the brainstem).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a stroke a 65-year-old patient has difficulty swallowing, liquid comes back through the nose, the voice is hoarse and speech is unintelligible. When protruded, the tongue deviates to the left, and fibrillations are seen in the tongue.
cases.ask: Which part of the brain is damaged? Which cranial nerves are affected? What is the main danger for the patient?
cases.answer: The medulla oblongata is damaged — bulbar syndrome. Impaired swallowing and elevation of the soft palate (return of liquid through the nose) and hoarseness — damage to the nuclei of nerves IX (glossopharyngeal) and X (vagus); deviation and fibrillation of the tongue — damage to the nucleus of nerve XII (hypoglossal) (the tongue deviates toward the damaged side). The main dangers: entry of food and saliva into the airways (aspiration, aspiration pneumonia) and, if the process spreads, damage to the nearby respiratory and circulatory centers.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient with a severe brain injury is unconscious; his arms and legs are stretched straight, the forearms rotated inward and the head thrown back, and this posture intensifies with painful stimuli.
cases.ask: What is this condition? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: Decerebrate posture (decerebrate rigidity). The injury is below the red nucleus and above the vestibular nuclei (at the midbrain–pons level). The inhibitory influence of the red nucleus and higher centers on the extensor muscles has been interrupted, while the activating influence of the vestibular (Deiters') nuclei and the pontine reticular formation is preserved and dominant — extensor muscle tone has risen sharply (mainly through the γ-motoneurons). This posture indicates serious brainstem damage and a poor prognosis; the unconsciousness is due to damage to the ascending activating system of the reticular formation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient under general anesthesia, the anesthesiologist regularly checks the state of the pupils and their reaction to light.
cases.ask: What is the pathway of the pupillary reflex? What might its loss indicate?
cases.answer: Light excites the photoreceptors of the retina; impulses travel along the optic nerve to the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain and from there to the Yakubovich–Edinger–Westphal nuclei on both sides; parasympathetic fibers in cranial nerve III go to the ciliary ganglion and from there to the pupillary constrictor muscle — the pupil constricts (direct and crossed reaction). Because the reflex center is in the midbrain, its loss and dilation of the pupils may indicate deep depression of brainstem function (excessively deep anesthesia), severe hypoxia or damage to the midbrain. That is why the state of the pupils is an important indicator of the depth of anesthesia and the condition of the brain.

topics.title: Activity of the different parts of the brain: the cerebellum, diencephalon, basal ganglia and cerebral cortex

goals.text: To teach the student the structure and connections of the cerebellum and its role in coordinating movements, the functions of the diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus), the importance of the basal (subcortical) ganglia in controlling movement, the sensory, motor and associative areas of the cerebral cortex, the limbic system and electroencephalography; to master performing tests of cerebellar function in humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the functional divisions of the cerebellum (archicerebellum, paleocerebellum, neocerebellum) and their connections;
the signs of cerebellar damage (Luciani's triad, ataxia, asynergia, dysmetria, intention tremor, nystagmus);
the types and functions of the thalamic nuclei;
the autonomic, endocrine and motivational centers of the hypothalamus;
the structure and connections of the basal ganglia and the syndromes of their damage;
the cytoarchitectonics and functional areas of the cortex;
the concept of the somatosensory and motor homunculus;
the functions of the limbic system;
the EEG rhythms and their significance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: perform and evaluate the Romberg test, the finger-to-nose and heel-to-knee tests and the adiadochokinesis test;
distinguish the main rhythms on an EEG recording.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Damage to the basal ganglia has **two kinds** of result: **reduced movement** (hypokinesia — Parkinson's disease; dopamine deficiency) or **excessive involuntary movements** (hyperkinesias — chorea, ballism). The difference from cerebellar damage: in basal ganglia disease the **initiation and amplitude** of movements are disturbed, whereas in the cerebellum their **accuracy and coordination** are disturbed.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: If swaying in the Romberg position increases when the eyes are **closed**, this is most often a sign of **sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia** (damage to the dorsal columns or peripheral nerves — visual control compensates). In cerebellar ataxia the swaying persists even with the eyes open.

blocks.text: The cerebellum lies behind the pons and medulla oblongata; it consists of two hemispheres and the vermis. Its cortex has three layers (molecular, Purkinje cell and granular), and inside there are nuclei: the **fastigial**, **globose**, **emboliform** and **dentate** nuclei.

blocks.label: Figure 25.1
blocks.caption: Cerebellar nuclei (A) and the connections of the cerebellum in the control of movement (B) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **The only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex are the Purkinje cells**; they exert an **inhibitory** (GABA) influence on the cerebellar nuclei. Information reaches the cerebellum through **mossy** fibers (mainly from the spinal cord and pontine nuclei) and **climbing** fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus).

blocks.title: Table 25.1. Functional divisions of the cerebellum
head: Branch
Structures
Main connections
Function
rows: The vermis and the paravermal part of the hemispheres
Spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts), red nucleus, reticular formation
Muscle tone, posture and correction of ongoing movements
The lateral part of the hemispheres, the dentate nucleus
Cortex (via the pons) → thalamus → motor cortex
Planning and programming of complex voluntary movements, motor memory, timing

blocks.text: **Functions of the cerebellum:** maintaining balance and posture; regulating muscle tone; coordinating voluntary movements (adjusting accuracy, smoothness, speed and force); motor learning (memory of motor skills); influence on autonomic functions.

**When the cerebellum is removed** (L. Luciani's experiments), three classic signs develop — **Luciani's triad**: **atonia** (reduced muscle tone), **asthenia** (reduced muscle strength and rapid fatigue), **astasia** (tremor-like muscle contractions — impaired standing). Later **ataxia** (incoordination of movements), **dysmetria**, **asynergia**, **intention tremor**, **dysarthria** (scanning speech) and **nystagmus** are added.

blocks.title: Table 25.2. Signs of cerebellar damage
head: Sign
Content
rows: Inability to keep balance when standing (swaying in the Romberg position, whether the eyes are open or closed)
Gait disturbance — walking with the legs wide apart, swaying (a “drunken gait”)
Misjudging the amplitude of a movement (hyper- and hypometria)
Tremor that increases as the target is approached (in the finger-to-nose test)
Inability to alternate opposite movements rapidly
Disturbance of the cooperative work of muscles
Speech broken into syllables, slow and explosive

parts.text: **In alcohol intoxication** cerebellar function is disturbed first: swaying gait, impaired speech, inaccurate movements — that is why the finger-to-nose test and walking along a straight line are used to examine an intoxicated person. In chronic alcoholism the cerebellar vermis atrophies.

blocks.text: The thalamus (optic thalamus)
The **thalamus** is the main “relay station” on the way of all sensory pathways (except smell) to the cortex and an integrative center (the “gateway to the cortex”).

blocks.title: Table 25.3. Thalamic nuclei
head: Group
Examples
Function
rows: Ventral posterolateral and posteromedial (somatosensory), lateral geniculate body (vision), medial geniculate body (hearing)
Transmit particular sensory information to the corresponding projection area of the cortex
From the cerebellum and basal ganglia to the motor cortex
Connected with the associative areas of the cortex; complex integration
From the reticular formation; diffusely activate the cortex and regulate its rhythm

parts.text: **Thalamic syndrome** (Dejerine–Roussy) — in damage to the thalamus (stroke): reduction of all types of sensation on the opposite side, but severe, agonizing, hard-to-treat pain (thalamic pain), hyperpathia and emotional changes.

blocks.text: Hypothalamus

The **hypothalamus** is the lower part of the diencephalon (≈ 4 g), the highest integrative center of **autonomic, endocrine and emotional-motivational** functions. It has more than 30 nuclei; it has a very rich blood supply and the blood–brain barrier is weak here — it senses changes in the blood directly.

blocks.title: Table 25.4. Functions of the hypothalamus
head: Function
Centers and mechanisms
rows: Anterior part — parasympathetic effects; posterior part — sympathetic effects
Liberins and statins (adenohypophysis), vasopressin and oxytocin (neurohypophysis) — topic 14
Anterior part — heat loss; posterior — heat production
Lateral nuclei — hunger center; ventromedial nuclei — satiety center; arcuate nucleus (leptin and ghrelin signals)
Suprachiasmatic nucleus — the “biological clock” (light information from the retina; melatonin via the pineal gland)
Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (sleep), lateral hypothalamus (orexin — wakefulness)
Together with the limbic system: anger, fear, sexual and parental behavior

parts.text: When the ventromedial nuclei of the hypothalamus are damaged (tumors, injury), appetite increases sharply and **hypothalamic obesity** develops; damage to the lateral nuclei leads to refusal of food and wasting. Loss of orexin neurons causes **narcolepsy** (sudden falling asleep during the day).

blocks.text: The **basal ganglia** are clusters of gray matter located within the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres: the **caudate nucleus** and the **putamen** — together the **striatum**; the **globus pallidus (pallidum)**; and, functionally related to them, the **subthalamic nucleus** and the **substantia nigra** in the midbrain.

**Connections:** cortex (almost all areas) → **striatum** → globus pallidus / substantia nigra → **thalamus** → cortex (motor and prefrontal). This **cortex–basal ganglia–thalamus–cortex loop** works through two pathways:

items: **The direct pathway** **enhances** the influence of the thalamus on the cortex — it “starts up” the required movements;

**The indirect pathway** (through the subthalamic nucleus) **inhibits** the thalamus — it suppresses unwanted movements. **Dopamine** from the **substantia nigra** activates the direct pathway (D~1~ receptors) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D~2~) — as a result it increases motor activity.

blocks.text: **Functions of the basal ganglia:** initiating and stopping movements; selecting motor programs; automatic movements (arm swing during walking, facial expression); regulating muscle tone; setting the amplitude and speed of movement; motor learning; cognitive and motivational functions.

blocks.title: Table 25.5. Syndromes of basal ganglia damage
head: Syndrome
Lesion
Signs
rows: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra
Hypokinesia, bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, poor facial expression (mask-like face), shuffling small-step gait
Involuntary rapid, irregular, dance-like movements, reduced muscle tone
Slow, worm-like involuntary movements (in the fingers)
Sharp, wide-amplitude flinging movements of the limbs (on one side — hemiballism)

parts.text: Damage to the basal ganglia has **two kinds** of result: **reduced movement** (hypokinesia — Parkinson's disease; dopamine deficiency) or **excessive involuntary movements** (hyperkinesias — chorea, ballism). The difference from cerebellar damage: in basal ganglia disease the **initiation and amplitude** of movements are disturbed, whereas in the cerebellum their **accuracy and coordination** are disturbed.

blocks.text: The cortex is a layer of gray matter 1.5–4.5 mm thick, with a surface area of ≈ 2200 cm^2^ and 14–16 billion neurons. Phylogenetically, the **ancient cortex (archicortex)**, the **old cortex (paleocortex)** and the **new cortex (neocortex — 96%)** are distinguished. The neocortex consists of **6 layers**; layer IV (internal granular) mainly receives afferent inputs (from the thalamus), and layer V (internal pyramidal — with the giant Betz pyramidal cells in the motor cortex) is the main efferent output. K. Brodmann divided the cortex cytoarchitectonically into **52 areas**.
**Functional organization:** neurons are grouped into **vertical columns** — each column processes a particular type of stimulus (V. Mountcastle).

blocks.title: Table 25.6. Functional areas of the cortex
head: Area
Location (Brodmann areas)
Function
Consequence of damage
rows: Skin and muscle-joint sensation; somatotopically organized
Sensory disturbance on the opposite side
Central paralysis on the opposite side
Planning of movements, complex movement sequences
Loss of visual fields, cortical blindness
Insula, parietal operculum (43); smell — paleocortex (parahippocampal gyrus, uncus)
Motor aphasia — understands but cannot speak
Sensory aphasia — fluent but meaningless speech; does not understand what is said
Anterior part of the frontal lobe
Planning, decision-making, control of behavior, working memory
Behavioral disturbance, lack of initiative, loss of self-criticism
Agnosia, neglect of the opposite side

blocks.text: Somatotopic organization — the homunculus

By stimulating the cortex electrically in patients during surgery, W. Penfield found that the sensory and motor areas are **somatotopically** organized: each part of the body is represented in a particular place of the cortex (on the opposite side). The projection area of a body part depends not on its size but on its **functional significance** (receptor density, precision of movements) — the hand, fingers, lips and tongue occupy a very large area.

blocks.label: Figure 25.2
blocks.caption: The sensory homunculus — projection of the body on the postcentral gyrus (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 25.3
blocks.caption: The motor homunculus — projection of the muscles on the precentral gyrus (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **limbic system** (the “visceral brain”, P. MacLean) is a set of cortical and subcortical structures: the **hippocampus**, the cingulate gyrus, the **amygdala**, the septum, the hypothalamus (mammillary bodies), the anterior thalamic nuclei and others. They are connected through the **Papez circuit** (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamic nuclei → cingulate gyrus → hippocampus).

blocks.label: Figure 25.4
blocks.caption: Structures of the limbic system (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: **Functions: emotions** (fear, anger, pleasure — amygdala); **motivation** and instinctive behavior (feeding, defensive, sexual); **memory** — the hippocampus transfers short-term memory into long-term memory (consolidation); coordination of autonomic and endocrine reactions with emotions.

parts.text: In bilateral damage to the **hippocampus** (the famous patient H.M. after epilepsy surgery), the ability to remember new events is lost (anterograde amnesia), while old memories and motor skills are preserved. **Alzheimer's disease** begins with the early death of hippocampal neurons.

blocks.text: **Electroencephalography (EEG)** is a method of recording the biopotentials of the brain from the scalp (H. Berger, 1929). EEG waves mainly reflect the sum of the **postsynaptic potentials** of cortical pyramidal neurons.

blocks.label: Figure 25.5
blocks.caption: Main EEG rhythms

blocks.title: Table 25.7. EEG rhythms
head: Rhythm
Frequency, Hz
Amplitude, µV
When observed
rows: Quiet wakefulness with the eyes closed; well expressed over the occipital region
High cognitive activity, binding of information
Light sleep, normal in children; pathological in awake adults
Deep (slow-wave) sleep, anesthesia, infants; severe pathology in awake adults

blocks.text: **α-rhythm blockade (desynchronization)** — when the eyes are opened or a new stimulus appears, the α-rhythm is replaced by the β-rhythm; this reflects the activation of the cortex by the reticular formation and the thalamus.

parts.text: EEG is the main method in the diagnosis of **epilepsy** — seizure activity appears as “spike-and-wave” complexes. EEG is also used to evaluate sleep disorders (polysomnography), the depth of anesthesia and the degree of coma, and to confirm **brain death** (electrical silence).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: examining cerebellar function in humans

items: **Romberg test**: the subject stands with the feet together, the arms stretched forward and the eyes closed (30–60 s). Observe swaying or a tendency to fall. A more difficult variant — standing with the feet in one line (heel to toe).
**Finger-to-nose test**: stretch the arm out to the side, then, with the eyes closed, touch the tip of the nose with the index finger (with each hand). Evaluate accuracy and tremor.
**Heel-to-knee test**: lying down, place the heel of one leg on the knee of the other and slide it down along the shin.
**Adiadochokinesis test**: rapidly turning the palms up and down alternately (supination–pronation).

**Gait**: walking along a straight line, heel-to-toe walking. **Interpretation:** normally stability is maintained in the Romberg position and the tests are performed accurately, without tremor and smoothly. In cerebellar damage — swaying, tremor on approaching the target (intention tremor), “overshooting” (dysmetria), slow and incorrect alternation of movements.

parts.text: If swaying in the Romberg position increases when the eyes are **closed**, this is most often a sign of **sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia** (damage to the dorsal columns or peripheral nerves — visual control compensates). In cerebellar ataxia the swaying persists even with the eyes open.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: analyzing an EEG recording (demonstration or a prepared recording)

items: The subject is at rest with the eyes closed — find the α-rhythm in the occipital leads and determine its frequency from the number of waves per 1 s.
The subject opens the eyes — observe the α-rhythm blockade (its replacement by the β-rhythm).
A mental load (calculation) is given — record the enhancement of the β-rhythm.
3 minutes of hyperventilation — observe the appearance of slow waves (a provocative test).

skills.title: Skill: determining the level of a motor disorder

items: Evaluate muscle strength and tone: weakness, spasticity and hyperreflexia — the pyramidal tract (upper motor neuron).
Rigidity (“cogwheel”), bradykinesia, resting tremor — the basal ganglia (extrapyramidal system).
Reduced muscle tone, ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria — the cerebellum.
Atrophy, fibrillations, loss of reflexes — the lower motor neuron.
Explain the result by linking it to the function of the corresponding structures.

skills.title: Skill: localizing a speech disorder

items: Evaluate whether the patient's speech is fluent, whether he understands what is said and whether he can repeat.
Speech not fluent, sparse, but comprehension preserved — Broca's area (motor aphasia).
Speech fluent but meaningless, comprehension impaired — Wernicke's area (sensory aphasia).
Only articulation impaired (dysarthria), language structure preserved — brainstem or cerebellum.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old patient sways when walking, walks with the legs wide apart, and his speech is broken into syllables and slow. In the finger-to-nose test the tremor increases as the target is approached and the finger “overshoots” the nose. In the Romberg position he sways even with the eyes open.
cases.ask: Which structure is damaged? Explain each sign.
cases.answer: The cerebellum is damaged (cerebellar ataxia). The cerebellum ensures the accuracy, smoothness and coordination of movements: it compares the planned movement with information about the ongoing movement (from proprioceptors) and corrects errors. When it is damaged: dynamic ataxia — a swaying, wide-based gait; intention tremor — on approaching the target the corrective movements overshoot and oscillation appears; dysmetria — misjudging the amplitude of a movement (“overshooting”); scanning speech — incoordination of the movements of the speech muscles; static ataxia persists regardless of visual control (the difference from sensory ataxia).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: For two years a 68-year-old man's movements have been slowing; he has a “pill-rolling” tremor of the hands at rest, a mask-like face, walks stooped with small steps, and uneven resistance is felt on passive flexion of his arms.
cases.ask: What is the disease? Explain its pathophysiological basis through the connections of the basal ganglia.
cases.answer: Parkinson's disease (akinetic-rigid syndrome). The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra die and the supply of dopamine to the striatum decreases. Normally dopamine activates the direct pathway (D~1~) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D~2~), facilitating the passage of movement-initiating signals through the thalamus to the motor cortex. In dopamine deficiency the indirect (inhibitory) pathway predominates — the activation of the cortex by the thalamus decreases: initiating movements becomes difficult (akinesia, bradykinesia), automatic movements disappear (mask-like face, no arm swing), muscle tone increases (“cogwheel” rigidity) and a resting tremor appears. Treatment — levodopa, dopamine agonists.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a left-sided stroke the patient understands what is said and follows instructions, but speaking is very difficult for him: few words, short, broken phrases; there is weakness in the right arm.
cases.ask: Which area of the cortex is damaged? Why is there weakness in the right arm?
cases.answer: Broca's area (areas 44–45) in the inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere is damaged — motor (expressive) aphasia: comprehension of speech (Wernicke's area) is preserved, but the construction of the motor program of speech is impaired. Broca's area lies close to the primary motor cortex (the lower part of the precentral gyrus — the projection of the face and arm); because this too is damaged and the pyramidal tracts cross in the medulla oblongata, weakness (central paresis) has developed in the opposite (right) arm.

cards.back: The only output of the cerebellar cortex; inhibitory
Balance, tone, accuracy and coordination of movements
Ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, adiadochokinesis, nystagmus

topics.title: The autonomic nervous system: sympathetic, parasympathetic and metasympathetic divisions. The adrenal medulla

goals.text: To teach the student the structural and functional features of the autonomic nervous system, its sympathetic, parasympathetic and metasympathetic divisions, the mediators and receptors in autonomic ganglia and synapses, the dual innervation of organs, autonomic reflexes and centers, and the effects of the hormones of the adrenal medulla; to master tests evaluating autonomic tone in humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the differences between the autonomic and somatic nervous systems;
the structure of the sympathetic, parasympathetic and metasympathetic divisions and the location of their centers;
the functions of autonomic ganglia and the axon reflex;
the mediators and receptors of autonomic synapses (N- and M-cholinergic receptors, α- and β-adrenergic receptors);
the effects of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions on organs;
the types of autonomic reflexes and the centers regulating autonomic functions;
the hormones of the adrenal medulla and their effects, the sympathoadrenal system.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: examine and evaluate dermographism;
perform the clino-orthostatic test and calculate the Kérdö index;
determine the type of autonomic tone.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Some organs have **only sympathetic** innervation: most blood vessels, the sweat glands, the adrenal medulla, the smooth muscles of the skin (piloerectors) and the splenic capsule. Their activity is regulated by an **increase or decrease** in sympathetic tone.

sections.title: 1. General description of the autonomic nervous system

blocks.text: The **autonomic nervous system (ANS)** is the part of the nervous system that regulates the activity of the internal organs, blood vessels, glands, smooth muscles and heart, and metabolism. It maintains homeostasis and ensures the body's adaptation to different conditions of activity (the **adaptive-trophic** function — L.A. Orbeli). Its activity is usually not subject to consciousness (“autonomic”).

blocks.title: Table 26.1. Differences between the somatic and autonomic nervous systems
head: Feature
Somatic nervous system
Autonomic nervous system

blocks.label: Figure 26.1
blocks.caption: The somatic and autonomic nervous systems: centers, ganglia and innervated organs (Alavia O.T., 2018)

sections.title: 2. Divisions of the autonomic nervous system

blocks.text: The sympathetic division

Its centers are in the lateral horns of the **thoracic and lumbar segments (Th~1~–L~2~ (L~3~))** of the spinal cord (the **thoracolumbar division**). The preganglionic fibers are **short**, and the ganglia lie close to the center: in the **paravertebral** (sympathetic trunk) and **prevertebral** (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric plexus) ganglia. The postganglionic fibers are **long**. One preganglionic fiber connects with many (≈ 1 : 10–30) postganglionic neurons — a **widespread (generalized)** effect.
The parasympathetic division

Its centers are in the **brainstem** (nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X) and in the **sacral segments (S~2~–S~4~)** of the spinal cord (the **craniosacral division**). The preganglionic fibers are **long**, and the ganglia lie next to or inside the organ (intramural); the postganglionic fibers are **short**. The effect is **local**. ≈ 75% of the parasympathetic fibers run in the **vagus nerve**.

blocks.title: Table 26.2. Parasympathetic fibers
head: Nerve
Center
Organs innervated
rows: Lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual salivary glands
Heart, bronchi, stomach, intestine (up to the left colic flexure), liver, pancreas, kidneys
Distal part of the large intestine, rectum, bladder, genital organs

parts.text: Some organs have **only sympathetic** innervation: most blood vessels, the sweat glands, the adrenal medulla, the smooth muscles of the skin (piloerectors) and the splenic capsule. Their activity is regulated by an **increase or decrease** in sympathetic tone.

blocks.text: The metasympathetic division

The **metasympathetic nervous system** (A.D. Nozdrachev) is the set of **intramural** nerve plexuses in the walls of hollow organs: the gastrointestinal tract (Auerbach and Meissner plexuses — the enteric nervous system), heart, bladder, uterus and bronchi. Its features:

items: it has its own sensory, inter- and efferent neurons — it **carries out local reflexes without the CNS** (for example, intestinal peristalsis);
**automaticity** (it has its own rhythm generators);
it innervates only internal organs and does not form part of somatic reflex arcs;
it connects with the sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers, “relays” and modulates their influence;
its mediators are diverse: acetylcholine, noradrenaline, serotonin, ATP (purinergic), VIP, NO, substance P.

blocks.text: Autonomic ganglia and the axon reflex

In addition to transmitting impulses, autonomic ganglia also function as **peripheral nerve centers**: convergence, multiplication, summation and rhythm transformation of impulses take place in them; **peripheral reflexes** can close through the ganglia.

The **axon reflex** is a reflex carried out through the branching of a sensory neuron's axon, without the participation of the CNS or even a ganglion: when the skin is stimulated, the impulse passes from one branch to another and dilates nearby vessels (reddening of the skin — dermographism, the “red flare” in inflammation).

parts.text: Remembering the mediators: **“In the ganglion — always acetylcholine (N)”**; **“Parasympathetic — acetylcholine at the end too (M)”**; **“Sympathetic — noradrenaline at the end (α, β)”**, the exception being the **sweat glands** (sympathetic, but acetylcholine, M).

Many drugs act on autonomic receptors: **atropine** (M-cholinergic blocker) — dilates the pupil, reduces salivation and sweating, increases HR, dilates the bronchi; **salbutamol** (β~2~-agonist) — dilates the bronchi in bronchial asthma; **metoprolol** (β~1~-blocker) — reduces HR and arterial pressure; **prazosin** (α~1~-blocker) — dilates vessels; **pilocarpine** (M-cholinomimetic) — constricts the pupil (in glaucoma). In poisoning with **organophosphorus compounds**, acetylcholine accumulates and a strong parasympathetic effect develops (pupil constriction, profuse salivation and sweating, bronchospasm, bradycardia, diarrhea).

sections.title: 4. Effects of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions on organs

blocks.text: Most organs have **dual innervation**; the divisions usually have **opposite (antagonistic)** effects, but their effects are **complementary (functional synergism)** and together finely adjust the organ's activity. Sometimes both divisions act in the same direction (salivary glands — topic 18).

parts.text: **The sympathetic division** — the “fight or flight” reaction: mobilization of energy, increased blood supply to the heart and skeletal muscles, inhibition of digestion. **The parasympathetic division** — “rest and digest”: saving and restoring energy, digestion, excretion.

Increased HR and breathing during physical work

parts.text: **Zakharyin–Head zones** — when an internal organ is diseased, pain is **referred** to the skin area innervated from the same segment (referred pain): in cardiac ischemia — to the left arm and under the scapula, in acute cholecystitis — to the right scapula and shoulder, in renal colic — to the groin. The cause is the **convergence** of visceral and skin afferents onto the same neurons of the spinal cord.

blocks.text: Centers regulating autonomic functions:

items: **The spinal cord** — centers of micturition, defecation, erection, sweating and vascular reflexes (segmental level).
**The medulla oblongata and pons** — the centers of breathing, circulation, the heart, salivation, swallowing, vomiting and coughing.
**The midbrain** — the pupillary reflex, accommodation.

**The hypothalamus** — the **highest autonomic center**: its anterior part — parasympathetic effects, its posterior part — sympathetic effects; thermoregulation, hunger, thirst; it integrates autonomic, endocrine and behavioral reactions.

**The limbic system, cerebellum, basal ganglia and cerebral cortex** — autonomic reactions associated with emotions and behavior (palpitations with excitement, pallor with fear), conditioned autonomic reflexes.

blocks.text: The adrenal medulla is embryologically and functionally a **modified sympathetic ganglion**: its chromaffin cells resemble postganglionic neurons, but instead of an axon they release hormones directly into the blood. They are innervated by **preganglionic sympathetic fibers** (acetylcholine, N~N~ receptors).

Hormones secreted: **adrenaline (≈ 80%)** and **noradrenaline (≈ 20%)**. Their synthesis: tyrosine → DOPA → dopamine → noradrenaline → adrenaline (the enzyme phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase — activated by cortisol; the blood flowing from the adrenal cortex helps this). Inactivation — by the enzymes MAO and COMT; the metabolite (vanillylmandelic acid) is excreted in the urine.

blocks.title: Table 26.7. Comparative effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline
head: Parameter
Adrenaline
Norepinephrine
rows: Mainly α and β~1~ (weak for β~2~)
May not change or may decrease reflexly
Does not change or decreases (muscle vessels dilate)

blocks.text: The **sympathoadrenal system** is the single functional union of the sympathetic nervous system and the adrenal medulla (W. Cannon). It is activated in stress, pain, fear, physical work, cold, blood loss and hypoglycemia and adapts the body to an emergency: cardiac work and arterial pressure increase, blood is redistributed to the muscles, heart and brain, the bronchi dilate, blood glucose and fatty acids increase, blood coagulation accelerates and fatigue decreases.

parts.text: **Pheochromocytoma** is a catecholamine-producing tumor of the adrenal medulla: paroxysmal severe arterial hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor, hyperglycemia. Diagnosis — metanephrines in blood and urine. **Adrenaline** is the first-line drug in anaphylactic shock (α — constricts vessels, β~1~ — strengthens the heart, β~2~ — dilates the bronchi and reduces the release of mediators from mast cells).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: examining dermographism

items: Draw a line on the skin of the subject's chest or forearm with a blunt spatula using moderate pressure.

After 10–20 s observe the color, width and persistence of the line that appears. **Interpretation: white dermographism** (a white line that disappears quickly) — predominance of sympathetic tone (constriction of skin vessels); **red dermographism** (a wide red line persisting for a long time — more than 1–3 minutes) — predominance of parasympathetic tone; **raised (urticarial)** dermographism — increased vascular permeability. Normally — a narrow pink line that disappears in 1–2 minutes. The axon reflex takes part in the mechanism of the red line.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: the clino-orthostatic test

items: **Orthostatic test:** measure the pulse and pressure after 5 minutes of lying down; measure them again 1 minute after standing up. Normally the pulse increases by 10–16 /min (sympathetic reactivity).

**Clinostatic test:** the pulse is measured after lying down from the standing position. Normally the pulse decreases by 4–12 /min (parasympathetic reactivity). **Interpretation:** an increase in pulse of > 16 in the orthostatic test — increased sympathetic reactivity; a decrease of > 12 in the clinostatic test — increased parasympathetic reactivity.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: calculating the Kérdö autonomic index

items: Measure the diastolic pressure (D) and pulse (P) at rest.
Kérdö index = (1 − D / P) × 100. **Interpretation:** close to 0 — autonomic balance (eutonia); positive — predominance of sympathetic tone; negative — predominance of parasympathetic tone.

blocks.text: **Example:** D = 80, P = 70 → (1 − 80/70) × 100 = −14 — parasympathetic predominance.
Exercise 4: reaction of the pupil to light and drugs (demonstration)

items: Compare the pupil size in light and in darkness.
Observe dilation of the pupil under the influence of fear or pain (for example, when the skin is pinched) (a sympathetic reflex).
Analyze the effect of atropine (dilates) and pilocarpine (constricts) in ophthalmology using videos or pictures.

skills.title: Skill: comprehensive evaluation of the type of autonomic tone

items: Determine the pulse, pressure and respiratory rate at rest.
Evaluate skin color, moisture and dermographism.
Calculate the Kérdö index.
Perform the orthostatic and clinostatic tests.
Add the Dagnini–Aschner reflex (topic 12).

Summarize the results and determine the type of autonomic tone: sympathicotonia (tachycardia, white dermographism, dry skin, wide pupils, positive Kérdö index), vagotonia (bradycardia, red dermographism, moist skin, negative Kérdö index), eutonia.

skills.title: Skill: predicting a drug's effect from the receptors

items: Determine which receptor the drug acts on (agonist or blocker).
Write down which organs the receptor is located in.
Determine the physiological effect of the receptor.
An agonist enhances that effect; with a blocker, the effect of the opposite division predominates.
List the expected and side effects (for example, a β-blocker may cause bronchospasm in asthma).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A farmer who had been working with an organophosphorus insecticide has sharply constricted pupils, profuse salivation and sweating, shortness of breath (bronchospasm), bradycardia, abdominal pain and diarrhea, and muscle twitching.
cases.ask: Explain the mechanism of poisoning. Which drug is used as an antidote, and why?
cases.answer: Organophosphorus compounds irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase — acetylcholine accumulates in the synapses without being broken down. The M-cholinergic receptors are excessively stimulated (muscarinic effects): miosis, profuse salivation and sweating, bronchoconstriction and increased mucus, bradycardia, increased intestinal motility. Stimulation of N-cholinergic receptors (nicotinic effects) — fasciculations in the skeletal muscles, then paralysis. The antidote is atropine (an M-cholinergic blocker): it eliminates the muscarinic effects; AChE reactivators (pralidoxime) are also used. In respiratory failure — artificial ventilation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Before an exam a student's heart is beating fast, his palms are sweating, his mouth is dry, his pupils are dilated and he has no appetite.
cases.ask: Which system is activated? Explain each sign in terms of mediators and receptors.
cases.answer: Because of stress the sympathoadrenal system has been activated (an emotional reaction — via the limbic system and hypothalamus). Tachycardia — the action of noradrenaline and adrenaline on β~1~ receptors in the heart. Sweating of the palms — the sympathetic cholinergic innervation of the sweat glands (acetylcholine, M receptors). Dry mouth — under sympathetic influence little thick saliva is secreted and the parasympathetic influence decreases. Pupil dilation — α~1~ receptors in the radial muscle. Lack of appetite and inhibition of digestion — the sympathetic division inhibits gastrointestinal motility and secretion. These are elements of the “fight or flight” reaction.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient with bronchial asthma was prescribed a non-selective β-blocker (propranolol) for hypertension, after which his attacks of breathlessness increased.
cases.ask: Why did the asthma worsen? Which drug would have been a better choice?
cases.answer: The smooth muscles of the bronchi contain β~2~-adrenergic receptors, which dilate the bronchi under the action of adrenaline. A non-selective β-blocker blocks the β~2~ receptors together with β~1~ (heart) — the bronchodilating sympathetic influence is lost and the parasympathetic (M~3~ — bronchoconstricting) influence predominates — bronchospasm increases. Non-selective β-blockers are contraindicated in asthmatic patients; if necessary, cardioselective β~1~-blockers are chosen with caution, or antihypertensive drugs of other groups (calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors).

goals.text: To teach the student the general doctrine of analyzers (sensory systems), the classification and properties of receptors, the structure of the visual system, the optical system of the eye, accommodation and refractive errors, the photoreceptor apparatus of the retina, phototransduction, theories of color vision, and the visual pathways and centers; in laboratory work, to master testing visual acuity, the visual field, color vision and the pupillary reflexes.

summary.text: **“Myope — Minus”**: nearsightedness is corrected with a “−” (concave) lens; **“Hypermetrope — Plus”** — farsightedness with a “+” (convex) lens.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Unlike other receptors, photoreceptors respond to light by **hyperpolarization**. Retinal is formed from **vitamin A** — that is why vitamin A deficiency causes **night blindness** (hemeralopia, “chicken blindness”).

sections.title: 1. General concept of the sensory systems

blocks.text: An **analyzer** (I.P. Pavlov) is the set of nervous structures that receive, process and analyze stimuli from the external and internal environment. It consists of three divisions:

items: **The peripheral (receptor) division** — converts the energy of the stimulus into a nerve impulse.
**The conducting division** — afferent pathways and intermediate centers (brainstem, thalamus).
**The central (cortical) division** — the corresponding area of the cerebral cortex; here the **sensation** is formed. In modern physiology the term “**sensory system**” is also used.

blocks.text: Receptors

blocks.title: Table 27.1. Classification of receptors
head: Feature
Types
rows: Exteroceptors (external environment), interoceptors (internal organs), proprioceptors (muscles, tendons, joints)
Distant (vision, hearing, smell) and contact (taste, touch)

Primary sensory (the receptor is the sensory neuron itself: touch, smell) and secondary sensory (a specialized receptor cell transmits to a neuron through a synapse: vision, hearing, taste, vestibular)
Rapidly adapting (phasic — touch, smell) and slowly adapting (tonic — pain, proprioceptors, baroreceptors)

blocks.text: Properties of receptors:

items: **High sensitivity to the adequate stimulus** (the eye can detect a few photons of light).

**Transformation** — the energy of the stimulus is converted into a **receptor potential** (a graded, local response) and then into action potentials; the strength of the stimulus is coded by the **frequency** of impulses.
**Adaptation** — a decrease in sensitivity to a constant stimulus.

**Rhythmic response** (spontaneous activity). **Weber–Fechner law:** the intensity of sensation is proportional to the **logarithm** of the stimulus strength. Weber's law: the smallest noticeable change in stimulus strength is a constant fraction of the initial strength (for example, ≈ 1/30 for a weight).

sections.title: 2. Structure and optical system of the eye

blocks.label: Figure 27.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the eyeball (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **optical (refracting) system** of the eye: the **cornea**, the aqueous humor of the anterior chamber, the **lens** and the **vitreous body**. Refractive power is measured in **diopters (D)**: D = 1 / focal length (m).

blocks.title: Table 27.2. Refractive power of the optical system of the eye
head: Structure
Refractive power, D
rows: Lens — looking at the nearest point
The whole eye (looking at a distance)

blocks.text: A **real, reduced and inverted** image is formed in the eye; the cortex perceives it in the upright position.
Accommodation
**Accommodation** is the adaptation of the eye to see objects at different distances clearly; it is achieved by changing the curvature of the lens.

items: **Looking at a distance**: the ciliary muscle is relaxed, the **zonules of Zinn** are taut — the lens is flattened (refracts less).

**Looking at a near object**: the **ciliary muscle contracts** (parasympathetic — nerve III, M-cholinergic receptors), the zonules of Zinn relax — the lens becomes **convex** owing to its own elasticity (refracts more). At the same time the pupil constricts and the eyes converge (the **near triad**).

blocks.label: Figure 27.2
blocks.caption: Mechanism of accommodation: A — looking at a distance; B — looking near (1 — lens, 2 — ciliary muscle, 3 — zonules of Zinn) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: The **near point of clear vision** recedes with age: ≈ 7 cm at 10 years, 10 cm at 20, 20–25 cm at 40, 80–100 cm at 60.

parts.text: **Presbyopia** (age-related farsightedness) — after 40–45 years the lens loses its elasticity and the ability to accommodate decreases: reading nearby text becomes difficult and it has to be held farther away. Correction — reading glasses with convex (converging) lenses.

blocks.text: The pupil and its reflexes

The pupil acts as the diaphragm of a camera: it regulates the amount of light entering the eye, reduces spherical aberration and increases the depth of focus. Its diameter is 1.5–8 mm. The **constrictor** muscle is parasympathetic (nerve III), the **dilator** muscle sympathetic (α~1~). The pupil constricts in light (direct and crossed reaction) and when looking near; it dilates in darkness, fear and pain.

sections.title: 3. The receptor apparatus of the eye

blocks.text: The **retina** is a 10-layer structure; the photoreceptors are located in its outermost layer (next to the pigment epithelium), and light passes through the other layers of the retina to reach them. Signal pathway: **photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells** (whose axons form the optic nerve); horizontal and amacrine cells provide **lateral inhibition** (contrast enhancement).

blocks.label: Figure 27.4
blocks.caption: Structure of the retina: photoreceptors (rods and cones), bipolar, ganglion, horizontal and amacrine cells (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 27.4. Comparative characteristics of rods and cones
head: Feature
Rods
Cones
rows: Mainly at the periphery of the retina; absent in the fovea
Low (many rods to one ganglion cell — convergence)
High (in the fovea 1 cone → 1 bipolar → 1 ganglion cell)

blocks.text: The **blind spot** is the exit point of the optic nerve (the disc); there are no photoreceptors there. The **fovea of the macula lutea** is the site of highest visual acuity.
Phototransduction

items: In darkness the photoreceptors contain much **cGMP**, and the cGMP-gated Na^+^ channels are open — the **“dark current”** flows; the membrane is relatively depolarized (−40 mV) and **glutamate** is released continuously.
Light converts **11-cis-retinal into all-trans-retinal** in **rhodopsin**; rhodopsin is activated.
Activated rhodopsin activates the G protein **transducin** → **phosphodiesterase** breaks down cGMP.
cGMP decreases and the Na^+^ channels close — the photoreceptor **hyperpolarizes** (−70 mV) and glutamate release decreases.
This change is processed in the bipolar and ganglion cells, and action potentials are generated in the ganglion cells.

parts.text: Unlike other receptors, photoreceptors respond to light by **hyperpolarization**. Retinal is formed from **vitamin A** — that is why vitamin A deficiency causes **night blindness** (hemeralopia, “chicken blindness”).

blocks.text: Dark and light adaptation

items: **Dark adaptation** — on passing from light to darkness, sensitivity increases thousands of times; first through the cones (5–10 minutes), then through the rods (up to 30–40 minutes) — resynthesis of rhodopsin, pupil dilation, neuronal convergence.
**Light adaptation** is fast (a few minutes): breakdown of rhodopsin, pupil constriction.

blocks.text: Color vision

**The three-component theory** (T. Young, H. Helmholtz): the retina has three kinds of cones, sensitive to **blue (short-wave, ≈ 420 nm)**, **green (medium, ≈ 530 nm)** and **red (long-wave, ≈ 560 nm)** light. Any color is perceived as a combination of their excitation to different degrees. **The opponent theory** (E. Hering) explains the processing of signals in the ganglion cells and thalamus in opposing pairs (red–green, blue–yellow, white–black); the two theories complement each other.

blocks.title: Table 27.5. Disorders of color vision
head: Disorder
Missing or weak cone
Frequency
rows: Very rare — only black and white

blocks.text: Red-green color blindness is inherited as an **X-linked recessive** trait — ≈ 8% of men and ≈ 0.5% of women.

parts.text: Disorders of color vision are tested with the **Rabkin polychromatic plates** (or Ishihara plates) in occupational selection for drivers, pilots, railway workers and some medical specialties.

blocks.text: The axons of the ganglion cells form the **optic nerve**. In the **optic chiasm** the fibers from the **nasal (medial) halves** of the retinas cross, while those from the temporal (lateral) halves do not. Thus each **optic tract** carries information about the opposite half of the visual field of both eyes. The fibers go to the **lateral geniculate body** (thalamus) and partly to the superior colliculi of the midbrain (orienting reflexes) and the pretectal area (pupillary reflex). From the lateral geniculate body the **optic radiation** (Gratiolet's bundle) goes to the **primary visual cortex** (area 17, V~1~) around the calcarine sulcus of the **occipital lobe**; areas 18–19 are the secondary (associative) visual areas.

blocks.caption: Visual pathways: optic nerve, chiasm, lateral geniculate body, midbrain and cortical centers, pathway of the pupillary reflex (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: In the cortex visual information is processed in two parallel streams: the **dorsal stream** (to the parietal lobe — “where?”: movement, spatial location) and the **ventral stream** (to the temporal lobe — “what?”: shape, color, face recognition).
**Binocular vision** is vision with both eyes: depth (stereoscopic) perception and judgment of distance; the images of the two eyes are fused in the cortex.
Exercise 1: determining visual acuity (Sivtsev chart)

items: The subject sits **5 m** from a well-lit chart; one eye is covered with an occluder.
The examiner points with a pointer to the letters on the chart from top to bottom; the subject reads them.
Write down the V number beside the lowest line the subject can read correctly; the second eye is also tested.

blocks.text: **Interpretation: Snellen formula**: V = d / D, where d is the test distance (5 m) and D the distance at which a normal eye should read that line. If line 10 is read from 5 m, V = 1.0 (normal). Visual acuity is the reciprocal of the smallest angle needed to see two points separately (normally 1 minute of arc).
Exercise 2: determining the visual field (perimetry)

items: The subject rests the chin on the support in front of the perimeter, with one eye closed, and looks at the central mark with the other.
A white (then red, green, blue) object is moved slowly along the perimeter arc from the periphery toward the center.

The angle at which the object is first seen is marked on the form; the arc is rotated every 15–30° and the test is repeated. **Interpretation:** normal limits for white: 90° outward, 60° inward, 50–55° upward, 65–70° downward. The field for colored objects is narrower (blue > red > green), because the cones are mainly in the center of the retina.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: detecting the blind spot (Mariotte's experiment)

items: Draw a cross on the left of a sheet of paper and a black circle 8–10 cm to its right.
Close the left eye and look at the cross with the right eye.

Slowly bring the paper closer to the eye and then move it away. **Result and analysis:** at a certain distance (≈ 20–25 cm) the circle disappears — its image falls on the optic disc (the blind spot), where there are no photoreceptors. In everyday life the blind spot is not noticed because of binocular vision, the constant small movements of the eyes and the “filling in” of the image by the cortex.

blocks.text: Exercise 4: testing color vision (Rabkin plates)

items: The subject sits 1 m from the plates in daylight.
Show each plate for 5–7 s; the subject names the number or shape on it.

Compare the results with the key in the instructions. **Interpretation:** if all plates are read correctly — normal trichromacy; errors on certain plates identify the type of protanopia or deuteranopia (anomaly).

blocks.text: Exercise 5: testing the pupillary reaction and accommodation

items: Test the direct and crossed reaction of the pupil to light (topic 24).
**Reaction to accommodation and convergence**: the subject looks into the distance, then at a finger 10–15 cm away — the pupils constrict and the eyes turn inward.
Determine the **near point of clear vision**: slowly bring small print toward the eye and measure the distance at which the letters become blurred.

items: Determine whether the visual field defect is in one eye or both.
Complete blindness of one eye — the optic nerve.
The temporal fields of both eyes — the chiasm (pituitary tumor).
The field on one side in both eyes — the tract, radiation or occipital cortex on the opposite side.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 46-year-old teacher complains that recently he has had to read text in books and on his phone with his arm outstretched, holding it farther away. He sees distant objects as well as before.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism and name the method of correction.
cases.answer: Presbyopia — an age-related decline in the ability to accommodate. To see a near object the ciliary muscle must contract, the zonules of Zinn relax and the lens become convex owing to its own elasticity. With age the lens becomes denser and loses its elasticity — it cannot become sufficiently convex, and the near point of clear vision recedes (more than 20–25 cm at 40 years). Distance vision (without accommodation) does not change. Correction — reading glasses with convex (converging, “+”) lenses.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 35-year-old woman has headaches, menstrual irregularity and milk discharge from the breasts. She says that on the road she fails to see cars coming from the side. On perimetry the temporal fields of both eyes are lost.
cases.ask: What is the type of visual field defect, and what is its cause? Explain on the basis of the structure of the visual pathways.
cases.answer: Bitemporal hemianopia. Here the central part of the optic chiasm is damaged — where the fibers from the nasal (medial) halves of the retinas cross. The nasal half of the retina receives the temporal (lateral) part of the visual field, so the temporal fields of both eyes are lost. Because the chiasm lies directly above the pituitary gland, the most common cause is a pituitary tumor; in this patient it may be a prolactin-producing tumor (prolactinoma): hyperprolactinemia leads to milk discharge (galactorrhea) and menstrual disturbance.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A young man undergoing a medical examination for a driving license could not see many of the numbers on the Rabkin plates, especially those made of red and green dots.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its cause and inheritance.
cases.answer: A red-green color vision defect (protanopia/protanomaly or deuteranopia/deuteranomaly — Daltonism). According to the three-component theory, colors are perceived through the excitation to different degrees of three kinds of cones (blue, green, red); if the red or green cone pigment is absent or altered, red and green cannot be distinguished. The genes for the green and red cone pigments are located on the X chromosome, and the defect is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait: it is common in men (who have one X chromosome) (≈ 8%), while women are most often carriers. Such people distinguish traffic lights not by color but by position and brightness; this is taken into account in occupational selection.

topics.title: Physiology of the auditory system and the vestibular apparatus

goals.text: To teach the student the structure of the auditory system, the conduction of sound in the outer, middle and inner ear, mechanoelectrical transduction in the organ of Corti, the theories of coding pitch and loudness, the auditory pathways and centers, binaural hearing, and the structure and receptors of the vestibular apparatus, vestibular reflexes and testing of vestibular excitability; in laboratory work, to master testing hearing acuity and bone and air conduction (Rinne and Weber tests).
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the structure and functions of the outer, middle and inner ear;
the sound-amplifying and protective mechanisms of the middle ear;
the structure of the cochlea, the composition of endolymph and perilymph, the endocochlear potential;
mechanoelectrical transduction in hair cells;
the theories of coding pitch (frequency) and loudness;
the limits of hearing, the auditory pathways and centers, sound localization;
the structure of the vestibular apparatus (otolith organs and semicircular canals) and their adequate stimuli;
vestibular reflexes and vestibulo-autonomic reactions.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine hearing acuity with whispered speech;
perform and evaluate the Rinne and Weber tests with a tuning fork;
read an audiogram;
evaluate the excitability of the vestibular apparatus with tests.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In hair cells depolarization is caused not by Na^+^, as in other cells, but by **K^+^ entry** — because the stereocilia are immersed in K^+^-rich endolymph. This is a special feature of the auditory and vestibular receptors.

blocks.text: **Sound** is mechanical vibration propagating in air (or another medium). Its physical characteristics: **frequency** (Hz) — perceived as pitch (low or high); **amplitude (intensity)** — perceived as loudness, measured in **decibels (dB)**; **timbre** — the composition of harmonics.

blocks.label: Figure 28.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the ear: outer, middle and inner ear (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.title: Table 28.1. Parts of the ear and their functions
head: Branch
Structures
Function
rows: Collecting and directing sound, helping to localize the sound source, resonance (2–4 kHz), protection (earwax)
Tympanic membrane, auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), muscles, Eustachian tube
Transmitting sound from air to fluid and amplifying it; protection

blocks.text: Functions of the middle ear

items: **Amplification of sound pressure (impedance matching)** — when sound passes from air into fluid, 99.9% of its energy is reflected. The middle ear overcomes this: the area of the tympanic membrane (≈ 55 mm^2^) is ≈ 17 times larger than that of the oval window (≈ 3.2 mm^2^), and with the lever system of the ossicles (≈ 1.3 times) the pressure increases **≈ 20–22 times**.

**Protection** — with loud sound (> 70–80 dB) the **tensor tympani** (nerve V) and the **stapedius muscle** (nerve VII) contract reflexly and limit the movement of the ossicles (the **acoustic reflex**; latency 10–40 ms — it does not protect against sudden explosions).
**Pressure equalization** — the **Eustachian (auditory) tube** opens during swallowing and yawning and equalizes the pressure in the middle ear with atmospheric pressure.

parts.text: When a plane is landing or when diving, the external pressure changes; if the Eustachian tube does not open (cold, inflammation), the tympanic membrane is pressed and pain and hearing loss occur (barotrauma). Swallowing, yawning or the Valsalva maneuver help. In children the Eustachian tube is short and wide, so pharyngeal infections quickly spread to the middle ear (**otitis**).

blocks.text: Bone conduction

Sound reaches the inner ear **through the air** (the main route) and **through vibration of the skull bones** (bone conduction). The fact that we hear our own voice differently on a recording is due to the contribution of bone conduction.

sections.title: 2. The inner ear: the cochlea and the organ of Corti

blocks.text: The **cochlea** is a bony canal coiled 2.5 times; it contains three cavities: the **scala vestibuli** (connected with the oval window) and the **scala tympani** (with the round window) — filled with **perilymph** (rich in Na^+^, similar to extracellular fluid); and the **scala media (cochlear duct)** — filled with **endolymph** (**rich in K^+^**, ≈ 150 mmol/l). The endolymph has a positive charge of **+80 mV** relative to the perilymph (the **endocochlear potential**; generated by the stria vascularis).

The **organ of Corti (spiral organ)** lies on the basilar membrane: **inner hair cells** (≈ 3500, one row — the main sensory receptors; 90–95% of the afferent fibers come to them) and **outer hair cells** (≈ 12,000, 3–4 rows — the **cochlear amplifier**: by contracting they enhance the vibration of the basilar membrane and increase sensitivity). Above the stereocilia of the hair cells lies the **tectorial membrane**.

blocks.label: Figure 28.2
blocks.caption: Structure of the organ of Corti (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Mechanoelectrical transduction

When the basilar membrane vibrates, the stereocilia of the hair cells shift relative to the tectorial membrane. When the stereocilia bend **toward the tallest stereocilium**, the tip links at their ends open the mechanosensitive channels and **K^+^ enters the cell from the endolymph** (because of the high K^+^ and the large electrical gradient) — the cell **depolarizes** (receptor potential), Ca^2+^ channels open, the mediator (**glutamate**) is released and action potentials arise in the neurons of the spiral ganglion. Bending in the opposite direction causes hyperpolarization.

parts.text: In hair cells depolarization is caused not by Na^+^, as in other cells, but by **K^+^ entry** — because the stereocilia are immersed in K^+^-rich endolymph. This is a special feature of the auditory and vestibular receptors.

blocks.label: Figure 28.3
blocks.caption: Stages of the conduction and reception of sound

blocks.text: Coding of pitch and loudness

items: **The place (resonance) theory** (H. Helmholtz; the modern **“traveling wave”** theory — G. von Békésy, Nobel Prize 1961): the width and stiffness of the basilar membrane change from its base to its apex. **High-frequency** sounds produce maximal vibration at the **base** of the membrane (next to the oval window, the narrow and stiff part), and **low-frequency** sounds at the **apex** (the wide and soft part). Each frequency excites a particular group of hair cells — **tonotopy** (preserved in the auditory pathways and cortex).

**The frequency (telephone, volley) theory** — at low frequencies (< 1000–4000 Hz) neurons fire impulses at a rhythm matching the frequency of the sound (several neurons in turn — the “volley” principle).
**Loudness** is coded by the number of excited neurons and the frequency of impulses.

blocks.text: Limits of hearing

Humans hear sounds **from 16–20 Hz to 20,000 Hz** (the upper limit falls with age — 10–12 kHz at 60). The highest sensitivity is in the **1000–4000 Hz** range (speech frequencies 300–4000 Hz). Below 16 Hz — **infrasound**; above 20 kHz — **ultrasound**.

blocks.caption: The human hearing area: thresholds of hearing and pain (approximate)

head: Sound
dB
rows: Rock concert, loud music in headphones
Threshold of pain, near a jet engine

parts.text: **Noise-induced hearing loss** — prolonged exposure to noise above 85 dB irreversibly damages the outer hair cells (first around 4000 Hz). Listening to loud music in headphones is increasing this problem among young people. Prevention — protective equipment, limiting volume. Aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin) also have an **ototoxic** effect on hair cells.

blocks.text: Axons of the spiral ganglion neurons (the cochlear part of nerve VIII) → **cochlear nuclei** in the medulla oblongata → **superior olivary complex** (pons; information from the two ears is compared for the first time) → lateral lemniscus → **inferior colliculi** (midbrain; auditory orienting reflexes) → **medial geniculate body** (thalamus) → **primary auditory cortex** (temporal lobe, Heschl's gyri, **areas 41–42**). The pathways partly cross, so each hemisphere receives information **from both ears** — unilateral cortical damage does not cause deafness.

**Binaural hearing and sound localization** — determining the direction of a sound source. Mechanisms: the **difference in arrival time** of the sound at the two ears (for low frequencies; differences down to 10 µs are detected) and the **difference in intensity** (for high frequencies — the head creates a “shadow”); these differences are analyzed by the superior olivary complex.

The **vestibular apparatus** is the organ that senses the position of the head in space and its movement (acceleration). It consists of the **vestibule** (otolith organs — the **utricle** and **saccule**) and three **semicircular canals** located in mutually perpendicular planes; all are filled with endolymph.

blocks.title: Table 28.3. Receptors of the vestibular apparatus
head: Structure
Receptor structure
Adequate stimulus
rows: Macula: an otolith membrane (calcium carbonate crystals — otoliths) above the hair cells
Tilting of the head (gravity) and horizontal linear acceleration
The cupula (a gelatinous partition) in the ampullae and the hair cells in it
Angular (rotational) acceleration — the start and end of head rotation

blocks.text: **Hair cells** have several stereocilia and one long **kinocilium**. When the stereocilia bend toward the kinocilium — depolarization (impulses increase); in the opposite direction — hyperpolarization (impulses decrease). Even at rest there is constant spontaneous firing.

**How the semicircular canals work:** when rotation starts, the endolymph lags behind the canal wall because of inertia and bends the cupula in the direction **opposite** to the rotation; during uniform rotation the endolymph moves together with the canal — the cupula returns to its initial position; on a sudden stop the endolymph continues to move and bends the cupula in the **opposite** direction — **post-rotational sensations** (a feeling of rotating the other way) and **nystagmus** appear.

**Vestibular pathways:** vestibular ganglion neurons → **vestibular nuclei** (medulla oblongata and pons) → the cerebellum (flocculonodular lobe), the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tract — extensor muscle tone), the nuclei of the oculomotor nerves (medial longitudinal fasciculus), the thalamus → cortex (parietal and temporal lobes), autonomic centers, the reticular formation.

blocks.title: Table 28.4. Vestibular reactions
head: Reaction
Content
rows: When the head moves, the eyes move in the opposite direction, keeping the image stable on the retina; nystagmus
Maintaining balance and posture by redistributing muscle tone (topic 24)
With strong or prolonged stimulation — nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating, changes in HR and pressure — motion sickness (sea, air, car sickness)

parts.text: **Motion sickness (kinetosis)** develops when there is a mismatch between vestibular, visual and proprioceptive information (for example, inside a ship — the eye sees a motionless room while the vestibular apparatus senses rocking). **Benign positional vertigo** (the most common form of dizziness) — otoliths falling into a semicircular canal; brief severe dizziness when the head position changes; treated with special maneuvers (the Epley maneuver).

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining hearing acuity with speech

items: The subject stands sideways to the examiner, closes the ear not being tested with a finger and closes the eyes (so as not to lip-read).
After expiration, using the residual air, the examiner **whispers** two-digit numbers (for example, 21, 47); starting from 6 m, he comes closer if the subject cannot repeat them.

Write down the greatest distance at which the subject repeated correctly; the other ear is also tested. **Interpretation:** normally whispered speech is heard from **6 m** or more, and ordinary conversational speech up to 20 m.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: the Rinne test

items: Place the stem of a vibrating tuning fork (128 or 512 Hz) on the mastoid process (bone conduction).
As soon as the subject stops hearing the sound, bring the tuning fork close to the ear canal (1–2 cm away) (air conduction).

Ask whether the sound is heard again. **Interpretation:** normally air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction (≈ 2 times) — **Rinne positive**. When the **sound-conducting** apparatus (outer and middle ear) is damaged, bone conduction is longer — **Rinne negative**. When the **sound-perceiving** apparatus (inner ear, nerve) is damaged, both are shortened but the ratio is preserved — Rinne positive.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: the Weber test (lateralization)

items: Place a vibrating tuning fork on the top of the head (in the midline).
Ask in which ear the sound is heard louder.

Close one ear with a finger and repeat the test. **Result and analysis:** normally the sound is heard equally in both ears (in the middle of the head). When the ear is closed or **conduction** is impaired (otitis, earwax plug), the sound lateralizes **toward the affected (closed) ear** — external noise does not act there and the sound coming through the bone is heard better. When **perception** is impaired, the sound lateralizes **toward the healthy ear**.

blocks.text: Exercise 4: testing the excitability of the vestibular apparatus

items: **Bárány rotation test** — as in topic 24: after 10 rotations in 20 s, the duration of nystagmus (normal 25–35 s), autonomic reactions and loss of balance are evaluated.
**Yashchenko (Voyachek) test** — after rotation, standing with the head bent forward and then walking along a straight line with the eyes open; the degree of deviation is evaluated.

Stability **in the Romberg position** is evaluated. **Interpretation:** prolonged nystagmus, severe nausea, pallor and sweating — high vestibular excitability (predisposition to motion sickness); important in occupational selection (pilots, cosmonauts, sailors).

skills.title: Skill: determining the type of hearing loss from tuning fork tests

items: Perform the Rinne test on both ears.
Perform the Weber test.
Rinne negative + Weber toward the affected ear — **conductive** hearing loss (outer or middle ear).
Rinne positive (both shortened) + Weber toward the healthy ear — **sensorineural** hearing loss (inner ear or auditory nerve).
State that the result needs to be confirmed by audiometry.

skills.title: Skill: reading an audiogram

items: Note that the horizontal axis shows frequency (125–8000 Hz) and the vertical axis the hearing threshold (dB, increasing from top to bottom).
Find the air conduction (o — right, x — left) and bone conduction lines.
Thresholds of 0–20 dB — normal; 20–40 — mild, 40–70 — moderate, 70–90 — severe, > 90 dB — profound hearing loss.
If there is a gap between the air and bone lines — conductive; if both are lowered together — a sensorineural disorder.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After a cold a child's right ear began to hurt, his hearing decreased and his temperature rose. The Rinne test is negative on the right and positive on the left; in the Weber test the sound is heard louder in the right ear.
cases.ask: What is the type and cause of the hearing loss? Explain the tuning fork tests.
cases.answer: Acute right-sided otitis media — conductive hearing loss. In children the Eustachian tube is short and wide, so infection easily passes from the nasopharynx to the middle ear; fluid accumulates in the middle ear and restricts the movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles — air conduction of sound is impaired. Rinne negative: bone conduction (directly to the inner ear) is heard longer than air conduction. Weber lateralizes toward the affected ear: external noise does not enter the affected ear, and the sound coming through the bone is perceived as relatively louder; the inner ear is healthy.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A patient treated with gentamicin for a long time developed ringing in the ears, bilateral hearing loss and unsteadiness when walking. Rinne is positive on both sides, and there is no Weber lateralization.
cases.ask: What disorder has developed? Explain its mechanism.
cases.answer: The ototoxic (and vestibulotoxic) effect of aminoglycosides — bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Gentamicin accumulates in the endolymph and damages the hair cells (first the outer hair cells at the base of the cochlea, which receive high frequencies) and the hair cells of the vestibular apparatus. Because the sound-conducting apparatus is healthy, Rinne is positive (air and bone conduction are shortened equally); because the damage is symmetrical, there is no lateralization in the Weber test. Damage to the vestibular hair cells leads to loss of balance. That is why doses and blood concentrations are monitored during treatment with aminoglycosides.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A passenger traveling by ship for the first time developed nausea, vomiting, pallor and cold sweat while sitting in the cabin. When he went out on deck and looked at the horizon, he felt better.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain its mechanism and why looking at the horizon helps.
cases.answer: Motion sickness (seasickness). When the ship rocks, the vestibular apparatus (otolith organs and semicircular canals) continuously registers changing accelerations, while in the cabin the eye sees motionless surroundings — a mismatch arises between vestibular, visual and proprioceptive information. Through the connections of the vestibular nuclei with the autonomic centers (the vomiting center, vagal nuclei), vestibulo-autonomic reactions develop: nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating. When looking at the horizon, visual information matches vestibular information (the eye also sees the rocking) — the mismatch decreases and the symptoms ease.
