test taste sensitivity in different regions of the tongue (gustometry);
determine and evaluate the pain threshold with an algometer;
evaluate pain intensity with scales.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The taste threshold is lowest for **bitter** substances (quinine ≈ 0.000008 M) and higher for salty and sweet ones (table salt ≈ 0.01 M, sucrose ≈ 0.01 M). This is an evolutionary defense: most poisons taste bitter.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The **“taste map”** of older textbooks (sweet at the tip of the tongue, sour and salty at the edges, bitter at the root) is, according to modern data, a **simplified** idea: all taste qualities are sensed by the buds in all regions of the tongue, with only slight differences in sensitivity (for example, the root of the tongue is slightly more sensitive to bitter). Testing sensitivity by region in laboratory work shows this.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex **bypassing the thalamus**, and it is directly connected with the **limbic system** (amygdala, hippocampus). That is why smells evoke strong emotions and memories (the “Proust effect”).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Reduced perception of pain during stress, heavy physical exertion or injury (for example, in battle or in a sports competition) is **stress analgesia**: endorphins and the descending inhibitory system are activated. The **placebo** effect is also partly due to the release of endogenous opioids (naloxone, an opioid antagonist, reduces it).

blocks.text: Taste receptors

**Taste buds** are onion-shaped structures located in the papillae of the tongue (fungiform, circumvallate, foliate) and in the mucosa of the soft palate, pharynx and epiglottis. Adults have ≈ 5000–10,000 buds. Each bud consists of **50–150 taste receptor cells** (renewed every 10–14 days), supporting cells and basal cells; at its tip there is a **taste pore** into which the microvilli of the receptor cells project. Taste receptors are **secondary sensory** receptors.
For taste to be sensed, substances must **dissolve in saliva**.

parts.text: The taste threshold is lowest for **bitter** substances (quinine ≈ 0.000008 M) and higher for salty and sweet ones (table salt ≈ 0.01 M, sucrose ≈ 0.01 M). This is an evolutionary defense: most poisons taste bitter.

The **“taste map”** of older textbooks (sweet at the tip of the tongue, sour and salty at the edges, bitter at the root) is, according to modern data, a **simplified** idea: all taste qualities are sensed by the buds in all regions of the tongue, with only slight differences in sensitivity (for example, the root of the tongue is slightly more sensitive to bitter). Testing sensitivity by region in laboratory work shows this.

blocks.text: Taste pathways and centers

Impulses from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue travel via the **facial nerve** (VII, chorda tympani), from the posterior 1/3 via the **glossopharyngeal nerve** (IX), and from the pharynx and epiglottis via the **vagus nerve** (X) to the **nucleus of the solitary tract** in the medulla oblongata → the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus → the taste area of the cortex (**insula and parietal operculum**, area 43). The nucleus of the solitary tract also has connections with the hypothalamus and limbic system (emotional evaluation of taste, appetite) and with the centers of salivation and digestive reflexes.

**Features of taste: adaptation** (especially rapid to sweet and salty); **contrast** (sour is felt more strongly after sweet); **mixed taste** (taste together with smell, temperature, texture and pungency — capsaicin sensations — forms “flavor”); sensitivity decreases with age.

parts.text: **Disorders of taste**: ageusia (loss), hypogeusia (reduction), dysgeusia (alteration — a metallic taste). Causes: facial nerve palsy (taste is lost in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue), dry mouth, some drugs (metronidazole, ACE inhibitors), zinc deficiency, radiation and chemotherapy, smoking, viral infections (loss of smell and taste in COVID-19).

blocks.text: The **olfactory epithelium** lies in the upper part of the nasal cavity (the superior nasal concha and the upper part of the septum), over an area of ≈ 5 cm^2^. It contains ≈ 10–20 million **olfactory receptor cells** — these are **primary sensory** receptors (bipolar neurons whose axons form the olfactory nerve) and the only neurons that are renewed, every 30–60 days. The **cilia** at the tip of their dendrite lie in the mucus.

**Transduction:** the odorant dissolves in the mucus and binds to **olfactory receptor proteins** on the cilia (≈ 350–400 functional genes in humans) → G protein (G~olf~) → adenylate cyclase → **cAMP** ↑ → cation channels open (Na^+^, Ca^2+^ enter) → Ca^2+^-dependent Cl^-^ channels open and Cl^-^ leaves → depolarization → action potentials. Each receptor cell expresses **one** type of receptor protein; but one odor excites many receptors to different degrees — odors are distinguished by a **combinatorial code** (R. Axel and L. Buck, Nobel Prize 2004). Humans can distinguish several thousand (according to some data more than a million) odors.

**Olfactory pathways:** the fibers of the olfactory nerve (I) pass through the openings of the ethmoid bone to the **olfactory bulb**; there, in the **glomeruli**, they synapse with mitral cells (all cells with the same receptor converge on one glomerulus) → **olfactory tract** → **primary olfactory cortex** (piriform cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex) — **bypassing the thalamus** (the only sense to do so). Then to the orbitofrontal cortex (also via the thalamus) — conscious discrimination of odors.

parts.text: Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex **bypassing the thalamus**, and it is directly connected with the **limbic system** (amygdala, hippocampus). That is why smells evoke strong emotions and memories (the “Proust effect”).

blocks.text: **Features of smell:** very high sensitivity (mercaptans are detected at 10^-11^ g per 1 l of air); **rapid adaptation** (ceasing to notice a constant smell within a few minutes); sensitivity is slightly higher in women; it decreases with age. A large part of food “flavor” is actually **retronasal smell** — that is why food seems “tasteless” during a cold.

parts.text: **Anosmia** (loss of smell) — in colds, polyps, head injury (the olfactory nerve fibers are torn at the ethmoid bone) and viral infections; it is also observed as an early sign **in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases**. Anosmia is dangerous: the person does not smell a gas leak, smoke or spoiled food. For safety, a strong-smelling substance (mercaptan) is added to household gas.

blocks.text: **Pain** is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage (International Association for the Study of Pain, IASP). Pain is a **protective signal**: it forces the body to escape the harmful factor and encourages it to protect the damaged organ. However, chronic pain may lose its protective significance and become a disease in its own right.

**Components of pain:** sensory-discriminative (location, intensity, character), emotional-affective (unpleasantness, fear), autonomic (tachycardia, rise in pressure, sweating, pupil dilation), motor (protective reflexes) and cognitive-evaluative components.

Types
rows: Superficial somatic (skin), deep somatic (muscle, joint, bone), visceral (internal organs)
Acute (signal, protective) and chronic (more than 3 months)

First (sharp, well localized — Aδ fibers) and second (aching, burning, poorly localized — C fibers)

blocks.text: Nociceptors and pain pathways

**Nociceptors** are **free nerve endings** (primary sensory receptors); they are present in almost all tissues (except brain tissue). Types: **mechanical**, **thermal** (> 45 °C or < 15 °C; TRPV1 — the capsaicin receptor) and the most widespread, **polymodal** (responding to mechanical, thermal and chemical stimuli). Nociceptors **adapt slowly** or not at all — pain persists as long as the stimulus lasts.

blocks.label: Figure 29.1
blocks.caption: Pain-conducting fibers and pathways

blocks.text: **Pain mediators (algogens)** are formed in damaged tissue and excite or sensitize nociceptors: **bradykinin**, **prostaglandins** (E~2~ — sensitizes nociceptors), **histamine**, **serotonin**, **K^+^ and H^+^ ions**, ATP, **substance P** and calcitonin gene-related peptide (released from nerve endings, causing neurogenic inflammation).

**Hyperalgesia** is increased pain sensitivity: **primary** (in the damaged area — sensitization of nociceptors by mediators) and **secondary** (in surrounding areas — **central sensitization** of spinal neurons). **Allodynia** — pain evoked by a normally painless stimulus (touch) (skin after a burn).

parts.text: **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs** (NSAIDs — ibuprofen, diclofenac) inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce the synthesis of **prostaglandins** — the sensitization of nociceptors decreases (a peripheral effect). **Local anesthetics** block Na^+^ channels in nerve fibers and stop the conduction of impulses.

sections.title: 4. The antinociceptive system and pain control

blocks.text: The gate theory

**The “gate theory”** (R. Melzack and P. Wall, 1965): in the dorsal horns of the spinal cord there is a “gate” for the transmission of pain signals; it is controlled by **inhibitory interneurons**. When the thick tactile **Aβ fibers** are activated, the inhibitory neurons are excited and the transmission of pain signals to the brain decreases (“the gate closes”). That is why rubbing a bruised spot reduces pain. This theory is the basis of **transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)**, massage and acupuncture.

blocks.label: Figure 29.2
blocks.caption: The “gate theory” of pain and descending inhibitory influences

blocks.text: The endogenous antinociceptive system
The **antinociceptive system** is the set of structures that limit and regulate pain sensation:

items: **Descending inhibitory pathways** from the **periaqueductal gray matter** (midbrain), the **raphe nuclei** (serotonin) and the **locus coeruleus** (noradrenaline) to the dorsal horns of the spinal cord; electrical stimulation of these areas causes strong analgesia (stimulation-produced analgesia).

**Endogenous opioid peptides** — **endorphins** (β-endorphin), **enkephalins** and **dynorphins**: they bind to opioid receptors (μ, δ, κ) and inhibit the transmission of pain signals presynaptically and postsynaptically.
**Non-opioid mechanisms** — serotonin, noradrenaline, GABA, cannabinoids.

parts.text: Reduced perception of pain during stress, heavy physical exertion or injury (for example, in battle or in a sports competition) is **stress analgesia**: endorphins and the descending inhibitory system are activated. The **placebo** effect is also partly due to the release of endogenous opioids (naloxone, an opioid antagonist, reduces it).

**Morphine** and other opioid analgesics bind to the μ receptors on which endogenous opioids act and produce strong analgesia; their side effects are depression of the respiratory center, pupil constriction, constipation and dependence. The antagonist in opioid poisoning is **naloxone**.

blocks.text: Referred and phantom pain

items: **Referred pain** — when an internal organ is diseased, pain is felt in the skin area innervated from the same segment (**Zakharyin–Head zones**): heart — left arm and scapula, diaphragm — shoulder, duodenum — epigastrium (topic 26). The cause is the **convergence** of visceral and somatic afferents onto the same neurons of the spinal cord.
**Phantom pain** is the sensation of pain in an amputated limb: it is associated with the damaged nerve endings and with reorganization of the somatotopic “map” in the spinal cord and cortex.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: determining the taste threshold

items: Prepare solutions of sucrose (sweet), table salt (salty), citric acid (sour) and quinine (bitter) in decreasing concentrations.
The subject rinses the mouth with water; starting with the lowest concentration, 1–2 drops are applied to the tongue with a pipette.
Write down the lowest concentration at which the subject identifies the taste — this is the **taste threshold**.
After each solution the mouth is rinsed with water and there is a 1–2-minute break. **Interpretation:** compare the thresholds of the different substances — the threshold for bitter is the lowest.

blocks.text: Exercise 2: testing taste sensitivity in different regions of the tongue (gustometry)

items: The subject keeps the tongue protruded.
One of the taste solutions is applied with a brush to the tip, lateral edges and root of the tongue in turn.
Without drawing the tongue into the mouth, the subject indicates the taste with a hand signal or a card.

Mark the results on a diagram. **Result and analysis:** all taste qualities are perceived in most regions of the tongue, with slight differences in sensitivity; in the central back part of the tongue there are few buds — sensitivity is low.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: determining olfactory acuity and adaptation

items: Vials of different odorous substances (vinegar, mint, vanillin, coffee) are brought in turn to one nostril (the other is closed), and the subject identifies the smell with the eyes closed.

Adaptation: the subject smells one odor continuously and the time until it is no longer perceived is recorded; then another odor is presented. **Result and analysis:** adaptation to a constant odor occurs in 1–3 minutes, but another odor is perceived immediately — adaptation is **selective** (only to that odor).

blocks.text: Exercise 4: determining the pain threshold — algometry

items: **Mechanical algometry** (tensoalgometer): the tip of the instrument is placed perpendicular to the skin (for example, the inner surface of the forearm or the palm) and the pressure is increased gradually.
The subject says when the pressure turns into a **sensation of pain** — this is the **pain threshold** (kg/cm^2^ or N).
Increasing the pressure further, the subject indicates the unbearable level — the **pain tolerance threshold** (under the instructor's supervision, with caution).
Repeat the measurement in different areas of the body (fingertip, palm, forearm, shoulder).

Measure the threshold again after local rubbing or applying cold. **Interpretation:** the pain threshold differs in different areas of the body (depending on nociceptor density); individual differences are large. An increase in the threshold after rubbing confirms the “gate theory”. Other types of algometry: **thermal** (a heat beam) and **electrical** algometry.

skills.title: Skill: evaluating pain intensity

items: **Visual analogue scale (VAS)**: the subject marks his pain on a 10 cm line (0 — no pain, 10 — the worst pain imaginable).
**Numerical rating scale (0–10)**: rating pain with a number.
In children the **faces scale** is used.
Ask about the location, character and duration of the pain and the factors that worsen and relieve it.
Evaluate the autonomic signs (pulse, pressure, sweating).

skills.title: Skill: distinguishing the type of pain by mechanism

items: Well localized, sharp, immediately after the stimulus — first (Aδ) pain.
Aching, poorly localized, delayed — second (C) pain.
Pain in a skin area in disease of an internal organ — referred pain.
Burning, “like an electric shock”, with allodynia — neuropathic pain.
Justify the appropriate analgesic approach for each type (NSAIDs, opioids, anticonvulsants).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Neighbors noticed a household gas leak in a patient's home, but the patient himself smelled nothing. A year earlier he had injured the back of his head in a car accident, and since then food has seemed “tasteless”.
cases.ask: What disorder has developed? Explain its mechanism. Why does food seem “tasteless”?
cases.answer: Post-traumatic anosmia. When the back of the head is struck, the brain shifts back and forth and the delicate olfactory nerve fibers passing through the openings of the ethmoid bone are torn — impulses from the olfactory receptors no longer reach the bulb. The “flavor” of food consists mainly of retronasal smell (odorants passing from the mouth through the pharynx into the nasal cavity); the taste receptors distinguish only the five basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami). When smell is lost, the complex flavor of food is not perceived. Anosmia is dangerous — the patient does not smell gas, smoke or spoiled food; installing gas and smoke detectors at home is recommended.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A footballer injured his leg during a match, but felt almost no pain until the end of the game. After the game the pain increased.
cases.ask: How can this phenomenon be explained?
cases.answer: Stress analgesia. The strong emotional and physical strain during competition activates the antinociceptive system: β-endorphin and enkephalins are released in the pituitary and CNS, and descending inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal gray matter, the raphe nuclei (serotonin) and the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline) to the dorsal horns of the spinal cord stop the transmission of pain signals. Activation of the sympathoadrenal system also contributes. When the stress passes these influences decrease, while in the damaged tissue inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin) have sensitized the nociceptors — the pain increases.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 50-year-old man complains of pressing pain behind the sternum during physical exertion, spreading to the left arm and under the scapula.
cases.ask: How can the spread of the pain to the left arm be explained?
cases.answer: This is referred pain — typical of angina pectoris. Visceral afferent fibers from the heart enter the Th~1~–Th~5~ segments of the spinal cord; somatic afferents from the skin of the inner surface of the left arm and the chest wall enter the same segments. They converge on the same projection neurons in the dorsal horn. Based on usual experience, the brain “interprets” the signals from these neurons as coming from a skin (somatic) source — the pain is felt in the left arm and scapular region (Zakharyin–Head zones). This sign is important in diagnosing myocardial ischemia.

topics.title: Higher nervous activity. Conditioned reflexes. Types of higher nervous activity. Signal systems. Functional asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres

goals.text: To teach the student I.P. Pavlov's doctrine of higher nervous activity (HNA), innate and acquired forms of behavior, the conditions, mechanisms and types of formation of conditioned reflexes, the inhibition of conditioned reflexes, the types of HNA, the first and second signal systems, memory, sleep and the functional asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres; to master methods of forming a conditioned reflex and determining the type of HNA in humans.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of higher and lower nervous activity;
the differences between unconditioned reflexes and instincts and conditioned reflexes;
the conditions and mechanism of formation of a conditioned reflex (temporary connection);
the classification of conditioned reflexes;
the external and internal inhibition of conditioned reflexes;
the types of HNA and their relationship to temperaments;
the first and second signal systems and the specifically human types of HNA;
the types and mechanisms of memory and the phases of sleep;
the functional asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: explain the formation of a pupillary or blink conditioned reflex in humans;
determine the capacity of short-term memory;
determine the type of HNA and functional asymmetry (dominant hand, eye, ear) with tests.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: External inhibition is **innate** (unconditioned) and develops immediately; internal inhibition is **acquired** (develops with practice) and arises in the cortex within the arc of the conditioned signal. Internal inhibition is weaker in youth and old age and in fatigue.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: “Pure” types of HNA are rare; most people have mixed features. The type is shaped not only by heredity but also by upbringing and living conditions (the phenotype). Therefore the type of HNA is not a diagnosis or a “label”, but a guide for an individual approach.

sections.title: 1. The concept of higher nervous activity

blocks.text: **Higher nervous activity (HNA)** (I.P. Pavlov) is the joint activity of the cerebral cortex and the subcortical structures; it ensures the most perfect individual adaptation (behavior) of animals and humans to a changing external environment. Its main mechanism is **conditioned reflexes**. **Lower nervous activity**, by contrast, coordinates the activity of the internal organs through the spinal cord and brainstem (mainly unconditioned reflexes).
The conceptual basis of Pavlov's doctrine was created by **I.M. Sechenov** in his work “Reflexes of the Brain” (1863): mental activity is also reflex in nature.
Innate and acquired forms of behavior

blocks.title: Table 30.1. Differences between unconditioned and conditioned reflexes
head: Feature
Unconditioned reflexes
Conditioned reflexes
rows: Common to the species (a species trait)
Any (indifferent) stimulus can become a signal

blocks.text: **Instincts** are complex innate programs of behavior (chains of unconditioned reflexes): feeding, defensive, sexual, parental and social instincts. They are triggered by **motivation** (a need — hunger, thirst).
Conditions for the formation of a conditioned reflex

items: **Coincidence in time of two stimuli**: an indifferent (neutral) stimulus (for example, light, a bell) must be given **before** the **unconditioned stimulus** (food) and applied **together with it several times** (reinforcement).
The conditioned signal must begin **1–5 s before** the unconditioned stimulus (if it is given after the unconditioned stimulus, the reflex is not formed).
The unconditioned stimulus must be biologically **stronger** (the animal must be hungry).
**An active, alert state of the cortex** and the absence of extraneous stimuli.
The indifferent stimulus must be of moderate strength.

blocks.label: Figure 30.1
blocks.caption: Formation of a conditioned salivary reflex: A — unconditioned reflex (food → saliva); B — orienting to light; C — combining light and food; D — conditioned reflex (saliva to light alone); E — extinction (without reinforcement); F — second-order reflex (bell) (O — food center, L — light center, ZV — sound center, 1 — food, 2 — salivary center, 3 — salivary gland) (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: Mechanism of formation of a conditioned reflex

According to Pavlov, when a conditioned reflex is formed, a **temporary connection** arises in the cortex between the **center of the conditioned signal** (for example, the visual center) and the **cortical representation of the unconditioned reflex** (the food center). The strong (dominant) unconditioned center “draws to itself” the excitation in the weaker center of the conditioned signal (Ukhtomsky's dominant). With repeated pairing this path is “worn in” — synaptic efficacy increases.

blocks.label: Figure 30.2
blocks.caption: Scheme of the temporary connection: connections between the center of the conditioned signal (KM — visual center) and the center of the unconditioned reflex (XM — taste center) in the cortex (a) and through subcortical structures (b, c); SB — salivary gland (Alavia O.T., 2018)

blocks.text: According to modern ideas, the temporary connection is formed not only in the cortex but in a **multilevel** system involving **cortical and subcortical** structures (thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, reticular formation, cerebellum). Its cellular basis is **synaptic plasticity**: long-term potentiation (in the hippocampus — NMDA glutamate receptors, Ca^2+^), synthesis of new proteins and formation of new synapses (E. Kandel, Nobel Prize 2000).
Classification of conditioned reflexes

parts.text: Conditioned reflexes are of great importance in medicine: nausea in a patient on entering the chemotherapy room (conditioned nausea), “white coat” hypertension (a rise in pressure at the sight of the doctor), part of the placebo effect, and the daily routine (regular times of eating and sleeping — a dynamic stereotype) are explained on the basis of conditioned reflexes. That is why the patient's environment and regimen are taken into account in treatment.

parts.text: External inhibition is **innate** (unconditioned) and develops immediately; internal inhibition is **acquired** (develops with practice) and arises in the cortex within the arc of the conditioned signal. Internal inhibition is weaker in youth and old age and in fatigue.

blocks.text: The **type of HNA** is the set of innate and acquired individual properties of the nervous system. Pavlov distinguished the types of HNA on the basis of three properties of the processes of **excitation and inhibition**: **strength**, **balance** and **mobility**. These types correspond to the temperaments of Hippocrates.

blocks.text: **Specifically human types of HNA** (according to the ratio of the signal systems): the **artistic type** (the first signal system predominates — imaginative, emotional thinking), the **thinking type** (the second signal system predominates — abstract, logical thinking) and the **intermediate (mixed) type**.

parts.text: “Pure” types of HNA are rare; most people have mixed features. The type is shaped not only by heredity but also by upbringing and living conditions (the phenotype). Therefore the type of HNA is not a diagnosis or a “label”, but a guide for an individual approach.

items: **The first signal system** is the perception of environmental stimuli in the form of concrete images through **direct sensations** (vision, hearing, smell, taste, skin). It is common to animals and humans.

**The second signal system** is signaling through **speech (the word)**; the word is the “signal of signals” (Pavlov). It is specific to humans and is the basis of **abstract thinking**, the formation of concepts, generalization, upbringing and education, and the transmission of social experience to the next generations. A word can evoke a conditioned reflex just like first-signal stimuli (for example, the word “lemon” increases salivation). The two signal systems are closely interconnected; the second signal system develops on the basis of the first and controls it.

blocks.text: **Speech centers:** Broca's (motor) and Wernicke's (sensory) areas — topic 25; for reading and writing, the angular gyrus and the corresponding areas of the frontal lobe.
Memory
**Memory** is the ability to receive, store and retrieve information.

blocks.title: Table 30.5. Types of memory
head: Type
Duration
Mechanism
rows: Trace processes in receptors and the primary cortex
Circulation of impulses in neuronal loops (reverberation), prefrontal cortex

blocks.text: Long-term memory is divided into **declarative** (explicit — facts and events; hippocampus and temporal lobe) and **nondeclarative** (implicit — skills, habits, conditioned reflexes; basal ganglia, cerebellum). **Consolidation** is the transfer of short-term memory into long-term memory; sleep (especially deep and paradoxical sleep) plays an important role in it.
Sleep

**Sleep** is a special active state, different from wakefulness — a periodic reorganization of brain activity; it is controlled by the hypothalamus (ventrolateral preoptic nucleus), the brainstem reticular formation and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (the “biological clock”); the pineal hormone **melatonin** is released in darkness and increases sleepiness.

blocks.text: 4–6 cycles (each 90–100 minutes) alternate during the night; toward morning the proportion of REM sleep increases. Adults need 7–9 hours of sleep.

sections.title: 7. Functional asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres

blocks.text: Although the cerebral hemispheres are similar in structure, they differ in function — **functional asymmetry**. This was clearly demonstrated by R. Sperry (Nobel Prize 1981) in studies of **“split-brain”** patients (with the corpus callosum severed).

blocks.title: Table 30.7. Functional specialization of the hemispheres (in right-handed people)
head: Left hemisphere
Right hemisphere
rows: Control of the right side of the body
Control of the left side of the body

blocks.text: The hemispheres are connected through the **corpus callosum** and work together. Asymmetry also appears in the **dominant hand** (≈ 90% of people are right-handed), and the dominant eye, ear and leg.

parts.text: When the left hemisphere is damaged (stroke) — right-sided paralysis and **aphasia**; when the right hemisphere is damaged — left-sided paralysis, neglect of the left side, impaired spatial orientation and face recognition, and sometimes denial of one's own illness (anosognosia). In children the speech centers are plastic: if the left hemisphere is damaged at an early age, speech may “move” to the right hemisphere.

blocks.text: Exercise 1: forming a conditioned blink reflex in humans (demonstration)

items: The subject sits in front of a device that blows a puff of air into the eye; the blinking movement is recorded.
An indifferent stimulus (a sound signal or light) is given, and it is checked that it does not cause blinking.
0.5–1 s after the sound signal a puff of air is blown into the eye (the unconditioned stimulus — the blink reflex); this is repeated 10–20 times.
Then the sound signal alone is given.

blocks.text: **Result and analysis:** after several pairings, blinking appears to the sound alone — a **conditioned defensive reflex** has been formed. Presenting the sound several times without reinforcement leads to **extinction** of the reflex (internal inhibition).
Exercise 2: determining the capacity of short-term memory

items: Twelve unrelated two-digit numbers (or words) are read to the subject at 1 s intervals.
The subject immediately writes down those he remembers, in any order.
The number written correctly is counted. **Interpretation:** normally **7 ± 2** items (Miller's number). Material linked by meaning (grouping) is easier to remember.

blocks.text: Exercise 3: determining functional asymmetry

items: **Dominant hand**: clapping the hands (which hand is on top), crossing the arms on the chest, interlocking the fingers (which thumb is on top).
**Dominant eye**: look at a distant object through a hole in a sheet of paper with both eyes, then close one eye at a time — the eye with which the object does not “shift” is dominant.
**Dominant leg**: kicking a ball, hopping on one leg.
Summarize the results: right-handed, left-handed or ambidextrous (using both hands equally).

blocks.text: Exercise 4: determining the type of HNA (based on questionnaires and observation)

items: Fill in the Eysenck or another temperament questionnaire (extraversion–introversion and emotional stability scales).

Place the result in the Eysenck circle and determine the temperament type (stable extravert — sanguine, unstable extravert — choleric, stable introvert — phlegmatic, unstable introvert — melancholic).
Perform a reaction speed (sensorimotor reaction time) test and compare the results.

skills.title: Skill: drawing up a plan for forming a conditioned reflex

items: Choose an unconditioned reflex (for example, food — salivation).
Choose an indifferent signal and check that it does not evoke a response by itself.
Give the signal 1–5 s before the unconditioned stimulus and repeat the pairing.
Ensure an alert state of the cortex, motivation (hunger) and the absence of extraneous stimuli.
Test with the signal alone to check that the reflex has formed; if you present it without reinforcement, observe its extinction.

skills.title: Skill: taking HNA features into account when working with patients

items: Observe the patient's temperament and emotional reactions.
Give information to a patient of the melancholic type step by step, calmly and in a supportive tone.
Speak patiently, clearly and briefly with a patient of the choleric type.
Help turn the treatment regimen (times of taking drugs, meals) into a dynamic stereotype.
Take into account the effect of the word (the second signal system): the doctor's word can both improve and worsen the patient's condition (iatrogenesis).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: After several courses of chemotherapy, a patient began to experience nausea and vomiting as soon as he entered the hospital building or saw the nurse (before the drug had been given).
cases.ask: Explain this phenomenon from the standpoint of HNA physiology. How can it be reduced?
cases.answer: This is a conditioned reflex (conditioned nausea). The chemotherapy drug is an unconditioned stimulus that excites the vomiting center; indifferent stimuli such as the hospital environment, the sight of the nurse and the smell of the room acted several times before and together with the drug administration — a temporary connection was formed in the cortical and subcortical structures. Now these signals by themselves excite the vomiting center. Ways to reduce it: effective use of antiemetic drugs from the first course (preventing the unconditioned response — the reflex is not formed), changing the environment, relaxation and psychotherapy (presenting the signal without reinforcement to develop extinctive inhibition).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student wakes up every morning at 7, has breakfast and goes to class at 8. Even on vacation he wakes at 7 without an alarm clock, and his appetite appears at that time. When he moved to a new country (a 5-hour time difference), he had daytime sleepiness and nighttime insomnia for a week.
cases.ask: How can these phenomena be explained?
cases.answer: On the basis of a regular daily routine, temporal conditioned reflexes and a dynamic stereotype have formed: waking at a certain time and the appearance of appetite (secretion of digestive juices) have become conditioned reflexes. Circadian rhythms (the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus — the “biological clock”, melatonin) also underlie this. When the time zone changes abruptly, the internal biological clock and the system of conditioned reflexes no longer match external time — desynchronosis (jet lag): the sleep–wake cycle is disturbed. Readjustment of the new stereotype and the biological clock (roughly 1 day for every hour of difference) takes several days; morning light and a regular new regimen speed up adaptation.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After a stroke a patient cannot move his right arm and leg and cannot speak, but he can hum tunes and songs and recognizes familiar people by their faces.
cases.ask: Which hemisphere is damaged? Why are some functions preserved?
cases.answer: The left hemisphere is damaged. Paralysis of the right arm and leg — damage to the motor cortex or pyramidal tract of the left hemisphere (the pathways cross). Loss of speech (aphasia) — in 95% of right-handed people the speech centers are in the left hemisphere. Humming the melody of tunes and songs and face recognition are mainly functions of the right hemisphere, which is not damaged. This demonstrates functional asymmetry; teaching patients to speak through singing (melodic intonation therapy) in speech rehabilitation is based on using the capacities of the right hemisphere.
